questions.s: Which of the following is a base unit of the SI?
questions.e: The seven SI base units are the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela, so the kelvin is a base unit. The newton (kg m s⁻²), joule (kg m² s⁻²) and coulomb (A s) are all derived from them. The coulomb is a common trap: the base electrical unit is the ampere, not the unit of charge.

questions.s: The SI base unit of luminous intensity is the
questions.e: Luminous intensity is one of the seven base quantities and its unit is the candela (cd). The lumen is the derived unit of luminous flux and the lux (lumen per square metre) is the unit of illuminance, so neither is a base unit. The watt measures power, not luminous intensity.

questions.s: The pascal, the SI unit of pressure, expressed in SI base units is
questions.e: Pressure = force/area, and 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², so 1 Pa = (kg m s⁻²)/m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻². The option kg m s⁻² is the newton itself (the area was not divided out), and kg m² s⁻² is the joule.

questions.s: The steradian is the SI unit of
questions.e: The steradian (sr) measures solid angle: a whole sphere subtends 4π sr at its centre. Plane angle is measured in radians, a different unit, and angular speed (rad s⁻¹) and angular momentum (kg m² s⁻¹) are derived quantities with other units.

questions.s: One kilowatt-hour (kWh), the unit used on electricity bills in Lahore, is equal to
questions.e: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. The value 3.6 × 10³ J forgets the factor 1000 from the kilo prefix (it is one watt-hour), and 6.0 × 10⁴ J uses 60 s instead of 3600 s for one hour.

questions.s: The prefix pico (p) stands for a factor of
questions.e: Pico means 10⁻¹², so 1 pF = 10⁻¹² F. Nano is 10⁻⁹, micro is 10⁻⁶ and femto is 10⁻¹⁵; nano is the usual confusion because it is the next prefix up.

questions.s: The thickness of a thin coating is 5 μm. In nanometres this is
questions.e: 5 μm = 5 × 10⁻⁶ m, and 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, so the thickness is 5 × 10⁻⁶/10⁻⁹ = 5 × 10³ = 5000 nm. Taking 1 μm as 100 nm gives 500 nm; each step between these prefixes is a factor of 1000, not 100.

questions.s: A density of 1 g cm⁻³ is equal to
questions.e: 1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm³ = (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, so 1 g cm⁻³ = 10⁻³/10⁻⁶ = 10³ kg m⁻³ (water is about 1000 kg m⁻³). The value 10⁻³ kg m⁻³ comes from multiplying by 10⁻⁶ instead of dividing by it; the centimetre factor must be cubed and then divided out.

questions.s: A bus on the Islamabad expressway moves at 72 km h⁻¹. Its speed in m s⁻¹ is
questions.e: 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 × 1000 m / 3600 s = 20 m s⁻¹ (multiply km h⁻¹ by 5/18). The value 259.2 m s⁻¹ comes from multiplying by 3.6 instead of dividing, and 7.2 m s⁻¹ divides by 10 instead of by 3.6.

questions.s: The number of significant figures in 0.004050 is
questions.e: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point and are not significant; the digits 4, 0, 5 and the trailing 0 after the decimal point are significant, giving 4. Answering 3 drops the final zero, but a trailing zero after a decimal point shows the precision of the reading and does count.

questions.s: Ayesha multiplies two measured values, 4.2 cm and 1.35 cm. The product written to the correct number of significant figures is
questions.e: 4.2 × 1.35 = 5.67, but in multiplication the result keeps as many significant figures as the least precise factor, here 2 (from 4.2), so the answer is 5.7 cm². Writing 5.67 cm² keeps three figures, which claims more precision than 4.2 cm allows, and 5.670 is even worse.

questions.s: The masses 12.4 g, 2.36 g and 0.115 g are added. Their sum, written correctly, is
questions.e: The exact sum is 14.875 g. In addition the result is rounded to the fewest decimal places among the values, which is one (12.4 g), giving 14.9 g. The rule for adding uses decimal places, not significant figures, so 15 g (two figures) rounds too far and 14.88 g keeps too many places.

questions.s: The value 0.0028749 rounded to three significant figures is
questions.e: The first three significant digits are 2, 8 and 7; the next digit is 4, which is less than 5, so the 7 stays and the result is 0.00287. The value 0.00288 wrongly rounds up because of the later 9, but only the first discarded digit (4) decides the rounding.

questions.s: Four students record the length of the same rod. Which recorded value was taken with the most precise instrument?
questions.e: Precision is shown by the smallest place recorded: 250.0 mm is read to 0.1 mm. The others are read only to 1 cm (25 cm), 1 mm (0.250 m) and 0.1 m (2.5 m). The value 0.250 m looks precise because of its three figures, but its last digit is in millimetres, ten times coarser than 0.1 mm.

questions.s: The length and breadth of a rectangular sheet are measured as (5.0 ± 0.1) cm and (2.0 ± 0.1) cm. The percentage uncertainty in its area is
questions.e: Percentage uncertainties add in a product: 0.1/5.0 = 2 % and 0.1/2.0 = 5 %, so the area has 2 % + 5 % = 7 %. The value 3.5 % averages the two instead of adding them, and 5 % keeps only the larger one.

questions.s: The radius of a steel ball is measured as (2.0 ± 0.1) cm. The percentage uncertainty in its volume is
questions.e: The radius has 0.1/2.0 = 5 % uncertainty, and V = (4/3)πr³ depends on r³, so the volume has 3 × 5 % = 15 %. The constants 4/3 and π have no uncertainty. The value 5 % forgets the power 3, and 10 % uses the power 2 of an area.

questions.s: When the jaws of a vernier calliper are closed, its zero does not coincide with the main-scale zero. This causes
questions.e: A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, which is the mark of a systematic error; it is removed by subtracting the zero correction. Random errors vary in size and sign from reading to reading, so averaging cannot remove a zero error.

questions.s: Random errors in an experiment are best reduced by
o: calibrating the instrument against a standard
taking the mean of several readings
questions.e: Random errors scatter readings on both sides of the true value, so the mean of many readings is closer to it. Calibration and zero-error correction remove systematic errors, which push all readings the same way, and changing the unit changes nothing physical.

questions.s: Hamza times 20 oscillations of a pendulum as 32.0 s with an uncertainty of 0.2 s. The time period with its uncertainty is
questions.e: T = 32.0/20 = 1.60 s, and the uncertainty in the total time is shared over the 20 oscillations: 0.2/20 = 0.01 s, so T = 1.60 ± 0.01 s. Writing ± 0.2 s ignores the division by 20, which is exactly why many oscillations are timed.

questions.s: In a simple pendulum experiment, g is found from g = 4π²L/T². If L has an uncertainty of 1 % and T has an uncertainty of 2 %, the uncertainty in g is
questions.e: For g ∝ L T⁻², the percentage uncertainties add with the powers taken as positive: 1 % + 2 × 2 % = 5 %. The value 3 % forgets that T is squared, and subtracting because T is in the denominator would be wrong, since uncertainties never cancel.

questions.s: The dimensions of force are
questions.e: F = ma, so [F] = [M][LT⁻²] = [MLT⁻²]. [MLT⁻¹] is momentum, [ML²T⁻²] is work or energy and [ML⁻¹T⁻²] is pressure.

questions.s: Planck's constant h appears in E = hf, where E is energy and f is frequency. The dimensions of h are
questions.e: h = E/f = [ML²T⁻²]/[T⁻¹] = [ML²T⁻¹], the same as angular momentum. [ML²T⁻²] is energy itself (the frequency was not divided out), and [ML²T] comes from multiplying by the frequency's dimensions instead of dividing.

questions.s: Which pair of quantities has the same dimensions?
questions.e: Torque = force × distance = [ML²T⁻²], which equals the dimensions of work, although torque is a vector and is never expressed in joules. Power is work per unit time [ML²T⁻³], momentum is [MLT⁻¹] against force [MLT⁻²], and pressure is force per area.

questions.s: In Newton's law of gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r², the dimensions of the constant G are
questions.e: G = Fr²/(m₁m₂) = [MLT⁻²][L²]/[M²] = [M⁻¹L³T⁻²]. The option [M⁻²L³T⁻²] divides the M² without first including the M from the force, and [M⁻¹L²T⁻²] forgets the L from the force.

questions.s: The frequency f of a vibrating liquid drop depends on its radius r, the density ρ of the liquid and the surface tension σ (unit N m⁻¹). By dimensional analysis f is proportional to
questions.e: [σ] = [MT⁻²] and [ρ] = [ML⁻³]. With f ∝ σᵃρᵇrᶜ: T gives −2a = −1 so a = ½; M gives a + b = 0 so b = −½; L gives −3b + c = 0 so c = −3/2. Hence f ∝ √(σ/(ρr³)). The option √(ρr³/σ) has the dimensions of time, the reciprocal of a frequency.

questions.s: Here u and v are speeds, a is acceleration, s is distance and t is time. Which equation is dimensionally incorrect?
questions.e: In s = ut + ½at³ the last term has dimensions [LT⁻²][T³] = [LT], which is not a length, so the equation cannot be right. In the other three every term matches: [LT⁻¹] for v = u + at, [L²T⁻²] for v² = u² + 2as and [L] for s = ut + ½at². The numerical factor ½ has no dimensions and is never checked.

questions.s: Which of the following can NOT be done by dimensional analysis?
o: check whether an equation is dimensionally consistent
derive a possible relation between quantities
find the value of a dimensionless constant such as 2π
convert a quantity from one system of units to another
questions.e: Pure numbers such as 2π or ½ have no dimensions, so dimensional analysis cannot find them; they come from experiment or theory. It can check consistency, suggest the form of a relation (for example T ∝ √(l/g)) and convert units, which is why the other three are possible.

questions.s: In the van der Waals equation (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT, P is pressure and V is volume. The dimensions of a/b are
questions.e: Only like quantities can be added, so a/V² is a pressure: a = PV² = [ML⁻¹T⁻²][L⁶] = [ML⁵T⁻²]. Likewise b is a volume, [L³]. Then a/b = [ML⁵T⁻²]/[L³] = [ML²T⁻²], the dimensions of energy. [ML⁵T⁻²] is a alone, without dividing by b.

questions.s: Which of the following quantities is dimensionless?
questions.e: Refractive index n = c/v is a ratio of two speeds, so its dimensions cancel. Wavelength is [L], frequency is [T⁻¹] and the speed of light is [LT⁻¹]. Frequency is tempting because it is a count per second, but the per second gives it dimensions.

questions.s: A wave is described by y = A sin(ωt − kx), where t is time and x is distance. The quantity ω/k has the dimensions of
questions.e: The argument of a sine must be dimensionless, so ωt and kx are pure numbers: [ω] = [T⁻¹] and [k] = [L⁻¹]. Then ω/k = [T⁻¹]/[L⁻¹] = [LT⁻¹], a speed (the wave speed). [L⁻¹T] is the reciprocal, k/ω.

questions.s: In a new system of units, the units of mass, length and time are each made twice as large as the SI units. The new unit of energy is
questions.e: Energy has dimensions [ML²T⁻²], so the new unit is 2 × 2² × 2⁻² = 2 times the joule. Getting 8 times treats every power as positive; the T⁻² makes the larger time unit reduce the energy unit by 4.

questions.s: Two lengths are measured as (25.4 ± 0.1) cm and (12.2 ± 0.1) cm. Their difference is
questions.e: 25.4 − 12.2 = 13.2 cm, and in a sum or a difference the absolute uncertainties always add: 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 cm. Subtracting the uncertainties to get 0.0 cm is the classic mistake; taking away one rough value from another can never make the result exact.

questions.s: Sana measures a length of 20.0 cm with a metre rule whose smallest division is 1 mm. The percentage uncertainty in her reading is
questions.e: The absolute uncertainty equals the least count, 1 mm = 0.1 cm, so the percentage uncertainty is (0.1/20.0) × 100 = 0.5 %. Using 1 cm as the uncertainty gives 5 %, and mixing millimetres with centimetres the other way gives 0.05 %.

questions.s: A measurement is said to be accurate when it
o: is close to the true value
questions.e: Accuracy means closeness to the true value. Agreement among repeated readings and a fine least count describe precision, which is different: a precise instrument with a zero error gives readings that agree closely but are all wrong by the same amount.

questions.s: A quantity is given by Q = a²b³/(c√d). If a, b, c and d are each measured with a 1 % uncertainty, the percentage uncertainty in Q is
questions.e: Multiply each percentage uncertainty by the magnitude of its power and add: 2(1 %) + 3(1 %) + 1(1 %) + ½(1 %) = 6.5 %. The value 7 % treats √d as d¹, and 4.5 % subtracts the denominator terms, but uncertainties in a quotient still add.

questions.s: On a vernier calliper, the main-scale divisions are 1 mm apart and 10 vernier divisions cover exactly 9 main-scale divisions. The least count of the calliper is
questions.e: One vernier division is 9/10 mm = 0.9 mm, so the least count = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = 1 − 0.9 = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm. The value 0.1 cm is 1 mm, the main-scale division itself, and 0.09 cm is the length of a vernier division, not the difference.

questions.s: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular (thimble) scale. Its least count is
questions.e: Least count = pitch/number of circular divisions = 0.5 mm/50 = 0.01 mm. Dividing 1 mm by 50 instead of the 0.5 mm pitch would give 0.02 mm, and 0.05 mm comes from dividing the pitch by 10.

questions.s: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.e: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Work and power are scalars even though they are calculated from vectors (work is the dot product F · d), and temperature has no direction at all.

questions.s: Bilal pulls a trolley with a force of 20 N along a rope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The horizontal component of the force is
questions.e: The horizontal component is F cos 30° = 20 × (√3/2) = 10√3 N (about 17 N). The value 10 N is F sin 30°, the vertical component, which comes from swapping sine and cosine.

questions.s: A vector has an x-component of 6 units and a y-component of −8 units. Its magnitude and direction are
questions.e: Magnitude = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 units. tan θ = 8/6 = 4/3 gives θ ≈ 53°, and since x is positive and y negative the vector lies in the fourth quadrant, below the +x-axis. 37° comes from tan⁻¹(6/8), the angle with the y-axis, and 14 simply adds the components.

questions.s: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a point at right angles to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.e: For perpendicular forces R = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 N. The value 7 N is the resultant only when the forces act in the same direction, and 1 N when they are opposite.

questions.s: Two forces, each of magnitude F, act on a particle with an angle of 120° between them. The magnitude of the resultant is
questions.e: R² = F² + F² + 2F² cos 120° = 2F² − F² = F², so R = F. √3 F is the resultant at 60°, where cos 60° = +½, and 2F holds only for parallel forces.

questions.s: The maximum resultant of two forces is 14 N and their minimum resultant is 2 N. When the two forces act at right angles, their resultant is
questions.e: P + Q = 14 and P − Q = 2 give P = 8 N and Q = 6 N. At right angles R = √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 N. The value 7 N halves the maximum, and 8 N is just the larger force.

questions.s: The unit vector in the direction of the vector 3î + 4ĵ is
questions.e: Divide the vector by its magnitude √(3² + 4²) = 5: (3î + 4ĵ)/5 = 0.6î + 0.8ĵ, whose magnitude is 1. The option 0.8î + 0.6ĵ also has magnitude 1 but points in a different direction because the components are swapped.

questions.s: If A = 2î + 3ĵ − k̂ and B = î − 2ĵ + 4k̂, then A − B is
questions.e: Subtract component by component: (2 − 1)î + (3 − (−2))ĵ + (−1 − 4)k̂ = î + 5ĵ − 5k̂. The option 3î + ĵ + 3k̂ is A + B, and î + ĵ − 5k̂ forgets that subtracting −2 gives +2.

questions.s: The value of k̂ · k̂ − î · ĵ is
questions.e: For unit vectors, k̂ · k̂ = 1 (angle 0°) and î · ĵ = 0 (angle 90°), so the result is 1 − 0 = 1. A dot product is a scalar, so a vector answer such as k̂ is impossible; that would come from confusing it with a cross product.

questions.s: If A = 2î + 3ĵ and B = 4î − ĵ, then A · B equals
questions.e: A · B = AₓBₓ + A_yB_y = (2)(4) + (3)(−1) = 8 − 3 = 5. The value 11 ignores the minus sign of B's y-component, and 8 keeps only the x-terms.

questions.s: The angle between the vectors A = î + ĵ and B = ĵ + k̂ is
questions.e: A · B = (1)(0) + (1)(1) + (0)(1) = 1, and |A| = |B| = √2, so cos θ = 1/(√2 × √2) = ½ and θ = 60°. Answering 90° assumes the vectors are perpendicular because they lie in different planes, but they share the ĵ component.

questions.s: The projection (scalar component) of A = 4î + 3ĵ along the direction of B = 3î + 4ĵ is
questions.e: The projection is A · B/|B| = (12 + 12)/5 = 24/5 = 4.8. The value 24 is the dot product itself, not divided by |B|, and 0.96 divides by |B|² = 25 instead of by |B|.

questions.s: A constant force of 10 N moves a box 5 m along a straight line making 60° with the direction of the force. The work done by the force is
questions.e: W = F · d = Fd cos θ = 10 × 5 × cos 60° = 25 J. The value 25√3 J uses sin 60°, and 50 J ignores the angle, which is right only when the force acts along the displacement.

questions.s: The cross product î × ĵ is equal to
questions.e: For the right-handed set î, ĵ, k̂ taken in cyclic order, î × ĵ = k̂. The result of a cross product is a vector, so 0 or 1 cannot be right; −k̂ is ĵ × î, the product taken in the reverse order.

questions.s: The value of ĵ × î + k̂ × k̂ is
questions.e: ĵ × î = −k̂ because the order is anticyclic, and k̂ × k̂ = 0 since sin 0° = 0. The sum is −k̂. Answering k̂ treats the cross product as commutative, which it is not.

questions.s: If A = î + 2ĵ and B = 3î + ĵ, then A × B is
questions.e: For vectors in the xy-plane, A × B = (AₓB_y − A_yBₓ)k̂ = (1 × 1 − 2 × 3)k̂ = −5k̂. Adding the two products instead of subtracting gives 7k̂, and reversing the order of subtraction gives 5k̂, which is B × A.

questions.s: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram are A = î + 2ĵ + 2k̂ and B = 2î + ĵ − 2k̂. The area of the parallelogram is
questions.e: A × B = (2(−2) − 2(1))î − (1(−2) − 2(2))ĵ + (1(1) − 2(2))k̂ = −6î + 6ĵ − 3k̂, whose magnitude is √(36 + 36 + 9) = 9 units². As a check, A · B = 2 + 2 − 4 = 0, so the sides are perpendicular and the area is |A||B| = 3 × 3 = 9. The value 4.5 is the area of the triangle on these sides, and 81 forgets the square root.

questions.s: For any two non-parallel vectors A and B, which of the following is correct?
questions.e: The cross product is anticommutative: reversing the order reverses the direction by the right-hand rule, so A × B = −(B × A). The dot product is commutative, so A · B = B · A, and A × A is the zero vector because the angle between them is 0°.

questions.s: For two vectors A and B, the magnitude of A × B equals A · B. The angle between the vectors is
questions.e: |A × B| = AB sin θ and A · B = AB cos θ, so sin θ = cos θ, giving tan θ = 1 and θ = 45°. At 90° the dot product is zero while the cross product is largest, and at 0° the reverse is true, so neither can make them equal.

questions.s: Vectors A and B have magnitudes 2 and 3, and |A × B| = √3 (A · B). The magnitude of A + B is
questions.e: AB sin θ = √3 AB cos θ gives tan θ = √3, so θ = 60°. Then |A + B|² = 2² + 3² + 2(2)(3) cos 60° = 4 + 9 + 6 = 19, so |A + B| = √19. √7 uses cos θ = −½ (that is |A − B|), and √13 assumes the vectors are perpendicular.

questions.s: The SI unit of torque is
questions.e: Torque = force × perpendicular distance, so its unit is the newton metre (N m). It is not written as the joule, even though the dimensions match, because torque is a vector. N s is the unit of impulse and J s of angular momentum or Planck's constant.

questions.s: Usman applies a force of 40 N at right angles to the end of a spanner 0.25 m long. The torque about the nut is
questions.e: τ = rF sin 90° = 0.25 × 40 = 10 N m. The value 160 N m divides the force by the length instead of multiplying, and 40 N m ignores the moment arm.

questions.s: A force of 50 N is applied at the handle of a door, 0.8 m from the hinge line, at an angle of 30° to the plane of the door. The torque about the hinge is
questions.e: Only the component perpendicular to the door turns it: τ = rF sin 30° = 0.8 × 50 × ½ = 20 N m. Using cos 30° gives 20√3 N m, which is the torque for a force at 30° to the normal of the door, not to the door itself.

questions.s: A force F = (î + 4ĵ) N acts at a point whose position vector is r = (3î + 2ĵ) m. The torque about the origin is
questions.e: τ = r × F = (xF_y − yFₓ)k̂ = (3 × 4 − 2 × 1)k̂ = 10k̂ N m. Taking F × r reverses the sign to −10k̂, and 11 N m is r · F, a scalar, which cannot be a torque.

questions.s: According to the first condition of equilibrium, a body is in translational equilibrium when
o: the net torque on it is zero
the net force on it is zero
its acceleration is constant but not zero
questions.e: The first condition is ΣF = 0, that is ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣF_y = 0, so the body has no linear acceleration. Zero net torque is the second condition, which concerns rotation. Constant non-zero acceleration needs a net force, and a body moving at steady velocity is in equilibrium although its kinetic energy is not zero.

questions.s: A paratrooper falls with constant velocity just before landing. He is in
o: no equilibrium, since he is moving
questions.e: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero (weight balanced by air resistance) and the body is in dynamic equilibrium. Static equilibrium needs the body to be at rest. Motion does not prevent equilibrium; acceleration does.

questions.s: Ali (40 kg) sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a light see-saw. For balance, Fatima (30 kg) must sit on the other side at a distance from the pivot of
questions.e: For rotational equilibrium the clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal: 40g × 1.5 = 30g × d, so d = 60/30 = 2 m. The value 1.125 m comes from inverting the ratio of the masses; the lighter child must sit farther away, not closer.

questions.s: Forces of 6 N towards east and 8 N towards south act on a ring. The third force that keeps the ring in equilibrium is
questions.e: The resultant of the two forces is √(6² + 8²) = 10 N, pointing 53° south of east (tan θ = 8/6). The equilibrant is equal and opposite: 10 N at 53° north of west. The option 10 N, 53° south of east is the resultant itself, which would double the net force instead of cancelling it.

questions.s: A 100 N weight hangs at rest from two strings tied to a ceiling. One string makes 30° and the other 60° with the horizontal. The tension in the string at 60° to the horizontal is
questions.e: Horizontal balance: T₁ cos 30° = T₂ cos 60°, so T₂ = √3 T₁. Vertical balance: T₁ sin 30° + T₂ sin 60° = 100 gives T₁/2 + 3T₁/2 = 100, so T₁ = 50 N and T₂ = 50√3 N. The steeper string carries more of the load; 50 N is the tension in the 30° string.

questions.s: A uniform plank 2.0 m long weighing 60 N rests on two supports at its ends. A 120 N load is placed 0.5 m from the left end. The force exerted by the right support is
questions.e: Take moments about the left support: R × 2.0 = 60 × 1.0 + 120 × 0.5 = 120, so R = 60 N. The left support then provides 180 − 60 = 120 N. 120 N is the left reaction; the load is near the left end, so the left support carries more.

questions.s: A uniform metre rule balances on a pivot at its 50 cm mark. A 20 g mass is hung at the 10 cm mark. To restore balance, a 40 g mass must be hung at the
questions.e: The rule's weight acts at the pivot, so only the hung masses matter: 20 × 40 = 40 × d gives d = 20 cm on the other side, at the 70 cm mark. The 90 cm mark balances only an equal 20 g mass at the same 40 cm distance.

questions.s: A uniform metre rule is pivoted at its 40 cm mark and balances horizontally when a 30 g mass hangs at its 10 cm mark. The mass of the metre rule is
questions.e: The rule's weight acts at its centre, the 50 cm mark, 10 cm from the pivot; the 30 g mass is 30 cm from the pivot on the other side. Moments: 30 × 30 = m × 10, so m = 90 g. Using 50 cm as the arm for the rule (measuring from the end) would give 18 g, and ignoring the rule's weight makes balance impossible.

questions.s: Two equal and opposite parallel forces of 5 N act on a steering wheel, with a perpendicular distance of 0.4 m between their lines of action. The torque of this couple is
questions.e: The torque of a couple is one force times the perpendicular distance between the forces: 5 × 0.4 = 2 N m. The net force is zero, but the net torque is not, so 0 N m is wrong; 4 N m counts each force with the full 0.4 m arm.

questions.s: A box of weight 50 N rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The component of its weight perpendicular to the plane is
questions.e: The perpendicular component is W cos 30° = 50 × √3/2 = 25√3 N, and the component along the slope is W sin 30° = 25 N. Choosing 25 N swaps the two components; at 0° the perpendicular component must equal the full weight, which only cos gives.

questions.s: A vector makes an angle of 60° with the x-axis and 45° with the y-axis. The angle it makes with the z-axis is
questions.e: Direction cosines satisfy cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1, so cos²γ = 1 − ¼ − ½ = ¼, giving cos γ = ½ and γ = 60°. Answering 90° assumes the vector lies in the xy-plane, but then the first two angles would have to add to 90°.

questions.s: A velocity of 10 m s⁻¹ is directed at 150° measured anticlockwise from the +x-axis. Its x- and y-components are
questions.e: vₓ = 10 cos 150° = −5√3 m s⁻¹ and v_y = 10 sin 150° = +5 m s⁻¹, because 150° lies in the second quadrant where x is negative and y positive. (−5, 5√3) uses the angle 120° instead, and (5√3, 5) drops the sign of the x-component.

questions.s: The number of significant figures in 4.200 × 10⁻³ is
questions.e: In scientific notation every digit of the number in front of the power of ten is significant, so 4.200 has 4 significant figures; the trailing zeros record that the value was read to the third decimal place. The power of ten never affects the count, and dropping the zeros (giving 2) loses that information.

questions.s: A radio transmitter in Karachi broadcasts at a frequency of 0.5 GHz. In hertz this frequency is
questions.e: Giga means 10⁹, so 0.5 GHz = 0.5 × 10⁹ Hz = 5 × 10⁸ Hz. The value 5 × 10⁹ Hz drops the 0.5 and keeps the 5 with the full power of ten, and 5 × 10⁶ Hz treats giga as mega (10⁶).

questions.s: In SI units the gravitational constant is G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Its value in the CGS system (centimetre, gram, second) is
questions.e: G has dimensions [M⁻¹L³T⁻²]. One SI unit = (1 kg)⁻¹(1 m)³(1 s)⁻² = (10³ g)⁻¹(10² cm)³ s⁻² = 10⁻³ × 10⁶ = 10³ CGS units, so G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 10³ = 6.67 × 10⁻⁸. The value 6.67 × 10⁻⁵ ignores the M⁻¹ factor, and 6.67 × 10⁻¹⁴ applies the factor 10³ the wrong way.

questions.s: The potential difference across a resistor is (6.0 ± 0.3) V and the current through it is (2.0 ± 0.1) A. The resistance R = V/I with its uncertainty is
questions.e: R = 6.0/2.0 = 3.0 Ω. In a quotient the percentage uncertainties add: 0.3/6.0 = 5 % and 0.1/2.0 = 5 %, total 10 %, and 10 % of 3.0 Ω is 0.3 Ω. Adding the absolute uncertainties (0.3 + 0.1) gives 0.4, which is valid only for sums and differences, and subtracting the percentages gives the impossible 0.0.

questions.s: The vectors A = pî − 2ĵ + k̂ and B = pî + pĵ − 3k̂ are perpendicular. The possible values of p are
questions.e: Perpendicular vectors have A · B = 0: p² − 2p − 3 = 0, which factorises as (p − 3)(p + 1) = 0, so p = 3 or p = −1. The pair −3 or 1 comes from a sign slip in the factors, and either single value alone misses a root of the quadratic.

questions.s: A uniform ladder 5 m long and weighing 200 N leans against a smooth vertical wall with its top 4 m above the rough ground and its foot 3 m from the wall. The friction force at the foot of the ladder is
questions.e: A smooth wall pushes only horizontally, with force N, and friction at the foot must balance it. Moments about the foot: N × 4 = 200 × 1.5 (the weight acts at the middle, 1.5 m from the wall horizontally), so N = 75 N and friction = 75 N. The value 150 N uses the full 3 m as the weight's moment arm instead of half of it.

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT a unit of energy?
questions.e: The watt (J s⁻¹) is the unit of power, the rate of doing work. The joule, the electronvolt (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) and the kilowatt-hour (3.6 × 10⁶ J) all measure energy; the kilowatt-hour is the usual trap because it contains the word watt, but power multiplied by time is energy.

questions.s: The SI base unit of the amount of substance is the
questions.e: The mole (mol) is one of the seven SI base units; one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The kilogram is the base unit of mass, not of amount, and gram per mole is the unit of molar mass, a derived quantity.

questions.s: A length of 3.5 mm expressed in metres is
questions.e: Milli means 10⁻³, so 3.5 mm = 3.5 × 10⁻³ m. The value 3.5 × 10⁻² m is 3.5 cm, and 3.5 × 10⁻⁶ m is 3.5 μm.

questions.s: Zainab divides a measured mass of 9.0 g by a measured volume of 3.00 cm³. The density, written with the correct number of significant figures, is
questions.e: In division the result keeps as many significant figures as the least precise value: 9.0 has 2, so the density is 3.0 g cm⁻³. Writing 3.00 follows the volume's three figures, but the answer can be no more precise than the 9.0 g mass.

questions.s: Impulse has the same dimensions as
questions.e: Impulse = force × time = [MLT⁻²][T] = [MLT⁻¹], which is the dimension of momentum; this is why impulse equals the change in momentum. Force is [MLT⁻²] without the factor of time, and energy is [ML²T⁻²].

questions.s: The product of pressure and volume has the dimensions of
questions.e: [P][V] = [ML⁻¹T⁻²][L³] = [ML²T⁻²], the dimensions of energy, which is why pV = nRT is in joules. [ML⁻¹T⁻²] is pressure alone, and [ML²T⁻³] is power.

questions.s: The speed v of sound in a gas is assumed to depend on the pressure P and the density ρ of the gas as v ∝ Pᵃρᵇ. Dimensional analysis gives
questions.e: [LT⁻¹] = [ML⁻¹T⁻²]ᵃ[ML⁻³]ᵇ. Matching T: −2a = −1, so a = ½. Matching M: a + b = 0, so b = −½; then L gives −a − 3b = −½ + 3/2 = 1, which checks. So v ∝ √(P/ρ). a = 1, b = −1 gives P/ρ, which is the square of a speed.

questions.s: Two forces of 5 N and 12 N act at right angles on a body. The magnitude of the resultant force is
questions.e: For perpendicular forces R = √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 N. Adding them gives 17 N, true only when they act in the same direction, and subtracting gives 7 N for opposite directions.

questions.s: The vectors A = 3î − 2ĵ + k̂ and B = î + aĵ − k̂ are perpendicular. The value of a is
questions.e: Perpendicular vectors have A · B = 0: 3(1) + (−2)(a) + (1)(−1) = 0, so 2 − 2a = 0 and a = 1. The value −1 comes from dropping the minus sign of −2ĵ when multiplying.

questions.s: For two non-zero vectors A and B, |A + B| = |A − B|. The angle between A and B is
questions.e: |A + B|² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ and |A − B|² = A² + B² − 2AB cos θ. These are equal only when cos θ = 0, so θ = 90°. At 0° the sum is largest and the difference smallest, so they cannot be equal there.

questions.s: A force F = (2î − ĵ + 3k̂) N acts at a point with position vector r = (î + ĵ + k̂) m. The magnitude of the torque about the origin is
questions.e: τ = r × F = (1·3 − 1·(−1))î − (1·3 − 1·2)ĵ + (1·(−1) − 1·2)k̂ = 4î − ĵ − 3k̂, so |τ| = √(16 + 1 + 9) = √26 N m. The value 4 N m is r · F, a scalar that cannot be a torque, and 26 forgets the square root.

questions.s: A uniform metre rule of mass 2 kg is pivoted at its 20 cm mark. The mass that must hang from its 0 cm end to keep it horizontal is
questions.e: The rule's weight acts at the 50 cm mark, 30 cm from the pivot; the hanging mass is 20 cm from the pivot on the other side. Moments: m × 20 = 2 × 30, so m = 3 kg. The value 1.33 kg inverts the ratio of the distances; the mass is closer to the pivot, so it must be heavier.

questions.s: A rigid body is in complete equilibrium when
questions.e: Complete equilibrium needs the first condition (net force zero, no linear acceleration) and the second condition (net torque zero, no angular acceleration). ΣF = 0 alone allows a couple to spin the body, and v = 0 is not required because a body moving at constant velocity is also in equilibrium.

questions.s: Four readings of the time for a ball to roll down a ramp are 2.31 s, 2.35 s, 2.33 s and 2.29 s. Taking the mean deviation as the uncertainty, the result is
questions.e: Mean = 9.28/4 = 2.32 s. The deviations are 0.01, 0.03, 0.01 and 0.03 s, whose mean is 0.08/4 = 0.02 s, so the result is (2.32 ± 0.02) s. The value 0.03 s is the largest single deviation, not the mean deviation, and 0.06 s is the full spread from 2.29 s to 2.35 s.

questions.s: Which of the following is a derived quantity?
questions.e: Velocity is defined from length and time (displacement per unit time), so it is derived. Mass, electric current and thermodynamic temperature are base quantities with base units kg, A and K.

questions.s: With a vernier calliper of least count 0.01 cm, the main-scale reading is 2.3 cm and the 7th vernier division coincides with a main-scale line. The calliper has a positive zero error of 0.02 cm. The corrected length is
questions.e: Observed reading = 2.3 + 7 × 0.01 = 2.37 cm. A positive zero error means the calliper reads too high, so it is subtracted: 2.37 − 0.02 = 2.35 cm. Adding the zero error gives 2.39 cm, and 2.37 cm forgets the correction altogether.

questions.s: Ali walks 30 m due east and then 40 m due north. The magnitude of his displacement is
questions.e: Displacement is the straight line from start to finish, the hypotenuse of a right triangle: √(30² + 40²) = √2500 = 50 m. 70 m is the total distance walked, not the displacement, and 2500 m forgets to take the square root.

questions.s: Hamza runs exactly one lap of a circular track of radius 50 m in 40 s. The magnitude of his average velocity for the lap is
questions.e: After one full lap he is back at the starting point, so his displacement is zero and average velocity = displacement/time = 0. The value 2.5π m/s (2π × 50/40) is his average speed, which uses the distance travelled, not the displacement.

questions.s: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.e: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Speed and distance are only magnitudes (scalars), and time has no direction at all.

questions.s: A bus travels from Islamabad to a town 60 km away at a steady 30 km/h and returns along the same road at a steady 60 km/h. Its average speed for the whole trip is
questions.e: Total distance = 120 km; total time = 60/30 + 60/60 = 2 h + 1 h = 3 h, so average speed = 120/3 = 40 km/h. 45 km/h is the simple mean of the two speeds, which is wrong because the bus spends more time at the lower speed.

questions.s: The position of a particle moving along the x-axis is x = 4t² − 2t, where x is in metres and t in seconds. Its velocity at t = 3 s is
questions.e: Velocity is v = dx/dt = 8t − 2, so at t = 3 s, v = 24 − 2 = 22 m/s. 30 m/s is the position value x(3) = 36 − 6, read wrongly as velocity, and 24 m/s forgets the −2 term.

questions.s: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of
questions.e: Acceleration a = Δv/Δt, the rate of change of velocity with time. The rate of change of displacement with time is velocity, not acceleration.

questions.s: A car starts from rest and moves with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s². Its velocity after 5 s is
questions.e: Using vf = vi + at = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 m/s. 5 m/s is the average velocity over the 5 s, not the final velocity, and 7 m/s wrongly adds a and t.

questions.s: A motorcycle starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 4 m/s². The distance it covers in the first 6 s is
questions.e: s = vit + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 4 × 36 = 72 m. 144 m forgets the factor ½, and 24 m is the final velocity (at = 24 m/s), not a distance.

questions.s: A train moving at 20 m/s applies its brakes and comes to rest with uniform deceleration after travelling 100 m. The magnitude of its deceleration is
questions.e: vf² = vi² − 2as gives 0 = 400 − 2a × 100, so a = 400/200 = 2 m/s². 4 m/s² comes from dividing 400 by 100 and forgetting the factor 2 in 2as.

questions.s: A stone dropped from rest from the top of a tower reaches the ground in 4 s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, the height of the tower is
questions.e: h = ½gt² = ½ × 10 × 16 = 80 m. 160 m forgets the factor ½, and 40 m is the final speed (gt = 40 m/s) mistaken for a height.

questions.s: Usman throws a ball vertically upward with a speed of 30 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, the ball returns to the point of projection after
questions.e: Time to reach the top is u/g = 30/10 = 3 s, and the fall back takes the same time, so total time = 2u/g = 6 s. 3 s is only the time of ascent.

questions.s: A car starts from rest and moves with a uniform acceleration of 4 m/s². The distance it covers during the 5th second of its motion is
questions.e: Distance in the 5th second = s(5) − s(4) = ½ × 4 × (25 − 16) = 2 × 9 = 18 m. 50 m is the total distance in the first 5 s, and 32 m is the total in the first 4 s.

questions.s: A body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration. It covers 10 m in the first 2 s. The distance it covers in the next 2 s is
questions.e: From rest, s ∝ t², so in 4 s it covers 10 × (4/2)² = 40 m. The distance in the next 2 s is 40 − 10 = 30 m (the 1 : 3 ratio for equal successive intervals). 40 m is the total in 4 s, not the distance in the second interval.

questions.s: A car at rest at a traffic light starts with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s² just as a truck moving at a constant 10 m/s passes it in the same direction. The car catches the truck at a distance from the light of
questions.e: They meet when ½ × 2 × t² = 10t, giving t = 10 s, and the distance is 10 × 10 = 100 m. 25 m is where the car is at t = 5 s, when the two speeds are equal and the gap is largest, not where they meet.

questions.s: The velocity of a car increases uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. The distance it travels in this time is
questions.e: For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (10 + 30)/2 = 20 m/s, so distance = 20 × 5 = 100 m. 150 m wrongly uses the final speed for the whole 5 s, and 50 m uses only the initial speed.

questions.s: The SI unit of acceleration is
questions.e: Acceleration = change in velocity (m s⁻¹) divided by time (s), giving m s⁻². m s⁻¹ is the unit of velocity and kg m s⁻¹ is the unit of momentum.

questions.s: A stone is dropped from rest and falls freely through 45 m. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, its speed just before it hits the ground is
questions.e: vf² = 2gh = 2 × 10 × 45 = 900, so vf = 30 m/s. √450 m/s forgets the factor 2, and 900 m/s forgets to take the square root.

questions.s: For a body moving with constant velocity, its acceleration is
questions.e: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; if velocity does not change in magnitude or direction, the acceleration is zero. A constant velocity does not mean a constant non-zero acceleration.

questions.s: A car moving at 30 m/s brakes with a uniform deceleration of 5 m/s² until it stops. The distance it covers in the last one second before stopping is
questions.e: The last second of a uniform deceleration to rest mirrors the first second of a uniform acceleration from rest: s = ½ × 5 × 1² = 2.5 m. 90 m is the total stopping distance (30²/(2 × 5)), and 5 m uses a × t without the ½.

questions.s: Bilal cycles in a straight line at 8 m/s for 6 s and then at 2 m/s for 12 s in the same direction. His average velocity for the whole motion is
questions.e: Total displacement = 8 × 6 + 2 × 12 = 48 + 24 = 72 m in a total time of 18 s, so average velocity = 72/18 = 4 m/s. 5 m/s is the simple mean of the two speeds, which ignores that the times are unequal.

questions.s: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m/s from the edge of a roof 25 m above the ground and falls to the ground beside the building. Taking g = 10 m/s², the time it takes to reach the ground is
questions.e: Taking up as positive, −25 = 20t − 5t², so t² − 4t − 5 = 0 and (t − 5)(t + 1) = 0, giving t = 5 s. 4 s is only the time to return to roof level (2u/g), and 2 s is the time to the highest point.

questions.s: A body is dropped from rest and falls freely. The distances it covers in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds of its fall are in the ratio
questions.e: Total distances after 1, 2, 3 s are in the ratio 1 : 4 : 9 (s ∝ t²), so the distances in each separate second are 1, 4 − 1 = 3 and 9 − 4 = 5. The ratio 1 : 4 : 9 is for total distances, not for each second.

questions.s: A balloon is rising vertically at a steady 10 m/s. When it is 40 m above the ground, a stone is released from it. Taking g = 10 m/s², the stone reaches the ground after
questions.e: The stone starts with the balloon's velocity, 10 m/s upward. Taking up as positive, −40 = 10t − 5t², so t² − 2t − 8 = 0 and (t − 4)(t + 2) = 0, giving t = 4 s. 2√2 s wrongly treats the stone as dropped from rest (40 = 5t²).

questions.s: A cyclist moving at 5 m/s accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 4 s. The distance covered in these 4 s is
questions.e: s = vit + ½at² = 5 × 4 + ½ × 2 × 16 = 20 + 16 = 36 m. 52 m forgets the ½ (20 + 32), while 16 m and 20 m each use only one of the two terms.

questions.s: Which pair consists of two scalar quantities?
questions.e: Speed and distance both have magnitude only, so both are scalars. Each of the other pairs contains a vector: velocity, displacement and force all have direction.

questions.s: The slope of a velocity-time graph gives the
questions.e: Slope = Δv/Δt, which is the definition of acceleration. Displacement is given by the area under the velocity-time graph, not its slope.

questions.s: The area between a velocity-time graph and the time axis represents the
questions.e: Area = velocity × time, which has the dimensions of displacement, so the area under a velocity-time graph gives the displacement. Acceleration is the slope of the graph, not the area.

questions.s: The velocity-time graph of a body is a straight line parallel to the time axis, above the axis. The body is moving with
questions.e: A horizontal line means the velocity has the same non-zero value at every instant, so the velocity is uniform and the slope (acceleration) is zero. Uniform acceleration would need a sloping straight line.

questions.s: The velocity-time graph of a car is a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 20 m/s at t = 4 s. The distance covered by the car in these 4 s is
questions.e: The distance is the area of the triangle under the graph: ½ × 4 × 20 = 40 m. 80 m forgets the ½ of the triangle, and 5 m is the slope (the acceleration in m/s²), not a distance.

questions.s: A velocity-time graph shows a van speeding up uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 3 s, moving at a constant 12 m/s for the next 4 s and then slowing uniformly to rest in a further 2 s. The total distance covered is
questions.e: Area = ½ × 3 × 12 + 4 × 12 + ½ × 2 × 12 = 18 + 48 + 12 = 78 m. 108 m treats the whole 9 s as if the speed were 12 m/s throughout, and 66 m leaves out the slowing-down triangle.

questions.s: A velocity-time graph shows a body speeding up uniformly from rest to 10 m/s in 4 s and then slowing uniformly to rest in the next 6 s. Its average speed over the 10 s is
questions.e: Total distance = area of the triangle = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 m, so average speed = 50/10 = 5 m/s. 50 m/s confuses the distance with the speed, and 10 m/s is the maximum speed, not the average.

questions.s: The velocity-time graph of a scooter is a straight line falling from 30 m/s at t = 0 to zero at t = 6 s. The magnitude of its deceleration is
questions.e: Deceleration = magnitude of slope = 30/6 = 5 m/s². 90 is the area under the graph (the stopping distance in metres), and 0.2 inverts the slope (6/30).

questions.s: The velocity-time graph of a particle is a straight line from +20 m/s at t = 0 to −20 m/s at t = 4 s. Over these 4 s, the particle's displacement and the distance it covers are respectively
questions.e: The line crosses the axis at t = 2 s. The area above the axis is ½ × 2 × 20 = +20 m and the area below is −20 m, so displacement = 0 while distance = 20 + 20 = 40 m. Adding the two areas as positive gives distance, not displacement.

questions.s: The displacement-time graph of a body is a straight line passing through the origin and inclined to the time axis. This shows that the body
questions.e: The slope of a displacement-time graph is velocity; a straight line has a constant slope, so the velocity is constant. Uniform acceleration would make the displacement-time graph a curve (a parabola).

questions.s: On a velocity-time graph, a curve whose slope keeps increasing with time shows a body with
questions.e: The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration, so a steadily steepening curve means the acceleration itself is increasing. Constant acceleration would give a straight line of fixed slope.

questions.s: A velocity-time graph shows a car moving at a constant 8 m/s from t = 0 to t = 4 s, then slowing uniformly to rest at t = 8 s. Its average velocity over the 8 s is
questions.e: Displacement = 8 × 4 + ½ × 4 × 8 = 32 + 16 = 48 m, so average velocity = 48/8 = 6 m/s. 4 m/s is the mean of the start and end velocities, which is valid only for uniform acceleration throughout, and 48 is the displacement in metres.

questions.s: A body starts from rest. Its acceleration-time graph is a horizontal line at 3 m/s² from t = 0 to t = 4 s. Its velocity at t = 4 s is
questions.e: The area under an acceleration-time graph gives the change in velocity: 3 × 4 = 12 m/s, and since it starts from rest, v = 12 m/s. 7 m/s wrongly adds 3 and 4, and 0.75 m/s divides instead of multiplying.

questions.s: The velocity-time graph of a bus is a straight line rising from 4 m/s at t = 0 to 16 m/s at t = 6 s. The distance covered by the bus in these 6 s is
questions.e: The area under the line is a trapezium: ½ × (4 + 16) × 6 = 60 m. 36 m counts only the triangle ½ × 6 × 12 and leaves out the rectangle 4 × 6 due to the initial velocity, and 96 m uses 16 m/s for the whole time.

questions.s: The velocity-time graph of a ball thrown upward is a straight line sloping downward that crosses the time axis. At the instant the line crosses the axis,
o: velocity is zero but acceleration is not zero
velocity and acceleration are both zero
acceleration is zero and speed is maximum
the ball is back at its starting point
questions.e: At the crossing the velocity is zero (the highest point), but the slope of the line, the acceleration g, is the same non-zero value as everywhere else. Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration: the ball is still being pulled down.

questions.s: Cars A and B leave the same point at the same instant along a straight road. On a velocity-time graph, A is a horizontal line at 10 m/s, while B is a straight line rising from 0 at t = 0 and reaching 10 m/s at t = 5 s. At t = 5 s, where the two lines cross,
o: A and B are side by side
B is 25 m ahead of A
A is 25 m ahead of B
questions.e: By t = 5 s, A has covered 10 × 5 = 50 m and B has covered ½ × 5 × 10 = 25 m, so A is 25 m ahead. Crossing lines on a velocity-time graph mean equal velocities, not equal positions; at this moment the gap is largest.

questions.s: Newton's first law of motion is also known as the law of
questions.e: The first law says a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts, which describes inertia. Action and reaction is the third law.

questions.s: A net force of 20 N acts on a body of mass 4 kg. The acceleration produced is
questions.e: From F = ma, a = F/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s². 80 m/s² multiplies instead of dividing, and 0.2 m/s² divides the wrong way round (m/F).

questions.s: The mass of a body is a measure of its
questions.e: Mass measures how strongly a body resists a change in its state of motion, that is, its inertia. Weight is the gravitational force mg, which changes from place to place while mass does not.

questions.s: Sana, of mass 60 kg, stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is accelerating upward at 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the scale reads
questions.e: For upward acceleration, R − mg = ma, so R = m(g + a) = 60 × 12 = 720 N. 480 N is m(g − a), which applies to downward acceleration, and 600 N is her weight when the lift is at rest or moving uniformly.

questions.s: A person stands on a weighing scale in a lift. The cable breaks and the lift falls freely. While it falls freely, the scale reads
questions.e: In free fall a = g downward, so R = m(g − a) = m(g − g) = 0: the person feels weightless. The true weight mg still acts, but the scale no longer pushes on the person, so it reads zero.

questions.s: Blocks of mass 2 kg and 3 kg are in contact on a smooth horizontal floor. A horizontal force of 10 N pushes the 2 kg block, which pushes the 3 kg block. The force exerted by the 2 kg block on the 3 kg block is
questions.e: Both move together with a = 10/(2 + 3) = 2 m/s². The only horizontal force on the 3 kg block is the contact force, so it equals 3 × 2 = 6 N. 4 N is the net force on the 2 kg block (10 − 6), not the contact force.

questions.s: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang on either side of a light string passing over a smooth, light pulley. Taking g = 10 m/s², the magnitude of their acceleration is
questions.e: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (3 − 2) × 10/5 = 2 m/s². Dividing the unbalanced weight of 10 N by only one of the masses (3 kg or 2 kg) gives 10/3 or 5 m/s², but the force must accelerate both masses together.

questions.s: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang vertically on either side of a light inextensible string over a smooth, light, fixed pulley and are released. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string is
questions.e: a = (3 − 2) × 10/5 = 2 m/s². For the 2 kg mass rising, T − 20 = 2 × 2, so T = 24 N (check: 30 − T = 3 × 2 also gives 24 N). 20 N and 30 N are the two weights; the tension lies between them because the masses accelerate.

questions.s: A block slides down a smooth (frictionless) plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its acceleration is
questions.e: Only the component of weight along the slope, mg sin θ, accelerates the block, so a = g sin 30° = 10 × ½ = 5 m/s². 5√3 m/s² wrongly uses cos 30°, which belongs to the component perpendicular to the slope.

questions.s: A book rests on a table. According to Newton's third law, the reaction to the weight of the book (the pull of the Earth on the book) is
o: the normal force of the table on the book
the force of the book on the table
the pull of the book on the Earth
questions.e: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies and are of the same type: the Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls the Earth with an equal and opposite gravitational force. The table's normal force balances the weight, but it acts on the same body (the book) and is a different type of force, so it is not the reaction.

questions.s: When a stationary bus suddenly starts moving, the standing passengers tend to fall backward. This is due to
questions.e: The bus floor moves forward but the upper body of a passenger tends to stay at rest, so it is left behind: this is inertia of rest. Inertia of motion explains falling forward when a moving bus stops suddenly.

questions.s: A body has a mass of 6 kg on the Earth. On the Moon, where the acceleration due to gravity is one-sixth of that on the Earth, its mass is
questions.e: Mass is the quantity of matter and does not depend on location, so it stays 6 kg. Only the weight mg becomes one-sixth on the Moon; 1 kg wrongly scales the mass as if it were weight.

questions.s: A constant net force of 12 N acts on a 3 kg body initially at rest. The distance moved by the body in the first 5 s is
questions.e: a = F/m = 12/3 = 4 m/s², so s = ½at² = ½ × 4 × 25 = 50 m. 100 m forgets the ½, and 20 m is the velocity after 5 s (at = 20 m/s), not the distance.

questions.s: A 5 kg box is pulled along a horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 30 N. The friction force on the box is 10 N. The acceleration of the box is
questions.e: Net force = 30 − 10 = 20 N, so a = 20/5 = 4 m/s². 6 m/s² ignores friction (30/5), and 8 m/s² wrongly adds friction to the pull.

questions.s: A 4 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is tied to a light string that passes over a smooth pulley at the table edge and carries a 1 kg mass hanging freely. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string while the system moves is
questions.e: The weight of the hanging mass (10 N) accelerates both masses: a = 10/(4 + 1) = 2 m/s². The only horizontal force on the 4 kg block is the tension, so T = 4 × 2 = 8 N. 10 N would be the tension only if the system were at rest; the falling mass needs T < mg.

questions.s: Zainab, of mass 50 kg, stands on a weighing scale in a lift moving downward with a constant velocity of 3 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the scale reads
questions.e: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero and R = mg = 50 × 10 = 500 N. The scale reading changes only when the lift accelerates; the value of the velocity itself does not matter.

questions.s: A rope can bear a maximum tension of 360 N. It is used to lift a 30 kg load vertically. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum upward acceleration the load can be given without breaking the rope is
questions.e: T − mg = ma gives 360 − 300 = 30a, so a = 2 m/s². 12 m/s² divides the whole tension by the mass and ignores that 300 N of it is needed just to support the weight.

questions.s: A net force acting on a body of constant mass always produces
o: a constant velocity in its own direction
a motion directly opposite to the force
no change in the body's momentum
questions.e: By Newton's second law, F = ma, so a net force produces an acceleration in the direction of the force. A constant velocity is what happens when the net force is zero.

questions.s: The momentum of a 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s is
questions.e: Momentum p = mv = 2 × 5 = 10 kg m s⁻¹. 25 is the kinetic energy ½mv² in joules, a different quantity.

questions.s: The SI unit of impulse is
questions.e: Impulse = force × time, so its unit is N s (equivalent to kg m s⁻¹, the unit of momentum). N m is the unit of work or torque, and kg m s⁻² is the newton itself.

questions.s: The impulse of a force acting on a body is equal to the
o: rate of change of its momentum
questions.e: Impulse = FΔt = Δp, the change in momentum. The rate of change of momentum is the force itself, and force × distance is work.

questions.s: A force of 50 N acts on a body for 0.2 s. The change in the momentum of the body is
questions.e: Change in momentum = impulse = FΔt = 50 × 0.2 = 10 N s. 250 N s divides 50 by 0.2 instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at right angles at 10 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 10 m/s. The magnitude of the change in its momentum is
questions.e: Taking the rebound direction as positive, Δp = 0.2 × 10 − 0.2 × (−10) = 4 kg m s⁻¹. Zero comes from ignoring that velocity reverses direction; momentum is a vector, so the change is double the initial momentum.

questions.s: A cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg moving at 20 m/s is hit straight back along its path at 30 m/s. The bat is in contact with the ball for 0.01 s. The average force exerted by the bat on the ball is
questions.e: Because the velocity reverses, Δp = 0.15 × (30 + 20) = 7.5 kg m s⁻¹, and F = Δp/Δt = 7.5/0.01 = 750 N. 150 N subtracts the speeds (30 − 20), forgetting that the direction has changed.

questions.s: A fielder pulls his hands backward while catching a fast cricket ball. He does this
o: to reduce the total change in the ball's momentum
to increase stopping time, lowering force
to increase the impulse given to the ball
to increase the momentum of the ball
questions.e: The change in momentum of the ball (from mv to zero) is fixed, so the impulse FΔt is fixed. Increasing the stopping time Δt reduces the average force on the hands. The change in momentum itself is not reduced by moving the hands.

questions.s: A force acts on a 0.5 kg body initially at rest. The force rises uniformly from 0 to 40 N in 0.1 s and then falls uniformly back to 0 in a further 0.1 s. The speed of the body afterwards is
questions.e: Impulse = area under the force-time graph = ½ × 0.2 × 40 = 4 N s, which equals the change in momentum, so v = 4/0.5 = 8 m/s. 16 m/s forgets the ½ in the triangle's area, and 4 m/s mistakes the impulse for the speed.

questions.s: A body of mass 2 kg has a kinetic energy of 100 J. The magnitude of its momentum is
questions.e: p = √(2mK) = √(2 × 2 × 100) = √400 = 20 kg m s⁻¹ (equivalently v = 10 m/s and p = 2 × 10). 10 kg m s⁻¹ confuses the speed with the momentum, and 400 forgets the square root.

questions.s: Two bodies of masses 1 kg and 4 kg have equal momenta. The ratio of their kinetic energies (1 kg body : 4 kg body) is
questions.e: K = p²/2m, so with equal p, kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass: K₁ : K₂ = 4 : 1. 1 : 4 assumes K is directly proportional to mass, which holds only for equal speeds.

questions.s: The rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to
questions.e: Newton's second law in its general form is F = Δp/Δt: the net force equals the rate of change of momentum. The impulse equals the change in momentum, not its rate of change.

questions.s: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest by its brakes in 5 s. The average braking force is
questions.e: F = Δp/Δt = (1000 × 20)/5 = 4000 N. 100 000 N multiplies the momentum by the time instead of dividing.

questions.s: The momentum of a 2 kg body moving in a straight line increases from 6 kg m s⁻¹ to 14 kg m s⁻¹ without changing direction. The increase in its kinetic energy is
questions.e: K = p²/2m, so ΔK = (14² − 6²)/(2 × 2) = (196 − 36)/4 = 40 J (speeds 3 m/s and 7 m/s give 9 J and 49 J). 16 J wrongly squares the change in momentum, (8²)/4, instead of taking the difference of the squares.

questions.s: A machine gun fires 10 bullets per second, each of mass 50 g, with a speed of 400 m/s. The average force needed to hold the gun in place is
questions.e: Force = momentum given to bullets per second = 10 × 0.05 × 400 = 200 N. 20 N is the momentum of a single bullet, and 200 000 N comes from using 50 g as 50 kg.

questions.s: The total momentum of a system of bodies remains constant when
o: the colliding bodies are at rest
questions.e: Momentum is conserved for an isolated system, one on which the net external force is zero. Kinetic energy need not be conserved; momentum is conserved in inelastic collisions too.

questions.s: A 4 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet with a muzzle speed of 400 m/s. The recoil speed of the rifle is
questions.e: Initial momentum is zero, so 4V = 0.02 × 400 = 8 kg m s⁻¹, giving V = 2 m/s backward. 8 m/s is the bullet's momentum value, not the rifle's speed.

questions.s: A 3 kg object at rest explodes into two pieces of 1 kg and 2 kg. The 1 kg piece moves off at 10 m/s. The velocity of the 2 kg piece is
o: 5 m/s, opposite to the 1 kg piece
5 m/s, same way as the 1 kg piece
10 m/s, opposite to the 1 kg piece
20 m/s, opposite to the 1 kg piece
questions.e: Total momentum stays zero: 1 × 10 + 2v = 0, so v = −5 m/s, that is 5 m/s opposite to the 1 kg piece. The pieces cannot move the same way, or the total momentum would no longer be zero.

questions.s: A 60 kg man jumps horizontally off the end of a 120 kg boat that was at rest on still water. If he leaves the boat at 4 m/s, the boat moves off in the opposite direction at
questions.e: Total momentum is zero before and after: 60 × 4 = 120V, so V = 2 m/s. 8 m/s swaps the masses (120 × 4/60); the heavier boat must move more slowly than the man.

questions.s: A 4 kg trolley moves at 5 m/s along a smooth horizontal track. A 1 kg bag of sand is dropped vertically onto it and stays on it. The new speed of the trolley is
questions.e: The sand has no horizontal momentum, so horizontal momentum is conserved: 4 × 5 = (4 + 1)v, giving v = 4 m/s. The speed cannot stay 5 m/s because the same momentum is now shared by a larger mass.

questions.s: A 10 g bullet moving horizontally at 500 m/s embeds itself in a 990 g wooden block resting on a smooth horizontal surface. The block and bullet move off together at
questions.e: 0.01 × 500 = (0.01 + 0.99)v, so v = 5/1 = 5 m/s. 5.05 m/s divides the momentum by the block's mass alone, forgetting that the bullet moves with the block.

questions.s: The backward kick (recoil) of a gun when it fires a bullet is explained by
questions.e: Before firing the total momentum of gun and bullet is zero; the bullet gains forward momentum, so the gun must gain an equal backward momentum. Energy is also conserved, but it does not fix the direction and size of the recoil velocity.

questions.s: A shell moving horizontally at 20 m/s explodes into two equal halves. Just after the explosion one half is at rest. The other half moves at
questions.e: Momentum is conserved: m × 20 = (m/2) × 0 + (m/2)v, so v = 40 m/s in the original direction. 20 m/s would keep the momentum only if the moving half had the full mass.

questions.s: A 50 kg boy running at 4 m/s jumps onto a 150 kg cart moving at 2 m/s in the same direction on a smooth road. The common speed of the boy and cart is
questions.e: 50 × 4 + 150 × 2 = 200v, so v = 500/200 = 2.5 m/s. 3 m/s is the simple mean of the two speeds, which ignores the different masses, and 0.5 m/s results from taking the motions as opposite.

questions.s: A 60 kg man stands at one end of a 140 kg boat floating at rest on still water. He walks 5 m to the other end of the boat. Ignoring water resistance, the distance the boat moves backward relative to the water is
questions.e: The centre of mass of man and boat stays fixed. If the man moves x forward and the boat moves 5 − x back, 60x = 140(5 − x), so x = 3.5 m and the boat moves 1.5 m. 3.5 m is the man's own movement relative to the water, and 15/7 m treats 5 m as the man's ground displacement.

questions.s: Two balls collide on a smooth horizontal table with no external horizontal force acting. Which quantity is always conserved in the collision?
questions.e: With no external force the total momentum of the system is conserved in every collision. Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions, and the momentum of each ball separately changes.

questions.s: An 80 kg astronaut at rest in space throws a 2 kg tool away from herself at 6 m/s. She moves in the opposite direction at
questions.e: Momentum is conserved: 80V = 2 × 6 = 12, so V = 12/80 = 0.15 m/s. 1.5 m/s and 0.015 m/s are decimal-place slips.

questions.s: In a perfectly elastic collision, the total kinetic energy is
questions.e: An elastic collision is defined as one in which kinetic energy is conserved, and momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system. Losing kinetic energy while conserving momentum describes an inelastic collision.

questions.s: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the colliding bodies
o: both come to rest in all cases
questions.e: A perfectly inelastic collision is one where the bodies move together with a common velocity afterwards, so the maximum kinetic energy is lost. They come to rest only if the total momentum was zero.

questions.s: A ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with an identical ball at rest. After the collision, the velocities of the first and second balls are respectively
questions.e: For equal masses in a one-dimensional elastic collision the balls exchange velocities, so the first stops and the second moves off at 6 m/s. 3 m/s each conserves momentum but loses half the kinetic energy, so it cannot be elastic.

questions.s: A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m/s collides with a 4 kg trolley at rest and they stick together. Their common velocity is
questions.e: 2 × 6 = (2 + 4)v, so v = 12/6 = 2 m/s. 3 m/s divides the speed by 2 as if the masses were equal.

questions.s: A 3 kg ball moving at 4 m/s collides with a 1 kg ball at rest and they stick together. The kinetic energy lost in the collision is
questions.e: Common velocity v = (3 × 4)/4 = 3 m/s. KE before = ½ × 3 × 16 = 24 J and KE after = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J, so 6 J is lost. 18 J is the kinetic energy remaining, not the loss, and zero would apply only to an elastic collision.

questions.s: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a 1 kg ball at rest. The velocity of the 1 kg ball after the collision is
questions.e: For an elastic collision with the target at rest, v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂) = 2 × 2 × 6/3 = 8 m/s (and v₁ = (2 − 1) × 6/3 = 2 m/s; momentum 12 = 2 × 2 + 1 × 8). 12 m/s (2u) is the limit only when the moving ball is very much heavier than the target.

questions.s: A 1 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a 2 kg ball at rest. Immediately after the collision, the 1 kg ball moves at
questions.e: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂) = (1 − 2) × 6/3 = −2 m/s, so it rebounds at 2 m/s; the 2 kg ball moves at 2 × 1 × 6/3 = 4 m/s. Zero would be correct only for equal masses; a lighter ball hitting a heavier one bounces back.

questions.s: A tennis ball hits a massive rigid wall head-on at 15 m/s in a perfectly elastic collision. It rebounds with a speed of
questions.e: In an elastic collision with a very massive body, the light ball's velocity simply reverses, so it rebounds at 15 m/s and its kinetic energy is unchanged. 30 m/s confuses the change in velocity with the final speed.

questions.s: In a one-dimensional elastic collision between two bodies, the relative velocity of separation after the collision is
questions.e: Combining conservation of momentum and kinetic energy gives u₁ − u₂ = v₂ − v₁: the speed of separation equals the speed of approach. Zero relative velocity after collision describes a perfectly inelastic collision.

questions.s: A 2 kg ball moving east at 5 m/s collides head-on with a 3 kg ball moving west at 5 m/s, and they stick together. Their common velocity is
questions.e: Taking east as positive, 2 × 5 + 3 × (−5) = 5v, so v = −5/5 = −1 m/s, which is 1 m/s west. Treating both velocities as positive would give 5 m/s, ignoring that momentum is a vector.

questions.s: Which of the following collisions is closest to perfectly elastic?
o: Clay hitting and sticking to a floor
Two cars crumpling in a crash
A bullet lodging in a wooden block
questions.e: Collisions between gas molecules lose essentially no kinetic energy, so they are treated as elastic. Clay, crashing cars and a lodged bullet all lose kinetic energy to heat, sound and deformation.

questions.s: Two identical balls move towards each other along a straight line, the first at 4 m/s and the second at 2 m/s, and collide elastically head-on. Taking the first ball's initial direction as positive, their velocities after the collision (first, second) are
questions.e: Equal masses in a one-dimensional elastic collision exchange velocities: the first takes −2 m/s and the second takes +4 m/s. 1 m/s each is the common velocity if they stuck together, which would lose kinetic energy.

questions.s: A 4 kg ball moving at 3 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a 2 kg ball at rest. The fraction of the initial kinetic energy transferred to the 2 kg ball is
questions.e: v₂ = 2 × 4 × 3/6 = 4 m/s, so the 2 kg ball gains ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J out of ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J, a fraction 16/18 = 8/9. 1/9 is the fraction kept by the 4 kg ball (it moves on at 1 m/s with 2 J).

questions.s: In an inelastic collision, the kinetic energy that is lost is mainly converted into
o: an increase in the bodies' mass
questions.e: The lost kinetic energy goes into heating, sound and permanent change of shape of the bodies. Momentum is not a form of energy, and it is conserved anyway.

questions.s: Water leaves a hose at 5 m/s at a rate of 2 kg/s and strikes a wall at right angles. The water does not rebound. The force exerted by the water on the wall is
questions.e: F = (mass per second) × change in velocity = 2 × 5 = 10 N. 20 N would apply only if the water bounced back at 5 m/s, doubling the change in velocity.

questions.s: Water flows out of a pipe of cross-sectional area 0.01 m² at 4 m/s and strikes a wall at right angles without rebounding. Taking the density of water as 1000 kg/m³, the force on the wall is
questions.e: Mass per second = ρAv = 1000 × 0.01 × 4 = 40 kg/s, and F = (mass per second) × v = 40 × 4 = ρAv² = 160 N. 40 N stops at the mass flow rate and forgets to multiply by the change in velocity, while 320 N assumes the water rebounds.

questions.s: A horizontal stream of water strikes a wall at right angles and comes to rest without splashing back. The force exerted on the wall equals
questions.e: Force = rate of change of momentum = (mass striking per second) × (change in velocity) = (Δm/Δt) × v. Mass × speed is momentum, not force; it must be divided by time, which is what the mass flow rate does.

questions.s: Water flows from a pipe of fixed cross-section and strikes a wall at right angles without rebounding. If the speed of the water is doubled, the force on the wall
questions.e: F = ρAv²: doubling v doubles both the mass arriving per second (ρAv) and the change in velocity of each kilogram, so F becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times. Choosing doubles counts only one of these two effects.

questions.s: Water leaves the nozzle of a fire hose at 20 m/s at a rate of 3 kg/s. The backward force that the firefighter must apply to hold the nozzle steady is
questions.e: The nozzle gives momentum to the water at a rate of (3 kg/s) × (20 m/s) = 60 N, so by the third law the water pushes back on the hose with 60 N. 6.7 N divides the speed by the flow rate instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A water jet delivers 0.5 kg of water per second at 8 m/s onto a flat plate held at right angles to it. The water bounces straight back at 2 m/s. The force exerted by the jet on the plate is
questions.e: Each kilogram changes velocity from +8 m/s to −2 m/s, a change of 10 m/s, so F = 0.5 × 10 = 5 N. 3 N subtracts the speeds (8 − 2), forgetting that the direction reverses, and 4 N ignores the rebound.

questions.s: The propulsion of a rocket is based on the principle of
questions.e: The rocket pushes exhaust gases backward and gains equal forward momentum, so the total momentum of rocket plus gases is conserved. Gravitation acts on the rocket but does not propel it.

questions.s: A rocket can accelerate in outer space, where there is no air, because
o: the air outside pushes on its exhaust
there is no gravity in outer space
its mass keeps increasing as it moves
questions.e: The rocket exerts a backward force on the gases it ejects, and by the third law the gases exert an equal forward force on the rocket. No outside air is needed; the rocket actually works better without air resistance.

questions.s: A rocket engine ejects 50 kg of exhaust gas per second at a speed of 2000 m/s relative to the rocket. The thrust on the rocket is
questions.e: Thrust = (Δm/Δt) × v = 50 × 2000 = 100 000 N = 1 × 10⁵ N. 40 N divides the speed by the mass rate instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A rocket of mass 5000 kg stands vertically on its launch pad. Its engines produce a thrust of 1.0 × 10⁵ N. Taking g = 10 m/s², its initial upward acceleration is
questions.e: Net upward force = thrust − weight = 100 000 − 50 000 = 50 000 N, so a = 50 000/5000 = 10 m/s². 20 m/s² ignores the rocket's weight, which must be overcome before it can accelerate upward.

questions.s: A rocket in deep space fires its engine with a constant thrust. As its fuel is used up, its acceleration
questions.e: a = thrust/mass; with constant thrust and a mass that falls as fuel is ejected, the acceleration keeps increasing. A constant acceleration would need the mass to stay constant.

questions.s: A 2000 kg rocket ejects exhaust gas at 1000 m/s relative to itself. Taking g = 10 m/s², the minimum rate at which it must eject gas to just lift off vertically is
questions.e: To just lift off, thrust must equal weight: (Δm/Δt) × 1000 = 2000 × 10, so Δm/Δt = 20 kg/s. 2 kg/s forgets to multiply the mass by g to get the weight.

questions.s: A ball is thrown at an angle above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, at the highest point of its path
questions.e: At the top the vertical component of velocity is zero but the horizontal component is unchanged, so the velocity is horizontal. The acceleration is still g vertically downward throughout the flight.

questions.s: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal component of the velocity of a projectile
questions.e: Gravity acts only vertically, so there is no horizontal force and the horizontal velocity u cos θ stays constant. It is the vertical component that becomes zero at the top.

questions.s: For a fixed speed of projection on level ground and no air resistance, the horizontal range of a projectile is greatest when the angle of projection is
questions.e: R = u² sin 2θ/g is largest when sin 2θ = 1, that is 2θ = 90° and θ = 45°. At 90° the range is zero because the projectile goes straight up and down.

questions.s: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its time of flight is
questions.e: T = 2u sin θ/g = 2 × 20 × ½/10 = 2 s. 4 s forgets sin θ (it is the flight time for a vertical throw), and 2√3 s wrongly uses cos 30°.

questions.s: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum height it reaches is
questions.e: H = u² sin²θ/2g = 400 × ¼/20 = 5 m. 10 m forgets to square sin θ, and 15 m uses cos²30° instead of sin²30°.

questions.s: A stone is projected from level ground at 40 m/s at 15° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its horizontal range is
questions.e: R = u² sin 2θ/g = 1600 × sin 30°/10 = 1600 × ½/10 = 80 m. 160 m is the maximum range u²/g at 45°, and 80√3 m uses sin 60° by doubling the angle twice.

questions.s: Two stones are projected from level ground with the same speed, one at 30° and the other at 60° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, the ratio of their horizontal ranges is
questions.e: R ∝ sin 2θ, and sin 60° = sin 120°, so complementary angles of projection give equal ranges: 1 : 1. The 60° stone goes higher and stays up longer, but moves more slowly horizontally.

questions.s: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a cliff 20 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s², it lands at a horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff of
questions.e: Vertical motion: 20 = ½ × 10 × t², so t = 2 s; horizontal distance = 15 × 2 = 30 m. 60 m comes from using t = 4 s (20 = 5t wrongly), and 20 m mistakes the height for the range.

questions.s: From the same height, Ayesha drops one ball and at the same instant throws an identical ball horizontally. Ignoring air resistance,
o: both land at the same time
questions.e: Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g, so they take the same time to fall; the horizontal velocity does not affect the vertical motion. Mass does not affect free-fall time either.

questions.s: A ball is thrown horizontally at 30 m/s from the top of a tower 80 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s², its speed just before it hits the ground is
questions.e: Fall time t = √(2 × 80/10) = 4 s, so vertical velocity = 40 m/s and speed = √(30² + 40²) = 50 m/s. 70 m/s adds the components as numbers instead of as perpendicular vectors.

questions.s: A projectile is launched from level ground so that its horizontal range equals its maximum height. The angle of projection θ satisfies
questions.e: Setting u² sin²θ/2g = 2u² sin θ cos θ/g gives sin θ/2 = 2 cos θ, so tan θ = 4 (about 76°). tan θ = 1 (45°) gives the maximum range, where the range is four times the height.

questions.s: Ignoring air resistance, the speed of a projectile at its highest point is half its speed of projection. The angle of projection above the horizontal is
questions.e: At the top only the horizontal component remains, so u cos θ = u/2, cos θ = ½ and θ = 60°. 30° would give a speed at the top of (√3/2)u, not u/2.

questions.s: A ball is projected from level ground at 20√2 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum height it reaches is
questions.e: Vertical component = 20√2 × (1/√2) = 20 m/s, so H = 20²/(2 × 10) = 20 m. 80 m is the range (u²/g = 800/10), and 40 m forgets the factor 2 in 2g.

questions.s: Hamza can throw a ball to a maximum horizontal range of 90 m on level ground. Ignoring air resistance, the greatest height he can throw the same ball vertically upward with the same speed is
questions.e: Maximum range R = u²/g = 90 m. Thrown straight up, H = u²/2g = 90/2 = 45 m. 22.5 m is the height reached at 45°, u² sin²45°/2g, not in a vertical throw.

questions.s: A ball is projected at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, its speed 1 s after projection is
questions.e: Components: uₓ = 20 cos 30° = 10√3 m/s and u_y = 10 m/s. After 1 s, v_y = 10 − 10 × 1 = 0, so the ball is at its highest point and the speed is just 10√3 m/s. Zero forgets the horizontal component, which never changes.

questions.s: Ball A is dropped from rest from the top of a 45 m tower. At the same instant ball B is thrown vertically upward at 30 m/s from the ground directly below. Ignoring air resistance, the balls meet after
questions.e: Both balls have the same acceleration g, so relative to each other they move uniformly: B approaches A at 30 m/s across a 45 m gap, giving t = 45/30 = 1.5 s. (Check: A falls 5 × 2.25 = 11.25 m and B rises 45 − 11.25 = 33.75 m.) 3 s is the time B would take to reach its own highest point.

questions.s: A ball thrown horizontally from a height h lands a horizontal distance d from the foot of the building. If the throwing speed is doubled and the height is made 4h, the ball lands at a horizontal distance of
questions.e: Fall time t = √(2h/g), so making the height 4h doubles t. Range = ut, and both u and t double, giving 4d. 2d accounts only for the doubled speed and forgets the longer fall time.

questions.s: According to Newton's third law, an action force and its reaction force
questions.e: Action and reaction are equal and opposite but act on two different bodies, so they never cancel each other. Forces that cancel must act on the same body, as in a balanced pair.

questions.s: A car's speed increases uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s while it travels 100 m. Its acceleration is
questions.e: vf² = vi² + 2as gives 900 = 100 + 200a, so a = 800/200 = 4 m/s². 8 m/s² forgets the 2 in 2as, and 0.2 m/s² divides the change in speed by the distance.

questions.s: The position of a particle moving along a straight line is x = 6t − t², where x is in metres and t in seconds. The particle comes momentarily to rest at
questions.e: v = dx/dt = 6 − 2t, which is zero at t = 3 s. At t = 6 s the particle is back at x = 0, which is a return to the start, not the instant of rest.

questions.s: The position of a particle moving along a straight line is x = 6t − t², where x is in metres and t in seconds. The distance it covers in the first 4 s is
questions.e: It moves forward until t = 3 s, reaching x = 9 m, then turns back: x(4) = 24 − 16 = 8 m. Distance = 9 + (9 − 8) = 10 m. 8 m is the displacement, which ignores the reversal of direction.

questions.s: The unit kg m s⁻¹ is equivalent to
questions.e: N s = (kg m s⁻²) × s = kg m s⁻¹, which is why impulse and momentum share a unit. The newton itself is kg m s⁻², and N m is the joule.

questions.s: The momentum of a body increases from 20 kg m s⁻¹ to 50 kg m s⁻¹ in 3 s along a straight line. The average net force on the body is
questions.e: F = Δp/Δt = (50 − 20)/3 = 10 N. 30 N is the change in momentum, not the force, and 70/3 N adds the momenta instead of subtracting.
