questions.s: A 2 kg block is pulled up a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal by a force of 20 N acting parallel to the plane. Taking g = 10 m/s², its acceleration up the plane is
questions.e: The weight component down the slope is mg sin 30° = 2 × 10 × ½ = 10 N, so net force = 20 − 10 = 10 N and a = 10/2 = 5 m/s². 10 m/s² ignores the weight component, and 15 m/s² adds it.

questions.s: A lift carrying Bilal, of mass 70 kg, is moving upward but slowing down at 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the force exerted by the floor on Bilal is
questions.e: Slowing while moving up means the acceleration is 2 m/s² downward, so mg − R = ma and R = 70 × (10 − 2) = 560 N. 840 N uses m(g + a), which is wrong because the direction of acceleration, not of motion, decides the sign.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg ball strikes the floor vertically at 6 m/s and rebounds vertically at 4 m/s. The magnitude of the impulse given to the ball by the floor is
questions.e: Taking upward as positive, Δp = 0.5 × 4 − 0.5 × (−6) = 2 + 3 = 5 N s. 1 N s subtracts the speeds (6 − 4), which ignores the reversal of direction.

questions.s: A 5 kg gun fires a 50 g bullet. The ratio of the kinetic energy of the bullet to the kinetic energy of the recoiling gun is
questions.e: Bullet and gun receive equal and opposite momenta, and K = p²/2m, so the ratio K(bullet)/K(gun) = M/m = 5/0.05 = 100. 1/100 inverts the ratio; the lighter body carries most of the kinetic energy.

questions.s: The forward force exerted on a rocket by the gases it ejects backward is called
questions.e: Thrust is the reaction force of the expelled gases on the rocket, equal to the rate at which momentum is given to the gases. Drag is air resistance, which opposes the motion.

questions.s: A ball is projected at 45° above the horizontal with kinetic energy K. Ignoring air resistance, its kinetic energy at the highest point is
questions.e: At the top only the horizontal component u cos 45° = u/√2 remains, so the kinetic energy is ½m(u²/2) = K/2. K/√2 forgets that kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed.

questions.s: A velocity-time graph is a straight line that starts at the origin and slopes upward with a constant slope. It shows a body moving with
questions.e: Starting at the origin means the body starts from rest, and a constant positive slope means a constant acceleration. Uniform velocity would show as a horizontal line.

questions.s: For any motion, the distance covered by a body is
o: at least as large as displacement
questions.e: Distance is the length of the actual path, and the straight-line displacement is the shortest possible path between the two points, so distance ≥ |displacement|. They are equal only for motion in one direction along a straight line; on a round trip the displacement, not the distance, is zero.

questions.s: A car covers 150 km in 2.5 hours. Its average speed is
questions.e: Average speed = distance/time = 150/2.5 = 60 km/h. 375 km/h multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.s: A body moving at 12 m/s decelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² until it stops. The distance it covers while stopping is
questions.e: 0 = vi² − 2as gives s = 144/(2 × 3) = 24 m. 48 m forgets the factor 2 in 2as, and 4 m is the stopping time in seconds (12/3).

questions.s: A stone thrown vertically upward returns to the thrower's hand after 4 s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, the speed with which it was thrown is
questions.e: The upward journey takes half the total time, 2 s, and the speed falls to zero in that time, so u = gt = 10 × 2 = 20 m/s. 40 m/s wrongly uses the whole 4 s as the time to the top.

questions.s: In a vacuum near the Earth's surface, a feather and a stone dropped together fall with
questions.e: Without air resistance the only force is the weight mg, so a = mg/m = g for every body regardless of mass. The feather falls slowly in air only because of air resistance.

questions.s: The velocity-time graph of a body is a straight line rising from 5 m/s at t = 0 to 15 m/s at t = 5 s. The acceleration of the body is
questions.e: Acceleration = slope = (15 − 5)/5 = 2 m/s². 3 m/s² divides the final velocity by the time and ignores the initial 5 m/s, and 50 is the area under the graph (the distance in metres).

questions.s: A velocity-time graph shows a rickshaw speeding up uniformly from rest to 10 m/s in 2 s, moving at 10 m/s for the next 6 s and then slowing uniformly to rest in 2 s. The total distance covered is
questions.e: Area = ½ × 2 × 10 + 6 × 10 + ½ × 2 × 10 = 10 + 60 + 10 = 80 m. 100 m treats all 10 s as if the speed were 10 m/s, and 60 m counts only the constant-speed part.

questions.s: Taking g = 10 m/s², the weight of a body of mass 8 kg is
questions.e: W = mg = 8 × 10 = 80 N. 8 N confuses mass in kilograms with weight in newtons.

questions.s: A certain force gives a 3 kg body an acceleration of 4 m/s². The same force acting on a 6 kg body gives it an acceleration of
questions.e: F = 3 × 4 = 12 N, so on 6 kg, a = 12/6 = 2 m/s²; for a fixed force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. 8 m/s² wrongly makes acceleration increase with mass.

questions.s: Fatima, of mass 40 kg, stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating downward at 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the scale reads
questions.e: For downward acceleration, mg − R = ma, so R = m(g − a) = 40 × 8 = 320 N. 480 N uses m(g + a), which applies to upward acceleration.

questions.s: Masses of 5 kg and 3 kg hang vertically on either side of a light string passing over a smooth, light, fixed pulley and are released. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string is
questions.e: a = (5 − 3) × 10/8 = 2.5 m/s². For the rising 3 kg mass, T − 30 = 3 × 2.5, so T = 37.5 N. 40 N is simply the mean of the two weights, which is not how the tension is found.

questions.s: A force of 100 N acts on a ball for 0.05 s. The impulse given to the ball is
questions.e: Impulse = FΔt = 100 × 0.05 = 5 N s. 2000 N s divides the force by the time instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A goalkeeper stops a 0.4 kg football moving at 15 m/s in 0.2 s. The average force exerted on the ball is
questions.e: Δp = 0.4 × 15 = 6 kg m s⁻¹, so F = 6/0.2 = 30 N. 60 N would apply if the ball were sent back at 15 m/s, and 1.2 N multiplies the momentum by the time.

questions.s: The momentum of a body of fixed mass is increased by 20%. Its kinetic energy increases by
questions.e: K = p²/2m, so K becomes (1.2)² = 1.44 times its value, an increase of 44%. 40% simply doubles the 20% and ignores the cross term (1.2² = 1 + 0.4 + 0.04).

questions.s: A 2 kg toy cannon at rest fires a 0.1 kg ball horizontally at 30 m/s. The recoil speed of the cannon is
questions.e: Total momentum stays zero: 2V = 0.1 × 30 = 3, so V = 1.5 m/s. 3 m/s is the ball's momentum value in kg m s⁻¹, not the cannon's speed.

questions.s: Blocks of 1 kg and 3 kg on a smooth floor are pushed apart from rest by a compressed spring between them. Their total kinetic energy afterwards is 24 J. The kinetic energy of the 1 kg block is
questions.e: The blocks get equal and opposite momenta, and K = p²/2m, so K is inversely proportional to mass: K(1 kg) : K(3 kg) = 3 : 1. The 1 kg block gets ¾ × 24 = 18 J. 6 J gives the larger share to the heavier block, which is the wrong way round.

questions.s: In an inelastic collision between two bodies with no external force acting, which statement is correct?
o: Kinetic energy is kept, momentum is not
Both momentum and kinetic energy are kept
Momentum is kept, kinetic energy is not
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is kept
questions.e: Total momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system, but in an inelastic collision some kinetic energy turns into heat, sound and deformation. Conservation of both is the definition of an elastic collision.

questions.s: A 1 kg ball moving at 8 m/s collides with a 3 kg ball at rest, and the two stick together. Their common velocity is
questions.e: 1 × 8 = (1 + 3)v, so v = 8/4 = 2 m/s. 8/3 m/s divides the momentum by the 3 kg mass alone, forgetting the 1 kg ball moves with it, and 4 m/s assumes equal masses.

questions.s: A very heavy ball moving at speed u collides head-on and elastically with a very light ball at rest. Just after the collision, the light ball moves at about
questions.e: v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂), which tends to 2u when m₁ is much larger than m₂; the heavy ball carries on at almost u. Speed u for the target is the result for equal masses, not for a very heavy striker.

questions.s: Water strikes a wall at right angles and stops. If the mass of water striking per second is doubled while its speed stays the same, the force on the wall
questions.e: F = (mass per second) × change in velocity; doubling the mass rate at the same speed doubles the force. Four times would need the speed to double as well.

questions.s: A rocket engine ejects gas at 1500 m/s relative to the rocket and produces a thrust of 3 × 10⁴ N. The mass of gas ejected per second is
questions.e: Thrust = (Δm/Δt) × v, so Δm/Δt = 30 000/1500 = 20 kg/s. 0.05 kg/s inverts the division (1500/30 000).

questions.s: Ignoring air resistance, the acceleration of a projectile throughout its flight is
questions.e: The only force on the projectile is its weight, so its acceleration is g vertically downward at every point, including the top. Zero velocity in the vertical direction at the top does not mean zero acceleration.

questions.s: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its horizontal range is
questions.e: R = u² sin 2θ/g = 400 × sin 90°/10 = 40 m. 80 m uses 2u²/g (an extra factor 2), and 10 m is the maximum height u² sin²45°/2g, not the range.

questions.s: A ball is projected from level ground at 40 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², the horizontal distance it has covered when it reaches its highest point is
questions.e: Time to the top = u sin θ/g = 20/10 = 2 s, and horizontal velocity = 40 cos 30° = 20√3 m/s, so the distance = 20√3 × 2 = 40√3 m (half the range). 80√3 m is the full range, reached only when the ball lands.

questions.s: A body moving with uniform acceleration covers 20 m in the 2nd second and 40 m in the 4th second of its motion. Its initial velocity is
questions.e: Distance in the nth second is u + a(2n − 1)/2, so 20 = u + 1.5a and 40 = u + 3.5a. Subtracting gives 2a = 20, a = 10 m/s², and then u = 20 − 15 = 5 m/s. 10 m/s is the acceleration value, not the initial velocity.

questions.s: A constant force of 20 N pushes a trolley 5 m along the direction of the force. The work done by the force is
questions.e: Force and displacement are parallel, so W = Fd = 20 × 5 = 100 J. Dividing 20 by 5 gives 4, which is not a work formula at all, and 200 J doubles the product for no reason.

questions.s: Ayesha pulls a suitcase with a force of 50 N directed at 60° to the floor and moves it 4 m along the floor. The work done by her pull is
questions.e: Only the component along the displacement does work: W = Fd cos θ = 50 × 4 × cos 60° = 200 × ½ = 100 J. Using sin 60° gives 100√3 J, and ignoring the angle gives 200 J.

questions.s: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. The work done by the tension in the string during one revolution is
o: zero, as force is perpendicular to motion
positive, as the force points to the centre
negative, as the direction keeps changing
questions.e: The tension points towards the centre while the displacement at every instant is along the tangent, so θ = 90° and F·d cos 90° = 0 throughout. The speed and kinetic energy stay constant, which confirms that no work is done. Multiplying mv²/r by 2πr wrongly assumes force and displacement are parallel.

questions.s: One watt is equal to
questions.e: Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, so 1 W = 1 joule per second = 1 J s⁻¹. The N s and kg m s⁻¹ are units of impulse and momentum, and J s is the unit of Planck's constant, not of power.

questions.s: The kinetic energy of a 4 kg ball moving at 3 m/s is
questions.e: K = ½mv² = ½ × 4 × 3² = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J. The value 12 is the momentum mv in kg m/s, and 6 J comes from ½mv, which forgets to square the speed.

questions.s: If the momentum of a body increases by 50 %, its kinetic energy increases by
questions.e: K = p²/2m, so K is proportional to p². The new momentum is 1.5p, so the new K is 1.5² = 2.25 times the old value, an increase of 125 %. The figure 225 % is the new energy as a percentage of the old, not the increase.

questions.s: Bilal lifts a 2 kg book from a table top 0.8 m above the floor to a shelf 2.3 m above the floor. Taking g = 10 m/s², the gain in gravitational potential energy of the book is
questions.e: Only the change in height matters: Δh = 2.3 − 0.8 = 1.5 m, so ΔU = mgΔh = 2 × 10 × 1.5 = 30 J. Using the shelf height alone gives 46 J, and adding the two heights gives 62 J.

questions.s: A 10 kg crate is pulled 6 m across a level floor at constant velocity. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done against friction is
questions.e: Friction f = μmg = 0.3 × 10 × 10 = 30 N, and the work against it is f × d = 30 × 6 = 180 J. The value 600 J is mgd, which ignores μ, and 30 is the friction force in newtons, not the work.

questions.s: A 2 kg ball is thrown vertically upwards and rises 5 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done by gravity on the ball during the rise is
questions.e: Gravity (20 N) acts downwards while the ball moves 5 m upwards, so θ = 180° and W = 20 × 5 × cos 180° = −100 J. The value +100 J is the work done against gravity, which equals the gain in potential energy, not the work done by gravity.

questions.s: Usman holds a 20 kg bag at a fixed height and walks 10 m along a level corridor at constant speed. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done by his upward supporting force on the bag is
questions.e: The supporting force is vertical while the displacement is horizontal, so W = Fd cos 90° = 0. The value 2000 J multiplies the weight (200 N) by the horizontal distance, which treats perpendicular vectors as parallel.

questions.s: The force on a body increases uniformly from 0 to 40 N as the body moves from x = 0 to x = 0.5 m along the direction of the force. The work done by the force is
questions.e: For a variable force, work is the area under the force-displacement graph. Here it is a triangle: ½ × 0.5 × 40 = 10 J. Taking the full rectangle 40 × 0.5 = 20 J forgets that the force was smaller at the start.

questions.s: A spring of spring constant 200 N/m is stretched by 10 cm from its natural length. The work done in stretching it is
questions.e: W = ½kx² = ½ × 200 × (0.1)² = 100 × 0.01 = 1 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 2 J, and 20 is the final force kx in newtons rather than the work.

questions.s: A spring with k = 500 N/m is already stretched by 2 cm. The extra work needed to stretch it further, from 2 cm to 4 cm, is
questions.e: W = ½k(x₂² − x₁²) = ½ × 500 × (0.04² − 0.02²) = 250 × (0.0016 − 0.0004) = 250 × 0.0012 = 0.3 J. The value 0.1 J is ½k(0.02)², which treats the extra 2 cm as if it started from the natural length; the restoring force is already larger there, so more work is needed.

questions.s: A crane lifts a 500 kg load vertically through 12 m in 20 s at steady speed. Taking g = 10 m/s², the power developed by the crane is
questions.e: Work done = mgh = 500 × 10 × 12 = 60 000 J, and P = W/t = 60 000/20 = 3000 W = 3 kW. The figure 60 kW forgets to divide by the time, and 0.3 kW leaves out g.

questions.s: A car engine provides a forward driving force of 2000 N while the car moves at a steady 25 m/s. The power delivered by the engine is
questions.e: P = W/t = F × (d/t) = Fv = 2000 × 25 = 50 000 W = 50 kW. Dividing force by speed gives 80 W (0.08 kW), which has no physical meaning here; 5 kW and 500 kW are power-of-ten slips.

questions.s: A car whose engine has a maximum power of 60 kW reaches a top speed of 30 m/s on a level road. At top speed, the total resistive force on the car is
questions.e: At top speed the driving force equals the resistance, and P = Fv gives F = P/v = 60 000/30 = 2000 N. Using 60 instead of 60 000 W gives 2 N, and multiplying P by v gives 1.8 × 10⁶, which is not a force.

questions.s: A pump raises 300 kg of water every minute from a well 20 m deep and delivers it at the top with a speed of 10 m/s. The pump is 50 % efficient. Taking g = 10 m/s², the input power of the pump is
questions.e: Each minute the water gains PE = 300 × 10 × 20 = 60 000 J and KE = ½ × 300 × 10² = 15 000 J, a total of 75 000 J. Useful output power = 75 000/60 = 1250 W, so input = 1250/0.5 = 2500 W = 2.5 kW. Ignoring the kinetic energy gives 2 kW, and 1.25 kW forgets the efficiency.

questions.s: According to the work-energy principle, the work done by the net force on a body is equal to the change in its
questions.e: The work-energy principle states W(net) = ½mv₂² − ½mv₁² = ΔK. The work done against gravity alone equals the change in potential energy, but the net force (all forces together) changes the kinetic energy. Momentum changes by the impulse, not by the work.

questions.s: A 20 g bullet moving at 400 m/s enters a wooden block and stops after penetrating 10 cm. The average resistive force exerted by the wood is
questions.e: By the work-energy principle F × d = ½mv² = ½ × 0.02 × 400² = 1600 J, so F = 1600/0.1 = 16 000 N. The value 1600 is the kinetic energy in joules, not the force, and 32 000 N forgets the ½.

questions.s: A 2 kg block starts from rest on a smooth horizontal surface and is acted on by a constant horizontal net force of 8 N over a distance of 4 m. Its final speed is
questions.e: Work done = 8 × 4 = 32 J = ½ × 2 × v², so v² = 32 and v = 4√2 m/s. Forgetting the ½ gives mv² = 32 and v = 4 m/s, and 16 m/s is the value of v² after that slip, before taking the square root.

questions.s: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², its speed when it is 5 m above the ground is
questions.e: It has fallen 20 − 5 = 15 m, so ½mv² = mg × 15 and v = √(2 × 10 × 15) = √300 = 10√3 m/s. Using the height above the ground (5 m) instead of the distance fallen gives 10 m/s, and 20 m/s is the speed on reaching the ground.

questions.s: A simple pendulum bob is released from rest at a point 45 cm above its lowest position. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², its speed at the lowest point is
questions.e: Loss of PE = gain of KE: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 0.45) = √9 = 3 m/s. The value 9 is v² without the square root, and 2.1 m/s comes from √(gh), which drops the factor 2.

questions.s: A block is released from rest at the top of a smooth curved track 5 m high. At the bottom it moves onto a rough horizontal floor where the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. The distance it slides on the floor before stopping is
questions.e: All the PE becomes work against friction on the floor: mgh = μmg d, so d = h/μ = 5/0.25 = 20 m. The mass and g cancel. Multiplying instead of dividing gives μh = 1.25 m.

questions.s: The escape velocity from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R is
questions.e: For escape the KE must equal the magnitude of the PE at the surface: ½mv² = GMm/R, giving v = √(2GM/R). The expression √(GM/R) is the orbital speed of a satellite just above the surface, which is smaller by a factor √2.

questions.s: The escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s. A planet has 8 times the mass of the Earth and twice its radius. The escape velocity from this planet is
questions.e: v = √(2GM/R), so v is proportional to √(M/R). Here M/R becomes 8/2 = 4 times larger, so v becomes √4 = 2 times larger: 2 × 11.2 = 22.4 km/s. Forgetting the square root gives 4 × 11.2 = 44.8 km/s.

questions.s: The escape velocity from the surface of a planet depends on
o: the mass of the escaping body
the angle of launch and the body's mass
the mass and radius of the planet
questions.e: From ½mv² = GMm/R the mass m of the body cancels, leaving v = √(2GM/R), which contains only the planet's mass and radius. Energy is a scalar, so the direction of projection does not matter either (ignoring air resistance).

questions.s: The escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s. A planet has the same average density as the Earth but half its radius. The escape velocity from this planet is
questions.e: With M = ρ(4/3)πR³, v = √(2GM/R) = √(8πGρR²/3), so v is proportional to R√ρ. With the same density and half the radius, v = 11.2/2 = 5.6 km/s. The value 7.9 km/s assumes v ∝ √R, forgetting that the mass also shrinks with R³.

questions.s: A satellite orbiting just above the surface of a planet moves at 8 km/s. The escape velocity from the surface of that planet is
questions.e: Orbital speed near the surface is √(GM/R) and escape velocity is √(2GM/R), so v(escape) = √2 × 8 = 8√2 km/s (about 11.3 km/s). Dividing by √2 instead gives 4√2 km/s, which would be slower than the orbit itself.

questions.s: Taking g = 10 m/s² at the surface and the Earth's radius as 6.4 × 10⁶ m, the minimum work needed to take a 1 kg body from the Earth's surface to infinity is
questions.e: The PE at the surface is −GMm/R, so the work needed is GMm/R. Since GM = gR², this is mgR = 1 × 10 × 6.4 × 10⁶ = 6.4 × 10⁷ J. The value 1.28 × 10⁸ J is 2gR, which is v² for escape, not ½v².

questions.s: A stone falls freely from a cliff with no air resistance. Which of the following is correct while it falls?
o: Its loss of PE equals its gain of KE
questions.e: With gravity as the only force, mechanical energy is conserved: as the stone loses height, every joule of PE lost appears as a joule of KE. The KE grows because the speed increases, and the PE falls because the height decreases.

questions.s: An electric motor takes 2 kW of electrical power and lifts a 100 kg load through 6 m in 4 s at steady speed. Taking g = 10 m/s², the efficiency of the motor is
questions.e: Useful output power = mgh/t = 100 × 10 × 6/4 = 1500 W, so efficiency = 1500/2000 × 100 % = 75 %. Inverting the ratio gives 133 %, which is impossible since no machine gives out more than it takes in; 7.5 % leaves out g.

questions.s: A 1000 kg car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s on a level road. Ignoring friction, the average power delivered to the car is
questions.e: Gain in KE = ½ × 1000 × 20² = 200 000 J, and average power = 200 000/10 = 20 000 W = 20 kW. Forgetting the ½ gives 40 kW; 200 is the energy in kJ, not the power.

questions.s: A 1000 kg car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s on a level road. Ignoring friction, the instantaneous power delivered at the end of the 10 s is
questions.e: a = 20/10 = 2 m/s², so the force is F = ma = 2000 N, and at t = 10 s the power is P = Fv = 2000 × 20 = 40 kW. The value 20 kW is the average power over the 10 s; with constant force the power rises linearly with v, so the final value is twice the average.

questions.s: Sana, of mass 60 kg, runs up a staircase that rises 4 m vertically over a horizontal distance of 3 m, taking 8 s. Taking g = 10 m/s², her average power against gravity is
questions.e: Work against gravity depends only on the vertical rise: mgh = 60 × 10 × 4 = 2400 J, so P = 2400/8 = 300 W. Using the slant length of 5 m gives 375 W, and using the horizontal 3 m gives 225 W.

questions.s: The kinetic energy K of a body of mass m is related to its linear momentum p by
questions.e: K = ½mv² and p = mv, so v = p/m and K = ½m(p/m)² = p²/2m. Writing p²m/2 puts the mass in the numerator, which gives the wrong units (kg³ m² s⁻²).

questions.s: Two bodies of masses 1 kg and 4 kg have equal kinetic energies. The ratio of their momenta (lighter : heavier) is
questions.e: p = √(2mK), so with equal K, p is proportional to √m: p₁/p₂ = √(1/4) = 1/2. The ratio 1 : 4 forgets the square root; the heavier body carries more momentum for the same energy.

questions.s: Two bodies of masses 2 kg and 8 kg have equal momenta. The ratio of their kinetic energies (lighter : heavier) is
questions.e: K = p²/2m, so with equal p, K is inversely proportional to m: K₁/K₂ = 8/2 = 4. The ratio 1 : 4 assumes the heavier body has more energy, which is true for equal speeds, not equal momenta.

questions.s: A car slows from 20 m/s to 10 m/s. The fraction of its kinetic energy that is lost is
questions.e: K is proportional to v², so the new energy is (10/20)² = ¼ of the original, and ¾ = 75 % is lost. Halving the speed does not halve the energy; 50 % treats K as proportional to v.

questions.s: With a certain constant braking force a car moving at 36 km/h stops in 10 m. With the same braking force, the stopping distance when it moves at 72 km/h is
questions.e: Work done by the brakes equals the KE: F d = ½mv², so d is proportional to v². Doubling the speed (10 m/s to 20 m/s) makes the distance 2² = 4 times larger: 40 m. The answer 20 m assumes d is proportional to v.

questions.s: A 5 kg block starts from rest and slides 4 m down a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The friction force on it is 10 N. Taking g = 10 m/s², its kinetic energy at the bottom is
questions.e: The vertical drop is 4 sin 30° = 2 m, so the PE lost is 5 × 10 × 2 = 100 J. Work against friction is 10 × 4 = 40 J, so KE = 100 − 40 = 60 J. Ignoring friction gives 100 J, and adding the friction work gives 140 J.

questions.s: A 2 kg block is projected up a rough inclined plane with 50 J of kinetic energy. It comes to rest after rising 2 m vertically. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done against friction during the ascent is
questions.e: The initial KE goes partly into PE and partly into work against friction: 50 = mgh + W(f) = 2 × 10 × 2 + W(f) = 40 + W(f), so W(f) = 10 J. The value 40 J is the gain in PE, not the friction loss.

questions.s: A small ball rolls without friction from rest down a track that leads into a vertical circular loop of radius r. The minimum starting height above the bottom of the loop for the ball to just complete the loop is
questions.e: At the top of the loop the weight alone must supply the centripetal force, so v² = gr there. Energy conservation gives mgh = mg(2r) + ½m(gr), so h = 2r + r/2 = 5r/2. The answer 2r ignores the speed the ball still needs at the top.

questions.s: A pendulum bob hangs on a light string 1.6 m long. It is pulled aside until the string makes 60° with the vertical and released. Taking g = 10 m/s², its speed at the lowest point is
questions.e: The bob rises h = L(1 − cos 60°) = 1.6 × ½ = 0.8 m, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 0.8) = √16 = 4 m/s. Taking h = L = 1.6 m gives 4√2 m/s, which would be the speed for a release from the horizontal position.

questions.s: A spring of spring constant 800 N/m is compressed by 5 cm and used to launch a 0.1 kg ball along a smooth horizontal surface. The speed of the ball as it leaves the spring is
questions.e: Elastic PE = ½kx² = ½ × 800 × 0.05² = 1 J, and this becomes ½mv², so v² = 2 × 1/0.1 = 20 and v = 2√5 m/s (about 4.5 m/s). The value 20 is v², before taking the square root.

questions.s: The expression U = mgh for gravitational potential energy is valid only when
o: h is small compared with the Earth's radius
h is greater than the Earth's radius
questions.e: U = mgh assumes g is constant, which is true only near the surface, where h is much less than R. For large heights g falls off with distance and the general form U = −GMm/r must be used. Motion or rest of the body does not affect PE.

questions.s: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
questions.e: Wind is driven by the Sun's uneven heating of the atmosphere and is continuously replenished. Coal and natural gas are fossil fuels formed over millions of years, and uranium is a mined nuclear fuel; all three are used up when consumed.

questions.s: Geothermal energy is obtained from
o: heat in the hot interior of the Earth
the rise and fall of ocean tides
questions.e: Geothermal energy uses heat stored in hot rocks below the Earth's surface, for example by producing steam to drive turbines. Tides give tidal energy, burning waste gives biomass energy, and solar cells give solar electricity.

questions.s: A solar cell converts
o: light energy directly into electrical energy
questions.e: A solar (photovoltaic) cell absorbs light and produces an electric current directly, without heating water or moving parts. Electrical to light is what a bulb does, and chemical to electrical is what a battery does.

questions.s: A body is dropped from rest from a height H. Ignoring air resistance and taking the ground as zero PE, at what height above the ground is its kinetic energy twice its potential energy?
questions.e: At height h, PE = mgh and KE = mg(H − h). Setting H − h = 2h gives h = H/3. The value 2H/3 is where the PE is twice the KE, the reverse of what is asked.

questions.s: The force on a body is 10 N (in the direction of motion) from x = 0 to x = 2 m, and then decreases uniformly to zero at x = 5 m. The total work done by the force from x = 0 to x = 5 m is
questions.e: Work is the area under the force-displacement graph: a rectangle 10 × 2 = 20 J plus a triangle ½ × 3 × 10 = 15 J, total 35 J. Treating the force as 10 N all the way gives 50 J, and 20 J counts only the first part.

questions.s: A uniform chain of mass m and length L lies on a smooth table with one third of its length hanging vertically over the edge. The work needed to pull the hanging part slowly back onto the table is
questions.e: The hanging part has mass m/3 and its centre of mass is L/6 below the table top, so the work is (m/3) × g × (L/6) = mgL/18. Taking the centre of mass at the bottom end (L/3 below) gives mgL/9, which overstates the lift.

questions.s: A 1200 kg car climbs a straight road that rises 1 m for every 20 m travelled along it, at a steady 15 m/s. The resistive forces total 600 N. Taking g = 10 m/s², the power of the engine is
questions.e: Along the slope the engine must balance mg sin θ = 1200 × 10 × (1/20) = 600 N plus the 600 N resistance, a total of 1200 N. Then P = Fv = 1200 × 15 = 18 000 W = 18 kW. Ignoring the slope gives 600 × 15 = 9 kW.

questions.s: A force F = (3i + 4j) N acts on a particle that undergoes a displacement d = (2i − j) m. The work done by the force is
questions.e: W = F·d = (3)(2) + (4)(−1) = 6 − 4 = 2 J. Missing the minus sign gives 6 + 4 = 10 J, and 5 is only the magnitude of the force in newtons.

questions.s: Work done by a constant force is defined as the
o: scalar product of force and displacement
vector product of force and displacement
product of force and the time it acts
questions.e: W = F·d = Fd cos θ, a scalar (dot) product, so work has magnitude but no direction. The product of force and time is impulse, and the vector (cross) product of force and a position vector gives torque.

questions.s: One kilowatt-hour (kWh) of energy is equal to
questions.e: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Using 60 instead of 3600 seconds (treating an hour as a minute) gives 6 × 10⁴ J.

questions.s: A 1.5 kW electric heater is used for 4 hours a day for 30 days. The electrical energy it uses is
questions.e: Energy = power × time = 1.5 kW × (4 × 30) h = 1.5 × 120 = 180 kWh. The value 6 kWh is the use for one day only, and 180 000 kWh wrongly converts kW to W while keeping the kWh unit.

questions.s: Taking 1 horsepower = 746 W, a motor rated at 2 hp has a power of about
questions.e: 2 hp = 2 × 746 = 1492 W, about 1.5 kW. Dividing by 2 instead of multiplying gives 373 W, and 2000 W treats 1 hp as 1 kW.

questions.s: A 5 kW pump that is 80 % efficient fills an overhead tank with 1000 kg of water raised through 20 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the time taken is
questions.e: Useful work = mgh = 1000 × 10 × 20 = 200 000 J and useful power = 0.8 × 5000 = 4000 W, so t = 200 000/4000 = 50 s. Ignoring efficiency gives 40 s, and 32 s multiplies that by 0.8 instead of dividing.

questions.s: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², the height at which its speed has fallen to half the initial value is
questions.e: Energy per kilogram: ½u² − ½v² = gh, so ½(400 − 100) = 10h and h = 15 m. Halving the speed leaves only a quarter of the KE, so three quarters has become PE; 10 m wrongly assumes half the KE has been used up.

questions.s: A ball is thrown vertically upwards from the ground at 20 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking the ground as zero PE, its speed at the point where its kinetic and potential energies are equal is
questions.e: Total energy is ½mu². Where KE = PE, KE is half of this, so ½mv² = ½ × ½mu², v = u/√2 = 20/√2 = 10√2 m/s. Taking half the speed (10 m/s) gives only a quarter of the KE, not half.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m and reaches the ground at 18 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the energy lost to air resistance is
questions.e: PE lost = 0.5 × 10 × 20 = 100 J and KE gained = ½ × 0.5 × 18² = 81 J, so 100 − 81 = 19 J went into work against air resistance. The value 81 J is the KE at the ground, not the loss.

questions.s: A raindrop falls through the air at its constant terminal speed. Which of the following is correct?
o: Its KE increases as its PE decreases
Its total mechanical energy is conserved
Its PE stays constant while its KE decreases
Its loss of PE goes into heating the air and the drop
questions.e: At terminal speed the KE is constant, yet the drop keeps losing height and PE. That lost PE is used up as work against air resistance and appears as internal energy (heat) of the air and the drop, so mechanical energy is not conserved.

questions.s: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang at the two ends of a light string passing over a smooth, light pulley. The system is released from rest. Taking g = 10 m/s², the speed of each mass when the 3 kg mass has descended 1 m is
questions.e: Net PE lost = (3 − 2) × 10 × 1 = 10 J, shared as KE by both masses moving at the same speed: ½(3 + 2)v² = 10, so v² = 4 and v = 2 m/s. The value 2√5 m/s is √(2gh), which treats the 3 kg mass as falling freely.

questions.s: A 1 kg block is dropped from rest from a height of 40 cm above the top of a light vertical spring of spring constant 1000 N/m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum compression of the spring is
questions.e: At maximum compression x the block is momentarily at rest, so mg(h + x) = ½kx²: 10(0.4 + x) = 500x². Trying x = 0.1 m: 10 × 0.5 = 5 J and 500 × 0.01 = 5 J, so x = 10 cm. About 9 cm comes from ignoring the extra drop x in the PE term, and 1 cm is the equilibrium compression mg/k.

questions.s: The area under a power-time graph represents
questions.e: P = dW/dt, so the area under the P-t graph is the sum of P × Δt, which is the work done (energy transferred). Momentum change is the area under a force-time graph instead.

questions.s: For a body moving in a straight line, the slope of a graph of its kinetic energy against displacement gives
o: the power delivered to the body
the net force on the body
questions.e: By the work-energy principle ΔK = F(net) × Δx, so ΔK/Δx = F(net), the slope of the K-x graph. The slope of K against time, not displacement, would give the power.

questions.s: Stretching a spring by x from its natural length needs work W. The extra work needed to stretch it further, from x to 2x, is
questions.e: Work = ½kx², so stretching to 2x from the natural length needs ½k(2x)² = 4W. The extra work from x to 2x is 4W − W = 3W. The answer 4W is the total from zero, not the extra.

questions.s: A small planet has surface gravity 1.6 m/s² and radius 1.8 × 10⁶ m. The escape velocity from its surface is
questions.e: With GM = gR², v = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) = √(2 × 1.6 × 1.8 × 10⁶) = √(5.76 × 10⁶) = 2400 m/s = 2.4 km/s. Leaving out the 2 gives √(gR), about 1.7 km/s, which is the orbital speed near the surface.

questions.s: Ignoring air resistance, a body projected from the Earth's surface with a speed slightly greater than 11.2 km/s will
o: escape from the Earth's gravitational field
orbit the Earth just above its surface
rise very high and then fall back
stop at a finite height and stay there
questions.e: 11.2 km/s is the Earth's escape velocity: with this KE the body can overcome the whole gravitational PE GMm/R and never return. A speed of about 7.9 km/s gives a low orbit, and speeds below 11.2 km/s (and not in orbit) make it fall back.

questions.s: A body is projected from the surface of a planet with a speed twice the escape velocity vₑ. Ignoring air resistance, its speed when it is very far from the planet is
questions.e: Energy conservation: ½mv² − GMm/R = ½mv∞², and GMm/R = ½mvₑ². So v∞² = (2vₑ)² − vₑ² = 3vₑ² and v∞ = √3 vₑ. Subtracting speeds directly (2vₑ − vₑ = vₑ) is wrong because energy depends on v².

questions.s: A body is projected vertically upwards from the surface of a planet of radius R with a speed equal to half the escape velocity. Ignoring air resistance, the maximum height it reaches above the surface is
questions.e: With vₑ² = 2GM/R, the initial KE is ½m(vₑ/2)² = GMm/4R. Energy conservation: GMm/4R − GMm/R = −GMm/(R + h), so 3/(4R) = 1/(R + h), R + h = 4R/3 and h = R/3. Using h = v²/2g with constant g gives R/4, which ignores the weakening of gravity with height.

questions.s: Hamza uses a pulley system to raise an 80 kg load through 1 m. He applies an effort of 250 N and pulls his end of the rope through 4 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the efficiency of the system is
questions.e: Useful output = mgh = 80 × 10 × 1 = 800 J and input = 250 × 4 = 1000 J, so efficiency = 800/1000 = 80 %. Inverting gives 125 %, which is impossible for a real machine.

questions.s: The efficiency of a real machine is always less than 100 % because
o: some input energy becomes heat and other unwanted forms
energy is destroyed inside the machine
its output work is greater than its input work
a machine cannot change the direction of a force
questions.e: Energy is never destroyed, but friction and other losses turn part of the input into heat, sound and other forms that are not useful output. So useful output is always less than input, and efficiency = output/input × 100 % is below 100 %.

questions.s: A thermal power station burns fuel at a rate that releases 500 MJ of energy every second and delivers 150 MW of electrical power. The energy wasted as heat every second is
questions.e: Input power is 500 MW and useful output is 150 MW (efficiency 30 %), so the waste is 500 − 150 = 350 MW, that is 350 MJ each second. Adding the two gives 650 MJ, which counts the output as a loss.

questions.s: At a small hydroelectric plant, 200 kg of water falls through 50 m every second onto a turbine. The plant converts 80 % of this energy into electrical energy. Taking g = 10 m/s², its electrical power output is
questions.e: Power available = (m/t)gh = 200 × 10 × 50 = 100 000 W = 100 kW, and output = 0.8 × 100 = 80 kW. The value 100 kW ignores the efficiency, and 125 kW divides by 0.8 instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A 2000 kg truck moves on a level road with its engine working at a constant 40 kW. The resistive forces total 1000 N. Its acceleration at the instant its speed is 10 m/s is
questions.e: Driving force F = P/v = 40 000/10 = 4000 N, net force = 4000 − 1000 = 3000 N, so a = 3000/2000 = 1.5 m/s². Forgetting the resistance gives 2 m/s².

questions.s: The work done by gravity on a body that moves along any closed path and returns to its starting point is
questions.e: Gravity is a conservative force: the work it does depends only on the start and end heights, W = mg(h₁ − h₂). For a closed path h₁ = h₂, so W = 0. Multiplying mg by the path length would be correct only for friction-like forces, which are non-conservative.

questions.s: From the top of a tower, Zainab throws one ball vertically upwards and another vertically downwards, both with the same speed. Ignoring air resistance, their speeds on reaching the ground are
o: greater for the one thrown upwards
greater for the one thrown downwards
questions.e: Both start with the same KE and the same height, so by energy conservation ½mv² = ½mu² + mgh gives the same v for both. The upward ball takes longer, but when it comes back down past the tower top it again has speed u downwards.

questions.s: A 2 kg block moving at 4 m/s slides 1 m across a rough floor (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3) and then onto a smooth section where it hits a light spring of spring constant 500 N/m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum compression of the spring is
questions.e: Initial KE = ½ × 2 × 4² = 16 J; work against friction = 0.3 × 2 × 10 × 1 = 6 J, leaving 10 J. Then ½ × 500 × x² = 10 gives x² = 0.04 and x = 0.2 m = 20 cm. Ignoring friction gives x² = 32/500, about 25 cm.

questions.s: The velocity of a 2 kg body changes from (3i + 4j) m/s to (6i + 8j) m/s. The work done by the net force on the body is
questions.e: Speeds are √(9 + 16) = 5 m/s and √(36 + 64) = 10 m/s, so W = ΔK = ½ × 2 × (10² − 5²) = 100 − 25 = 75 J. The value 25 J uses ½m(Δv)² with |Δv| = 5 m/s, which is not the change in kinetic energy, and 100 J is the final KE alone.

questions.s: A book slides across a rough table and comes to rest. The work done by friction on the book is
questions.e: Friction acts opposite to the displacement, so θ = 180° and W = fd cos 180° = −fd. This negative work removes the book's kinetic energy, which is why it stops. It is not zero, because the force is along the line of motion.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg cricket ball is moving at 30 m/s. Its kinetic energy is
questions.e: K = ½mv² = ½ × 0.2 × 30² = 0.1 × 900 = 90 J. The value 6 is the momentum mv in kg m/s, and 3 J comes from ½mv without squaring the speed.

questions.s: A boy does 1200 J of work in 1 minute. His average power is
questions.e: P = W/t = 1200/60 = 20 W, with the time in seconds. Leaving the time as 1 gives 1200 W, and multiplying by 60 gives 72 000 W, which is not a power at all.

questions.s: A water tank holding 2000 kg of water is placed on a roof 15 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s², the gravitational PE of the water relative to the ground is
questions.e: U = mgh = 2000 × 10 × 15 = 300 000 J = 3 × 10⁵ J. Leaving out g gives 3 × 10⁴ J, one power of ten too small.

questions.s: If the speed of a moving car is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes
questions.e: K = ½mv² is proportional to v², so doubling v multiplies K by 2² = 4. Twice as large would be true only if K were proportional to v, as momentum is.

questions.s: A 10 kg box is lifted vertically through 2 m with a constant upward acceleration of 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done by the lifting force is
questions.e: Lifting force F = m(g + a) = 10 × 12 = 120 N, so W = 120 × 2 = 240 J. Of this, 200 J becomes PE and 40 J becomes KE. The value 200 J would apply only for lifting at constant speed.

questions.s: A swing passes through its lowest point at 2 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², the greatest height it rises above the lowest point is
questions.e: ½mv² = mgh gives h = v²/2g = 4/20 = 0.2 m = 20 cm. Forgetting the 2 in the denominator gives 40 cm.

questions.s: Crane A lifts a load to a certain height in 10 s; crane B lifts an identical load to the same height in 20 s. Which statement is correct?
o: A does twice as much work as B
B develops twice the power of A
Both do equal work, but A has twice the power
questions.e: Work = mgh is the same for both, since the load and height are the same. Power = W/t, so A, taking half the time, has twice the power. Taking longer does not mean doing more work.

questions.s: A force of 20 N stretches a spring by 4 cm. The elastic potential energy stored in the spring is
questions.e: k = F/x = 20/0.04 = 500 N/m, so U = ½kx² = ½ × 500 × 0.04² = 0.4 J (equivalently ½Fx = ½ × 20 × 0.04). The value 0.8 J is Fx, which treats the force as 20 N from the very start, and 40 J keeps x in centimetres.

questions.s: The Moon has practically no atmosphere mainly because
o: its low escape velocity lets gas molecules escape
it has no gravitational field at all
it is too cold for any gas to exist
its surface reflects most of the sunlight
questions.e: The Moon's escape velocity is only about 2.4 km/s, and fast-moving gas molecules heated by the Sun can reach such speeds and leave. The Moon does have gravity (about one sixth of the Earth's), just not enough to hold an atmosphere.

questions.s: A 60 W filament lamp gives out light energy at a rate of 6 W. The energy wasted as heat in one minute is
questions.e: Wasted power = 60 − 6 = 54 W, and in 60 s the waste is 54 × 60 = 3240 J (the efficiency is only 10 %). The value 3600 J is the total input in a minute, and 54 J is the waste in one second.

questions.s: A 1500 kg car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest by its brakes. The work done by the braking force is
questions.e: By the work-energy principle, W = 0 − ½mv² = −½ × 1500 × 400 = −3 × 10⁵ J. It is negative because the braking force opposes the motion; forgetting the ½ gives −6 × 10⁵ J.

questions.s: A 2 kg block slides from rest down a rough plane 10 m long, inclined at 30° to the horizontal, and reaches the bottom at 8 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the average friction force on the block is
questions.e: Height = 10 sin 30° = 5 m, so PE lost = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J and KE gained = ½ × 2 × 64 = 64 J. Work against friction = 36 J over 10 m, so f = 3.6 N. The value 36 is the friction work in joules, and 6.4 N divides the KE by the length.

questions.s: A pump draws water from a tank and ejects it through a nozzle 5 m higher at 10 m/s, at a rate of 2 kg every second. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring losses, the power of the pump is
questions.e: Each second the water gains PE = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J and KE = ½ × 2 × 10² = 100 J, so P = 200 W. Using mv² instead of ½mv² for the KE gives 300 W, and 100 W counts only one of the two energies.

questions.s: The escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s. A planet has twice the Earth's surface gravity and half its radius. The escape velocity from this planet is
questions.e: v = √(2gR), so v is proportional to √(gR). Here gR becomes 2 × ½ = 1 times the Earth's value, so the escape velocity is unchanged at 11.2 km/s. Taking only the change in g gives √2 × 11.2 ≈ 15.8 km/s.

questions.s: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length equals the radius of the circle is
questions.e: By definition θ = s/r, so an arc equal to the radius gives θ = r/r = 1 radian (about 57.3°). One degree is a much smaller angle, 1/360 of a full turn, so 1° is wrong.

questions.s: A bicycle wheel makes 3 complete revolutions. Its angular displacement is
questions.e: One revolution is 2π rad, so 3 revolutions give 3 × 2π = 6π rad. Taking one revolution as π rad gives 3π rad, which is only half the correct value.

questions.s: A wheel of radius 0.5 m turns through an angle of 4 rad. The distance moved by a point on its rim is
questions.e: Arc length s = rθ = 0.5 × 4 = 2 m. Dividing instead of multiplying (θ/r = 8) gives 8 m, which has the wrong form for the relation s = rθ.

questions.s: A ceiling fan in Lahore turns at a steady 120 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity is
questions.e: 120 rev/min = 2 rev/s, and ω = 2πf = 2π × 2 = 4π rad/s. Writing 2π rad/s uses 1 rev/s, and 240π rad/s forgets to convert minutes to seconds.

questions.s: The angular velocity of the minute hand of a clock is
questions.e: The minute hand turns 2π rad in 3600 s, so ω = 2π/3600 = π/1800 rad/s. π/30 rad/s belongs to the seconds hand (2π in 60 s), and π/21600 rad/s to the hour hand (2π in 12 h).

questions.s: A wheel accelerates uniformly from rest to an angular velocity of 20 rad/s in 4 s. The angle it turns through in this time is
questions.e: With uniform acceleration θ = ½(ωi + ωf)t = ½(0 + 20)(4) = 40 rad. Using the final angular velocity for the whole time gives 80 rad, double the true value.

questions.s: A wheel of radius 0.4 m has an angular acceleration of 5 rad/s². The tangential acceleration of a point on its rim is
questions.e: Tangential acceleration aT = rα = 0.4 × 5 = 2 m/s². The value 12.5 m/s² comes from α/r, dividing instead of multiplying.

questions.s: The direction of the angular velocity vector of a rotating body is
o: Along the tangent to the path
questions.e: Angular velocity is an axial vector: it lies along the axis of rotation, with its sense given by the right-hand rule (curl the fingers along the rotation, the thumb points along ω). The tangent is the direction of the linear velocity of a particle, not of ω.

questions.s: A flywheel rotating at 600 rev/min is brought to rest with uniform deceleration in 10 s. The magnitude of its angular deceleration is
questions.e: ωi = 600/60 rev/s = 10 rev/s = 20π rad/s, so α = (0 − 20π)/10 = −2π rad/s², magnitude 2π rad/s². Answering 20π rad/s² gives the initial angular velocity, not the deceleration.

questions.s: A wheel starts from rest with a constant angular acceleration of π rad/s². The number of revolutions it makes during the 10th second is
questions.e: θ(t) = ½αt², so θ(10) − θ(9) = ½π(100 − 81) = 9.5π rad. Dividing by 2π gives 4.75 revolutions. The value 25 is the total number of revolutions in the first 10 s, and 9.5 forgets to divide by 2π.

questions.s: The Earth spins once about its axis in 24 hours. Its angular speed of rotation is about
questions.e: ω = 2π/T = 6.28/86400 s ≈ 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s. 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s forgets the factor 2π, and 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ rad/s is the angular speed of the Earth's yearly orbit round the Sun.

questions.s: The dimensions of angular velocity are
questions.e: ω = θ/t and the radian is dimensionless, so [ω] = [T⁻¹]. [LT⁻¹] is the dimension of linear velocity and [T⁻²] that of angular acceleration.

questions.s: A car of mass 1000 kg moves at 20 m/s round a curve of radius 100 m. The centripetal force on it is
questions.e: F = mv²/r = 1000 × 400/100 = 4000 N. The value 200 N comes from mv/r, which forgets to square the speed.

questions.s: A body moves with uniform speed v in a circle of radius r. The work done by the centripetal force in one complete revolution is
questions.e: The centripetal force always acts towards the centre, perpendicular to the velocity, so W = Fd cos 90° = 0 at every instant. The kinetic energy stays constant, which confirms that no work is done; ½mv² is the kinetic energy itself, not work.

questions.s: A body moving in a circle has its speed doubled while the radius of the circle is halved. The centripetal force required becomes
questions.e: F = mv²/r; doubling v multiplies v² by 4 and halving r multiplies 1/r by 2, so F becomes 4 × 2 = 8 times. Answering 4 times accounts for the speed but ignores the change in radius.

questions.s: Ignoring gravity, a stone of mass 0.2 kg is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string 0.5 m long at 2 revolutions per second. The tension in the string is
questions.e: ω = 2πf = 4π rad/s, so T = mω²r = 0.2 × 16π² × 0.5 = 1.6π² N. 0.4 N treats 2 rev/s as 2 rad/s, and 3.2π² N uses 1 m (the diameter) instead of the radius.

questions.s: A road curve of radius 40 m is banked so that a car at 20 m/s needs no friction. Taking g = 10 m/s², the banking angle is
questions.e: For a frictionless banked curve tan θ = v²/(rg) = 400/(40 × 10) = 1, so θ = 45°. A 90° bank would be a vertical wall, which no car speed requires.

questions.s: A particle moves in a circle of radius 2 m with a constant angular speed of 3 rad/s. Its centripetal acceleration is
questions.e: ac = ω²r = 9 × 2 = 18 m/s². 6 m/s² is ωr, which is the linear speed in m/s, not an acceleration.

questions.s: A small ball on a string moves in a vertical circle of radius 2.5 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the minimum speed it must have at the top of the circle to keep the string just taut is
questions.e: At the top with zero tension, gravity alone supplies the centripetal force: mg = mv²/r, so v = √(gr) = √25 = 5 m/s. 25 m/s is gr itself, the value of v² without the square root.

questions.s: Bilal swings a bucket of water in a vertical circle of radius 0.4 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the least frequency of rotation for the water not to fall out at the top is
questions.e: At the top mg ≤ mω²r, so ω ≥ √(g/r) = √25 = 5 rad/s. Then f = ω/2π = 5/(2π) rev/s, a little under 1 rev/s. Writing 5 rev/s confuses the angular speed in rad/s with the frequency.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg mass tied to a string 1 m long moves in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is 4 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string at that point is
questions.e: At the lowest point T − mg = mv²/r, so T = 5 + 0.5 × 16/1 = 5 + 8 = 13 N. The value 3 N subtracts the weight instead of adding it, which is the condition at the top of the circle.

questions.s: When a car takes a sharp turn, a passenger feels pushed towards the outside of the turn. This is because
o: A real outward force acts on him
His inertia keeps him moving straight
Gravity acts sideways on the car
Friction from the seat pushes him out
questions.e: By Newton's first law the passenger tends to continue in a straight line, while the car turns beneath him, so he seems to move outward relative to the car. No real outward force acts in the ground frame; the only real horizontal force (friction from the seat) points inward and provides his centripetal force.

questions.s: A disc rotates at 10 rad/s about its axis. The linear speed of a point 20 cm from the axis is
questions.e: v = rω = 0.20 m × 10 rad/s = 2 m/s. Using r = 20 without converting centimetres to metres gives 200 m/s.

questions.s: A car takes an unbanked circular turn of radius 80 m. The coefficient of friction between tyres and road is 0.5. Taking g = 10 m/s², the greatest speed at which it can take the turn without skidding is
questions.e: Friction provides the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r, so v = √(μgr) = √(0.5 × 10 × 80) = √400 = 20 m/s. 400 m/s is v² mistaken for v.

questions.s: A particle starts from rest and moves in a circle of radius 2 m with a constant angular acceleration of 2 rad/s². The magnitude of its total acceleration after 1 s is
questions.e: After 1 s, ω = αt = 2 rad/s, so ac = ω²r = 8 m/s² and aT = αr = 4 m/s². These are perpendicular, so a = √(64 + 16) = √80 = 4√5 m/s². Adding them directly gives 12 m/s², which ignores that they are at right angles.

questions.s: The moment of inertia of a rigid body about a given axis depends on
questions.e: I = Σmr², so it depends on how much mass there is and how far each part lies from the axis. Two bodies of equal mass can have very different I, so the total mass alone is not enough; I does not depend on ω or on the torque.

questions.s: The SI unit of moment of inertia is
questions.e: I = Σmr² has units kg × m² = kg m². kg m² s⁻¹ is the unit of angular momentum (Iω), and N m is the unit of torque.

questions.s: Two point masses of 2 kg each are fixed at the ends of a light rod 1 m long. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis through the centre of the rod and perpendicular to it is
questions.e: Each mass is 0.5 m from the axis, so I = 2 × (2 × 0.5²) = 2 × 0.5 = 1 kg m². Taking r = 1 m for each mass gives 4 kg m², which uses the rod length instead of the distance from the axis.

questions.s: A uniform disc and a thin ring have the same mass and the same radius. The ratio of the moment of inertia of the disc to that of the ring, each about its central axis perpendicular to its plane, is
questions.e: Idisc = ½MR² and Iring = MR², so Idisc : Iring = ½ : 1 = 1 : 2. The ring has all its mass at distance R, while much of the disc's mass lies nearer the axis; 2:1 inverts the ratio.

questions.s: A solid sphere of mass 5 kg and radius 0.2 m rotates about a diameter. Its moment of inertia (I = 2MR²/5) is
questions.e: I = 2MR²/5 = (2/5)(5)(0.04) = 0.08 kg m². 0.4 kg m² comes from forgetting to square the radius, and 0.2 kg m² is simply MR².

questions.s: A thin uniform rod of mass 3 kg and length 2 m rotates about an axis through its centre perpendicular to its length (I = ML²/12). Its moment of inertia is
questions.e: I = ML²/12 = 3 × 4/12 = 1 kg m². 4 kg m² is ML²/3, the value about one end, and 12 kg m² is ML² with no factor.

questions.s: A body of mass 4 kg has a moment of inertia of 1 kg m² about an axis. Its radius of gyration about that axis is
questions.e: I = Mk², so k = √(I/M) = √(1/4) = 0.5 m. 0.25 m is I/M, which forgets the square root.

questions.s: A solid disc is released from rest and rolls without slipping down a slope of vertical height 0.3 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², its speed at the bottom is
questions.e: mgh = ½mv² + ½(½mr²)(v/r)² = ¾mv², so v = √(4gh/3) = √(4 × 10 × 0.3/3) = √4 = 2 m/s. √6 m/s is √(2gh), which ignores the rotational KE, and √3 m/s is the result for a ring.

questions.s: The SI unit of angular momentum is
questions.e: L = Iω has units kg m² s⁻¹, which equals (kg m² s⁻²)(s) = J s. J s⁻¹ is the watt, and kg m s⁻¹ is the unit of linear momentum.

questions.s: The angular momentum of a system remains constant when
questions.e: τ = ΔL/Δt, so L is conserved when the net external torque is zero. Zero net force conserves linear momentum, not angular momentum, so that option is the common confusion.

questions.s: An ice skater spins at 1.5 rev/s with her arms stretched out, her moment of inertia being 6 kg m². She pulls her arms in, reducing it to 2 kg m². Her new rate of spin is
questions.e: No external torque acts, so I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ gives ω₂ = 6 × 1.5/2 = 4.5 rev/s. 0.5 rev/s inverts the ratio, as if a smaller I meant slower rotation.

questions.s: A particle of mass 0.1 kg moves at 5 m/s in a circle of radius 2 m. Its angular momentum about the centre is
questions.e: L = mvr = 0.1 × 5 × 2 = 1 J s. 0.5 J s is only the linear momentum mv, and 2 J s wrongly uses r² instead of r.

questions.s: A diver in the air pulls her knees to her chest and starts somersaulting faster. This happens because
o: Gravity exerts a torque about her centre
questions.e: Tucking brings mass closer to the axis, so I falls; with no external torque L = Iω is constant, so ω rises. Gravity acts at her centre of mass and gives no torque about it, so her angular momentum cannot increase.

questions.s: If the Earth suddenly shrank to half its present radius with its mass unchanged, and it were treated as a uniform sphere, the length of a day would become
questions.e: I = 2MR²/5 becomes one quarter when R is halved. Angular momentum is conserved, so ω becomes 4 times and the period becomes 24/4 = 6 h. 12 h would follow if I were proportional to R instead of R².

questions.s: A disc spins freely with angular velocity ω about a vertical axle. An identical disc at rest is dropped onto it along the same axle, and the two then turn together. The fraction of the original kinetic energy lost is
questions.e: Angular momentum is conserved: Iω = 2Iω′, so ω′ = ω/2. New KE = ½(2I)(ω/2)² = ¼Iω², half of the original ½Iω², so half the KE is lost (to friction between the discs). Answering zero wrongly assumes KE is conserved along with L.

questions.s: A planet moves round the Sun in an elliptical orbit. Which quantity of the planet stays constant throughout its orbit?
questions.e: Gravity on the planet points towards the Sun, so it exerts no torque about the Sun and L = mvr stays constant. Because r changes, the speed must change too: the planet moves faster when nearer the Sun, so its speed and KE are not constant.

questions.s: A constant torque of 2 N m acts on a wheel initially at rest for 3 s. The angular momentum gained by the wheel is
questions.e: τ = ΔL/Δt, so ΔL = τΔt = 2 × 3 = 6 J s. 0.67 J s and 1.5 J s divide the quantities instead of multiplying, and 5 J s adds them.

questions.s: A flywheel of moment of inertia 2 kg m² rotates at 3 rad/s. Its rotational kinetic energy is
questions.e: KErot = ½Iω² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J. 18 J forgets the factor ½, and 6 J is Iω, which is angular momentum, not energy.

questions.s: A uniform disc rolls without slipping on a level floor. The fraction of its total kinetic energy that is rotational is
questions.e: Translational KE = ½mv² and rotational KE = ½(½mr²)(v/r)² = ¼mv², so the total is ¾mv². The rotational fraction is (¼)/(¾) = 1/3. 1/2 is the fraction for a ring, whose two parts are equal.

questions.s: A thin ring (hoop) of mass 2 kg rolls without slipping at 3 m/s. Its total kinetic energy is
questions.e: For a hoop I = mr², so rotational KE = ½mr²(v/r)² = ½mv², equal to the translational KE. Total = mv² = 2 × 9 = 18 J. 9 J counts only the translational part, and 13.5 J uses the disc result ¾mv².

questions.s: The angular speed of a flywheel of moment of inertia 0.5 kg m² is raised from 10 rad/s to 20 rad/s. The work done on it is
questions.e: W = ΔKE = ½I(ω₂² − ω₁²) = ½ × 0.5 × (400 − 100) = 75 J. 25 J uses ½I(ω₂ − ω₁)², squaring the change instead of taking the change of squares, and 100 J is the final KE alone.

questions.s: A solid sphere rolls without slipping at 5 m/s on level ground and then rolls up a rough slope. Taking g = 10 m/s², the greatest vertical height it reaches is
questions.e: Total KE = ½mv² + ½(2mr²/5)(v/r)² = (7/10)mv². Setting this equal to mgh gives h = 7v²/(10g) = 7 × 25/100 = 1.75 m. 1.25 m is v²/2g, which ignores the rotational KE that also turns into potential energy.

questions.s: For a body of fixed moment of inertia, its rotational kinetic energy is directly proportional to
questions.e: KErot = ½Iω², so with I fixed it is proportional to ω². Proportionality to ω applies to angular momentum L = Iω, not to energy.

questions.s: A spinning body has angular momentum L. If its moment of inertia is halved while L stays constant, its rotational kinetic energy becomes
questions.e: KE = ½Iω² = L²/(2I). With L fixed, halving I doubles the KE; the extra energy comes from the work the body does pulling its mass inward. Four times would follow from ω doubling if I were unchanged, but I is halved.

questions.s: A torque of 6 N m acts on a wheel of moment of inertia 2 kg m². Its angular acceleration is
questions.e: τ = Iα gives α = τ/I = 6/2 = 3 rad/s². 12 rad/s² multiplies τ by I instead of dividing.

questions.s: The SI unit of the gravitational constant G is
questions.e: From F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = Fr²/(m₁m₂), so its unit is N m²/kg² = N m² kg⁻². N kg² m⁻² inverts the rearrangement.

questions.s: If the distance between the centres of two bodies is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes
questions.e: F ∝ 1/r², so doubling r divides the force by 2² = 4, giving 1/4 of the original. 1/2 times would be true only for an inverse (not inverse-square) law.

questions.s: Two lead spheres of 100 kg each have their centres 1 m apart. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², the gravitational force between them is
questions.e: F = Gm₁m₂/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 100 × 100/1² = 6.67 × 10⁻⁷ N. 6.67 × 10⁻⁹ N uses only one of the masses.

questions.s: If g is the acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface and R the Earth's radius, the mass of the Earth is given by
questions.e: At the surface mg = GMm/R², so g = GM/R² and M = gR²/G. g/(GR²) inverts the rearrangement, and gR/G uses R instead of R².

questions.s: The Earth pulls a falling mango of mass 1 kg with a force of 10 N. The force that the mango exerts on the Earth is
questions.e: Gravitational forces between two bodies form a Newton's third law pair, equal in size and opposite in direction, so the mango pulls the Earth with 10 N. The Earth's acceleration is tiny only because its mass is huge, not because the force is small.

questions.s: The mass of the Earth is 81 times that of the Moon and the distance between their centres is d. The point on the line joining them where the net gravitational force on a body is zero lies at a distance from the Earth's centre of
questions.e: Set GM/x² = G(M/81)/(d − x)²; taking square roots, 1/x = 1/(9(d − x)), so d − x = x/9 and x = 9d/10. 81d/82 comes from forgetting to take the square root of the mass ratio.

questions.s: A planet has twice the mass and twice the radius of the Earth. A man who weighs 600 N on the Earth would weigh on that planet
questions.e: g = GM/R², so g′/g = 2/2² = 1/2 and the weight becomes 600/2 = 300 N. 600 N assumes the doubled mass and doubled radius cancel, which ignores that R is squared.

questions.s: The gravitational force between two masses is
questions.e: Mass comes in one kind only, so gravity always pulls masses together. Unlike electric force, it cannot be repulsive, and it acts between all masses whether charged or not.

questions.s: At a height above the Earth's surface equal to twice the Earth's radius, the acceleration due to gravity is
questions.e: gh = gR²/(R + h)² = gR²/(3R)² = g/9. The tempting g/4 uses the height 2R instead of the distance 3R from the Earth's centre.

questions.s: The acceleration due to gravity at the centre of the Earth is
questions.e: Inside the Earth gd = g(1 − d/R); at the centre d = R, so g = 0, because the mass around the centre pulls equally in all directions. Infinite would come from wrongly using 1/r² with r = 0.

questions.s: Taking g = 10 m/s² at the surface, the acceleration due to gravity at a depth equal to one quarter of the Earth's radius is
questions.e: Below the surface gd = g(1 − d/R) = 10(1 − 1/4) = 7.5 m/s². 5.6 m/s² squares the factor 3/4, wrongly copying the inverse-square form used above the surface.

questions.s: Using gh ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) for small heights and R = 6400 km, the height above the Earth's surface at which g is 1 % less than at the surface is about
questions.e: A 1 % drop means 2h/R = 0.01, so h = 0.005 × 6400 km = 32 km. 64 km forgets the factor 2 in the approximation (h/R = 0.01).

questions.s: On the Earth's surface, the value of g is greatest at
questions.e: The poles are nearest the Earth's centre (the Earth is slightly flattened) and have no rotational effect, so g is largest there. At the equator the radius is largest and the spin reduces the effective g most.

questions.s: For heights and depths small compared with the Earth's radius, g decreases by the same amount at a height h above the surface and at a depth of
questions.e: At height h the decrease is about 2gh/R; at depth d it is gd/R. Equal decreases need d/R = 2h/R, so d = 2h. Answering h assumes g falls at the same rate above and below the surface.

questions.s: A planet has the same average density as the Earth but twice its radius. The acceleration due to gravity on its surface is
questions.e: g = GM/R² with M = (4/3)πR³ρ gives g = (4/3)πGρR, so g ∝ R at fixed density and doubles to 2g. 4g wrongly uses g ∝ R², and g/2 treats the mass as unchanged.

questions.s: If g is the value at the Earth's surface and R is the Earth's radius, the acceleration due to gravity at height h above the surface is
questions.e: g varies as 1/r², so gh/g = R²/(R + h)², giving gh = g(R/(R + h))². g((R + h)/R)² inverts the ratio and would make g grow with height.

questions.s: Taking g = 10 m/s² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, the orbital speed of a satellite moving just above the Earth's surface is
questions.e: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: mg = mv²/R, so v = √(gR) = √(6.4 × 10⁷) = 8000 m/s = 8 km/s. 11.2 km/s is the escape velocity, which is √2 times larger.

questions.s: A satellite orbits close to the Earth's surface at 8 km/s. Another satellite orbits the Earth in a circle of radius four times the Earth's radius. Its orbital speed is
questions.e: v = √(GM/r), so v ∝ 1/√r; making r four times larger divides v by √4 = 2, giving 4 km/s. 2 km/s divides by 4, forgetting the square root.

questions.s: Two satellites of masses m and 2m move in the same circular orbit round the Earth. The ratio of their orbital speeds is
questions.e: From GMm/r² = mv²/r, v = √(GM/r); the satellite's own mass cancels, so both move at the same speed. 1:√2 wrongly keeps the satellite's mass in the formula.

questions.s: If the radius of a satellite's circular orbit is made four times larger, its period of revolution becomes
questions.e: T = 2π√(r³/GM), so T ∝ r^(3/2); with r four times larger, T is 4^(3/2) = 8 times larger. 16 times uses T ∝ r².

questions.s: For a satellite to remain above the same point on the Earth (a geostationary satellite), it must have
questions.e: It must turn with the Earth: period 24 h, moving west to east, in the plane of the equator. A polar orbit with a 24 h period would carry the satellite north and south over the ground, so it would not stay above one point.

questions.s: The radius of the orbit of a geostationary satellite, measured from the centre of the Earth, is about
questions.e: A 24 h orbit has radius about 42 300 km from the Earth's centre, which is about 36 000 km above the surface (42 300 − 6400). 36 000 km is the height, not the orbital radius, and 384 000 km is the Moon's distance.

questions.s: Taking g = 10 m/s² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, a satellite orbiting at a height above the surface equal to the Earth's radius has an orbital speed of
questions.e: v = √(GM/r) = √(gR²/2R) = √(gR/2) = 8/√2 = 4√2 km/s (about 5.7 km/s). 4 km/s would follow from v ∝ 1/r, forgetting the square root.

questions.s: Taking g = 10 m/s², the centripetal acceleration of a satellite orbiting just above the Earth's surface is
questions.e: The only force on the satellite is its weight, which provides the centripetal force, so its centripetal acceleration equals g = 10 m/s². Zero confuses the feeling of weightlessness with having no acceleration.

questions.s: Taking g = 10 m/s² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, the period of a satellite orbiting just above the Earth's surface is about
questions.e: T = 2πR/v = 2π√(R/g) = 2π√(6.4 × 10⁵) = 2π × 800 = 1600π s ≈ 5000 s ≈ 84 min. 24 h is the period of a geostationary satellite, which orbits much farther out.

questions.s: A girl of mass 50 kg stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is moving upward with a constant velocity. Taking g = 10 m/s², the scale reads
questions.e: At constant velocity the acceleration is zero, so R − mg = 0 and R = mg = 50 × 10 = 500 N. Motion alone does not change the reading; only acceleration does. 50 N confuses the mass in kg with the weight in newtons.

questions.s: A man of mass 60 kg stands in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², his apparent weight is
questions.e: R − mg = ma, so R = m(g + a) = 60 × 12 = 720 N. 480 N uses m(g − a), which applies when the acceleration is downward.

questions.s: Ayesha, of mass 40 kg, stands on a scale in a lift that accelerates downward at 2.5 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the scale reads
questions.e: mg − R = ma, so R = m(g − a) = 40 × 7.5 = 300 N. 500 N adds the acceleration, which is correct only for upward acceleration, and 100 N is just ma.

questions.s: If the cable of a lift breaks and the lift falls freely, the apparent weight of a passenger inside becomes
questions.e: In free fall a = g downward, so R = m(g − a) = 0 and the passenger feels weightless. His real weight mg still acts; only the support force (the apparent weight) disappears.

questions.s: A 5 kg mass hangs from a spring balance fixed to the roof of a lift. The balance reads 60 N. Taking g = 10 m/s², the acceleration of the lift is
questions.e: T − mg = ma gives a = (60 − 50)/5 = 2 m/s², positive, so it is upward. A reading above the true weight always means upward acceleration; 12 m/s² wrongly divides the whole reading by the mass.

questions.s: A lift carrying a 70 kg man is moving downward and slowing down at 2 m/s² as it approaches a floor. Taking g = 10 m/s², his apparent weight is
questions.e: Slowing while moving down means the acceleration points upward, so R = m(g + a) = 70 × 12 = 840 N. 560 N uses m(g − a) because the lift is moving down, but it is the direction of acceleration, not of motion, that matters.

questions.s: A body of mass m is in a lift accelerating upward. Its real weight
questions.e: Real weight is the Earth's gravitational pull, mg, which does not depend on the lift's motion. What increases is the apparent weight, the reading of the scale, R = m(g + a).

questions.s: Fatima stands on a weighing scale in a lift. The scale reads one quarter of her real weight. Taking g = 10 m/s², the acceleration of the lift is
questions.e: A reading below the real weight means downward acceleration: m(g − a) = mg/4, so a = 3g/4 = 7.5 m/s² downward. 2.5 m/s² is g/4, which is the remaining reading per kg, not the acceleration.

questions.s: An astronaut in a satellite orbiting the Earth feels weightless because
o: He and the craft fall together
questions.e: Both the astronaut and the satellite are in free fall towards the Earth with the same acceleration, so the floor exerts no reaction force on him. Gravity in a low orbit is still almost as strong as at the surface, so it is not zero.

questions.s: A space station orbits 400 km above the Earth's surface. Taking R = 6400 km, the acceleration due to gravity at the station is
questions.e: g′/g = (R/(R + h))² = (6400/6800)² = (16/17)² ≈ 0.89, so g is about 90 % of the surface value. Astronauts there float because they are in free fall, not because gravity has vanished.

questions.s: A plastic bottle full of water has a small hole near its bottom. If the bottle is dropped and falls freely, the water
o: Flows out at the same rate
questions.e: In free fall the water and the bottle accelerate together at g, so the water is weightless relative to the bottle and there is no pressure difference to push it out. Water flows out only when the water presses on the walls, which needs a support force.

questions.s: A ring-shaped space station of radius 40 m rotates to give its crew an artificial gravity of 10 m/s² at the rim. Its angular speed must be
questions.e: The floor supplies the centripetal force, so the required ω²R = g gives ω = √(g/R) = √(10/40) = 0.5 rad/s. 0.25 rad/s is g/R without the square root.

questions.s: A spaceship has a rotating ring of radius 250 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the period of rotation needed to produce artificial gravity equal to g at the ring is
questions.e: ω = √(g/R) = √(10/250) = √0.04 = 0.2 rad/s, so T = 2π/ω = 2π/0.2 = 10π s (about 31 s). 5π s forgets the factor 2 in T = 2π/ω.

questions.s: Inside a satellite in a circular orbit, which of the following can still be done normally?
o: Measuring mass with a beam balance
questions.e: A thermometer works by thermal expansion of mercury, which does not depend on weight. A beam balance, a pendulum and pouring all depend on an effective weight, which is zero in the freely falling satellite.

questions.s: Compared with its value on the Earth, the mass of an astronaut in an orbiting spacecraft is
questions.e: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with place or state of motion. Only the apparent weight becomes zero in orbit; answering zero mixes up mass and weight.

questions.s: Two satellites orbit the Earth in circles of radius r and 4r. If the inner one has a period of 2 h, the period of the outer one is
questions.e: T ∝ r^(3/2), so T₂ = 2 × 4^(3/2) = 2 × 8 = 16 h. 8 h uses T ∝ r, and 4 h uses T ∝ √r.

questions.s: Taking the Earth's radius as 6400 km, the height above the surface at which g becomes one quarter of its surface value is
questions.e: g′/g = R²/(R + h)² = 1/4 gives R + h = 2R, so h = R = 6400 km. 12800 km is 2R, the distance from the Earth's centre, mistaken for the height above the surface.

questions.s: A horizontal platform of moment of inertia 200 kg m² rotates freely at 2 rad/s. A boy of mass 50 kg, standing at its centre, walks out to a point 2 m from the axis. Treating the boy as a point mass, the new angular speed is
questions.e: No external torque acts, so Iω is conserved. The boy adds mr² = 50 × 4 = 200 kg m², so 200 × 2 = 400 × ω and ω = 1 rad/s. 2 rad/s ignores the increase in moment of inertia.

questions.s: A ring, a disc and a solid sphere of the same mass and radius are released together from rest at the top of the same slope and roll down without slipping. The first to reach the bottom is
questions.e: v² = 2gh/(1 + I/mr²); I/mr² is 2/5 for the sphere, 1/2 for the disc and 1 for the ring, so the sphere is fastest. All would reach together only if they slid without rolling, so that no energy went into rotation.

questions.s: The angle turned through by the seconds hand of a clock in 20 s is
questions.e: The seconds hand turns 2π rad in 60 s, so in 20 s it turns (20/60) × 2π = 2π/3 rad. π/3 rad uses π instead of 2π for a full turn.

questions.s: Two points P and Q on a rotating disc are at distances r and 2r from the axis. The ratio of their linear speeds vP : vQ is
questions.e: Every point of a rigid disc has the same ω, and v = rω, so vP : vQ = r : 2r = 1 : 2. 1:1 confuses equal angular speeds with equal linear speeds.

questions.s: Satellite A orbits the Earth in a circle of radius r and satellite B in a circle of radius 2r. The ratio of their centripetal accelerations aA : aB is
questions.e: The centripetal acceleration of a satellite is the local value of g, GM/r², so aA : aB = (2r)² : r² = 4 : 1. 2:1 uses v²/r with the same v for both, but the outer satellite also moves more slowly.

questions.s: A stone of mass 0.2 kg is whirled on a string in a vertical circle, just keeping the string taut. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, the tension at the lowest point exceeds that at the highest point by
questions.e: Energy conservation gives vb² = vt² + 4gr. Then Tb − Tt = (mvb²/r + mg) − (mvt²/r − mg) = 4mg + 2mg = 6mg = 6 × 0.2 × 10 = 12 N. 4 N (2mg) ignores the greater speed at the bottom.

questions.s: A wheel has rotational kinetic energy 100 J and angular momentum 20 J s about its axle. Its angular speed is
questions.e: KE = ½Iω² and L = Iω, so KE = ½Lω and ω = 2KE/L = 200/20 = 10 rad/s (then I = 2 kg m²). 5 rad/s is KE/L, which forgets the factor ½ in the energy.

questions.s: Satellite P orbits the Earth in a circle of radius r and satellite Q in a circle of radius 2r. The ratio of their periods TQ/TP is
questions.e: T² ∝ r³, so TQ/TP = (2)^(3/2) = 2√2. √2 is the ratio of their speeds vP/vQ, not of their periods, and 2 assumes T ∝ r.

questions.s: A wheel turns through an angle of 540°. Its angular displacement in radians is
questions.e: Multiply by π/180: 540 × π/180 = 3π rad (one and a half turns). 6π rad would be three full turns, 1080°.

questions.s: Hamza's car moves at 15 m/s. Its wheels of radius 0.3 m roll without slipping. The angular speed of each wheel is
questions.e: For rolling without slipping v = rω, so ω = v/r = 15/0.3 = 50 rad/s. 25 rad/s divides by the diameter instead of the radius, and 4.5 rad/s multiplies v by r.

questions.s: A wheel spinning at 4 rad/s has a constant angular acceleration of 3 rad/s². Its angular velocity after 2 s is
questions.e: ωf = ωi + αt = 4 + 3 × 2 = 10 rad/s. 6 rad/s is only the gain αt, which leaves out the initial angular velocity.

questions.s: For a body moving with uniform speed in a circle, the centripetal acceleration is directed
questions.e: The velocity keeps changing direction towards the centre, so the acceleration v²/r points along the radius towards the centre. The velocity, not the acceleration, is along the tangent.

questions.s: Ignoring gravity, a 2 kg ball on a string 1 m long moves in a horizontal circle, completing one revolution every π seconds. The tension in the string is
questions.e: ω = 2π/T = 2π/π = 2 rad/s, so T = mω²r = 2 × 4 × 1 = 8 N. 4 N comes from mωr, which forgets to square ω.

questions.s: A thin ring of mass 0.5 kg and radius 0.2 m rotates about an axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane. Its moment of inertia is
questions.e: All the mass of a thin ring is at distance R, so I = MR² = 0.5 × 0.04 = 0.02 kg m². 0.01 kg m² uses the disc formula ½MR², and 0.1 kg m² forgets to square R.

questions.s: Bodies of the same mass and the same radius rotate about their central axes. Which one has the largest moment of inertia?
questions.e: In a thin ring all the mass lies at the greatest distance R, so I = MR², larger than the disc (½MR²) and the sphere (2MR²/5). A point mass on the axis has zero moment of inertia.

questions.s: A disc of moment of inertia 0.5 kg m² spins at 8 rad/s. Its angular momentum is
