questions.e: L = Iω = 0.5 × 8 = 4 J s. 16 J s is the number ½Iω², which is the rotational KE in joules, not angular momentum.

questions.s: A merry-go-round of moment of inertia 300 kg m² turns freely at 1 rad/s. Sana, of mass 50 kg, steps on to it at 2 m from the axis. Treating her as a point mass, the new angular speed is
questions.e: Angular momentum is conserved: 300 × 1 = (300 + 50 × 2²)ω = 500ω, so ω = 0.6 rad/s. 0.4 rad/s wrongly takes Sana's share 200/500 instead of the platform's 300/500, and 1 rad/s ignores the added moment of inertia.

questions.s: If the angular speed of a flywheel is tripled, its rotational kinetic energy becomes
questions.e: KErot = ½Iω², so tripling ω multiplies the KE by 3² = 9. 3 times would be the change in angular momentum, which is proportional to ω.

questions.s: A uniform disc of mass 4 kg rolls without slipping at 2 m/s. Its total kinetic energy is
questions.e: Total KE = ½mv² + ½(½mr²)(v/r)² = ¾mv² = ¾ × 4 × 4 = 12 J. 8 J counts only the translational part ½mv².

questions.s: The orbital speed of an artificial satellite in a circular orbit does not depend on
questions.e: From GMm/r² = mv²/r, v = √(GM/r): the satellite's mass m cancels, while M, r and G all remain. This is why a heavy and a light satellite in the same orbit move together.

questions.s: Two satellites move in circular orbits whose radii are in the ratio 1 : 4. The ratio of their orbital speeds is
questions.e: v = √(GM/r), so v₁/v₂ = √(r₂/r₁) = √4 = 2, giving 2 : 1. 1:2 forgets that the inner satellite, being closer, moves faster.

questions.s: Taking g = 10 m/s² and R = 6400 km, a satellite in a circular orbit has a speed of 4 km/s. Its height above the Earth's surface is
questions.e: v² = GM/r = gR²/r, so r = gR²/v² = 10 × (6.4 × 10⁶)²/(1.6 × 10⁷) = 2.56 × 10⁷ m = 4R. The height is r − R = 3R = 19 200 km; 25 600 km is the orbital radius, not the height.

questions.s: Usman stands on a weighing scale in a lift that starts moving upward from rest. While the lift is speeding up, the scale reads
questions.e: With upward acceleration R − mg = ma, so R = m(g + a), which is more than mg. Less than his weight would apply to downward acceleration.

questions.s: An 8 kg bag hangs from a spring balance in a lift that is moving upward but slowing down at 2.5 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the balance reads
questions.e: Slowing while moving up means the acceleration is downward, so T = m(g − a) = 8 × 7.5 = 60 N. 100 N uses m(g + a) because the lift moves up, but only the direction of acceleration matters.

questions.s: Ignoring air resistance, in which situation does a person feel weightless?
o: Standing in a lift at rest
Falling freely from a diving board
Sitting in a car at constant speed
questions.e: In free fall the person and everything around him accelerate at g, so no support force acts and the apparent weight is zero. On the Moon gravity is weaker but a person standing there still presses on the ground, so he is not weightless.

questions.s: Two masses attract each other with a gravitational force F. If each mass is doubled and the distance between them is halved, the force becomes
questions.e: F ∝ m₁m₂/r²: doubling both masses multiplies F by 4, and halving r multiplies it by another 4, giving 16F. 8F treats the distance as entering the law only once (1/r), not squared.

questions.s: The depth below the Earth's surface at which g has the same value as at a height R above the surface (R = radius of the Earth) is
questions.e: At height R, g′ = gR²/(2R)² = g/4. Inside, g(1 − d/R) = g/4 gives d = 3R/4. R/4 sets d/R equal to 1/4 instead of 1 − d/R.

questions.s: A grinding wheel spinning at 20 rad/s slows down uniformly and stops after turning through 40 rad. The time it takes to stop is
questions.e: With uniform deceleration θ = ½(ωi + ωf)t, so 40 = ½(20 + 0)t and t = 4 s (the deceleration is 5 rad/s²). 2 s comes from θ/ωi, which wrongly assumes the wheel keeps its initial speed.

questions.s: According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag force on a small sphere of radius r moving slowly with speed v through a fluid of viscosity η is
questions.e: Stokes' law states F = 6πηrv: the drag is proportional to the radius and to the speed, each to the first power. A dependence on r² or v² is wrong for slow (streamline) motion; checking dimensions, ηrv = [ML⁻¹T⁻¹][L][LT⁻¹] = [MLT⁻²], a force, while ηr²v is not.

questions.s: The SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity is
questions.e: From F = 6πηrv, η = F/(rv) has units N/(m × m s⁻¹) = N s m⁻², which is the pascal second (Pa s). The option N m⁻² s⁻¹ puts the second in the denominator, and kg m s⁻¹ is the unit of momentum.

questions.s: A sphere of radius 2 mm moves at 0.5 m s⁻¹ through water of viscosity 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s, slowly enough for Stokes' law to hold. The drag force on it is
questions.e: F = 6πηrv = 6π × (1.0 × 10⁻³) × (2 × 10⁻³) × 0.5 = 6π × 10⁻⁶ N. The value 12π × 10⁻⁶ N uses the diameter 4 mm instead of the radius, and 6π × 10⁻³ N leaves the radius in millimetres.

questions.s: A small sphere moves through a viscous liquid. If its radius is halved and its speed is doubled, the Stokes' drag force on it becomes
questions.e: F = 6πηrv is proportional to the product rv, and (r/2)(2v) = rv, so the drag is unchanged. Thinking that drag depends on the cross-sectional area (r²) would give half; in Stokes' law the radius appears only to the first power.

questions.s: A raindrop falling through air reaches its terminal velocity when
o: the air drag balances its weight
questions.e: As the drop speeds up, the drag force grows until it equals the weight (upthrust in air is negligible); the net force is then zero and the drop falls with constant terminal velocity. The acceleration is g only at the start, when the drop is at rest and there is no drag.

questions.s: For a small sphere falling through a viscous fluid, the terminal velocity is vₜ = 2r²ρg/(9η), upthrust being neglected. If the radius of the sphere is doubled, the terminal velocity becomes
questions.e: vₜ ∝ r², so doubling r multiplies vₜ by 2² = 4. The weight grows as r³ (volume) while the drag at a given speed grows only as r, so their ratio gives r². Answering eight times uses the r³ of the weight and forgets the drag.

questions.s: A water droplet of radius 3 × 10⁻⁶ m falls through air of viscosity 2 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s. Using vₜ = 2r²ρg/(9η) with ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 10 m s⁻², and neglecting upthrust, its terminal velocity is
questions.e: vₜ = 2 × (9 × 10⁻¹²) × 1000 × 10 / (9 × 2 × 10⁻⁵) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁷ / 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹. Using the diameter 6 × 10⁻⁶ m gives four times this, 4.0 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹, and dropping the factor 2/9 gives 4.5 × 10⁻³ m s⁻¹.

questions.s: Two identical small raindrops, each falling with terminal velocity v, merge to form a single larger drop. Assuming Stokes' law, the terminal velocity of the larger drop is
questions.e: The volume doubles, so the new radius is 2^(1/3) r. Since vₜ ∝ r², the new terminal velocity is (2^(1/3))² v = 2^(2/3) v = ∛4 v (about 1.6v). Answering 2v assumes the speed doubles with the mass, but the drag also grows with the larger radius.

questions.s: Which statement is true for streamline (laminar) flow of a fluid?
o: the velocity at a given point does not change with time
the fluid moves in irregular eddies
it occurs only at very high speeds
questions.e: In streamline flow every particle passing a given point has the same velocity, so the velocity at each point stays constant in time and the layers slide smoothly past each other. Streamlines never cross, because a particle cannot have two velocities at one point. Eddies and high speeds are features of turbulent flow.

questions.s: Smoke rising from an incense stick moves smoothly at first and then breaks into swirls higher up. The swirling part is an example of
questions.e: As the hot smoke speeds up, its smooth motion breaks into irregular, changing eddies: this is turbulent flow. The smooth lower column is laminar (streamline), which is the same as steady flow in which the velocity at each point does not change.

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the assumptions made for an ideal fluid when deriving the equation of continuity and Bernoulli's equation?
questions.e: An ideal fluid is taken as incompressible (constant density), non-viscous (no energy lost to friction) and in steady, streamline flow. Turbulent flow is the opposite of the steady flow assumed, so it is not an assumption. Incompressibility is the one most often forgotten; it is what lets the volume flow rate stay constant.

questions.s: The equation of continuity, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, is a consequence of the conservation of
questions.e: For an incompressible fluid in steady flow, the mass entering one end of a pipe each second must leave the other end: ρA₁v₁ = ρA₂v₂, giving A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Bernoulli's equation, not the continuity equation, comes from conservation of energy.

questions.s: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross-sectional area falls to half its value at a narrow section. Compared with the wide section, the speed of the water in the narrow section is
questions.e: From A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, halving the area doubles the speed. Four times would apply if the diameter (not the area) were halved, since the area then falls to a quarter.

questions.s: Water flows at 2 m s⁻¹ in a pipe of diameter 4 cm. The pipe narrows to a diameter of 2 cm. The speed of the water in the narrow part is
questions.e: Area ∝ d², so halving the diameter makes the area one quarter and, by A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, the speed four times: v₂ = 2 × (4/2)² = 8 m s⁻¹. The value 4 m s⁻¹ treats the diameter ratio as the area ratio, forgetting to square it.

questions.s: Water comes out of a pipe of cross-sectional area 5 cm² at a speed of 2 m s⁻¹. The time taken to fill a 60 litre bucket is
questions.e: Volume flow rate = Av = (5 × 10⁻⁴ m²)(2 m s⁻¹) = 1 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹ = 1 L s⁻¹, so 60 L takes 60 s. The value 600 s comes from taking 5 cm² as 5 × 10⁻⁵ m²; since 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², the correct area is 5 × 10⁻⁴ m².

questions.s: While watering a lawn, Hamza partly covers the open end of a hose with his thumb, and the water shoots out much faster. This is explained by
questions.e: The volume of water passing per second, Av, is fixed by the supply, so reducing the outlet area A increases the exit speed v, as the equation of continuity requires. Stokes' law concerns drag on a moving sphere, and Archimedes' and Pascal's principles concern fluids at rest.

questions.s: A hose of radius 1 cm carries water at 1 m s⁻¹ to a sprinkler head with 20 holes, each of radius 1 mm. The speed of the water leaving each hole is
questions.e: Continuity: π(1 cm)² × 1 = 20 × π(0.1 cm)² × v, so 1 = 20 × 0.01 × v and v = 5 m s⁻¹. The value 100 m s⁻¹ forgets that the flow is shared among 20 holes, 0.5 m s⁻¹ uses the radius ratio 10 instead of its square, and 0.2 m s⁻¹ inverts the area ratio.

questions.s: Blood flows through the aorta, of cross-sectional area 3 cm², at 30 cm s⁻¹. If the total cross-sectional area of all the capillaries it feeds is 900 cm², the average speed of blood in the capillaries is
questions.e: Continuity: 3 × 30 = 900 × v, so v = 90/900 = 0.1 cm s⁻¹. Although each capillary is very narrow, their combined area is huge, so the blood slows down; expecting it to speed up, as in a single narrow pipe, is the usual mistake.

questions.s: Bernoulli's equation for a fluid in steady flow is a statement of the conservation of
questions.e: Bernoulli's equation, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, comes from applying the work-energy principle to a moving fluid: the work done by pressure equals the change in kinetic and potential energy. Conservation of mass leads to the equation of continuity instead.

questions.s: Air flows steadily through a horizontal tube. According to Bernoulli's principle, where the speed of the air is greater, its pressure is
questions.e: At the same height P + ½ρv² is constant, so a larger speed means a lower pressure. Many students expect faster air to push harder, but the extra kinetic energy is gained at the expense of pressure energy.

questions.s: In Bernoulli's equation, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, each of the three terms represents
questions.e: Each term has the units of pressure, N m⁻² = J m⁻³, so each is an energy per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy (½ρv²) and potential energy (ρgh) of one cubic metre of fluid. Energy per unit mass would be ½v² and gh, without the density ρ.

questions.s: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows through a horizontal pipe. At one point its speed is 2 m s⁻¹ and its pressure is 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. At a narrower point the speed is 4 m s⁻¹. The pressure there is
questions.e: For a horizontal pipe P₂ = P₁ − ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 2.0 × 10⁵ − 500 × (16 − 4) = 2.0 × 10⁵ − 6000 = 1.94 × 10⁵ Pa. Forgetting the ½ gives 1.88 × 10⁵ Pa, and squaring the difference of the speeds, (4 − 2)², gives 1.98 × 10⁵ Pa.

questions.s: Water flows through a horizontal pipe whose cross-sectional area changes from 0.02 m² to 0.01 m². The speed in the wider part is 3 m s⁻¹. Taking the density of water as 1000 kg m⁻³, the pressure difference between the wide and narrow parts is
questions.e: Continuity gives the narrow-part speed: v₂ = 3 × (0.02/0.01) = 6 m s⁻¹. Bernoulli then gives P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (36 − 9) = 1.35 × 10⁴ Pa. Dropping the ½ gives 2.7 × 10⁴ Pa, and using (6 − 3)² = 9 instead of 36 − 9 gives 4.5 × 10³ Pa.

questions.s: A water tank on a house roof in Peshawar has a small hole in its side 5 m below the water surface. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the speed with which water leaves the hole is
questions.e: By Torricelli's theorem v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 5) = √100 = 10 m s⁻¹. The value 100 m s⁻¹ forgets the square root, and √50 m s⁻¹ leaves out the factor 2, which comes from ½v² = gh.

questions.s: Water flows out of a small hole near the bottom of a wide tank. If the depth of the hole below the water surface is made four times as great, the speed of efflux becomes
questions.e: Torricelli's theorem gives v = √(2gh), so v ∝ √h and a fourfold depth doubles the speed: √4 = 2. Answering four times assumes v is proportional to h itself, which is true of the pressure at the hole, not of the speed.

questions.s: An open tank standing on the ground is filled with water to a height of 1.0 m. A small hole is made in its side 0.2 m below the water surface. The horizontal distance from the tank at which the jet strikes the ground is
questions.e: Efflux speed v = √(2gh) with h = 0.2 m; the hole is 0.8 m above the ground, so the fall time is t = √(2 × 0.8/g). Range = vt = 2√(h × 0.8) = 2√0.16 = 0.8 m, independent of g. The value 0.4 m drops the factor 2 in the formula 2√(h(H − h)).

questions.s: In deriving Torricelli's theorem v = √(2gh) for water leaving a hole in a wide tank, it is assumed that
o: the pressure at the hole exceeds atmospheric
the flow through the hole is turbulent
the speed of the top surface is negligible
questions.e: Applying Bernoulli's equation between the water surface and the hole, both are at atmospheric pressure, and because the tank is much wider than the hole the surface falls so slowly that its speed is taken as zero. This leaves ½v² = gh. The pressure at the free jet is atmospheric, not greater, and viscosity and turbulence are ignored, not assumed.

questions.s: A Venturi meter fitted in a water main is used to measure
o: the speed of flow in the pipe
questions.e: A Venturi meter has a narrow throat; the pressure difference between the wide part and the throat, read from manometer tubes, gives the flow speed (and hence the flow rate) through Bernoulli's equation and continuity. It assumes a known density rather than measuring it, and viscosity is neglected.

questions.s: In a horizontal Venturi meter carrying water (density 1000 kg m⁻³), the area of the wide section is twice the area of the throat. The pressure in the wide section is 6000 Pa greater than in the throat. The speed of water in the wide section is
questions.e: Continuity gives v₂ = 2v₁ in the throat. Bernoulli: 6000 = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (4v₁² − v₁²) = 1500v₁², so v₁² = 4 and v₁ = 2 m s⁻¹. The value 4 m s⁻¹ is the throat speed, and √12 m s⁻¹ comes from ignoring v₁ and writing 6000 = 500v².

questions.s: The two vertical manometer tubes of a Venturi meter show water levels that differ by 15 cm. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and the density of water as 1000 kg m⁻³, the pressure difference between the wide part and the throat is
questions.e: ΔP = ρgΔh = 1000 × 10 × 0.15 = 1500 Pa. Using 15 cm as 1.5 m gives 1.5 × 10⁴ Pa, and dropping g gives 150 Pa; the height must be converted to metres first.

questions.s: The lift on the wing of an aeroplane in flight is mainly due to
o: higher pressure above the wing, where air moves faster
lower pressure below the wing, where air moves slower
equal pressure on both faces of the wing
lower pressure above the wing, where air moves faster
questions.e: The wing's shape and tilt make air flow faster over the top surface than under it. By Bernoulli's principle, faster air has lower pressure, so the pressure below the wing is greater and the difference pushes the wing up. Slower air has higher, not lower, pressure.

questions.s: In the carburettor of a petrol engine, petrol is drawn into the air stream because
o: air slows in a narrow throat, raising its pressure
petrol becomes less viscous in the throat
air speeds up in a narrow throat, lowering its pressure
the throat heats the petrol until it boils
questions.e: Air passing through the narrow throat (a Venturi) speeds up by continuity, so by Bernoulli's principle its pressure falls below that above the petrol, and petrol is pushed into the air stream through a jet. In a narrow section the air speeds up rather than slowing down, so its pressure falls rather than rises.

questions.s: During a strong windstorm, the light tin roof of a hut is lifted off. This happens because
o: pressure above the roof drops below that inside
pressure above the roof rises above that inside
pressure inside the hut drops sharply
the wind pushes directly upward on the roof
questions.e: Fast wind over the roof has low pressure (Bernoulli), while the still air inside stays near atmospheric pressure. The higher pressure underneath pushes the roof upward. The wind blows horizontally, so it cannot push straight up, and the inside pressure does not suddenly fall.

questions.s: Two boats moving side by side, close together and parallel to each other, tend to be
questions.e: Water squeezed into the narrow gap between the boats flows faster than the water on their outer sides, so the pressure between them is lower (Bernoulli). The higher outside pressure pushes the boats towards each other. Expecting faster water to push them apart is the usual error.

questions.s: In a perfume spray, squeezing the bulb sends a jet of air across the top of a narrow tube dipping into the perfume, and the perfume rises up the tube. This is mainly due to
o: capillary rise of the liquid in the narrow tube
high pressure produced by the fast air above the tube
viscous drag of the moving air pulling the liquid up
low pressure above the tube caused by the fast air
questions.e: The fast air jet has low pressure (Bernoulli), so atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface in the bottle pushes the perfume up the tube, where the jet breaks it into a spray. Fast air lowers the pressure rather than raising it, and capillary rise is far too small to lift the liquid out of the tube.

questions.s: Honey flows much more easily on a hot day in Lahore than on a cold winter morning. This shows that, as the temperature of a liquid rises, its viscosity
questions.e: Viscosity is internal friction between layers of the liquid; heating weakens the attraction between molecules, so the viscosity of a liquid decreases and it flows more easily. Increasing viscosity would make warm honey flow more slowly, which is the opposite of what is observed.

questions.s: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows up a pipe. At the lower end the speed is 2 m s⁻¹ and the pressure is 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa. The upper end is 2 m higher and has half the cross-sectional area. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the pressure at the upper end is
questions.e: Continuity gives v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹. Bernoulli: P₂ = P₁ − ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) − ρgΔh = 1.5 × 10⁵ − 500 × 12 − 1000 × 10 × 2 = 1.5 × 10⁵ − 6000 − 20 000 = 1.24 × 10⁵ Pa. Leaving out the speed change gives 1.30 × 10⁵ Pa, and leaving out the height gives 1.44 × 10⁵ Pa.

questions.s: A steel ball of radius 3 mm and density 7800 kg m⁻³ falls through glycerine of density 1300 kg m⁻³ and viscosity 1.3 Pa s. Using vₜ = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), where σ is the density of the liquid, and g = 10 m s⁻², the terminal velocity is
questions.e: vₜ = 2 × (3 × 10⁻³)² × (7800 − 1300) × 10 / (9 × 1.3) = 2 × 9 × 10⁻⁶ × 6500 × 10 / 11.7 = 1.17/11.7 = 0.10 m s⁻¹. Ignoring the upthrust (using 7800 instead of 6500) gives 0.12 m s⁻¹, and using the diameter 6 mm gives 0.40 m s⁻¹.

questions.s: Two steel balls of radii 1 mm and 3 mm fall through the same oil. Assuming Stokes' law holds, the ratio of their terminal velocities is
questions.e: vₜ ∝ r² for the same materials, so the ratio is 1² : 3² = 1 : 9. The ratio 1 : 27 follows the weights (∝ r³) but forgets that the drag also grows with r, and 1 : 3 forgets the square.

questions.s: Smoke goes up a chimney more quickly when a wind blows across the top of the chimney, because
o: the wind raises the pressure at the chimney top
the wind cools and thickens the smoke
the wind lowers the pressure at the chimney top
the wind blocks outside air from entering
questions.e: Moving air across the top of the chimney has lower pressure than the still air in the room below (Bernoulli), so the smoke is pushed up faster. A rise in pressure at the top would slow the smoke instead, and cooling would make the smoke denser and rise more slowly.

questions.s: The viscosity of a fluid is a measure of
o: the mass of fluid per unit volume
how much its volume shrinks under pressure
the friction between its moving layers
questions.e: Viscosity is the internal friction that resists one layer of fluid sliding over another; honey has a high viscosity and water a low one. Mass per unit volume is density and weight per unit volume is weight density, neither of which describes how easily the fluid flows.

questions.s: A ball of radius 1 cm moves slowly at 2 cm s⁻¹ through glycerine of viscosity 0.5 Pa s. Using Stokes' law, the drag force on the ball is
questions.e: F = 6πηrv = 6π × 0.5 × 0.01 × 0.02 = 6π × 10⁻⁴ N, with r and v first converted to metres. Using the diameter 2 cm gives 1.2π × 10⁻³ N, and leaving the radius in centimetres gives 6π × 10⁻² N.

questions.s: Fatima drops a small steel ball from rest into a tall jar of oil. As the ball falls through the oil, its velocity
questions.e: At first the ball accelerates, but the viscous drag grows with speed until drag plus upthrust equal the weight; then the net force is zero and the ball falls at constant terminal velocity. It cannot keep accelerating without limit because the drag keeps rising, and it starts from rest, so it is not constant from the start.

questions.s: A river of uniform depth becomes narrower as it passes between two rocks. In the narrow part the water flows
questions.e: By the equation of continuity the volume of water passing each second, Av, stays the same, so where the cross-section A is smaller the speed v is greater. More slowly would mean less water passing per second through the gap, which would make water pile up upstream.

questions.s: Oil flows at 0.5 m s⁻¹ in a pipe of radius 3 cm, which then narrows to a radius of 1 cm. The speed of the oil in the narrow pipe is
questions.e: Area ∝ r², so the area falls by a factor 3² = 9 and the speed rises by 9: v₂ = 0.5 × 9 = 4.5 m s⁻¹. The value 1.5 m s⁻¹ uses the radius ratio without squaring, and 13.5 m s⁻¹ cubes it.

questions.s: A large water tank in Quetta has a small tap 0.45 m below the water surface. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the speed of water flowing out of the open tap is
questions.e: Torricelli's theorem: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 0.45) = √9 = 3 m s⁻¹. The value 9 m s⁻¹ forgets the square root, and √4.5 m s⁻¹ leaves out the factor 2.

questions.s: Air of density 1.2 kg m⁻³ flows over the top of a horizontal wing at 60 m s⁻¹ and under it at 50 m s⁻¹. The pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces is
questions.e: ΔP = ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²) = 0.6 × (3600 − 2500) = 0.6 × 1100 = 660 Pa. Forgetting the ½ gives 1320 Pa, and squaring the difference of speeds, ½ρ(10)², gives only 60 Pa.

questions.s: A model aeroplane has a total wing area of 10 m². Air of density 1.2 kg m⁻³ moves over the upper surface at 70 m s⁻¹ and under the lower surface at 60 m s⁻¹. The lift force on the wings is
questions.e: ΔP = ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²) = 0.6 × (4900 − 3600) = 780 Pa, and lift = ΔP × A = 780 × 10 = 7800 N. The value 780 N forgets to multiply by the area, 15 600 N forgets the ½, and 600 N uses (70 − 60)² instead of the difference of the squares.

questions.s: Bernoulli's equation in its simple form applies to
o: turbulent flow of a highly viscous fluid
any flow of a compressible gas at high speed
steady flow of an ideal fluid
a fluid at rest, never a moving one
questions.e: Bernoulli's equation is derived for steady (streamline) flow of an ideal fluid, that is incompressible and non-viscous, so that no energy is lost to friction. Viscous, turbulent flow loses energy, and the equation also holds for a fluid at rest, where it reduces to P + ρgh = constant.

questions.s: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows at 2 litres per second through a horizontal pipe that narrows from a cross-sectional area of 4 cm² to 1 cm². The pressure difference between the wide and narrow parts is
questions.e: Speeds: v₁ = (2 × 10⁻³)/(4 × 10⁻⁴) = 5 m s⁻¹ and v₂ = (2 × 10⁻³)/(1 × 10⁻⁴) = 20 m s⁻¹. Then ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (400 − 25) = 1.875 × 10⁵ Pa. Using (20 − 5)² gives 1.125 × 10⁵ Pa, and forgetting the ½ gives 3.75 × 10⁵ Pa.

questions.s: A body executes simple harmonic motion when its acceleration is
o: proportional to displacement, directed away from the mean position
constant in size and directed towards the mean position
proportional to the square of displacement, towards the mean position
proportional to displacement, directed towards the mean position
questions.e: SHM is defined by a = −ω²x: the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from the mean position and always points back towards it (the minus sign). An acceleration directed away from the mean position would push the body further out, so it would not oscillate.

questions.s: A vibrating body completes one oscillation in 0.2 s. Its frequency is
questions.e: Frequency is the number of oscillations per second, f = 1/T = 1/0.2 = 5 Hz. Writing 0.2 Hz confuses the period with the frequency.

questions.s: When a body in simple harmonic motion passes through its mean position, its
o: speed is maximum and acceleration is zero
speed is zero and acceleration is maximum
speed and acceleration are both maximum
speed and acceleration are both zero
questions.e: At x = 0, a = −ω²x = 0, while v = ω√(A² − x²) takes its largest value ωA. Zero speed with maximum acceleration describes the extreme positions instead.

questions.s: At an extreme position of a body in simple harmonic motion, the
o: restoring force on the body is zero
questions.e: At x = ±A the body is momentarily at rest, so KE = 0 and all the energy is potential, ½kA², its largest value. The restoring force −kx is also at its maximum there, not zero.

questions.s: A 0.4 kg mass attached to a spring of spring constant 40 N/m oscillates on a smooth horizontal surface. Its time period is
questions.e: T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(0.4/40) = 2π√0.01 = 2π × 0.1 = 0.2π s (about 0.63 s). Inverting the ratio to √(k/m) = 10 gives 20π s.

questions.s: Taking g = 10 m/s², the time period of a simple pendulum of length 2.5 m is
questions.e: T = 2π√(l/g) = 2π√(2.5/10) = 2π√0.25 = 2π × 0.5 = π s. Forgetting the square root gives 2π × 0.25 = π/2 s.

questions.s: Taking g = π² m/s², the length of a seconds pendulum (time period 2 s) is
questions.e: From T = 2π√(l/g), l = gT²/4π² = π² × 4/4π² = 1 m. Using T = 1 s (the time for one swing, not a full oscillation) gives 0.25 m.

questions.s: If the length of a simple pendulum is made four times as great, its time period becomes
questions.e: T = 2π√(l/g) is proportional to √l, so multiplying l by 4 multiplies T by √4 = 2. Four times as large would be true only if T were proportional to l.

questions.s: Fatima replaces the bob of a simple pendulum by one of twice the mass, keeping the length and the small amplitude the same. The time period becomes
questions.e: T = 2π√(l/g) contains no mass: a heavier bob needs more force to accelerate, but its weight (the restoring force) increases in the same ratio. The √2 factor would apply to a mass-spring system, where T = 2π√(m/k).

questions.s: The mass attached to a spring is increased to four times its original value. The frequency of oscillation becomes
questions.e: f = (1/2π)√(k/m), so f is proportional to 1/√m; with 4m, f becomes 1/√4 = ½ of the original. One quarter forgets the square root, and twice as large applies to the period, not the frequency.

questions.s: A particle executes SHM with amplitude 0.05 m and angular frequency 20 rad/s. Its maximum speed is
questions.e: v(max) = ωA = 20 × 0.05 = 1 m/s, reached at the mean position. The value 20 is ω²A, the maximum acceleration in m/s², not the speed.

questions.s: A body oscillates in SHM with amplitude 8 cm and angular frequency 5 rad/s. Its maximum acceleration is
questions.e: a(max) = ω²A = 25 × 0.08 = 2 m/s², at the extreme positions. The value 0.4 is ωA, the maximum speed in m/s, and 62.5 divides ω² by A instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A particle in SHM has amplitude 10 cm and angular frequency 4 rad/s. Its speed when its displacement is 6 cm is
questions.e: v = ω√(A² − x²) = 4√(100 − 36) = 4 × 8 = 32 cm/s. The value 40 cm/s is the maximum speed ωA at the mean position, and 24 cm/s is ωx, which wrongly makes the speed grow with displacement.

questions.s: A particle executes SHM of amplitude A. Its speed is half of its maximum speed when its displacement from the mean position is
questions.e: Set ω√(A² − x²) = ωA/2: A² − x² = A²/4, so x² = 3A²/4 and x = (√3/2)A. The tempting A/2 assumes speed falls linearly with displacement, which it does not.

questions.s: A particle executes SHM of amplitude A. Its kinetic energy equals its potential energy when its displacement is
questions.e: PE = ½kx² and total E = ½kA². KE = PE means PE = E/2, so x² = A²/2 and x = A/√2. At x = A/2 the PE is only a quarter of the total energy.

questions.s: If the amplitude of a simple harmonic oscillator is doubled, keeping the spring and mass the same, its total energy becomes
questions.e: Total energy E = ½kA² = ½mω²A² is proportional to A², so doubling A multiplies E by 4. The period does not change with amplitude, which is why one might wrongly think the energy is unchanged.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg block attached to a spring of spring constant 200 N/m oscillates with amplitude 10 cm on a smooth surface. Its kinetic energy when the displacement is 5 cm is
questions.e: Total energy = ½kA² = ½ × 200 × 0.1² = 1 J, and PE at x = 0.05 m = ½ × 200 × 0.05² = 0.25 J, so KE = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75 J. The value 0.25 J is the PE at that point, and 0.5 J wrongly assumes energy shares in proportion to x rather than x².

questions.s: In simple harmonic motion, the phase difference between the displacement and the velocity is
questions.e: With x = A sin ωt, v = ωA cos ωt = ωA sin(ωt + π/2), so velocity leads displacement by π/2. That is why v is maximum when x = 0 and zero when x is maximum.

questions.s: In simple harmonic motion, the phase difference between the displacement and the acceleration is
questions.e: a = −ω²x, so acceleration is always opposite to displacement: a = ω²A sin(ωt + π). The phase difference is π. A difference of π/2 is between displacement and velocity, not acceleration.

questions.s: The displacement of a particle is given by x = 0.04 sin(10πt) metre, with t in seconds. The frequency of the motion is
questions.e: Compare with x = A sin ωt: ω = 10π rad/s, so f = ω/2π = 10π/2π = 5 Hz. Reading 10π directly as the frequency mistakes angular frequency for frequency, and 0.2 is the period in seconds.

questions.s: A particle moves according to x = 3 sin(2t + π/4) cm, with t in seconds. Its maximum acceleration is
questions.e: Here A = 3 cm and ω = 2 rad/s, so a(max) = ω²A = 4 × 3 = 12 cm/s². The initial phase π/4 does not affect the maximum value. The value 6 is ωA, the maximum speed in cm/s.

questions.s: A particle moves round a circle of radius 5 cm at a steady 2 revolutions per second. The projection of the particle on a diameter executes SHM. The maximum speed of this projection is
questions.e: The projection has amplitude equal to the radius, 5 cm, and ω = 2πf = 4π rad/s, so v(max) = ωA = 4π × 5 = 20π cm/s. This equals the particle's own speed on the circle. Using ω = 2π (1 rev/s) gives 10π cm/s.

questions.s: A spring stretches by 10 cm when a mass is hung from it at rest. Taking g = 10 m/s², the time period with which the mass oscillates up and down on this spring is
questions.e: At equilibrium kx = mg, so m/k = x/g = 0.1/10 = 0.01 s², and T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π × 0.1 = 0.2π s. The mass itself is not needed. The option 0.1π s drops the 2 of 2π, and 2π s comes from putting the extension in centimetres, √(10/10) = 1.

questions.s: A mass on a single spring oscillates with period T₀. The same mass is now hung from two such identical springs joined end to end (in series). The new period is
questions.e: Two identical springs in series have effective constant k/2 (each stretches by the same force, so the extension doubles). T = 2π√(m/(k/2)) = √2 × 2π√(m/k) = √2 T₀. T₀/√2 is the result for the parallel arrangement, where the effective constant is 2k.

questions.s: A mass on a spring oscillates with period T₀. The spring is cut into two equal halves and the same mass is attached to one half. The new period is
questions.e: Half the spring stretches half as much for the same force, so its spring constant is 2k. T = 2π√(m/2k) = T₀/√2. The answer T₀/2 forgets the square root in the period formula.

questions.s: Free oscillations of a body are oscillations
o: at its natural frequency with no external periodic force
at the frequency of an applied periodic force
that grow in amplitude without any limit
that occur only when the body is in a vacuum
questions.e: A body displaced and then left alone oscillates freely at its own natural frequency, which depends only on its properties (for example m and k, or l and g). Oscillations at the frequency of an applied periodic force are forced oscillations.

questions.s: When a body is made to oscillate by an external periodic force, it vibrates with
o: its own natural frequency in every case
the frequency of the driving force
a frequency that keeps on rising
questions.e: In forced oscillations the driver imposes its own frequency on the body after the initial motion dies away. The natural frequency matters only in deciding how large the amplitude is; when the two are equal, resonance occurs.

questions.s: Resonance occurs when
o: the driving frequency equals the natural frequency
the driving force is removed completely
the damping force becomes very large
the amplitude of the driver is zero
questions.e: At resonance the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, so energy is fed in at exactly the right moment in each cycle and the amplitude becomes maximum. Large damping reduces the resonant amplitude rather than causing resonance.

questions.s: Damping in an oscillating system
o: gradually reduces the amplitude as energy is lost
questions.e: Damping forces such as friction and air resistance do negative work, converting the oscillator's mechanical energy into heat. Since E is proportional to A², the amplitude steadily decreases. A constant amplitude would need no losses, or an energy supply as in forced oscillations.

questions.s: Tuning a radio receiver to pick up one particular station is an example of
questions.e: Turning the tuning knob changes the natural frequency of the receiver's electrical circuit. When it equals the frequency of the station's waves, that signal produces a large response while other stations produce very little, which is resonance.

questions.s: For a driven oscillator, increasing the damping makes the graph of amplitude against driving frequency
questions.e: With more damping, more energy is lost per cycle, so the maximum amplitude at resonance is smaller and the response is spread over a wider range of frequencies. Light damping gives the high, sharp peak.

questions.s: Soldiers marching across a bridge are told to break step. The main reason is to avoid
questions.e: Marching in step applies a periodic force to the bridge. If its frequency matched the bridge's natural frequency, resonance would build up a dangerously large amplitude. Breaking step makes the forces irregular, so no single frequency is driven.

questions.s: Shock absorbers in a car's suspension are a practical use of
o: forced oscillation at the natural frequency
questions.e: Shock absorbers convert the energy of the springs' oscillations into heat in oil, so the car body stops bouncing quickly after a bump. Resonance or driving at the natural frequency would make the bouncing worse, not better.

questions.s: A displaced oscillating system that returns to its equilibrium position in the shortest possible time, without oscillating, is said to be
questions.e: Critical damping is just enough to prevent any overshoot, so the system returns to equilibrium fastest without oscillating; car suspensions are designed close to it. Light damping still allows several oscillations of falling amplitude, and an undamped system oscillates forever.

questions.s: A simple pendulum has a period T on the Earth. On the Moon, where the acceleration due to gravity is one sixth of that on the Earth, the period of the same pendulum is
questions.e: T = 2π√(l/g) is proportional to 1/√g, so with g/6 the period becomes √6 times larger, about 2.45T. The pendulum swings more slowly where gravity is weaker; T/√6 would mean it swings faster.

questions.s: A simple pendulum has period T in a stationary lift. Taking g = 10 m/s², its period when the lift accelerates upwards at 5 m/s² is
questions.e: In a lift accelerating upwards the effective gravity is g + a = 15 m/s². Since T is proportional to 1/√g, T′ = T√(10/15) = T√(2/3), shorter than T. Using g − a = 5 m/s² would give T√2, the result for downward acceleration.

questions.s: A simple pendulum with period T on the ground is taken into a lift that is falling freely. In the lift, the pendulum
questions.e: In free fall the effective gravity is g − g = 0, so there is no restoring force and T = 2π√(l/0) becomes infinite: displaced, the bob simply stays where it is. A period of zero would mean infinitely fast swings, the opposite of what happens.

questions.s: Two simple pendulums at the same place have lengths 1 m and 4 m. The ratio of their frequencies (shorter : longer) is
questions.e: f = (1/2π)√(g/l), so f is proportional to 1/√l: f₁/f₂ = √(4/1) = 2. The shorter pendulum swings faster. The ratio 1 : 2 is for the periods, not the frequencies.

questions.s: A mass on a spring of spring constant 50 N/m is displaced 4 cm from its equilibrium position. The restoring force on it is
o: 2 N away from the mean position
questions.e: By Hooke's law F = −kx = −50 × 0.04 = −2 N: magnitude 2 N, directed opposite to the displacement, that is towards the mean position. Using x = 4 (in cm) gives 200 N, and the force can never point away from the mean position in SHM.

questions.s: A particle executes SHM with angular frequency 10 rad/s. The magnitude of its acceleration when its displacement is 3 cm is
questions.e: a = ω²x = 100 × 0.03 = 3 m/s² (directed towards the mean position). Using ωx instead of ω²x gives 0.3 m/s², and leaving x in centimetres gives 300.

questions.s: A body in SHM has an acceleration of 16 m/s² when its displacement is 4 cm. Its time period is
questions.e: ω² = a/x = 16/0.04 = 400, so ω = 20 rad/s and T = 2π/ω = 2π/20 = π/10 s. Taking T = π/ω forgets the factor 2 and gives π/20 s.

questions.s: A particle in SHM has a maximum speed of 2 m/s and a maximum acceleration of 8 m/s². Its amplitude is
questions.e: a(max)/v(max) = ω²A/ωA = ω = 8/2 = 4 rad/s, and then A = v(max)/ω = 2/4 = 0.5 m. The value 4 is ω, not the amplitude, and 0.25 m divides by ω twice.

questions.s: A particle in SHM of period T starts from the mean position. The shortest time it takes to reach a displacement of half the amplitude is
questions.e: x = A sin ωt = A/2 gives ωt = π/6, so t = (π/6)/(2π/T) = T/12. It is not T/8 (half of the quarter period T/4), because the particle moves fastest near the mean position and covers the first half-amplitude quickly.

questions.s: A particle in SHM of period T starts from an extreme position. The shortest time it takes to reach a displacement of half the amplitude is
questions.e: From the extreme, x = A cos ωt = A/2 gives ωt = π/3, so t = (π/3)/(2π/T) = T/6. The particle is slow near the extreme, so it takes longer than the T/12 needed for the half-amplitude next to the mean position.

questions.s: A particle in SHM of amplitude A and angular frequency ω is at its positive extreme position at t = 0. Its displacement at time t is
questions.e: At t = 0, A cos 0 = A, the positive extreme, as required. A sin ωt and A sin(ωt + π) both give x = 0 at t = 0 (start at the mean position), and −A cos ωt starts at the negative extreme.

questions.s: The phase of a particle executing SHM tells us
o: its displacement and direction of motion at that instant
questions.e: The phase, the angle ωt + φ in x = A sin(ωt + φ), fixes where the particle is in its cycle: its displacement and which way it is moving. The energy depends on amplitude, not on phase.

questions.s: For a mass-spring system in SHM, a graph of potential energy against displacement is
o: a parabola with its minimum at the mean position
a straight line through the origin
a parabola with its maximum at the mean position
questions.e: U = ½kx² is a parabola, zero at x = 0 and rising to ½kA² at the extremes. A horizontal line describes the total energy, and the kinetic energy curve is the inverted parabola with its maximum at the mean position.

questions.s: A body oscillates in SHM with frequency f. Its kinetic energy varies periodically with frequency
questions.e: K = ½mv² with v = ωA cos ωt gives K = ½mω²A² cos²ωt = ¼mω²A²(1 + cos 2ωt), which repeats at 2ω, that is frequency 2f. Physically, KE is maximum twice per oscillation, once each way through the mean position.

questions.s: In an undamped simple harmonic oscillator, the total mechanical energy
o: is maximum at the mean position only
is zero at the extreme positions
varies as the square of the displacement
questions.e: Without damping, energy only changes form: KE + PE = ½kA² at every point. It is the PE, not the total, that varies as x², and the KE, not the total, that is zero at the extremes.

questions.s: The motion of a simple pendulum is simple harmonic only for small amplitudes because
o: the tension in the string vanishes at small angles
air resistance disappears for small swings
the mass of the bob changes at large angles
sin θ ≈ θ (in radians) only when θ is small
questions.e: The restoring force is mg sin θ. Only for small θ is sin θ ≈ θ = x/l, giving F = −(mg/l)x, which is proportional to displacement as SHM requires. At large angles sin θ is noticeably less than θ, so the motion is periodic but not simple harmonic.

questions.s: The time period of a mass-spring system does not depend on
o: the mass attached to the spring
questions.e: T = 2π√(m/k) contains only the mass and the spring constant, so a larger or smaller amplitude gives the same period (as long as Hooke's law holds). A bigger amplitude simply means a larger maximum speed.

questions.s: A body vibrates with a frequency of 50 Hz. Its angular frequency is
questions.e: ω = 2πf = 2π × 50 = 100π rad/s. Writing ω = πf gives 50π, and 25/π comes from dividing by 2π instead of multiplying.

questions.s: The amplitude of a simple harmonic motion is
o: the maximum displacement from the mean position
the total distance covered in one full oscillation
the distance between the two extreme positions
the time taken for one oscillation
questions.e: Amplitude A is the greatest distance of the body from its mean position, reached at each extreme. The distance between the two extremes is 2A, and the distance covered in one full oscillation is 4A.

questions.s: A particle executes SHM with amplitude 5 cm. The total distance it travels in one complete oscillation is
questions.e: In one oscillation the particle goes from the mean position to one extreme, back, to the other extreme and back: 4A = 4 × 5 = 20 cm. Zero is its displacement after a full cycle, not the distance travelled.

questions.s: Which of the following motions is simple harmonic (for small displacements)?
o: A mass vibrating on a light spring
A ball bouncing on a hard floor
The Earth moving round the Sun
A car moving at constant speed on a road
questions.e: A mass on a spring feels F = −kx, a restoring force proportional to displacement, which is the condition for SHM. A bouncing ball has a constant downward acceleration between bounces, and the Earth's orbit is periodic but its acceleration is not proportional to a displacement from a mean position.

questions.s: The displacement-time graph of a particle executing SHM is
questions.e: The displacement is x = A sin(ωt + φ), so the graph is a sine (sinusoidal) curve repeating every period T. A parabola is the PE-displacement graph, not the displacement-time graph.

questions.s: The length of a simple pendulum is increased by 21 %. Its time period increases by
questions.e: T is proportional to √l, so the new period is √1.21 = 1.1 times the old one, an increase of 10 %. Forgetting the square root gives 21 %, and squaring instead (1.21² ≈ 1.46) gives 46 %.

questions.s: A 2 kg body executes SHM with angular frequency 5 rad/s and amplitude 0.2 m. Its total energy is
questions.e: E = ½mω²A² = ½ × 2 × 25 × 0.04 = 1 J. Dropping the ½ gives 2 J, and forgetting to square the amplitude gives ½ × 2 × 25 × 0.2 = 5 J.

questions.s: When an extra 0.3 kg is added to the mass hanging on a spring, the period of vertical oscillation doubles. The original mass was
questions.e: T is proportional to √m, so doubling T needs four times the mass: m + 0.3 = 4m, giving m = 0.1 kg. Assuming T proportional to m gives m + 0.3 = 2m and m = 0.3 kg.

questions.s: A pendulum clock keeps correct time in winter. In summer its pendulum is 0.2 % longer. There are 86 400 s in a day. In summer the clock
questions.e: T is proportional to √l, so a 0.2 % longer pendulum has a period about 0.1 % longer (√1.002 ≈ 1.001). The clock ticks slower and loses 0.001 × 86 400 ≈ 86 s per day. Forgetting the square root gives 173 s, and a longer period can never make the clock gain.

questions.s: For small swings, the time period of a simple pendulum depends on
o: the length of the string and g
questions.e: T = 2π√(l/g): only the length and the acceleration due to gravity appear. Mass and material cancel out, and for small angles the period is independent of amplitude.

questions.s: A pendulum makes 30 complete oscillations in 15 s. Its time period is
questions.e: T = total time/number of oscillations = 15/30 = 0.5 s. The value 2 is the frequency in hertz (30/15), not the period.

questions.s: For a mass oscillating on a horizontal spring, at the equilibrium position
questions.e: At x = 0 the spring is at its natural length, so elastic PE, restoring force and acceleration are all zero, and all the energy is kinetic. The PE, force and acceleration are greatest at the extreme positions.

questions.s: A singer holds a note that shatters a thin wine glass. This happens because of
questions.e: When the frequency of the note equals the natural frequency of the glass, the sound drives the glass at resonance and its vibration amplitude builds up until the glass breaks. Damping would reduce the vibration, not increase it.

questions.s: For a mass m on a spring of spring constant k, the angular frequency of oscillation is
questions.e: From ma = −kx, a = −(k/m)x, and comparing with a = −ω²x gives ω = √(k/m). The expression 2π√(m/k) is the time period, not the angular frequency.

questions.s: A 1 kg mass oscillates on a spring of spring constant 100 N/m. Its frequency of oscillation is
questions.e: ω = √(k/m) = √100 = 10 rad/s, so f = ω/2π = 10/2π = 5/π Hz (about 1.6 Hz). The value π/5 is the period in seconds, and 10 is ω, not f.

questions.s: On the Earth (taking g = π² m/s²) a seconds pendulum is 1 m long. On a planet where the acceleration due to gravity is one quarter of the Earth's value, the length of a seconds pendulum is
questions.e: For the same period T = 2π√(l/g), l/g must stay the same, so l is proportional to g: 1 × ¼ = 0.25 m. Taking l proportional to √g gives 0.5 m, and 4 m inverts the relation.

questions.s: A 1 kg mass on a spring of spring constant 400 N/m oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Its maximum speed is
questions.e: ω = √(k/m) = √400 = 20 rad/s, so v(max) = ωA = 20 × 0.1 = 2 m/s. Using ω² = 400 instead of ω gives 40, which is the maximum acceleration in m/s².

questions.s: A spring of spring constant 100 N/m carries a mass that oscillates with amplitude 0.2 m. The total energy of the oscillation is
questions.e: E = ½kA² = ½ × 100 × 0.04 = 2 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 4 J, and forgetting to square A gives ½ × 100 × 0.2 = 10 J.

questions.s: The displacement of a particle is x = 5 sin(4πt + π/3) cm, with t in seconds. Its phase at t = 1/12 s is
questions.e: Phase = 4πt + π/3 = 4π/12 + π/3 = π/3 + π/3 = 2π/3. The value π/3 is only the initial phase (at t = 0).

questions.s: A pendulum left swinging in air gradually comes to rest. Its mechanical energy has mainly been
o: destroyed by the pull of gravity
stored as extra PE of the bob
given to the Earth as kinetic energy
changed into heat by air resistance and friction
questions.e: Air resistance and friction at the support damp the motion: they do negative work and turn the oscillation energy into internal energy (heat) of the air and the support. Energy is not destroyed, and the bob ends at its lowest point, so it has less PE, not more.

questions.s: Bilal wants a child's swing to go higher using only small pushes. The pushes should be given
o: once every natural period of the swing
whenever the swing moves towards him
questions.e: Pushing once each cycle, always in the direction of motion, drives the swing at its natural frequency, so energy is added every cycle and the amplitude grows (resonance). Pushing when the swing moves towards him opposes the motion and takes energy out.

questions.s: A particle executes SHM of amplitude A. When its displacement is A/2, the ratio of its kinetic energy to its potential energy is
questions.e: PE = ½k(A/2)² = ¼ of the total ½kA², so KE = ¾ of the total and KE : PE = 3 : 1. Reversing the ratio to 1 : 3 gives the situation at x = (√3/2)A.

questions.s: A particle in SHM has amplitude 5 cm and maximum speed 10 cm/s. Its speed when the displacement is 3 cm is
questions.e: ω = v(max)/A = 10/5 = 2 rad/s, so v = ω√(A² − x²) = 2√(25 − 9) = 2 × 4 = 8 cm/s. Using ω(A − x) = 2 × 2 gives 4 cm/s, and 6 cm/s is ωx, which makes the speed grow with displacement.

questions.s: A mass hung on a spring produces a static extension of 25 cm. A simple pendulum has the same time period as the mass oscillating on this spring. The length of the pendulum is
questions.e: At equilibrium kx = mg, so m/k = x/g and T = 2π√(x/g). A pendulum has T = 2π√(l/g), so equal periods need l = x = 25 cm. Doubling to 50 cm or quadrupling to 100 cm would wrongly bring in factors from the spring energy formula.

questions.s: A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels is called a
questions.e: In a transverse wave the particle motion is perpendicular to the direction of propagation, as on a stretched string. In a longitudinal (pressure) wave such as sound in air, particles vibrate along the direction of travel. A stationary wave is a superposition pattern, not a type defined by vibration direction.

questions.s: A sound of frequency 680 Hz travels in air at 340 m/s. Its wavelength is
questions.e: λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. Dividing the other way, f/v = 2, gives 2.0 m⁻¹, which is not even a wavelength; 0.25 m would need a frequency of 1360 Hz.

questions.s: When a wave passes from one medium into another, which quantity stays the same?
questions.e: The frequency is fixed by the source, so it does not change at the boundary. The speed depends on the medium, and since v = fλ the wavelength changes with it. Direction can change by refraction, so it is not conserved either.

questions.s: A progressive wave is described by y = 0.05 sin(20πt − 0.5πx), where x and y are in metres and t in seconds. The speed of the wave is
questions.e: Comparing with y = A sin(ωt − kx): ω = 20π rad/s and k = 0.5π rad/m, so v = ω/k = 20π/0.5π = 40 m/s. Using ω × k or k/ω gives wrong values such as 0.025 m/s; 10 m/s comes from taking f = 10 Hz and λ = 1 m instead of λ = 2π/k = 4 m.

questions.s: For the wave y = 0.02 sin(100πt − 4πx) in SI units, the frequency and wavelength are
questions.e: ω = 100π gives f = ω/2π = 50 Hz, and k = 4π gives λ = 2π/k = 0.5 m. Reading the coefficients directly as f = 100 Hz or λ = 4 m forgets the factor 2π.

questions.s: In a sound wave, the distance between the centre of a compression and the centre of the next rarefaction is
questions.e: A compression and the next compression are one wavelength apart, and a rarefaction lies midway between them, so the compression-to-rarefaction distance is λ/2. λ is the compression-to-compression distance, not this one.

questions.s: Two points on a progressive wave of wavelength 1.0 m are 0.25 m apart along the direction of travel. The phase difference between them is
questions.e: Phase difference Δφ = (2π/λ)Δx = 2π × 0.25/1.0 = π/2 rad. A separation of λ/2 would give π, and a full wavelength 2π; π/4 comes from forgetting the factor 2.

questions.s: Which of the following cannot travel through a vacuum?
questions.e: Sound is a mechanical wave: it needs particles of a medium to pass on compressions and rarefactions, so it cannot cross a vacuum. Light, radio waves and X-rays are electromagnetic waves and travel through empty space.

questions.s: A source makes 30 complete vibrations in 6 s and produces waves of wavelength 2 m. The speed of the waves is
questions.e: f = 30/6 = 5 Hz, so v = fλ = 5 × 2 = 10 m/s. Multiplying 30 × 2 = 60 m/s forgets to divide by the time, and 2.5 m/s comes from dividing f by λ.

questions.s: The amplitude of a sound wave is doubled while its frequency stays the same. The intensity of the wave becomes
questions.e: The energy carried by a wave, and so its intensity, is proportional to the square of the amplitude: I ∝ A². Doubling A gives 2² = 4 times the intensity. Choosing 2 times assumes intensity is proportional to amplitude itself.

questions.s: A wave on a rope is given by y = 0.04 sin(50t − 2x) in SI units. The maximum speed of a particle of the rope is
questions.e: Particle velocity is ∂y/∂t = 0.04 × 50 cos(50t − 2x), so its maximum is Aω = 0.04 × 50 = 2 m/s. The wave speed ω/k = 25 m/s is a different quantity: it is how fast the shape moves, not how fast a particle moves. 0.08 m/s wrongly uses Ak.

questions.s: The tension in a stretched string is made four times larger, with nothing else changed. The speed of transverse waves on the string becomes
questions.e: v = √(T/μ), so v ∝ √T. Four times the tension gives √4 = 2 times the speed. Four times would mean v ∝ T, which forgets the square root.

questions.s: A string 50 cm long has a mass of 5 g and is kept under a tension of 100 N. The speed of transverse waves on it is
questions.e: μ = 0.005 kg / 0.5 m = 0.01 kg/m, so v = √(T/μ) = √(100/0.01) = √10⁴ = 100 m/s. 10⁴ m/s is T/μ without the square root, and 10 m/s uses √T alone.

questions.s: In deriving his formula for the speed of sound in air, Newton assumed that the compressions and rarefactions take place
questions.e: Newton took the changes to be isothermal, so he used the isothermal bulk modulus E = P and got v = √(P/ρ), about 280 m/s for air at 0 °C. Laplace later showed the changes are adiabatic because they are too fast for heat exchange.

questions.s: Laplace's correction changes Newton's value of the speed of sound in a gas by a factor of (γ = ratio of the molar specific heats)
questions.e: For adiabatic changes the bulk modulus is γP instead of P, so v = √(γP/ρ) = √γ × √(P/ρ). The speed rises by √γ, not by γ, because the modulus sits under the square root.

questions.s: A gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa has a density of 1.0 kg/m³ and γ = 1.6. Using Laplace's formula, the speed of sound in the gas is
questions.e: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(1.6 × 10⁵/1.0) = √(16 × 10⁴) = 400 m/s. Newton's formula √(P/ρ) gives about 316 m/s, which is the uncorrected value; 250 m/s comes from dividing by γ.

questions.s: The speed of sound in air at 27 °C is v. At what temperature will the speed of sound in air be 2v?
questions.e: v ∝ √T with T in kelvin, so doubling v needs T = 4 × 300 K = 1200 K, which is 1200 − 273 = 927 °C. 108 °C multiplies the Celsius value by 4, and 1200 °C forgets to convert back from kelvin.

questions.s: For an ideal gas kept at a fixed temperature, the speed of sound in it does NOT depend on
o: the molar mass of the gas
the value of γ for the gas
questions.e: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(γRT/M). At fixed temperature, raising P raises ρ in the same ratio, so P/ρ and hence v are unchanged. Temperature, molar mass and γ all appear in √(γRT/M), so v does depend on them.

questions.s: The speed of sound in air is 332 m/s at 0 °C and increases by about 0.61 m/s for every 1 °C rise. In Lahore on a day when the air is at 20 °C, the speed of sound is about
questions.e: v ≈ 332 + 0.61 × 20 = 332 + 12.2 ≈ 344 m/s. Adding 20 m/s directly (352 m/s) treats the rate as 1 m/s per °C, and 332.6 m/s adds the rate only once.

questions.s: Hydrogen (molar mass 2 g/mol) and oxygen (molar mass 32 g/mol) are both diatomic and at the same temperature. The ratio of the speed of sound in hydrogen to that in oxygen is
questions.e: v = √(γRT/M) with the same γ and T, so v ∝ 1/√M and vH/vO = √(32/2) = √16 = 4. 16 forgets the square root, and 1/4 inverts the ratio: the lighter gas carries sound faster.

questions.s: When two waves overlap in a medium, the resultant displacement of a particle at any instant equals
o: the sum of the individual displacements
the product of the individual displacements
the larger of the two displacements
the difference of the two amplitudes
questions.e: By the principle of superposition, the resultant displacement is the algebraic (vector) sum of the displacements each wave would produce alone. Signs are included, so the sum can be smaller than either one; it is not a product or simply the larger value.

questions.s: Two coherent sources in phase emit waves of wavelength 0.4 m. At a point where the path difference from the two sources is 1.0 m, the interference is
questions.e: Path difference/λ = 1.0/0.4 = 2.5, so the path difference is 5λ/2, an odd multiple of λ/2. For in-phase sources this gives destructive interference. Constructive interference would need a whole number of wavelengths such as 0.8 m or 1.2 m.

questions.s: A steady interference pattern can be obtained only if the two sources have
questions.e: The sources must be coherent: same frequency and a constant phase difference, so the positions of maxima and minima do not shift. Equal amplitudes improve the contrast but are not enough, and a random phase makes the pattern wash out.

questions.s: Two coherent sound waves of the same frequency have amplitudes 3 mm and 5 mm. The ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity in their interference pattern is
questions.e: Maximum amplitude = 5 + 3 = 8 mm and minimum = 5 − 3 = 2 mm. Intensity ∝ amplitude², so Imax/Imin = (8/2)² = 16 : 1. 4 : 1 is only the amplitude ratio, and 25 : 9 compares the two separate waves instead of the maxima and minima.

questions.s: Two in-phase sources emit waves of wavelength 0.6 m. The smallest path difference that gives destructive interference is
questions.e: Destructive interference needs a path difference of (n + ½)λ; the smallest is λ/2 = 0.3 m. A path difference of 0.6 m = λ gives constructive interference, and 0.15 m = λ/4 gives neither a maximum nor a minimum.

questions.s: Beats are heard when two sound waves travelling in the same direction have
o: the same frequency but opposite directions
questions.e: Beats are the regular rise and fall of loudness when two waves of slightly different frequencies superpose; the beat frequency is f₁ − f₂. Equal frequencies give no beats, and waves of the same frequency moving in opposite directions form a stationary wave instead.

questions.s: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. The number of beats heard per second is
questions.e: Beat frequency = f₁ − f₂ = 260 − 256 = 4 per second. 258 Hz is the average frequency, which is the pitch heard, not the beat rate, and 516 adds the frequencies.

questions.s: Two sources of frequencies 300 Hz and 304 Hz sound together. The time between two successive moments of maximum loudness is
questions.e: The beat frequency is 304 − 300 = 4 Hz, so the time between successive loud sounds is 1/4 = 0.25 s. 4 s confuses the beat frequency with the beat period, and 0.5 s halves the frequency difference wrongly.

questions.s: A tuning fork of unknown frequency gives 5 beats per second with a fork of 400 Hz. When the prongs of the unknown fork are filed slightly, it gives 3 beats per second with the same 400 Hz fork. The original frequency of the unknown fork was
questions.e: Filing a fork makes its prongs lighter and raises its frequency. The original frequency was 405 Hz or 395 Hz; raising 405 Hz would give more than 5 beats, but raising 395 Hz to about 397 Hz gives 3 beats. So it was 395 Hz; 397 Hz is the value after filing.

questions.s: Which of the following is a practical use of beats?
o: tuning a guitar to a reference note
finding the depth of the sea by echo
questions.e: A musician sounds a string with a reference note and adjusts the tension until the beats slow down and vanish, which means the frequencies match. Depth finding uses echoes, not beats, and the speed of light has nothing to do with sound beats.

questions.s: Two sound waves of frequencies 500 Hz and 506 Hz superpose. The listener hears a tone whose loudness rises and falls 6 times a second. The frequency (pitch) of this tone is
questions.e: The resultant vibration has frequency (f₁ + f₂)/2 = (500 + 506)/2 = 503 Hz, and its amplitude varies at the beat frequency f₂ − f₁ = 6 Hz. 6 Hz is the beat rate, not the pitch, and 1006 Hz forgets to halve the sum.

questions.s: In a stationary wave of frequency 1000 Hz, adjacent nodes are 15 cm apart. The speed of the waves that form it is
questions.e: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart, so λ = 2 × 0.15 = 0.30 m and v = fλ = 1000 × 0.30 = 300 m/s. Taking the node spacing as a full wavelength gives 150 m/s.

questions.s: In a stationary wave, the points where the displacement is always zero are called
questions.e: Nodes are points of permanent zero displacement where the two component waves always cancel. Antinodes are the points of maximum amplitude, midway between nodes; crests and compressions describe progressive waves.

questions.s: In a stationary wave, the distance between a node and the nearest antinode is
questions.e: Nodes are λ/2 apart and each antinode lies halfway between two nodes, so a node and the next antinode are λ/4 apart. λ/2 is the node-to-node (or antinode-to-antinode) spacing.

questions.s: Which statement about a stationary wave on a string is correct?
o: all particles have the same amplitude
particles in adjacent loops move in phase
it carries energy along the string at speed v
particles within one loop vibrate in phase
questions.e: All particles between two adjacent nodes move up and down together, in phase, while particles in neighbouring loops are in antiphase. Amplitude varies from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes, and a stationary wave does not transport energy along the string.

questions.s: A string 1.2 m long is fixed at both ends. Transverse waves travel on it at 240 m/s. The frequency of its fundamental mode is
questions.e: In the fundamental, L = λ/2, so λ = 2.4 m and f₁ = v/2L = 240/2.4 = 100 Hz. Using f = v/L gives 200 Hz (the second harmonic), and v/4L = 50 Hz is the closed-pipe formula.

questions.s: A stretched string has a fundamental frequency of 150 Hz. The frequency of its second overtone is
questions.e: A string fixed at both ends gives all harmonics f, 2f, 3f, …; the first overtone is 2f and the second overtone is the third harmonic, 3 × 150 = 450 Hz. 300 Hz is the first overtone, the common mix-up of overtone number with harmonic number.

questions.s: A string 40 cm long with mass per unit length 0.01 kg/m is fixed at both ends under a tension of 64 N. Its fundamental frequency is
questions.e: v = √(T/μ) = √(64/0.01) = √6400 = 80 m/s, then f₁ = v/2L = 80/0.8 = 100 Hz. Using f = v/L gives 200 Hz, and v/4L gives 50 Hz, which applies to a pipe closed at one end.

questions.s: A string fixed at both ends vibrates at 240 Hz with four loops (segments) between its ends. Its fundamental frequency is
questions.e: With n loops the frequency is n f₁, so f₁ = 240/4 = 60 Hz. Multiplying by 4 (960 Hz) treats the four-loop mode as the fundamental instead of the fourth harmonic.

questions.s: A stationary wave on a string is given by y = 0.06 sin(5πx) cos(200πt), with x and y in metres and t in seconds. The distance between adjacent nodes is
questions.e: Nodes occur where sin(5πx) = 0, i.e. 5πx = nπ, so x = n/5 m; adjacent nodes are 0.2 m apart. Equivalently k = 5π gives λ = 2π/k = 0.4 m and node spacing λ/2 = 0.2 m. 0.4 m is the wavelength, not the node spacing.

questions.s: A pipe 0.85 m long is open at both ends. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, its fundamental frequency is
questions.e: An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so L = λ/2 in the fundamental and f₁ = v/2L = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz. 100 Hz uses v/4L, the formula for a pipe closed at one end.

questions.s: A pipe 25 cm long is closed at one end. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, the frequency of its fundamental note is
questions.e: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so L = λ/4 and f₁ = v/4L = 340/1.0 = 340 Hz. 680 Hz uses v/2L, which is the open-pipe formula.

questions.s: A pipe closed at one end can produce
questions.e: The closed end must be a node and the open end an antinode, so L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4, …, giving frequencies f₁, 3f₁, 5f₁, … only. A pipe open at both ends (or a string fixed at both ends) gives all harmonics.

questions.s: For the air column in a pipe closed at one end, the closed end and the open end are respectively a
questions.e: Air cannot move at the closed end, so it is a displacement node, while air at the open end is free to move, giving a displacement antinode. Putting the antinode at the closed end reverses the physical situation.

questions.s: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 200 Hz. If the closed end is opened, keeping the length the same, the new fundamental frequency is
questions.e: Closed pipe: f₁ = v/4L = 200 Hz, so v/L = 800 Hz. Open pipe: f₁ = v/2L = 400 Hz. Opening the pipe halves the effective wavelength of the fundamental (from 4L to 2L), so the frequency doubles rather than halves.

questions.s: Two successive resonance frequencies of a pipe closed at one end are 450 Hz and 750 Hz. The fundamental frequency of the pipe is
questions.e: A closed pipe has only odd harmonics, so successive resonances differ by 2f₁: 750 − 450 = 300 Hz gives f₁ = 150 Hz. Check: 450 = 3 × 150 and 750 = 5 × 150. Taking the difference itself as f₁ (300 Hz) is the open-pipe rule.

questions.s: In a resonance tube experiment with a tuning fork of 500 Hz, the first resonance occurs when the air column is 16 cm long. Ignoring end correction, the speed of sound is
questions.e: The first resonance of a closed column is at L = λ/4, so λ = 4 × 0.16 = 0.64 m and v = 500 × 0.64 = 320 m/s. Taking L = λ/2 gives 160 m/s, and taking L = λ gives 80 m/s.

questions.s: In a resonance tube with a 500 Hz tuning fork, the first and second resonances occur at air-column lengths of 15 cm and 48 cm. The speed of sound in the air is
questions.e: Successive resonances of a closed column differ by λ/2, which also cancels the end correction: 48 − 15 = 33 cm = λ/2, so λ = 0.66 m and v = 500 × 0.66 = 330 m/s. Using 4 × 15 cm directly gives 300 m/s, which ignores the end correction.

questions.s: A pipe 1.0 m long is open at both ends. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, the frequency of its first overtone is
questions.e: Open pipe: f₁ = v/2L = 340/2 = 170 Hz, and all harmonics are present, so the first overtone is 2f₁ = 340 Hz. 170 Hz is the fundamental, and 510 Hz is the second overtone.

questions.s: On a hot day, the fundamental frequency of an organ pipe compared with a cold day is
questions.e: The speed of sound rises with temperature (v ∝ √T) while the pipe length, and so the wavelength of its fundamental, stays almost fixed. Since f = v/λ, the frequency rises. Choosing 'the same' ignores the change in the speed of sound.

questions.s: A source of sound moves towards a stationary listener. Compared with the actual frequency of the source, the frequency heard by the listener
o: is lower at first, then higher
questions.e: As the source approaches, each wave is emitted closer to the previous one, so the wavelength reaching the listener is shorter and the frequency heard is higher (Doppler effect). The pitch drops only after the source has passed and is moving away.

questions.s: A source emitting sound of 600 Hz moves at 40 m/s directly towards a stationary listener. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. The frequency heard is
questions.e: For a moving source, f′ = f × v/(v − u) = 600 × 340/300 = 680 Hz. 671 Hz uses the moving-observer formula f(v + u)/v, which applies when the listener moves, and 560 Hz simply subtracts the speed from the frequency.

questions.s: Ali rides a motorbike at 33 m/s directly towards a stationary siren of frequency 500 Hz. The speed of sound is 330 m/s. The frequency Ali hears is
questions.e: For a moving observer, f′ = f(v + u)/v = 500 × 363/330 = 550 Hz. 556 Hz uses the moving-source formula f × v/(v − u), and 450 Hz is the value for moving away.

questions.s: A train moving at 20 m/s away from a stationary listener blows a whistle of 720 Hz. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, the frequency heard is
questions.e: For a source moving away, f′ = f × v/(v + u) = 720 × 340/360 = 680 Hz. 765 Hz = 720 × 340/320 is the value while the train approaches, and 700 Hz wrongly subtracts the speed from the frequency.

questions.s: A car's horn is heard at 480 Hz by a roadside listener while the car approaches and at 400 Hz after it has passed and is moving away. If the speed of sound is 330 m/s, the speed of the car is
A source of frequency 330 Hz and a listener move directly towards each other, each at 10 m/s, in still air where the speed of sound is 340 m/s. The frequency heard is
questions.e: f′ = f(v + u_o)/(v − u_s) = 330 × 350/330 = 350 Hz. Both motions raise the frequency because the separation is decreasing; 310 Hz would be the result if they moved apart.

questions.s: There is no Doppler change in frequency when
o: both move with the same velocity
questions.e: The Doppler effect depends on relative motion between source and observer. If both move with the same velocity, their separation stays constant and the heard frequency equals the source frequency. In each other case the separation changes, so the frequency changes.

questions.s: Spectral lines in the light from a distant galaxy are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum. This shows that the galaxy is
o: at rest relative to the Earth
questions.e: A red shift means longer wavelength and lower frequency, which by the Doppler effect means the source is receding. A source moving towards us would show a blue shift, and temperature does not shift the positions of spectral lines in this way.

questions.s: A bat flies at 30 m/s directly towards a wall, emitting ultrasound of 40 kHz. The speed of sound is 330 m/s. The frequency of the echo heard by the bat is
questions.e: The wall receives f₁ = 40 × 330/300 = 44 kHz (moving source). The wall re-emits 44 kHz to the bat, which moves towards it: f₂ = 44 × 360/330 = 48 kHz. Combined, f₂ = f(v + u)/(v − u) = 40 × 360/300. 44 kHz stops after the first shift.

questions.s: Steel has Young's modulus 2 × 10¹¹ Pa and density 8000 kg/m³. The speed of longitudinal sound waves along a steel rod is
questions.e: v = √(E/ρ) = √(2 × 10¹¹/8000) = √(2.5 × 10⁷) = 5000 m/s. 2.5 × 10⁷ m/s is E/ρ without the square root. This high speed is why sound travels much faster in solids than in air.

questions.s: At room temperature, sound travels fastest in
questions.e: Solids such as steel have a very large elastic modulus compared with their density, giving speeds of about 5000 m/s. Water gives about 1500 m/s, hydrogen about 1300 m/s and air about 340 m/s.

questions.s: A wave is described by y = 0.1 sin(4πx − 20πt) in SI units. This wave travels
questions.e: For a form sin(kx − ωt) the phase stays constant when x increases with t, so the wave moves along +x. Its speed is ω/k = 20π/4π = 5 m/s. A plus sign between the terms would mean travel along −x, and 80 m/s multiplies ω and k.

questions.s: At the same temperature and pressure, the speed of sound in moist air compared with dry air is
o: less, because moist air is denser
greater, because moist air is less dense
equal, because the pressure is the same
greater, because moist air is denser
questions.e: Water vapour (M = 18 g/mol) is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen it replaces (M ≈ 29 g/mol on average), so moist air has a lower density. Since v = √(γP/ρ), a lower density gives a higher speed. The common belief that humid air is heavier is the trap.

questions.s: Hamza stands 170 m from a tall cliff and claps once. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, he hears the echo after
questions.e: The sound travels to the cliff and back, 2 × 170 = 340 m, so t = 340/340 = 1.0 s. 0.5 s counts only the one-way distance.

questions.s: For air, γ = 1.44. The ratio of the speed of sound given by Laplace's formula to that given by Newton's formula is
questions.e: v_Laplace/v_Newton = √(γP/ρ)/√(P/ρ) = √γ = √1.44 = 1.2. 1.44 forgets the square root, and 0.83 = 1/1.2 is the inverse ratio.

questions.s: The speed of sound in air at 0 °C is 332 m/s. At 273 °C its value is about
questions.e: 273 °C is 546 K, twice 273 K, and v ∝ √T, so v = 332 × √2 ≈ 332 × 1.414 ≈ 470 m/s. 664 m/s assumes v ∝ T, forgetting the square root.

questions.s: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels at 360 m/s. The shortest distance between two points on the wave that differ in phase by π/3 is
questions.e: λ = 360/500 = 0.72 m. Δx = (Δφ/2π)λ = (1/6) × 0.72 = 0.12 m. Treating π/3 as a third of a cycle gives 0.24 m, but π/3 is only one-sixth of 2π.

questions.s: In the wave equation y = A sin(ωt − kx), the quantity k = 2π/λ is called the
questions.e: k = 2π/λ is the (angular) wave number or propagation constant, measured in rad/m. ω = 2πf is the angular frequency, and (ωt − kx) as a whole is the phase.

questions.s: The pitch of a musical note depends mainly on its
questions.e: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds and is set by frequency. Amplitude decides loudness, and the waveform (overtones present) decides the quality or timbre; the speed is the same for all notes in the same air.

questions.s: A ship's sonar sends a pulse straight down and receives the echo from the sea bed 4 s later. If sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water, the depth of the sea is
questions.e: The pulse goes down and back in 4 s, so the one-way time is 2 s and depth = 1500 × 2 = 3000 m. 6000 m forgets that the echo covers the distance twice.

questions.s: A string 0.5 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrating in its fundamental mode is in unison with the fundamental of a pipe 0.25 m long closed at one end. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. The speed of transverse waves on the string is
questions.e: Pipe: f = v/4L = 340/1.0 = 340 Hz. String: f = v_s/2L = v_s/1.0, so v_s = 340 m/s. Using v/2L for the closed pipe gives 680 Hz and hence 680 m/s, which is wrong for a closed pipe.

questions.s: An open pipe and a closed pipe have the same length. The ratio of the fundamental frequency of the open pipe to that of the closed pipe is
questions.e: Open: f = v/2L; closed: f = v/4L. Their ratio is (v/2L)/(v/4L) = 2 : 1. 1 : 2 inverts it: the closed pipe has the longer fundamental wavelength (4L), so the lower frequency.

questions.s: The third harmonic of a pipe closed at one end has the same frequency as the fundamental of a pipe open at both ends. The ratio of the length of the closed pipe to that of the open pipe is
questions.e: Closed third harmonic: 3v/4L_c. Open fundamental: v/2L_o. Setting them equal: 3/4L_c = 1/2L_o, so L_c/L_o = 3/2. 2 : 3 is the inverse ratio.

questions.s: A string 0.9 m long fixed at both ends vibrates in a mode with three antinodes. The wavelength of the waves on the string is
questions.e: Three antinodes means three loops, each λ/2 long, so 3λ/2 = 0.9 m and λ = 0.6 m. 1.8 m is the wavelength of the fundamental (one loop), and 0.3 m is the length of one loop.

questions.s: Human hearing ranges roughly from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s, the corresponding wavelengths are
questions.e: λ = v/f: 340/20 = 17 m and 340/20 000 = 0.017 m = 1.7 cm. A slip in the powers of ten on either value gives the other options.

questions.s: Two waves y₁ = A sin(kx − ωt) and y₂ = A sin(kx + ωt) superpose on a string, giving y = 2A sin kx cos ωt. The amplitude of vibration at x = λ/4 is
questions.e: At x = λ/4, kx = (2π/λ)(λ/4) = π/2 and sin(π/2) = 1, so the amplitude 2A sin kx equals 2A: this point is an antinode. Zero amplitude occurs at x = 0, λ/2, λ, …, which are the nodes.

questions.s: Two loudspeakers driven in phase by the same 340 Hz oscillator stand in an open field; the speed of sound is 340 m/s. Sana stands 3.0 m from one speaker and 4.5 m from the other. At her position the sound is
questions.e: λ = 340/340 = 1.0 m, so the path difference 4.5 − 3.0 = 1.5 m = 1.5λ, an odd multiple of λ/2. The waves arrive in antiphase and interfere destructively, so the sound is quiet. A whole number of wavelengths would be needed for a loud point.

questions.s: A source of sound moves directly away from a stationary listener. The listener hears half the frequency emitted by the source when the speed of the source is (v = speed of sound)
questions.e: For a receding source f′ = fv/(v + u). Setting f′ = f/2 gives v + u = 2v, so u = v. Choosing v/2 assumes the frequency falls in proportion to u/v, which is not what the formula says: u = v/2 gives f′ = 2f/3.

questions.s: Two identical strings are both tuned to 200 Hz. The tension in one of them is then increased slightly, and 4 beats per second are heard when both are plucked. The frequency of the tightened string is now
