questions.e: Increasing tension raises the frequency (f ∝ √T), and the beat frequency is the difference, so the tightened string is at 200 + 4 = 204 Hz. 196 Hz would require the tension to be reduced.

questions.s: A string 0.75 m long fixed at both ends has two successive resonant frequencies of 300 Hz and 400 Hz. The speed of transverse waves on the string is
questions.e: For a string fixed at both ends, successive harmonics differ by f₁, so f₁ = 400 − 300 = 100 Hz. Then v = 2Lf₁ = 2 × 0.75 × 100 = 150 m/s. Using v = Lf₁ gives 75 m/s, which forgets that the fundamental wavelength is 2L.

questions.s: Transverse waves of frequency 50 Hz on a long stretched wire have a wavelength of 4 m. Their speed is
questions.e: v = fλ = 50 × 4 = 200 m/s. 12.5 m/s divides f by λ, and 0.08 m/s divides λ by f; neither is the wave equation v = fλ.

questions.s: Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
questions.e: In sound the air particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, producing compressions and rarefactions, so it is longitudinal. Light and radio waves are transverse electromagnetic waves, and waves on a guitar string are transverse mechanical waves.

questions.s: A wave is given by y = 0.03 sin(40πt − πx/2) in SI units. The time period of the wave is
questions.e: ω = 40π rad/s, so f = ω/2π = 20 Hz and T = 1/f = 0.05 s. 20 s confuses the frequency with the period, and 4 s comes from the x-term, which gives the wavelength λ = 2π/(π/2) = 4 m.

questions.s: Newton's formula gives the speed of sound in air at 0 °C as 280 m/s. For air γ = 1.44. The value after Laplace's correction is
questions.e: Laplace's correction multiplies by √γ = √1.44 = 1.2, so v = 280 × 1.2 = 336 m/s, close to the measured 332 m/s. 403 m/s multiplies by γ itself, forgetting the square root.

questions.s: The speed of sound in a gas is 320 m/s at 0 °C. The temperature at which it becomes 640 m/s is
questions.e: v ∝ √T (kelvin), so doubling v needs T = 4 × 273 = 1092 K, which is 1092 − 273 = 819 °C. 273 °C (546 K) only doubles T and gives √2 times the speed, and 1092 °C forgets to convert from kelvin.

questions.s: A string gives 6 beats per second with a 384 Hz tuning fork. When the string is tightened slightly, the beats become fewer. The original frequency of the string was
questions.e: The string was 384 ± 6 Hz, i.e. 390 Hz or 378 Hz. Tightening raises its frequency; the beats decrease only if it moves closer to 384 Hz, so it started below, at 378 Hz. Starting at 390 Hz, tightening would increase the beats.

questions.s: Two waves of equal amplitude and frequency meet at a point. Complete destructive interference occurs there when the phase difference between them is
questions.e: A phase difference of π (or any odd multiple of π) means one wave is at a crest when the other is at a trough, so equal amplitudes cancel. A phase difference of 0 or 2π gives constructive interference.

questions.s: A string 60 cm long is fixed at both ends, and waves travel on it at 120 m/s. The frequency of its second harmonic is
questions.e: f₁ = v/2L = 120/1.2 = 100 Hz, so the second harmonic is 2f₁ = 200 Hz. 100 Hz is the fundamental (first harmonic).

questions.s: A sitar string vibrates at 250 Hz. If its tension is made four times larger without changing its length, its new fundamental frequency is
questions.e: f = (1/2L)√(T/μ), so f ∝ √T. Four times the tension gives √4 = 2 times the frequency: 500 Hz. 1000 Hz treats f as proportional to T.

questions.s: A pipe 0.5 m long is closed at one end. Taking the speed of sound as 320 m/s, the frequency of its first overtone is
questions.e: f₁ = v/4L = 320/2 = 160 Hz, and a closed pipe has only odd harmonics, so the first overtone is 3f₁ = 480 Hz. 320 Hz would be the second harmonic, which a closed pipe cannot produce.

questions.s: In the fundamental mode of a pipe open at both ends, the number of displacement nodes in the air column is
questions.e: Both open ends are displacement antinodes, and the fundamental (L = λ/2) has a single node in the middle. Two nodes would belong to the second harmonic, with L = λ.

questions.s: Fatima travels in a car at 32 m/s directly away from a stationary horn of frequency 400 Hz. The speed of sound is 320 m/s. The frequency she hears is
questions.e: For an observer moving away, f′ = f(v − u)/v = 400 × 288/320 = 360 Hz. 364 Hz uses the moving-source formula fv/(v + u), and 440 Hz is the value for moving towards the horn.

questions.s: An ambulance siren of 480 Hz approaches a stationary listener at 20 m/s. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. The frequency heard is
questions.e: For an approaching source, f′ = fv/(v − u) = 480 × 340/320 = 510 Hz. 453 Hz is the receding value 480 × 340/360, and 500 Hz just adds the speed to the frequency.

questions.s: A stationary wave is given by y = 0.02 sin(2πx) cos(100πt) in SI units. The amplitude of vibration of the particle at x = 1/12 m is
questions.e: Amplitude at x is 0.02 sin(2πx) = 0.02 sin(π/6) = 0.02 × ½ = 0.01 m. 0.02 m is the amplitude only at an antinode (x = 1/4 m), and 0.017 m uses cos instead of sin.

questions.s: Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. A gas with the same γ, at the same pressure, has a density four times that of air. The speed of sound in this gas is
questions.e: v = √(γP/ρ); with γ and P the same, v ∝ 1/√ρ. Four times the density gives v = 340/√4 = 170 m/s. 85 m/s forgets the square root, dividing by 4.

questions.s: Light from a point source reaches the Earth from a very distant star. Over a small region near the Earth, the wavefront is
questions.e: A point source gives spherical wavefronts, but at a very large distance the radius is so large that a small part of the sphere is practically flat, so the wavefront is plane. Spherical is the shape close to the source, not far away.

questions.s: According to Huygens' principle, each point on a wavefront
o: reflects the wave back towards the source
acts as a source of secondary wavelets
questions.e: Huygens' principle says every point of a wavefront behaves as a source of secondary spherical wavelets; the new wavefront is the surface tangent to these wavelets after a time t. It says nothing about points absorbing or reflecting the wave.

questions.s: The direction of propagation of light (a ray) is always
o: along the tangent to the wavefront
questions.e: A ray shows the direction in which the wave energy travels, and it is always normal (at 90°) to the wavefront. A ray along the wavefront or tangent to it would mean the wave moves sideways along its own surface of constant phase, which does not happen.

questions.s: Two points P and Q lie on the same wavefront of a light wave. The phase difference between the vibrations at P and Q is
questions.e: A wavefront is defined as the locus of all points vibrating in the same phase, so any two points on it have zero phase difference. A phase difference of π would hold for points half a wavelength apart along the ray, not on one wavefront.

questions.s: A long, narrow illuminated slit acts as a line source of light. Close to the slit, the wavefronts it produces are
questions.e: Every point of a line source sends out wavelets, and together they form surfaces of equal distance from the line, which are cylinders with the slit as axis. Spherical wavefronts come from a point source, and plane wavefronts appear only very far from the source.

questions.s: Two light sources are said to be coherent if they
o: have exactly the same intensity only
questions.e: Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference, which requires the same frequency (wavelength); only then does a steady interference pattern form. Equal intensity or amplitude alone is not enough, because two separate lamps of equal brightness still change phase randomly.

questions.s: In Young's double slit experiment, with slit separation d, screen distance L and wavelength λ, the fringe spacing is
questions.e: Bright fringes lie at y = mλL/d, so neighbouring fringes are separated by Δy = λL/d. Writing λd/L inverts the role of d and L: a larger slit separation actually brings the fringes closer together.

questions.s: In Young's double slit experiment, light of wavelength 600 nm falls on slits 0.3 mm apart and the screen is 1.5 m away. The fringe spacing is
questions.e: Δy = λL/d = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5)/(0.3 × 10⁻³) = 3 × 10⁻³ m = 3 mm. The value 6 mm comes from using half the slit separation, as if d were measured from the centre line.

questions.s: In Young's experiment, the slit separation is doubled and the distance to the screen is halved, with the same light. The fringe spacing becomes
questions.e: Δy = λL/d. Halving L halves Δy and doubling d halves it again, so Δy becomes (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4 of the original. Thinking the two changes cancel gives unchanged, but both act in the same direction.

questions.s: In a Young's double slit set-up, the fringe spacing is 2.0 mm with light of wavelength 500 nm. If the light is changed to wavelength 600 nm and nothing else changes, the fringe spacing becomes
questions.e: Δy is proportional to λ, so Δy = 2.0 × 600/500 = 2.4 mm. The value 1.67 mm uses the inverse ratio 500/600, as if a longer wavelength gave narrower fringes.

questions.s: In Young's experiment, λ = 500 nm, the slit separation is 0.5 mm and the screen is 1 m away. The distance of the third dark fringe from the centre of the pattern is
questions.e: λL/d = (500 × 10⁻⁹ × 1)/(0.5 × 10⁻³) = 1 mm. Dark fringes lie at (m + ½)λL/d, and the third dark fringe has m = 2, so y = 2.5 × 1 mm = 2.5 mm. The value 3 mm is the third bright fringe, and 3.5 mm would be the fourth dark fringe.

questions.s: A complete Young's double slit apparatus is moved from air into water of refractive index 4/3. The fringe spacing
questions.e: In water the wavelength becomes λ/n = 3λ/4 while d and L are unchanged, so Δy = λL/d becomes 3/4 of its value in air. Choosing 4/3 multiplies by n instead of dividing; light slows down and its wavelength shortens in water.

questions.s: Young's double slit experiment is performed with white light. The central fringe is
questions.e: At the centre the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all colours interfere constructively there and the central fringe is white. Coloured fringes appear only away from the centre, where different wavelengths have their maxima at different places.

questions.s: In Young's experiment with light of wavelength 600 nm, the path difference between the waves reaching a point P on the screen is 1.5 μm. At P there is the
questions.e: Path difference/λ = 1.5 μm/0.6 μm = 2.5, an odd number of half wavelengths, so the point is dark. Dark fringes occur at path differences 0.5λ, 1.5λ and 2.5λ, so this is the third dark fringe. Calling it the second dark fringe starts the count at 1.5λ and misses the dark fringe next to the centre.

questions.s: In a Young's double slit experiment, the slits are 2 mm apart and the screen is 2 m away. A span of 10 fringe widths on the screen measures 6 mm. The wavelength of the light is
questions.e: One fringe width is 6/10 = 0.6 mm, and λ = Δy d/L = (0.6 × 10⁻³ × 2 × 10⁻³)/2 = 6 × 10⁻⁷ m = 600 nm. The value 667 nm comes from dividing 6 mm by 9, as if the 10 fringes enclosed only 9 widths.

questions.s: In a Young's double slit experiment, two wavelengths are used together. The third bright fringe of light of wavelength 600 nm falls exactly on the fourth bright fringe of the second light. The second wavelength is
questions.e: Bright fringes lie at y = mλL/d, so coincidence needs 3 × 600 = 4 × λ₂, giving λ₂ = 1800/4 = 450 nm. The value 800 nm comes from writing 4 × 600 = 3λ₂, which swaps the fringe orders.

questions.s: In Young's experiment, either slit alone gives an intensity I at the centre of the screen. With both slits open and the light coherent, the intensity at the central bright fringe is
questions.e: At the central maximum the two waves arrive in phase, so the amplitudes add to 2A, and intensity, being proportional to amplitude squared, becomes 4I. The value 2I adds intensities, which is correct only for incoherent light.

questions.s: Two identical bulbs placed side by side do not produce an interference pattern on a wall because
questions.e: Light from two separate bulbs is emitted by independent atoms whose phases change randomly many millions of times a second, so the phase difference is not constant and any pattern washes out. Brightness, wavelength and speed do not stop interference.

questions.s: The bright colours seen on a thin soap film in sunlight are due to
questions.e: Light reflected from the front and back surfaces of the film interferes; for each thickness some wavelengths reinforce and others cancel, giving colours. Dispersion by a prism also gives colours, but the soap film has no prism action and the colours change with thickness.

questions.s: When light travelling in air is reflected from the surface of glass, the reflected wave undergoes a phase change of
questions.e: Reflection at the boundary with an optically denser medium produces a phase change of π, equivalent to an extra path of λ/2. Reflection from a rarer medium (glass to air inside the glass) gives no phase change, so 'zero' is the case for the other direction.

questions.s: A thin film of refractive index 1.5 is surrounded by air and is lit normally by light of wavelength 600 nm. The minimum thickness for which the film looks bright in reflected light is
questions.e: Reflection from the top surface has a π phase change and from the bottom surface none, so brightness needs 2nt = λ/2, giving t = λ/(4n) = 600/(4 × 1.5) = 100 nm. The value 200 nm comes from 2nt = λ, which ignores the phase change.

questions.s: A soap film in air becomes extremely thin (much thinner than the wavelength of light) just before it bursts. In reflected light it then appears
questions.e: For thickness close to zero the path difference 2nt is negligible, but the wave reflected from the front surface has an extra phase change of π, so the two reflected waves cancel and the film looks dark. Without the phase change one would wrongly expect constructive interference and a white film.

questions.s: A thin oil film of refractive index 1.25 floats on water of refractive index 1.33. For normal incidence, the minimum non-zero thickness of oil that strongly reflects light of wavelength 500 nm is
questions.e: Both reflections (air to oil, oil to water) are from a denser medium, so both have a π change and they cancel out. Constructive reflection then needs 2nt = λ, so t = 500/(2 × 1.25) = 200 nm. The value 100 nm, λ/(4n), wrongly applies the rule for a film with air on both sides.

questions.s: In thin film interference seen in reflected light, the interfering waves are the waves reflected from
o: the top and bottom faces of the film
only the upper surface of the film
two separate lamps placed near the film
only the lower surface of the film
questions.e: Part of the light reflects from the top surface and part enters, reflects from the bottom surface and comes back out; these two coherent parts interfere. A single reflected wave cannot interfere with itself to produce colours.

questions.s: A lens is coated with a thin layer of refractive index 1.38 (the glass has index 1.5) to reduce reflection of light of wavelength 552 nm at normal incidence. The minimum thickness of the coating is
questions.e: Both reflections (air to coating, coating to glass) have a π phase change, so cancellation needs 2nt = λ/2, giving t = λ/(4n) = 552/(4 × 1.38) = 100 nm. The value 138 nm is λ/4 without dividing by n; the wavelength inside the coating is shorter.

questions.s: In the Newton's rings arrangement, a convex lens rests on a flat glass plate. The thin film whose interference produces the rings is
o: a glass film inside the lens
an oil film spread over the lens surface
an air film between lens and plate
a water film below the plate
questions.e: The curved lens surface and the flat plate enclose a wedge-shaped air film whose thickness grows from zero at the point of contact. Light reflected from the top and bottom of this air film interferes and gives the rings. No oil or water is used in the standard arrangement.

questions.s: Newton's rings are viewed in reflected monochromatic light. The central spot, at the point where the lens touches the plate, is
questions.e: At the point of contact the air film has zero thickness, but the wave reflected from the glass plate has an extra phase change of π, so the two reflected waves cancel and the centre is dark. Ignoring this phase change would wrongly predict a bright centre.

questions.s: The fringes in the Newton's rings experiment are circular because
o: the lamp used has a circular shape
the lens absorbs some of the light along circular zones
the plate is polished in circular strokes
the air film thickness is constant along circles
questions.e: Each fringe is a locus of equal film thickness. The air gap below a spherical lens has the same thickness at all points equidistant from the point of contact, that is, along circles. The shape of the lamp has no effect on the fringe shape.

questions.s: In a Newton's rings experiment, the air between the lens and the plate is replaced by water. The rings
questions.e: The condition for a given ring is 2nt = mλ; with water (n = 4/3) the same m is reached at a smaller thickness t, which lies closer to the centre, so the rings shrink. Expecting larger rings treats the higher refractive index as if it lengthened the wavelength.

questions.s: In Newton's rings seen in reflected light, the radius of a dark ring is proportional to the square root of its order. The ratio of the radius of the 1st dark ring to that of the 4th dark ring is
questions.e: Since r ∝ √n, r₁/r₄ = √1/√4 = 1/2, so the ratio is 1:2. The ratio 1:4 takes r proportional to n itself, forgetting the square root.

questions.s: Newton's rings are formed in reflected light of wavelength 600 nm, with an air film. Counting the central dark spot as order zero, the thickness of the air film at the 5th dark ring is
questions.e: With the π phase change at the lower surface, dark rings occur where 2t = mλ, so for m = 5, t = 5 × 600/2 = 1500 nm = 1.5 μm. The value 3.0 μm forgets that the light crosses the film twice, and 1.65 μm uses the bright-ring condition (m + ½)λ.

questions.s: In a Michelson interferometer, the incoming beam of light is divided into two beams by
questions.e: A half-silvered plate (beam splitter) reflects about half the light towards one mirror and transmits the other half to the second mirror, giving two coherent beams. A prism would disperse the light rather than split it into two equal coherent parts.

questions.s: In a Michelson interferometer using light of wavelength 600 nm, the movable mirror is moved through 0.15 mm. The number of fringes that pass the reference mark is
questions.e: Each fringe shift corresponds to a mirror movement of λ/2, so m = 2d/λ = (2 × 0.15 × 10⁻³)/(600 × 10⁻⁹) = 500. The value 250 uses m = d/λ, forgetting that the light travels to the mirror and back.

questions.s: In a Michelson interferometer, the movable mirror is moved through a distance of λ/4. The fringe pattern shifts by
questions.e: Moving the mirror by λ/4 changes the path of that beam by 2 × λ/4 = λ/2, which shifts the pattern by half a fringe, so a bright fringe is replaced by a dark one. One fringe needs a path change of λ, that is, a mirror movement of λ/2.

questions.s: When the movable mirror of a Michelson interferometer is moved through 0.29 mm, 1000 fringes cross the field of view. The wavelength of the light is
questions.e: 2d = mλ gives λ = 2d/m = (2 × 0.29 × 10⁻³)/1000 = 5.8 × 10⁻⁷ m = 580 nm. The value 290 nm uses λ = d/m, missing the factor 2 for the return path.

questions.s: A Michelson interferometer is mainly used to
o: find the focal length of a lens
find the critical angle of glass
find the magnifying power of a telescope
questions.e: By counting fringes as the mirror moves a measured distance, the interferometer gives the wavelength of light (or very small lengths) with high precision. Focal lengths and critical angles are measured with simple ray optics, not interference.

questions.s: Diffraction of light through a slit is most noticeable when the width of the slit is
o: about the size of the wavelength
about a thousand times the wavelength
about a million times the wavelength
about the size of the screen
questions.e: Spreading of light past an opening is significant only when the opening is comparable to the wavelength; for much wider openings the light travels on almost straight. This is why visible light (λ ≈ 500 nm) shows little diffraction through a door or window.

questions.s: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a single slit of width 1.2 μm. The angle of the first minimum from the central direction is
questions.e: For a single slit, the first minimum is at a sin θ = λ, so sin θ = 0.6/1.2 = 0.5 and θ = 30°. The value 60° comes from using cos θ = 0.5.

questions.s: Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through a single slit of width 0.2 mm onto a screen 2 m away. The width of the central bright band is
questions.e: The first minima lie at y = ±λL/a = ±(500 × 10⁻⁹ × 2)/(0.2 × 10⁻³) = ±5 mm, so the central band is 2 × 5 = 10 mm wide. The value 5 mm is only the distance from the centre to one minimum.

questions.s: In a single slit diffraction experiment, the slit is made narrower while the wavelength and screen distance stay the same. The central maximum
questions.e: The angular half-width of the central maximum is given by sin θ = λ/a, so a smaller slit width a gives a larger θ and a wider central band. Expecting a narrower band treats the slit as an aperture that simply casts a smaller shadow image.

questions.s: In the single slit diffraction pattern, the width of the central maximum compared with the width of each secondary maximum is
questions.e: Minima occur at sin θ = λ/a, 2λ/a, 3λ/a, … on both sides. The central maximum stretches from −λ/a to +λ/a, a width of 2λ/a, while each secondary maximum spans only λ/a, so the central one is twice as wide.

questions.s: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through a single slit of width 0.1 mm. The angle between the first minima on the two sides of the central maximum is about
questions.e: For small angles θ ≈ λ/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.1 × 10⁻³) = 6 × 10⁻³ rad to each side, so the angle between the two first minima is 2θ = 1.2 × 10⁻² rad. The value 6 × 10⁻³ rad is the angle on one side only.

questions.s: In single slit diffraction, at a certain angle the path difference between the light from the two edges of the slit is 2λ. In this direction there is the
questions.e: Minima occur where a sin θ = mλ; a path difference of 2λ between the edges gives m = 2, the second minimum. A path difference of 2λ would mean a bright fringe in a double slit, which is the tempting but wrong analogy.

questions.s: For a diffraction grating with grating element d, the condition for the nth order bright line of wavelength λ at angle θ is
questions.e: Light from neighbouring slits of a grating reinforces when its path difference d sin θ is a whole number of wavelengths, so d sin θ = nλ. The cosine form would give the maximum light at θ = 90°, which is not observed.

questions.s: A diffraction grating has 5000 lines per centimetre. Its grating element is
questions.e: d = 1/(5000 per cm) = 2 × 10⁻⁴ cm = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m = 2 μm. The value 0.2 μm comes from treating the figure as lines per millimetre.

questions.s: A grating with 5000 lines per centimetre is lit normally by light of wavelength 500 nm. The angle of the second-order maximum is
questions.e: d = 2 μm, so sin θ = nλ/d = (2 × 0.5)/2 = 0.5 and θ = 30°. The value 15° halves the angle for the first order, but sin θ, not θ, is proportional to n.

questions.s: A grating with grating element 2 μm is lit normally by light of wavelength 450 nm. The highest order of maximum that can be seen is
questions.e: Since sin θ cannot exceed 1, n ≤ d/λ = 2000/450 ≈ 4.4, so the highest whole order is 4. Rounding 4.4 up to 5 would need sin θ greater than 1, which is impossible.

questions.s: Light of wavelength 500 nm falls normally on a diffraction grating, and the first-order maximum appears at 30°. The number of lines per millimetre on the grating is
questions.e: d = nλ/sin θ = 500 nm/0.5 = 1000 nm = 10⁻³ mm, so there are 1/10⁻³ = 1000 lines per mm. The value 2000 comes from taking d = λ = 500 nm, which forgets to divide by sin θ.

questions.s: A grating is lit by light containing wavelengths 400 nm and 600 nm. The third-order maximum of the 400 nm light falls at the same angle as which order of the 600 nm light?
questions.e: Same angle means the same d sin θ, so 3 × 400 = n × 600, giving n = 2. Choosing the third order assumes equal orders always overlap, which happens only for equal wavelengths.

questions.s: The fact that light can be polarised shows that light waves are
questions.e: Polarisation means restricting the vibrations to one plane perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is possible only for transverse waves. Longitudinal waves such as sound vibrate along the direction of travel and cannot be polarised.

questions.s: Sound waves in air cannot be polarised because they are
questions.e: In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate along the direction of travel, so there is no sideways vibration that a polariser could select. Speed or wavelength has nothing to do with it: long radio waves can still be polarised because they are transverse.

questions.s: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ falls on an ideal polaroid sheet. The intensity of the transmitted light is
questions.e: Unpolarised light has vibrations equally in all directions, and a polaroid passes only the component along its axis; averaging cos²θ over all directions gives 1/2, so I = I₀/2. Taking I₀ assumes the polaroid lets all light through, which happens only for light already polarised along its axis.

questions.s: Unpolarised light passes through two ideal polaroids whose transmission axes are perpendicular to each other. The intensity of light coming out of the second polaroid is
questions.e: The first polaroid passes light vibrating along its own axis; the second polaroid, with its axis at 90°, has no component of that vibration to pass (cos² 90° = 0), so no light emerges. One-half is the intensity after the first sheet only.

questions.s: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polariser and then an analyser whose axis makes 60° with that of the polariser. The final intensity is (use Malus's law I = I₁ cos² θ)
questions.e: After the polariser I₁ = I₀/2. Then I = I₁ cos² 60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8. The value 3I₀/8 uses sin² 60° = 3/4 instead of cos² 60°, and I₀/4 forgets that the first sheet already halves the intensity.

questions.s: Light reflected from a glass surface of refractive index √3 is completely plane polarised when the angle of incidence θ satisfies tan θ = n. This angle is
questions.e: tan θ = √3 gives θ = 60°, the polarising (Brewster) angle; at this angle the reflected and refracted rays are at 90° to each other. The value 30° is the angle whose tangent is 1/√3, obtained by inverting n.

questions.s: Which of the following waves cannot be polarised?
questions.e: Ultrasound in air is a sound wave, which is longitudinal, so it cannot be polarised. Radio waves, X-rays and light are all electromagnetic waves, which are transverse and can be polarised even though some of them are invisible.

questions.s: Polaroid sunglasses reduce the glare of sunlight reflected from a wet road mainly because the reflected light is
questions.e: Light reflected from a horizontal surface is partly polarised with its vibrations mostly horizontal; the polaroid lenses have vertical transmission axes and block much of it. Reflection does not change the wavelength, and coherence has nothing to do with glare.

questions.s: Plane polarised light is passed through each of the following. Which one rotates the plane of polarisation?
questions.e: A sugar solution is optically active: it rotates the plane of polarisation by an angle depending on its concentration, which is used to measure sugar content. Pure water and ordinary glass are not optically active and leave the plane unchanged.

questions.s: An object 2 cm tall forms an image 6 cm tall through a lens. The linear magnification is
questions.e: Linear magnification = image height/object height = 6/2 = 3. The value 1/3 divides the other way round, object height by image height.

questions.s: The angular magnification (magnifying power) of an optical instrument is defined as the ratio of the
o: image height to object height, both measured on a screen
image distance to object distance, both measured from the lens
focal length of the objective to the focal length of the eyepiece
angle at the eye due to the image to that due to the object
questions.e: Magnifying power M = θ′/θ, where θ′ is the angle subtended at the eye by the image and θ is the angle subtended by the object when seen directly (at the near point for a microscope). Image height over object height is the linear magnification, a different quantity.

questions.s: The least distance of distinct vision (near point) for a normal adult eye is taken as
questions.e: A normal eye can focus clearly on objects from about 25 cm out to infinity, so d = 25 cm is used in microscope formulas. Objects held nearer than this look blurred.

questions.s: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. The magnification of the real image formed is
questions.e: 1/q = 1/f − 1/p = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so q = 60 cm and M = q/p = 60/30 = 2. The value 1.5 is p/f, which is not a magnification, and 0.5 is p/q, the ratio inverted.

questions.s: In a simple microscope (magnifying glass), the object is placed
o: between F and 2F of the lens
questions.e: A convex lens forms a virtual, erect, magnified image only when the object is inside its focal length, between the lens and F. Objects beyond F give real, inverted images, as in a projector or camera.

questions.s: A convex lens of focal length 5 cm is used as a simple microscope with the final image at the near point (25 cm). Its magnifying power is
questions.e: M = 1 + d/f = 1 + 25/5 = 6. The value 5 is d/f, which is correct only when the image is formed at infinity, not at the near point.

questions.s: A simple microscope must give a magnifying power of 11 with the final image at the near point (25 cm). The focal length of the lens should be
questions.e: From M = 1 + d/f, 11 = 1 + 25/f gives f = 25/10 = 2.5 cm. The value 2.27 cm uses M = d/f (25/11), the formula for an image at infinity.

questions.s: A lens of power +10 dioptres is used as a magnifying glass, with the final image at the near point (25 cm). The magnifying power is
questions.e: f = 1/P = 1/10 m = 10 cm, so M = 1 + d/f = 1 + 25/10 = 3.5. The value 2.5 is d/f, the result for an image at infinity.

questions.s: The image formed by a simple microscope is
questions.e: With the object inside the focal length of a convex lens, the rays leave diverging and appear to come from a virtual, upright, enlarged image on the same side as the object. A real, inverted image needs the object beyond F.

questions.s: Which statement about a compound microscope is correct?
o: The eyepiece has the shorter focal length
The objective has a shorter focal length
The objective is a concave lens
questions.e: Both lenses are convex; the objective has a very short focal length so the object can be placed just outside its focus and give a large real image, which the eyepiece then magnifies. In a telescope, by contrast, the objective has the longer focal length.

questions.s: Compared with the object, the final image seen in a compound microscope is
questions.e: The objective forms a real, inverted, magnified image; the eyepiece acts as a magnifier on it and gives a virtual image without inverting it again. So the final image is virtual, inverted relative to the object and magnified. It is not real, because no screen can catch it.

questions.s: In a compound microscope, the objective produces a linear magnification of 10 and the eyepiece a magnification of 5. The total magnification is
questions.e: The eyepiece magnifies the image already magnified by the objective, so the total is the product, 10 × 5 = 50. Adding them to get 15 treats the lenses as working side by side instead of one after the other.

questions.s: In a compound microscope, the objective (f = 1 cm) has the object 1.25 cm in front of it. The eyepiece (f = 5 cm) forms the final image at the near point, 25 cm. The magnifying power is
questions.e: Objective: 1/q = 1/1 − 1/1.25 = 0.2, so q = 5 cm and M₀ = q/p = 5/1.25 = 4. Eyepiece: Mₑ = 1 + 25/5 = 6. Total M = 4 × 6 = 24. The value 20 takes Mₑ = 25/5 = 5, the result for a final image at infinity.

questions.s: To increase the magnifying power of a compound microscope, one should use
o: an objective and an eyepiece of short focal length
an objective and an eyepiece of long focal length
an objective of long and an eyepiece of short focal length
a concave lens as the eyepiece
questions.e: M ≈ (L/f₀)(1 + d/fₑ), so a smaller f₀ and a smaller fₑ each increase M. A long-focus objective with a short-focus eyepiece describes a telescope, where M = f₀/fₑ.

questions.s: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. In normal adjustment its magnifying power is
questions.e: M = f₀/fₑ = 100/5 = 20. The value 105 cm is f₀ + fₑ, which is the length of the telescope, not its magnifying power.

questions.s: An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has a magnifying power of 15 and an objective of focal length 90 cm. The distance between the objective and the eyepiece is
questions.e: fₑ = f₀/M = 90/15 = 6 cm, and in normal adjustment the lens separation is f₀ + fₑ = 90 + 6 = 96 cm. The value 84 cm subtracts the focal lengths instead of adding them.

questions.s: The objective of a good astronomical telescope has
o: a long focal length and a large aperture
a short focal length and a small aperture
a long focal length and a small aperture
a short focal length and a large aperture
questions.e: A long focal length gives a high magnifying power f₀/fₑ, and a large aperture collects more light and improves the resolving power. A short focal length objective belongs to a microscope.

questions.s: A telescope objective has a diameter of 0.122 m. For light of wavelength 500 nm, the smallest angular separation it can resolve (Rayleigh criterion θ = 1.22λ/D) is
questions.e: θ = 1.22 × 500 × 10⁻⁹/0.122 = 1.22 × 5 × 10⁻⁷/0.122 = 5 × 10⁻⁶ rad. The value 4.1 × 10⁻⁶ rad drops the factor 1.22, which applies to a circular aperture.

questions.s: The resolving power of a telescope can be increased by
o: using an eyepiece of shorter focal length
using an objective of larger diameter
questions.e: The smallest resolvable angle is θ = 1.22λ/D, so a larger objective diameter D (or a shorter wavelength) improves resolving power. A shorter-focus eyepiece only increases magnification; it enlarges a blurred image without separating close objects.

questions.s: An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.60 and a cladding of refractive index 0.8√3 (about 1.39). The critical angle at the core-cladding boundary is
questions.e: sin C = n₂/n₁ = 0.8√3/1.6 = √3/2, so C = 60°. Light hitting the boundary at more than 60° to the normal is totally internally reflected. The value 30° comes from reading √3/2 as the cosine instead of the sine.

questions.s: Light travels along the axis of a straight optical fibre whose core has refractive index 1.5. Take c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. The time taken to travel 1 km of fibre is
questions.e: v = c/n = 3 × 10⁸/1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ m/s, so t = 1000/(2 × 10⁸) = 5 × 10⁻⁶ s = 5 μs. The value 3.3 μs uses the speed of light in vacuum, ignoring the core's refractive index.

questions.s: A graded-index optical fibre reduces the spreading of light pulses (multipath dispersion) compared with a step-index multimode fibre because
o: longer-path rays travel faster in the outer, lower-index glass
the core absorbs every ray that is not along the axis
the cladding reflects only one colour and absorbs the others
the refractive index of the core is highest at its outer edges
questions.e: In a graded-index fibre the refractive index falls from the centre outwards, so rays that zigzag far from the axis travel through lower-index glass at higher speed and arrive nearly together with the axial ray. The index is highest at the centre, not the edges, and the core does not absorb oblique rays.

questions.s: Huygens' principle is used mainly to find
o: the speed of light in vacuum
the new position of a wavefront
the mass of a light photon
the focal length of a mirror
questions.e: Huygens' construction draws secondary wavelets from every point of a known wavefront; the surface touching them all after time t is the new wavefront. It is a geometric method and does not give the speed of light or photon properties.

questions.s: In Young's experiment, the slits are 1 mm apart, the screen is 2 m away and the fringe spacing is 1.1 mm. The wavelength of the light is
questions.e: λ = Δy d/L = (1.1 × 10⁻³ × 1 × 10⁻³)/2 = 5.5 × 10⁻⁷ m = 550 nm. The value 1100 nm forgets to divide by the screen distance of 2 m.

questions.s: When an astronomical telescope is in normal adjustment, the final image is formed
o: at the near point of the eye
at the focus of the objective
questions.e: In normal adjustment the objective's image lies at the focus of the eyepiece, so rays leave the eyepiece parallel and the final image is at infinity, which the relaxed eye views comfortably. The intermediate (first) image, not the final one, is at the focus of the objective.

questions.s: In Young's double slit experiment, the path difference between the two waves reaching a point on the screen is 3λ. The point lies on the
questions.e: A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths, mλ, gives a bright fringe; m = 3 gives the third bright fringe counted from the central one (m = 0). Dark fringes need an odd number of half wavelengths, such as 2.5λ.

questions.s: A soap film of refractive index 4/3 in air is lit normally by light of wavelength 640 nm. The least thickness for which it looks bright in reflected light is
questions.e: With a π phase change at the front surface only, brightness needs 2nt = λ/2, so t = λ/(4n) = 640/(4 × 4/3) = 640 × 3/16 = 120 nm. The value 160 nm is λ/4, which forgets that the wavelength inside the film is λ/n.

questions.s: Newton's rings and the colours of thin films are examples of interference produced by
questions.e: In thin films and Newton's rings one beam is split at a surface into a reflected and a transmitted part, which share the amplitude; this is division of amplitude. Young's double slit, where two parts of one wavefront pass through two slits, is division of wavefront.

questions.s: In a Michelson interferometer with light of wavelength 500 nm, 200 fringes cross the field of view as the movable mirror is displaced. The mirror moved through
questions.e: Each fringe corresponds to a mirror movement of λ/2, so d = mλ/2 = 200 × 500 nm/2 = 50 000 nm = 50 μm. The value 100 μm uses d = mλ, forgetting that the light covers the extra distance twice.

questions.s: In the diffraction pattern of a single slit, the central band is
o: as bright as each of the other bands
dark, with bright bands on either side
the narrowest band of the pattern
the brightest and the widest band
questions.e: All parts of the slit send light in phase straight ahead, so the centre is brightest, and it spans from the first minimum on one side to the first on the other, twice the width of the other bands. A dark centre is never found for a single slit.

questions.s: A grating has 4000 lines per centimetre and is lit normally by light of wavelength 600 nm. For the second-order maximum, sin θ equals
questions.e: d = 1/4000 cm = 2.5 μm, so sin θ = nλ/d = (2 × 0.6)/2.5 = 0.48. The value 0.24 is the first-order result.

questions.s: A polaroid sheet is slowly rotated through a full turn in front of a beam of light, and the transmitted intensity stays the same throughout. The incident beam is
questions.e: Unpolarised light has vibrations equally in all directions, so a polaroid passes half of it in every orientation. Plane polarised light would go from bright to dark twice per turn, and partly polarised light would vary between a maximum and a non-zero minimum.

questions.s: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 0.8 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm, and the final image is at the near point (25 cm). Using M = (L/f₀)(1 + d/fₑ), the length L needed for a magnifying power of 150 is
questions.e: 1 + d/fₑ = 1 + 25/5 = 6, so L/f₀ = 150/6 = 25 and L = 25 × 0.8 = 20 cm. The value 24 cm uses d/fₑ = 5 instead of 6, giving L/f₀ = 30.

questions.s: Light is guided along an optical fibre by
questions.e: Light in the core meets the boundary with the lower-index cladding at angles greater than the critical angle and is totally internally reflected again and again along the fibre. Dispersion is actually a drawback in fibres because it spreads pulses.

questions.s: The pupil of an eye has a diameter of 2 mm. Taking λ = 500 nm and the Rayleigh criterion θ = 1.22λ/D, the greatest distance at which two car headlights 1.22 m apart can just be seen as separate is
questions.e: θ = 1.22 × 500 × 10⁻⁹/(2 × 10⁻³) = 3.05 × 10⁻⁴ rad. The distance is separation/θ = 1.22/(3.05 × 10⁻⁴) = 4000 m = 4 km. The value 8 km comes from using the pupil radius, 1 mm, in place of the diameter, which halves θ.

questions.s: A grating with grating element 2 μm is lit normally by light of wavelength 600 nm. The total number of bright maxima seen, including the central one, is
questions.e: n ≤ d/λ = 2000/600 ≈ 3.3, so orders 1, 2 and 3 appear on each side of the central maximum, giving 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 maxima. The value 3 counts the highest order on one side only.

questions.s: A single-mode optical fibre differs from a multimode step-index fibre mainly because
o: its core is very narrow, so light follows almost one path
its cladding has a higher refractive index than the core
its core is made of plastic with a large diameter
light in it travels by refraction rather than reflection
questions.e: A single-mode fibre has a core only a few micrometres across, so light travels essentially along one path and pulses do not spread by taking different routes; this suits long-distance links. In every fibre the cladding has the lower refractive index, otherwise total internal reflection could not occur.

questions.s: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas, collisions of the molecules with each other and with the walls are assumed to be
o: inelastic, with loss of kinetic energy
questions.e: Kinetic theory assumes perfectly elastic collisions, so the total kinetic energy of the molecules is not lost and a gas left alone keeps its temperature and pressure. If collisions lost kinetic energy, an isolated gas would cool down by itself, which is not observed.

questions.s: According to kinetic theory, the pressure exerted by a gas on the walls of its container is due to
o: molecules changing momentum as they hit the walls
the weight of the gas pressing down on the base of the box
the attraction between molecules and the walls
questions.e: Each molecule that hits a wall and rebounds has its momentum changed; the total rate of change of momentum per unit area of wall is the pressure. The weight of a gas is far too small to explain it, and pressure acts equally on the top wall too.

questions.s: A gas of density 1.2 kg m⁻³ exerts a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Using P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩, the root mean square speed of its molecules is
questions.e: ⟨v²⟩ = 3P/ρ = 3 × 10⁵/1.2 = 2.5 × 10⁵ m² s⁻², so v_rms = √(2.5 × 10⁵) = 500 m/s. The value 2.5 × 10⁵ m/s forgets the square root, and 289 m/s omits the factor 3.

questions.s: The temperature of a gas is raised from 27 °C to 927 °C. The root mean square speed of its molecules becomes
questions.e: v_rms ∝ √T with T in kelvin: T rises from 300 K to 1200 K, a factor of 4, so v_rms increases by √4 = 2. The value 34 uses the Celsius ratio 927/27, and 4 forgets the square root.

questions.s: Hydrogen (molar mass 2 g/mol) and oxygen (molar mass 32 g/mol) are at the same temperature. The ratio of the rms speed of hydrogen molecules to that of oxygen molecules is
questions.e: At the same temperature v_rms = √(3RT/M) ∝ 1/√M, so v_H/v_O = √(32/2) = √16 = 4. The value 16 forgets the square root, and 1/4 inverts the ratio: the lighter molecules are faster.

questions.s: The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at absolute temperature T is (k = Boltzmann constant)
questions.e: Kinetic theory gives ⟨½mv²⟩ = (3/2)kT, which is (1/2)kT for each of the three directions of motion. (1/2)kT is the share for only one direction, and 2/3 is the factor in P = (2/3)(N/V)⟨KE⟩, not in the energy.

questions.s: For an ideal gas, the pressure is equal to what fraction of the total translational kinetic energy of the molecules per unit volume?
questions.e: P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩ = (2/3)(½ρ⟨v²⟩), and ½ρ⟨v²⟩ is the kinetic energy per unit volume, so P is two-thirds of it. The factor 1/3 belongs to the form in terms of ρ⟨v²⟩, before the ½ of the kinetic energy is brought in.

questions.s: A gas is at 27 °C. The temperature at which the average kinetic energy of its molecules is doubled is
questions.e: Average kinetic energy ∝ T in kelvin, so it doubles when T goes from 300 K to 600 K, which is 600 − 273 = 327 °C. The value 54 °C doubles the Celsius figure, and 600 °C forgets to convert back from kelvin.

questions.s: The rms speed of hydrogen molecules (M = 2 g/mol) at 300 K equals the rms speed of oxygen molecules (M = 32 g/mol) at a temperature of
questions.e: v_rms = √(3RT/M) is the same when T/M is the same, so T_O = 300 × 32/2 = 4800 K. The value 1200 K uses √16 = 4 as the factor, but it is T itself, not its square root, that must scale with M.

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
o: Molecules move randomly in all directions
The size of molecules is negligible
questions.e: Kinetic theory assumes no intermolecular forces except during collisions, so strong attraction is not an assumption; it is a feature of real gases that leads to liquefaction. Random motion, elastic collisions and negligible molecular size are all standard assumptions.

questions.s: A temperature of 300 K on the Celsius scale is
questions.e: T(°C) = T(K) − 273 = 300 − 273 = 27 °C. The value 573 °C adds 273 instead of subtracting it.

questions.s: A gas at a pressure of 2 atm occupies 6 L. It is compressed at constant temperature to 1.5 L. Its new pressure is
questions.e: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so P₂ = 2 × 6/1.5 = 8 atm. The value 0.5 atm treats pressure as proportional to volume, but squeezing a gas raises its pressure.

questions.s: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C. It is heated at constant pressure to 127 °C. Its new volume is
questions.e: Charles's law: V/T is constant with T in kelvin, so V = 300 × 400/300 = 400 cm³. The value 1411 cm³ uses the Celsius ratio 127/27, and 225 cm³ inverts the temperature ratio.

questions.s: An ideal gas at a pressure of 2 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 400 K occupies 8.31 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the number of moles of gas is
questions.e: n = PV/RT = (2 × 10⁵ × 8.31 × 10⁻³)/(8.31 × 400) = 1662/3324 = 0.5 mol. The value 2 comes from inverting the fraction, RT/PV.

questions.s: A gas occupies 3 L at 27 °C and 1 atm. It is heated to 127 °C and its pressure is raised to 2 atm. Its new volume is
questions.e: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ gives V₂ = 3 × (1/2) × (400/300) = 2 L. The value 1.5 L ignores the temperature change, and 1.13 L uses the temperature ratio upside down.

questions.s: The internal energy of a fixed mass of an ideal gas depends on its
questions.e: An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so it has no potential energy between molecules and its internal energy is only the kinetic energy of the molecules, which depends on T alone. Changing pressure or volume at constant temperature leaves U unchanged.

questions.s: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas are heated so that the temperature rises by 10 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and U = (3/2)nRT, the increase in internal energy is
questions.e: ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT = 1.5 × 2 × 8.3 × 10 = 249 J. The value 166 J is nRΔT without the factor 3/2, and 415 J uses 5/2, the factor for a diatomic gas.

questions.s: If Q is the heat supplied to a system, ΔU the increase in its internal energy and W the work done by the system, the first law of thermodynamics is
questions.e: Energy is conserved: the heat supplied partly raises the internal energy and partly leaves as work done by the system, so Q = ΔU + W. Q = ΔU − W would be correct only if W meant work done on the system.

questions.s: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. The change in its internal energy is
questions.e: ΔU = Q − W = 500 − 200 = +300 J. The value 700 J adds the work instead of subtracting it; work done by the gas uses up part of the heat.

questions.s: 300 J of work is done on a gas while it gives out 100 J of heat to the surroundings. The change in its internal energy is
questions.e: Q = −100 J (heat lost) and W = −300 J (work done on the gas), so ΔU = Q − W = −100 + 300 = +200 J. The value +400 J treats the heat lost as heat gained.

questions.s: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa from 1 L to 3 L. The work done by the gas is
questions.e: W = PΔV = 1.5 × 10⁵ × (3 − 1) × 10⁻³ = 300 J. The value 450 J uses the final volume 3 L instead of the change in volume.

questions.s: Heat is supplied to a gas kept in a closed rigid container (constant volume). Which statement is correct?
o: All the heat raises the internal energy
The work done by the gas equals the heat supplied
The internal energy of the gas stays constant
questions.e: At constant volume ΔV = 0, so W = PΔV = 0 and the first law gives Q = ΔU: all the heat raises the internal energy, and the temperature rises. Work equal to heat supplied describes an isothermal process instead.

questions.s: In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas,
o: no heat at all enters the gas
the internal energy of the gas increases
heat absorbed equals work done by the gas
questions.e: At constant temperature the internal energy of an ideal gas does not change, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W: all the heat absorbed is used to do work. 'No heat enters' describes an adiabatic process, not an isothermal one.

questions.s: A process in which no heat enters or leaves the system is called
questions.e: Adiabatic means Q = 0, as when a gas is compressed very quickly or is well insulated. Isothermal means constant temperature, isochoric constant volume and isobaric constant pressure.

questions.s: A gas at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa absorbs 500 J of heat and its volume increases by 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. The increase in its internal energy is
questions.e: W = PΔV = 10⁵ × 2 × 10⁻³ = 200 J, so ΔU = Q − W = 500 − 200 = 300 J. The value 200 J is the work done, not the change in internal energy.

questions.s: When an ideal gas expands adiabatically, its temperature
questions.e: With Q = 0, the first law gives ΔU = −W; the gas does positive work in expanding, so its internal energy, and hence its temperature, falls. A constant temperature would need heat to flow in, which is the isothermal case.

questions.s: For a reversible adiabatic change of an ideal gas with γ = Cp/Cv, the relation between pressure and volume is
questions.e: In an adiabatic change the temperature also changes, and the result is PV^γ = constant. PV = constant is Boyle's law, which holds only for an isothermal change.

questions.s: When Bilal pumps up a bicycle tyre quickly, the barrel of the pump becomes warm. The main reason is that
o: heat flows into the air from his hands
friction between the air molecules creates heat
the air expands quickly inside the pump
work done on the air raises its internal energy
questions.e: Fast compression is nearly adiabatic: there is no time for heat to escape, so Q ≈ 0 and ΔU = work done on the air, which raises its temperature. The air is being compressed, not expanded, and molecular collisions in an ideal gas are elastic, so they do not create heat by friction.

questions.s: On a P–V diagram, an isothermal curve and an adiabatic curve for the same gas start from the same point. The adiabatic curve is
o: less steep than the isothermal curve
exactly as steep as the isothermal curve
a straight line parallel to the V-axis
questions.e: The slope of an isothermal is −P/V while that of an adiabatic is −γP/V; since γ > 1 the adiabatic curve is steeper. Physically, in an adiabatic expansion the gas also cools, so its pressure falls faster than at constant temperature.

questions.s: A monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its original volume. Its pressure increases by a factor of
questions.e: PV^γ = constant gives P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^γ = 8^(5/3) = (8^(1/3))⁵ = 2⁵ = 32. The value 8 is the isothermal (Boyle's law) result, which ignores the heating of the gas.

questions.s: A monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its volume. Using TV^(γ−1) = constant, its final temperature is
questions.e: T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^(γ−1) = 300 × 8^(2/3) = 300 × 4 = 1200 K. The value 9600 K uses the exponent γ = 5/3 (a factor of 32), which belongs to the pressure relation.

questions.s: An ideal gas is compressed slowly at constant temperature, and 400 J of work is done on it. During the compression,
o: 400 J of heat is given out by the gas
400 J of heat is absorbed by the gas
no heat is exchanged with the surroundings
800 J of heat is given out by the gas
questions.e: Isothermal means ΔU = 0, so Q = W = −400 J (W done by the gas is −400 J): the gas must give out 400 J of heat. No heat exchange would describe an adiabatic compression, in which the gas would warm up.

questions.s: A gas expands adiabatically and does 150 J of work. The change in its internal energy is
questions.e: For an adiabatic process Q = 0, so ΔU = Q − W = 0 − 150 = −150 J; the gas uses its own internal energy to do the work and cools. Zero would be the change for an isothermal process of an ideal gas.

questions.s: The molar specific heat of a gas at constant pressure, Cp, is greater than that at constant volume, Cv, because at constant pressure
o: the gas also does work as it expands
less heat is lost to the surroundings
questions.e: At constant pressure the heat supplied must raise the internal energy and also provide the work PΔV done as the gas expands, so more heat is needed per kelvin. At constant volume no work is done and all the heat raises the temperature.

questions.s: For one mole of an ideal gas, the molar specific heats Cp and Cv are related by
questions.e: Cp − Cv = R, because at constant pressure the extra heat per mole per kelvin equals the work done, PΔV = RΔT. The ratio Cp/Cv is γ, not R.

questions.s: For a monatomic ideal gas, the ratio γ = Cp/Cv is
questions.e: For a monatomic gas Cv = (3/2)R and Cp = Cv + R = (5/2)R, so γ = (5/2)/(3/2) = 5/3. The value 7/5 is for a diatomic gas, whose molecules can also rotate.

questions.s: The molar specific heat at constant volume of a monatomic ideal gas is
questions.e: The internal energy of a monatomic gas is U = (3/2)nRT, so raising 1 mol by 1 K at constant volume needs (3/2)R of heat. (5/2)R is Cp for a monatomic gas, which includes the work of expansion.

questions.s: For a diatomic ideal gas at room temperature, Cv = (5/2)R. The value of γ = Cp/Cv is
questions.e: Cp = Cv + R = (7/2)R, so γ = (7/2)/(5/2) = 7/5 = 1.4. The value 1.67 is 5/3, the result for a monatomic gas.

questions.s: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas are heated at constant pressure so that the temperature rises by 50 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the heat supplied is
questions.e: Cp = (5/2)R for a monatomic gas, so Q = nCpΔT = 2 × 2.5 × 8.3 × 50 = 2075 J. The value 1245 J uses Cv = (3/2)R, which would be correct only at constant volume.

questions.s: Heat is supplied to a monatomic ideal gas at constant pressure. The fraction of this heat that goes into increasing the internal energy of the gas is
questions.e: ΔU = nCvΔT and Q = nCpΔT, so ΔU/Q = Cv/Cp = (3/2)R/(5/2)R = 3/5; the remaining 2/5 is the work done in expanding. 2/5 is the work fraction, and 5/3 is greater than 1, which is impossible for a fraction of the heat.

questions.s: For every ideal gas, the ratio γ = Cp/Cv is
o: equal to the gas constant R
questions.e: Since Cp = Cv + R, Cp is always larger than Cv, so γ > 1 (5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for diatomic gases). A value of exactly 1 would mean no work is done on expansion at constant pressure, which is not true.

questions.s: On a P–V diagram, the work done by a gas during an expansion is equal to
o: the pressure at the end of the process
the product of the final pressure and final volume
the area between the curve and the volume axis
questions.e: W = ∫P dV, which is the area under the P–V curve between the initial and final volumes. The product of final P and V is PV = nRT, which relates to temperature, not to the work done.

questions.s: A gas is taken clockwise round a cycle that forms a rectangle on the P–V diagram: pressures 1 × 10⁵ Pa and 3 × 10⁵ Pa, volumes 1 L and 3 L, with the expansion at the higher pressure. The net heat absorbed by the gas in one cycle is
questions.e: Net work = area enclosed = ΔP × ΔV = (2 × 10⁵)(2 × 10⁻³) = 400 J. In a complete cycle ΔU = 0, so the net heat absorbed equals the net work, 400 J. The value 600 J is only the work done during the expansion at 3 × 10⁵ Pa.

questions.s: When a gas is taken through a complete cycle and returns to its initial state, the change in its internal energy is
questions.e: Internal energy depends only on the state of the gas, so returning to the starting state means ΔU = 0. The heat supplied equals the work done in a cycle, but neither of them is the change in internal energy.

questions.s: The number of gas molecules in a rigid container is doubled while the temperature is kept constant. The pressure of the gas
questions.e: P = (N/V)kT, so at fixed V and T the pressure is proportional to the number of molecules: twice as many molecules strike the walls each second with the same average momentum. Four times would follow only if the speeds also doubled.

questions.s: Taking k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 300 K is
questions.e: ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)kT = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 = 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J. The value 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ J is kT without the factor 3/2.

questions.s: According to kinetic theory, the absolute temperature of a gas is a measure of the
o: total energy of all the molecules taken together
mean translational kinetic energy per molecule
number of molecules per unit volume
questions.e: Kinetic theory gives ⟨½mv²⟩ = (3/2)kT, so T is directly proportional to the average translational kinetic energy per molecule. The total energy also depends on how much gas there is, but temperature does not.

questions.s: A gas in a closed rigid vessel is at 27 °C. The temperature to which it must be heated for its pressure to become three times as large is
questions.e: At constant volume P ∝ T in kelvin, so T = 3 × 300 = 900 K = 900 − 273 = 627 °C. The value 81 °C triples the Celsius temperature, and 900 °C forgets to convert back.

questions.s: The law stating that the pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature is
questions.e: P ∝ T at constant V is the pressure law (also called Gay-Lussac's law). Boyle's law relates P and V at constant T, and Charles's law relates V and T at constant P.

questions.s: Ayesha watches smoke particles in air under a microscope and sees them moving about in a jerky, random way. This Brownian motion is evidence that
o: smoke particles are alive and move on their own
the smoke particles attract each other strongly
the light from the lamp pushes the particles about
air molecules move randomly and hit the particles
questions.e: Fast, invisible air molecules hit each smoke particle unevenly from different sides, giving it a random, jerky motion; this supports the kinetic theory assumption of random molecular motion. The particles are not alive, and light pressure is far too weak and steady to cause the jerks.

questions.s: A heat engine is a device that
o: converts part of the heat it absorbs into work
converts all of the heat it absorbs into work
moves heat from a cold body to a hot body
questions.e: A heat engine takes heat from a hot source, turns part of it into mechanical work and rejects the rest to a cold sink. Converting all the heat into work in a cycle is forbidden by the second law, and moving heat from cold to hot is what a refrigerator does.

questions.s: A heat engine absorbs heat Q₁ from the source and rejects heat Q₂ to the sink in each cycle. Its efficiency is
questions.e: Work per cycle is W = Q₁ − Q₂, so efficiency = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁. The ratio Q₂/Q₁ is the fraction of heat wasted, not the fraction turned into work.

questions.s: In each cycle, an engine absorbs 1000 J of heat from the source and rejects 600 J to the sink. Its efficiency is
questions.e: W = 1000 − 600 = 400 J, so efficiency = 400/1000 = 40%. The value 60% is the wasted fraction Q₂/Q₁, and 167% is Q₁/Q₂, which cannot be an efficiency.

questions.s: An engine of efficiency 25% does 200 J of work in each cycle. The heat it rejects to the sink in each cycle is
questions.e: Q₁ = W/η = 200/0.25 = 800 J, so Q₂ = Q₁ − W = 800 − 200 = 600 J. The value 800 J is the heat absorbed from the source, not the heat rejected.

questions.s: A Carnot engine works between a source at absolute temperature T₁ and a sink at absolute temperature T₂. Its efficiency is
questions.e: For a Carnot engine Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁, so η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁ with temperatures in kelvin. 1 − T₁/T₂ would be negative because T₁ > T₂.

questions.s: A Carnot engine works between 527 °C and 127 °C. Its efficiency is
questions.e: In kelvin T₁ = 800 K and T₂ = 400 K, so η = 1 − 400/800 = 0.5 = 50%. The value 76% comes from using Celsius temperatures, 1 − 127/527.

questions.s: The efficiency of a Carnot engine could be 100% only if
o: the sink were at absolute zero
the source and sink were at the same temperature
questions.e: η = 1 − T₂/T₁ equals 1 only when T₂ = 0 K, which cannot be reached, so no engine can be 100% efficient. With source and sink at the same temperature the efficiency would be zero, and the working substance does not affect Carnot efficiency.

questions.s: A Carnot engine takes heat from a source at 600 K and has an efficiency of 40%. The temperature of its sink is
questions.e: 1 − T₂/T₁ = 0.4 gives T₂ = 0.6 × 600 = 360 K. The value 240 K comes from T₂ = 0.4 × 600, using the efficiency instead of 1 − η.

questions.s: A Carnot engine with its sink at 300 K has an efficiency of 50%. Keeping the sink fixed, by how much must the source temperature be raised to make the efficiency 60%?
questions.e: At 50%, T₁ = 300/0.5 = 600 K; at 60%, T₁ = 300/0.4 = 750 K. The rise is 750 − 600 = 150 K. The value 750 K is the new source temperature, not the increase.

questions.s: The Carnot cycle consists of
o: two isothermal and two adiabatic processes
two isobaric and two isochoric processes
four isothermal processes in a row
two isochoric and two adiabatic processes only
questions.e: The Carnot cycle is isothermal expansion at T₁, adiabatic expansion to T₂, isothermal compression at T₂ and adiabatic compression back to T₁. Two isochoric and two adiabatic processes make up the Otto cycle of a petrol engine, not the Carnot cycle.

questions.s: Carnot's theorem states that, between the same two temperatures,
o: a petrol engine is always more efficient than a Carnot engine
the efficiency depends on the working gas
questions.e: Carnot's theorem says a reversible engine has the highest possible efficiency for given source and sink temperatures, and this efficiency does not depend on the working substance. Real engines such as petrol engines lose energy to friction and heat leaks, so they are less efficient.

questions.s: A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K and absorbs 1000 J of heat from the source in each cycle. The work done per cycle is
questions.e: η = 1 − 300/500 = 0.4, so W = 0.4 × 1000 = 400 J. The value 600 J is the heat rejected to the sink, Q₂ = Q₁T₂/T₁.

questions.s: Which of the following is a statement of the second law of thermodynamics?
o: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature
No cyclic engine can turn all the heat absorbed into work
The pressure of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature
questions.e: The Kelvin statement of the second law says it is impossible for a cyclic engine to turn all the heat it absorbs into work; some must be rejected to a colder sink. Conservation of energy is the first law, which would allow 100% conversion.

questions.s: A refrigerator moves heat from its cold interior to the warmer kitchen. This does not break the second law of thermodynamics because
o: work is done on it by the compressor
the heat moves on its own from cold to hot
the refrigerant has no internal energy
questions.e: The Clausius statement says heat cannot flow by itself from a colder to a hotter body; a refrigerator needs external work from the compressor to make it happen. If heat flowed on its own from cold to hot, that would violate the second law.

questions.s: In a four-stroke petrol engine, the stroke in which the fuel-air mixture burns and pushes the piston outwards is the
questions.e: After the compression stroke, a spark ignites the mixture; the hot gases expand and drive the piston out in the power stroke, which is the only stroke that delivers work. In the compression stroke the piston does work on the gas instead.

questions.s: In a diesel engine, the fuel injected into the cylinder is ignited by
o: a spark from a spark plug
a small gas flame in the cylinder
questions.e: A diesel engine compresses air so strongly (nearly adiabatically) that its temperature rises above the ignition temperature of the fuel, which then burns as soon as it is sprayed in. Ignition by a spark plug is the method used in a petrol engine.

questions.s: Entropy of a system is a measure of its
questions.e: Entropy measures the disorder (randomness) of a system; for example, it rises when ice melts and the molecules become free to move. Temperature and internal energy are related to entropy changes through ΔS = Q/T, but they are different quantities.

questions.s: A system absorbs 546 J of heat reversibly at a constant temperature of 273 K. Its change in entropy is
questions.e: ΔS = Q/T = 546/273 = 2 J/K. The value 0.5 J/K is T/Q, the ratio inverted.

questions.s: In all natural (irreversible) processes, the total entropy of the universe
questions.e: The second law in entropy form says the total entropy of an isolated system, such as the universe, increases in every irreversible process and stays constant only in an ideal reversible one. Entropy of one part may fall, but the total never decreases.

questions.s: 1200 J of heat flows by conduction from a large body at 600 K to another large body at 300 K. The total change in entropy of the two bodies is
questions.e: The hot body loses entropy 1200/600 = 2 J/K and the cold body gains 1200/300 = 4 J/K, so the total change is −2 + 4 = +2 J/K, positive as expected for an irreversible process. The value +4 J/K counts only the gain of the cold body.

questions.s: In a reversible adiabatic process, the change in entropy of the gas is
questions.e: ΔS = Q/T for a reversible change, and Q = 0 in an adiabatic process, so ΔS = 0; such a process is called isentropic. A positive change would need heat to enter or the process to be irreversible.

questions.s: When water at 0 °C freezes into ice at 0 °C, the entropy of the water
questions.e: Freezing releases latent heat (Q is negative), so ΔS = Q/T is negative; the molecules also become more ordered in the crystal. Entropy increases in the reverse change, melting.

questions.s: A Carnot engine works between 400 K and 300 K. Which change gives the higher efficiency?
questions.e: Raising the source: η = 1 − 300/450 = 1/3 ≈ 33%. Lowering the sink: η = 1 − 250/400 = 3/8 = 37.5%. Lowering the sink by the same amount helps more because T₂ appears in the numerator of T₂/T₁.

questions.s: 500 J of heat is given to a monatomic ideal gas at constant pressure. The work done by the gas is
questions.e: At constant pressure W = nRΔT and Q = nCpΔT, so W/Q = R/Cp = R/(5R/2) = 2/5 and W = 0.4 × 500 = 200 J. The value 300 J is the increase in internal energy, the other 3/5 of the heat.

questions.s: To make the expansion of a gas nearly isothermal, it should be carried out
o: slowly, in a conducting container touching a heat reservoir
quickly, in a conducting container kept far away from any heat source
questions.e: An isothermal process needs heat to flow in all the time to keep the temperature constant, so the walls must conduct, a large reservoir must be in contact and the change must be slow. A quick change in an insulated container is the recipe for an adiabatic process.

questions.s: Absolute zero on the Celsius scale is approximately
questions.e: 0 K corresponds to −273 °C (more exactly −273.15 °C), since T(K) = T(°C) + 273. 0 °C is the melting point of ice, which is 273 K.

questions.s: The SI unit of molar specific heat is
questions.e: Molar specific heat is the heat needed per mole per kelvin, so its unit is J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. J K⁻¹ is the unit of heat capacity of a whole body, and also of entropy.

questions.s: A gas is heated in a cylinder closed by a light, frictionless piston that is free to move under constant atmospheric pressure. The process is
questions.e: The free piston keeps the gas pressure equal to atmospheric pressure, so the process is isobaric (constant pressure) while the volume and temperature both rise. Isochoric would need a fixed piston.

questions.s: After a long drive from Islamabad to Lahore, the pressure of the air in a car tyre has risen. In terms of kinetic theory, the main reason is that
o: more air molecules have entered the tyre
the air molecules have become larger
the air molecules now attract each other more strongly than before
the warmer molecules hit the walls harder and more often
questions.e: Friction warms the tyre and its air; at higher temperature the molecules move faster, so they strike the walls more often and with more momentum, raising the pressure. The number of molecules stays the same in a sealed tyre, and their size does not change.

questions.s: In a car's petrol engine regarded as a heat engine, the sink (cold reservoir) is
o: the fuel tank of the car
the spark plug in the cylinder
questions.e: The exhaust gases and the radiator give the waste heat to the surrounding air, which acts as the cold sink. The burning fuel inside the cylinder is the hot source, not the sink.

questions.s: Kinetic theory assumes that, compared with the time between collisions, the duration of a collision between molecules is
questions.e: Collisions are treated as instantaneous: their duration is negligible compared with the time a molecule spends moving freely between collisions. If collisions lasted long, the molecules would spend much of their time in contact, as in a liquid.

questions.s: The molecules of a gas of density 0.3 kg m⁻³ have an rms speed of 1000 m/s. Using P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩, the pressure of the gas is
questions.e: P = ⅓ × 0.3 × (1000)² = 0.1 × 10⁶ = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. The value 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa leaves out the factor ⅓, and 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa uses ½ρv², which is the kinetic energy per unit volume.

questions.s: The Boltzmann constant k is related to the gas constant R and the Avogadro number N_A by
questions.e: R is the gas constant per mole and k is the gas constant per molecule, so k = R/N_A = 8.31/(6.02 × 10²³) ≈ 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. Multiplying by N_A would give a huge number, not the tiny k.

questions.s: A gas is at 127 °C. The temperature at which the rms speed of its molecules is halved is
questions.e: v_rms ∝ √T, so halving v_rms needs T/4: 400 K/4 = 100 K = −173 °C. The value −73 °C (200 K) halves the temperature, which would reduce the speed only by a factor of √2.

questions.s: An ideal gas expands at constant temperature from 2 L to 6 L. Its initial pressure was 3 atm. Its final pressure is
questions.e: Boyle's law: P₂ = P₁V₁/V₂ = 3 × 2/6 = 1 atm. The value 9 atm multiplies by the volume ratio instead of dividing; a gas that expands at constant temperature loses pressure.

questions.s: A gas does 250 J of work on its surroundings while its internal energy falls by 50 J. The heat exchanged by the gas is
questions.e: Q = ΔU + W = (−50) + 250 = +200 J, so the gas absorbs 200 J. The value 300 J comes from adding the magnitudes, which ignores the sign of ΔU.

questions.s: Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the molar specific heat at constant pressure of a monatomic ideal gas is
questions.e: Cv = (3/2)R and Cp = Cv + R = (5/2)R = 2.5 × 8.3 = 20.75 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The value 12.45 is Cv, which applies at constant volume.

questions.s: In a process at constant volume, the work done by the gas is
questions.e: Work done by a gas is PΔV, and at constant volume ΔV = 0, so no work is done. The heat supplied then goes entirely into internal energy, which is why 'equal to the heat supplied' describes ΔU, not W.

questions.s: One mole of a diatomic ideal gas (Cv = (5/2)R) is heated at constant volume from 300 K to 340 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the heat supplied is
questions.e: Q = nCvΔT = 1 × 2.5 × 8.3 × 40 = 830 J. The value 1162 J uses Cp = (7/2)R, which applies at constant pressure, and 498 J uses the monatomic value (3/2)R.

questions.s: An engine of efficiency 30% absorbs 2000 J of heat in each cycle. The work it does per cycle is
questions.e: W = ηQ₁ = 0.30 × 2000 = 600 J. The value 1400 J is the heat rejected to the sink, Q₁ − W.

questions.s: A Carnot engine has an efficiency of 25% and its sink is at 27 °C. The temperature of its source is
questions.e: 1 − T₂/T₁ = 0.25 gives T₁ = 300/0.75 = 400 K = 127 °C. The value 36 °C applies the formula to Celsius temperatures (27/0.75), and 102 °C comes from T₁ = 1.25 × 300 = 375 K.

questions.s: When a gas is compressed adiabatically, its temperature
questions.e: With Q = 0, the work done on the gas goes entirely into its internal energy (ΔU = −W > 0), so the temperature rises. It stays constant only if heat can escape, as in an isothermal compression.

questions.s: In each cycle an engine absorbs 1200 J from a reservoir at 400 K and gives out 900 J to a reservoir at 300 K. The total entropy change of the two reservoirs per cycle is
questions.e: The hot reservoir loses 1200/400 = 3 J/K and the cold reservoir gains 900/300 = 3 J/K, so the total is zero; the engine behaves as a reversible (Carnot) engine, and indeed its efficiency 300/1200 = 25% equals 1 − 300/400. The value +3 J/K counts only the cold reservoir.

questions.s: Which of the following would violate the second law of thermodynamics?
o: an engine turning all heat from one reservoir into work
a refrigerator whose compressor is driven by an electric motor
an engine that rejects part of its heat to a colder sink
heat flowing on its own from a hot cup of tea to cool air
questions.e: The Kelvin statement forbids a cyclic engine that takes heat from a single reservoir and converts it completely into work. A motor-driven refrigerator, an engine with a cold sink and heat flowing from hot to cold are all allowed.

questions.s: An ideal gas with γ = 1.5 is compressed adiabatically from 4 L to 1 L. Its pressure increases by a factor of
questions.e: P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^γ = 4^1.5 = (√4)³ = 2³ = 8. The value 4 is the isothermal result from Boyle's law, which ignores the rise in temperature.

questions.s: Two point charges repel each other with a force F. If the distance between them is doubled, the force becomes
questions.e: Coulomb's law gives F ∝ 1/r², so doubling r divides the force by 2² = 4, giving F/4. F/2 treats the force as inversely proportional to r instead of r².

questions.s: Two point charges of 2 μC and 3 μC are 3 m apart in air. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the force between them is
questions.e: F = kq₁q₂/r² = (9 × 10⁹)(2 × 10⁻⁶)(3 × 10⁻⁶)/3² = 5.4 × 10⁻²/9 = 6 × 10⁻³ N. 1.8 × 10⁻² N divides by r instead of r², and 5.4 × 10⁻² N forgets to divide by r² at all.

questions.s: The SI unit of the permittivity of free space ε₀ is
questions.e: From F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²), ε₀ = q₁q₂/(4πFr²), so its unit is C²/(N m²) = C² N⁻¹ m⁻². N m² C⁻² is the unit of k = 1/(4πε₀), the reciprocal quantity.

questions.s: Two identical small metal spheres carry charges +6 μC and −2 μC and attract each other with a force F. They are touched together and then put back at the same separation. The new force is
questions.e: On contact the total charge +4 μC is shared equally, so each sphere has +2 μC. The force goes from k(6)(2)/r² to k(2)(2)/r², i.e. from 12 to 4 units, so it becomes F/3, and like charges now repel. Keeping it attractive ignores that both spheres end up positive.

questions.s: If each of two point charges is doubled and the distance between them is halved, the Coulomb force between them becomes
questions.e: F ∝ q₁q₂/r². Doubling both charges multiplies F by 4, and halving r multiplies it by another 4, so the force becomes 16F. 8F comes from treating the distance effect as a factor of 2 instead of 2².

questions.s: Point charges of +4 μC and +9 μC are fixed 10 cm apart. A third charge placed on the line between them feels no net force. Its distance from the 4 μC charge is
questions.e: Equal forces need 4/x² = 9/(10 − x)², so x/(10 − x) = 2/3, giving 3x = 20 − 2x and x = 4 cm. 6 cm is the distance from the 9 μC charge, and 5 cm (the midpoint) would only work for equal charges.

questions.s: The number of electrons that make up a charge of 1 C is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: n = q/e = 1/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.25 × 10¹⁸. 1.6 × 10¹⁹ wrongly takes the reciprocal of the power only, and 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the charge of one electron, not a count.

questions.s: A plastic rod is found to carry a charge of −3.2 μC. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the rod has
questions.e: n = q/e = 3.2 × 10⁻⁶/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2 × 10¹³, and a negative charge means electrons were gained. 'Lost' gives the sign wrongly, and 2 × 10¹⁹ forgets the micro (10⁻⁶) prefix.

questions.s: For two protons at any separation, the ratio of the electrostatic repulsion to the gravitational attraction between them is of the order of
questions.e: Fₑ/F_g = ke²/(Gm_p²) = (9 × 10⁹)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)²/[(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(1.67 × 10⁻²⁷)²] ≈ 1.2 × 10³⁶, independent of distance since both forces vary as 1/r². About 10⁴² is the figure for two electrons, whose mass is much smaller.

questions.s: Three point charges, each +1 μC, lie on a straight line at x = 0, x = 0.1 m and x = 0.2 m. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the net force on the charge at x = 0.2 m is
questions.e: From the charge 0.1 m away: (9 × 10⁹)(10⁻¹²)/0.01 = 0.9 N; from the charge 0.2 m away: 9 × 10⁻³/0.04 = 0.225 N. Both push in the +x direction, so the total is 1.125 N. 0.675 N wrongly subtracts two forces that act in the same direction.

questions.s: Three equal charges of 1 μC sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.3 m. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the magnitude of the net force on any one charge is
