questions.e: Each pair force is kq²/a² = 9 × 10⁻³/0.09 = 0.1 N, and the two forces on one charge are 60° apart. The resultant is 2(0.1)cos 30° = 0.1√3 N. 0.2 N simply adds the magnitudes as if the forces were parallel.

questions.s: A total charge Q is split into two parts, q and Q − q, which are then held a fixed distance apart. The Coulomb force between the parts is greatest when q equals
questions.e: F ∝ q(Q − q) = Qq − q². Setting dF/dq = Q − 2q = 0 gives q = Q/2, and the second derivative is negative, so this is a maximum. Any unequal split, such as Q/3 and 2Q/3, gives a smaller product (2Q²/9 < Q²/4).

questions.s: Two fixed charges exert a force of 12 N on each other in air. When the space between them is filled completely with an insulating liquid, the force drops to 3 N. The relative permittivity of the liquid is
questions.e: In a medium F = F_air/εᵣ, so εᵣ = 12/3 = 4. The value 16 squares the ratio as if εᵣ acted like distance, and 1/4 inverts the ratio; εᵣ of any medium is at least 1.

questions.s: The constant k in Coulomb's law, F = kq₁q₂/r², is equal to
questions.e: In SI units k = 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², with ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻². 4πε₀ is the reciprocal and would give a tiny value of about 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰.

questions.s: If F₁₂ is the force on charge q₁ due to charge q₂, then the force F₂₁ on q₂ due to q₁ is
questions.e: Coulomb forces obey Newton's third law: they are equal in magnitude, act along the line joining the charges and are opposite in direction, so F₂₁ = −F₁₂. Writing F₁₂ ignores that the two forces point in opposite directions.

questions.s: Which of the following is a unit of electric field intensity?
questions.e: E = V/d for a uniform field, so V m⁻¹ is a unit of E, equivalent to N C⁻¹. J C⁻¹ is the volt, the unit of potential, and C N⁻¹ is the reciprocal of N C⁻¹.

questions.s: The electric field at a distance of 3 m from a point charge of 4 μC in air is (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
questions.e: E = kq/r² = (9 × 10⁹)(4 × 10⁻⁶)/9 = 4 × 10³ N C⁻¹. 1.2 × 10⁴ divides by r instead of r², and 3.6 × 10⁴ is kq without dividing by r² at all.

questions.s: A particle of mass 4 mg and charge 2 μC is placed in a uniform electric field of 500 N C⁻¹. Ignoring gravity, its acceleration is
questions.e: F = qE = (2 × 10⁻⁶)(500) = 10⁻³ N and m = 4 mg = 4 × 10⁻⁶ kg, so a = 10⁻³/(4 × 10⁻⁶) = 250 m s⁻². 0.25 m s⁻² treats 4 mg as 4 g, and 2.5 × 10⁵ uses 10⁻⁹ kg for a milligram.

questions.s: Which statement about electric field lines is correct?
o: They start on negative charges and end on positive ones
They start on positive charges and end on negative ones
They form closed loops around an isolated point charge
They may cross each other at a neutral point
questions.e: Field lines show the direction of force on a positive test charge, so they leave positive charges and end on negative charges. They never cross, because the field has one direction at each point, and electrostatic field lines never form closed loops.

questions.s: A hollow conducting sphere of radius R carries a charge Q on its surface. The electric field at a point inside it, at distance r from the centre, is
questions.e: A Gaussian sphere drawn inside the shell encloses no charge, so by Gauss's law the flux and hence E inside is zero. kQ/R² is the field just outside the surface, and kQ/R is the potential, which is constant inside.

questions.s: An oil drop of mass 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg stays at rest between two horizontal plates where the upward electric field is 2 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the number of excess electronic charges on the drop is
questions.e: Balance gives qE = mg, so q = (6.4 × 10⁻¹⁵)(10)/(2 × 10⁵) = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, which is 3.2/1.6 = 2 electronic charges. Forgetting to multiply by g gives a non-integer 0.2, and 4 comes from halving E by mistake.

questions.s: Charges of +2 μC and −2 μC are 0.2 m apart in air. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the electric field at the midpoint between them is
o: 1.8 × 10⁶ N C⁻¹ towards the negative charge
3.6 × 10⁶ N C⁻¹ towards the negative charge
3.6 × 10⁶ N C⁻¹ towards the positive charge
questions.e: Each charge is 0.1 m away and gives E = (9 × 10⁹)(2 × 10⁻⁶)/0.01 = 1.8 × 10⁶ N C⁻¹. The field of +q points away from it and that of −q points towards it, so both point towards the negative charge and add to 3.6 × 10⁶ N C⁻¹. Zero would be right only for two like charges.

questions.s: An electron enters a uniform electric field moving at right angles to the field lines. Inside the field its path is a
questions.e: The electron moves at constant velocity across the field and has constant acceleration eE/m along it, exactly like a horizontally thrown ball under gravity, so the path is a parabola. A circle needs a force always perpendicular to the velocity, as in a magnetic field.

questions.s: An electron is placed in a uniform electric field of 1000 N C⁻¹ directed vertically upwards. The force on it is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: F = eE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(10³) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ N, and because the electron is negative the force is opposite to E, i.e. downwards. 'Upwards' would be the direction for a proton.

questions.s: Equal charges +q are placed at three corners of a square of side a; the fourth corner is empty. The electric field at the centre of the square is
questions.e: The two charges on opposite corners cancel at the centre, leaving the charge opposite the empty corner. Its distance is a/√2, so E = kq/(a²/2) = 2kq/a², pointing away from that charge, i.e. towards the empty corner. kq/a² wrongly uses the side a instead of the half-diagonal.

questions.s: Two large parallel plates carry uniform surface charge densities +σ and −σ. The electric field in the region between the plates is
questions.e: Each sheet alone gives σ/(2ε₀); between the plates the two fields point the same way (from + to −) and add to σ/ε₀. Outside the plates they cancel, which is where the field is zero. σ/(2ε₀) counts only one plate.

questions.s: Using Gauss's law, the electric field near a large, flat, isolated non-conducting sheet with uniform surface charge density σ is
questions.e: A cylindrical Gaussian surface through the sheet has flux out of both flat ends: 2EA = σA/ε₀, so E = σ/(2ε₀). σ/ε₀ forgets that the field lines leave from both faces of the sheet.

questions.s: A flat surface of area 0.5 m² is placed in a uniform electric field of 200 N C⁻¹ so that its normal makes an angle of 60° with the field. The electric flux through it is
questions.e: Φ = EA cos θ = 200 × 0.5 × cos 60° = 100 × ½ = 50 N m² C⁻¹. 50√3 uses sin 60° (the angle with the surface, not the normal), and 100 ignores the angle entirely.

questions.s: The electric flux through a flat surface placed in a uniform electric field is zero when
o: the field lines are parallel to the surface
the surface is perpendicular to the field
the area vector is parallel to the field
questions.e: Φ = EA cos θ, where θ is the angle between E and the area vector (the normal). If the field lines run parallel to the surface, θ = 90° and no lines pass through, so Φ = 0. A surface perpendicular to the field has its normal along E, which gives the maximum flux.

questions.s: A charge of 8.85 μC is enclosed by a closed surface. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the total electric flux through the surface is
questions.e: Gauss's law gives Φ = q/ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻⁶/8.85 × 10⁻¹² = 10⁶ N m² C⁻¹. 10⁻⁶ inverts the ratio, and 7.8 × 10⁻¹⁷ multiplies q by ε₀ instead of dividing.

questions.s: A point charge q is placed at the centre of a cube. The electric flux through any one face of the cube is
questions.e: The total flux through the closed cube is q/ε₀ (Gauss's law), and by symmetry the six faces share it equally, giving q/(6ε₀) per face. q/ε₀ is the flux through the whole cube, not one face.

questions.s: A closed surface encloses charges of +3 μC and −5 μC, while a charge of +7 μC lies outside it. The net electric flux through the surface is
questions.e: Only enclosed charge counts in Gauss's law: Φ = (3 − 5) μC/ε₀ = −2 μC/ε₀, meaning a net inward flux. +5 μC/ε₀ wrongly includes the outside charge, whose field lines enter and leave the surface equally.

questions.s: A point charge sits at the centre of a spherical Gaussian surface. If the radius of the sphere is doubled, the electric flux through it
questions.e: By Gauss's law Φ = q/ε₀ depends only on the enclosed charge. The field falls as 1/r² while the area grows as r², so the product EA stays constant. 'One quarter' looks only at the weaker field and forgets the larger area.

questions.s: A solid insulating sphere of radius R has charge spread uniformly through its volume, and the field at its surface is E₀. The field at a distance R/2 from the centre is
questions.e: A Gaussian sphere of radius r encloses Q(r/R)³, so E = kQ(r³/R³)/r² = kQr/R³, which grows linearly with r inside. At r = R/2 the field is E₀/2. Zero applies to a hollow conducting shell, and E₀/4 wrongly uses the 1/r² outside law.

questions.s: A metal sphere of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 2 μC. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the electric field at a point 30 cm from its centre is
questions.e: Outside a charged sphere the field is that of a point charge at the centre: E = (9 × 10⁹)(2 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.3)² = 1.8 × 10⁴/0.09 = 2 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. 4.5 × 10⁵ uses 20 cm (the distance from the surface), and 1.8 × 10⁶ uses the radius 10 cm.

questions.s: Two large parallel plates carry equal and opposite charges with surface density 8.85 × 10⁻⁸ C m⁻². Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the field between them is
questions.e: Between oppositely charged plates E = σ/ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻⁸/8.85 × 10⁻¹² = 10⁴ N C⁻¹. 5 × 10³ uses σ/(2ε₀), the field of a single isolated sheet.

questions.s: A hemispherical bowl of radius R is placed in a uniform electric field E that is parallel to its axis of symmetry. The magnitude of the flux through its curved surface is
questions.e: The bowl plus its flat circular rim form a closed surface with no charge inside, so the flux through the curved part equals that through the flat circle: E × πR². 2πR²E wrongly multiplies E by the curved area, ignoring that the field is not normal to most of it.

questions.s: The SI unit of electric flux is
questions.e: Φ = EA has unit (N C⁻¹)(m²) = N m² C⁻¹, which is also V m. N m² C⁻² is the unit of Coulomb's constant k, not of flux.

questions.s: A closed cylinder of radius r and length L is placed in a uniform electric field E with its axis parallel to the field. The net electric flux through the whole cylinder is
questions.e: Flux πr²E enters one flat end and the same amount leaves the other, while the curved side is parallel to E and carries none. The net flux is zero, as Gauss's law requires since no charge is enclosed. 2πr²E adds the two ends instead of giving them opposite signs.

questions.s: The net electric flux through a closed surface is found to be zero. Which conclusion is certain?
o: There is no charge anywhere inside
The net charge inside is zero
The field is zero all over the surface
There is no charge outside the surface
questions.e: Gauss's law says Φ = Q_enclosed/ε₀, so zero flux only means the algebraic sum of enclosed charges is zero; equal + and − charges could be inside. The field on the surface can still be non-zero, for example when an outside charge sends lines in and out.

questions.s: The electric potential at a distance of 0.3 m from a point charge of 2 nC is (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
questions.e: V = kq/r = (9 × 10⁹)(2 × 10⁻⁹)/0.3 = 18/0.3 = 60 V. 200 V divides by r² (that is the field formula), and 5.4 V multiplies by r instead of dividing.

questions.s: The work done in moving a charge of 3 μC through a potential difference of 200 V is
questions.e: W = qV = (3 × 10⁻⁶)(200) = 6 × 10⁻⁴ J. 6 × 10² J forgets the micro prefix, and 1.5 × 10⁻⁸ J divides q by V instead of multiplying.

questions.s: Charges +q and −q are fixed a short distance apart. At the midpoint of the line joining them
questions.e: Potential is a scalar: kq/r + k(−q)/r = 0. Field is a vector: both fields point from +q towards −q at the midpoint, so they add and E ≠ 0. Taking E = 0 too confuses this with two like charges, where the fields cancel.

questions.s: Two parallel plates 5 cm apart are connected to a 250 V supply. The magnitude of the uniform electric field between them is
questions.e: E = V/d = 250/0.05 = 5000 V m⁻¹. 50 V m⁻¹ divides by 5 without converting centimetres to metres, and 12.5 multiplies V by d.

questions.s: A charge of 5 μC is moved between two points that lie on the same equipotential surface at 100 V. The work done is
questions.e: W = qΔV and ΔV = 0 between points on one equipotential surface, so no work is done. 5 × 10⁻⁴ J uses the potential 100 V itself instead of the potential difference.

questions.s: The work needed to bring a +2 μC charge from infinity to a point 0.3 m from a fixed +3 μC charge is (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
questions.e: W = U = kq₁q₂/r = (9 × 10⁹)(6 × 10⁻¹²)/0.3 = 0.054/0.3 = 0.18 J. 0.6 J divides by r² as in the force formula, and 0.054 J forgets to divide by r.

questions.s: Charges +q, +q and −q are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. The electrostatic potential energy of the system is
questions.e: Add the three pairs: (+q)(+q) gives +kq²/a, and each of the two (+q)(−q) pairs gives −kq²/a. The total is kq²/a − 2kq²/a = −kq²/a. −3kq²/a treats all three pairs as unlike.

questions.s: Four equal charges +q are placed at the corners of a square of side a. The electric potential at the centre of the square is
questions.e: Each corner is a/√2 from the centre, so each charge gives kq√2/a, and potentials add as scalars: 4√2 kq/a. Zero is the electric field there (the vectors cancel), not the potential, and 4kq/a uses the side instead of the half-diagonal.

questions.s: A uniform electric field of 400 V m⁻¹ points along the +x axis. Point A is at the origin and point B is at (3 cm, 4 cm). The potential difference V_A − V_B is
questions.e: Only displacement along the field changes the potential: V_A − V_B = E Δx = 400 × 0.03 = 12 V (A is higher, since the field points from A towards larger x). 20 V wrongly uses the full distance AB = 5 cm, and 16 V uses the y-displacement, which is perpendicular to E.

questions.s: An alpha particle starting from rest is accelerated through a potential difference of 1000 V. The kinetic energy it gains is
questions.e: K = qV and an alpha particle carries charge 2e, so K = 2e × 1000 V = 2000 eV. 1000 eV would be correct for a proton or electron, which carry a single charge e.

questions.s: One electron volt is equal to
questions.e: 1 eV is the energy gained by a charge e moving through 1 V: W = eV = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1 V) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. 6.25 × 10¹⁸ is the number of electrons in 1 C, and 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ is the electron's mass in kg.

questions.s: An electron starting from rest is accelerated through a potential difference of 500 V. Its kinetic energy in joules is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: K = eV = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(500) = 800 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8 × 10⁻¹⁷ J, i.e. 500 eV. 8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J writes 800 × 10⁻¹⁹ with the wrong power of ten.

questions.s: An energy of 1 MeV expressed in joules is
questions.e: 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV = 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J. 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J is 1 keV (10³ eV), and 1.6 × 10⁻²⁵ J divides by 10⁶ instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A proton and an alpha particle, both starting from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference. Taking the alpha particle's mass as four proton masses, the ratio of their final speeds, v_proton/v_alpha, is
questions.e: ½mv² = qV gives v = √(2qV/m), so v ∝ √(q/m). For the proton q/m = e/m; for the alpha it is 2e/4m = ½(e/m). The ratio is √(1/½) = √2. The value 2 forgets the square root, and 1/√2 inverts the ratio.

questions.s: The electron volt is a unit of
questions.e: An electron volt is charge × potential difference, (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1 V), which is work or energy, equal to 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Its name contains 'volt', which tempts students to choose potential.

questions.s: The electric potential along the x-axis is V = 5x² volts, with x in metres. The electric field at x = 2 m is
questions.e: E = −dV/dx = −10x, which is −20 V m⁻¹ at x = 2 m: magnitude 20 V m⁻¹ in the −x direction, since the field points towards falling potential. 'Along +x' drops the minus sign, and 10 V m⁻¹ divides V = 20 V by x.

questions.s: A hollow metal sphere of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 1 nC. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the potential at its centre is
questions.e: The field inside is zero, so the potential inside is constant and equal to the surface value: V = kQ/R = (9 × 10⁹)(10⁻⁹)/0.1 = 90 V. Zero confuses potential with field, and 900 V divides by R².

questions.s: A charge of +2 μC is at x = 0 and a charge of −4 μC is at x = 6 cm. The point between them where the electric potential is zero is at
questions.e: V = 0 needs k(2)/x = k(4)/(6 − x), so 12 − 2x = 4x and x = 2 cm, nearer the smaller charge. x = 4 cm puts the point nearer the larger charge, where its potential would dominate.

questions.s: The potential 2 m from a point charge is 60 V. The potential 6 m from the same charge is
questions.e: V ∝ 1/r, so tripling the distance divides the potential by 3: 60/3 = 20 V. 6.7 V divides by 9, which is how the field (∝ 1/r²) would change, not the potential.

questions.s: At a certain point near an isolated point charge, the potential is 600 V and the field strength is 200 V m⁻¹. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the charge is
questions.e: V/E = (kq/r)/(kq/r²) = r, so r = 600/200 = 3 m. Then q = Vr/k = 600 × 3/(9 × 10⁹) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ C. 6.7 × 10⁻⁸ C takes r = 1 m, and 6 × 10⁻⁷ C uses r = 9 m.

questions.s: A capacitor stores a charge of 60 μC when connected to a 12 V battery. Its capacitance is
questions.e: C = Q/V = 60 μC/12 V = 5 μF. 0.2 μF inverts the ratio (V/Q), and 720 μF multiplies Q by V.

questions.s: One farad is equal to
questions.e: C = Q/V, so 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹: a capacitor of 1 F stores 1 C for each volt across it. One joule per coulomb is the volt, the unit of potential.

questions.s: A parallel-plate capacitor in air has plates of area 0.1 m² separated by 0.885 mm. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, its capacitance is
questions.e: C = ε₀A/d = (8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(0.1)/(8.85 × 10⁻⁴) = 10⁻⁹ F = 1 nF. Using d = 0.885 m (forgetting to convert millimetres) gives 1 pF.

questions.s: The plate area of a parallel-plate capacitor C is doubled and the plate separation is halved. Its new capacitance is
questions.e: C = ε₀A/d, so doubling A doubles C and halving d doubles it again: 4C. The answer C wrongly lets the two changes cancel, but C rises with A and falls with d, so both changes increase it.

questions.s: A parallel-plate capacitor is charged to a potential difference V and then disconnected from the battery. A slab of dielectric constant 5 is then inserted to fill the gap. The potential difference between the plates
questions.e: Once disconnected the charge Q cannot change, while C rises to 5C, so V = Q/C falls to V/5. 'Remains V' would be true only if the battery stayed connected, in which case Q would rise instead.

questions.s: An isolated charged parallel-plate capacitor stores energy U. A dielectric slab of dielectric constant 5 is slid in to fill the space between the plates, with no battery connected. The stored energy becomes
questions.e: With Q fixed, U = Q²/(2C), and C becomes 5C, so U falls to U/5 (the slab is pulled in and the field does work on it). 5U uses ½CV² with V held constant, which applies only while a battery stays connected.

questions.s: Filling the gap of a parallel-plate capacitor with a dielectric increases its capacitance because
o: it lets charge leak between plates
it adds free electrons to the plates
it moves the plates further apart
questions.e: The dielectric's molecules polarise, and their bound surface charges set up a field opposing the plates' field. For the same charge the field and so the voltage fall, and C = Q/V rises by the factor εᵣ. A dielectric is an insulator, so no charge leaks or flows through it.

questions.s: Capacitors of 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series. Their equivalent capacitance is
questions.e: In series 1/C = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so C = 2 μF, which is less than the smaller capacitor. 9 μF adds them as if they were in parallel, and 4.5 μF is just their average.

questions.s: Capacitors of 2 μF, 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.e: 1/C = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = (3 + 2 + 1)/6 = 1, so C = 1 μF. 11 μF is the parallel value, and 1/11 μF takes the reciprocal of the sum of capacitances instead of summing reciprocals.

questions.s: A 3 μF capacitor and a 6 μF capacitor are connected in series across a 12 V battery. The potential difference across the 3 μF capacitor is
questions.e: C_eq = 2 μF, so each capacitor carries Q = 2 μF × 12 V = 24 μC. Then V₃ = 24/3 = 8 V and V₆ = 24/6 = 4 V. 4 V swaps them: in series the smaller capacitor takes the larger share of the voltage.

questions.s: Capacitors of 4 μF and 6 μF are connected in parallel across a 10 V supply. The charge on the 4 μF capacitor is
questions.e: In parallel each capacitor has the full 10 V, so Q = CV = 4 × 10 = 40 μC. 100 μC is the total charge of the pair, and 24 μC is the charge a series connection would give.

questions.s: Two 4 μF capacitors are connected in parallel, and this pair is connected in series with an 8 μF capacitor. The equivalent capacitance of the network is
questions.e: The parallel pair gives 4 + 4 = 8 μF; 8 μF in series with 8 μF gives 8 × 8/(8 + 8) = 4 μF. 16 μF adds all three as if in parallel, and 8 μF stops after the first step.

questions.s: A 10 μF capacitor charged to 100 V is connected across an identical uncharged capacitor. The energy lost as heat and radiation in the connecting wires is
questions.e: Initially U = ½(10 × 10⁻⁶)(100)² = 0.05 J. Charge is conserved, so the 20 μF pair settles at 50 V with U = ½(20 × 10⁻⁶)(50)² = 0.025 J; the loss is 0.025 J. 'Zero' assumes energy is conserved like charge, which it is not when charge flows through the wires.

questions.s: The energy stored in a 4 μF capacitor charged to 50 V is
questions.e: U = ½CV² = ½(4 × 10⁻⁶)(2500) = 5 × 10⁻³ J. 1 × 10⁻² J forgets the ½, and 1 × 10⁻⁴ J forgets to square V.

questions.s: The energy density in a region of uniform electric field 10⁶ V m⁻¹ in vacuum is approximately (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹)
questions.e: u = ½ε₀E² = ½(8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(10¹²) ≈ 4.4 J m⁻³. 8.85 J m⁻³ forgets the ½, and 8.85 × 10⁻⁶ J m⁻³ both drops the ½ and uses E instead of E².

questions.s: A 5 μF capacitor is charged through a 2 MΩ resistor. The time constant of the circuit is
questions.e: τ = RC = (2 × 10⁶ Ω)(5 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 10 s. Reading MΩ as kΩ gives 10 ms; the mega and micro prefixes cancel here, leaving 2 × 5 = 10 s.

questions.s: An uncharged capacitor is charged through a resistor from a d.c. supply. After one time constant (t = RC), its charge is about what percentage of the final charge?
questions.e: While charging, q = Q₀(1 − e⁻ᵗ/ᴿᶜ); at t = RC this is Q₀(1 − 1/e) ≈ 0.63Q₀. 37 % is the fraction left after one time constant of discharging, and 100 % is reached only after a very long time.

questions.s: A capacitor holding charge Q₀ discharges through a resistor R. The charge remaining after a time equal to RC is about
questions.e: On discharge q = Q₀e⁻ᵗ/ᴿᶜ, so at t = RC, q = Q₀/e ≈ 0.37Q₀. 0.63Q₀ is the charge gained in one time constant when charging, and 0.5Q₀ is reached at t = 0.69RC.

questions.s: A 100 μF capacitor discharges through a 10 kΩ resistor. The time taken for its charge to fall to half its initial value is about (ln 2 ≈ 0.69)
questions.e: τ = RC = (10⁴)(10⁻⁴) = 1 s. Setting e⁻ᵗ/ᴿᶜ = ½ gives t = RC ln 2 ≈ 0.69 s. 1.0 s is the time constant itself, after which only 37 % of the charge is left, not 50 %.

questions.s: A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor R. The time taken for its stored energy to fall to one quarter of the initial value is (ln 2 ≈ 0.69)
questions.e: U = q²/(2C) ∝ e⁻²ᵗ/ᴿᶜ. Setting e⁻²ᵗ/ᴿᶜ = ¼ gives 2t/RC = ln 4 = 2 ln 2, so t = RC ln 2 ≈ 0.69 RC; this is when the charge has halved. 1.39 RC = RC ln 4 is the time for the charge itself to fall to a quarter.

questions.s: An uncharged capacitor is connected in series with a 4 kΩ resistor to a 12 V battery. The current at the instant the circuit is completed is
questions.e: At t = 0 the uncharged capacitor has no voltage across it, so the whole 12 V is across R: I₀ = 12/4000 = 3 mA. The current is zero only at the end, once the capacitor is fully charged.

questions.s: The product of resistance and capacitance, RC, has the unit of
questions.e: Ω × F = (V/A)(C/V) = C/A = C/(C s⁻¹) = s, so RC is a time, the time constant. Hertz is the reciprocal unit, s⁻¹.

questions.s: A capacitor is charged through a resistor from a 20 V supply. One time constant after the switch is closed, the potential difference across the capacitor is about
questions.e: V_C = E(1 − e⁻¹) ≈ 0.63 × 20 = 12.6 V. 7.4 V (0.37E) is the voltage left across the resistor at that moment, and 10 V is reached earlier, at 0.69RC.

questions.s: An uncharged capacitor is connected through a resistor to a 10 V battery. At t = RC, the potential difference across the resistor is about
questions.e: The capacitor voltage has risen to 0.63 × 10 = 6.3 V, and the two voltages always add up to the emf, so V_R = 10 − 6.3 = 3.7 V (V_R = Ee⁻¹). 6.3 V is the capacitor's share, not the resistor's.

questions.s: Which change makes a charged capacitor discharge more slowly through a resistor?
questions.e: The rate of discharge is set by τ = RC, so a larger C (or a larger R) slows it. The initial voltage does not change τ: a higher voltage gives a larger current but the same fractional decay in each time constant.

questions.s: A 20 μF capacitor discharges through two 50 kΩ resistors connected in parallel. The time constant is
questions.e: The parallel resistors give R = 50/2 = 25 kΩ, so τ = (25 × 10³)(20 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.5 s. 2 s treats the resistors as series (100 kΩ), and 1 s uses only one resistor.

questions.s: A 3 μF capacitor carries a charge of 6 μC. The energy stored in it is
questions.e: U = Q²/(2C) = (6 × 10⁻⁶)²/(2 × 3 × 10⁻⁶) = 36 × 10⁻¹²/(6 × 10⁻⁶) = 6 × 10⁻⁶ J (check: V = 2 V and ½QV = 6 × 10⁻⁶ J). 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ J forgets the ½, and 9 × 10⁻¹² J multiplies Q by C.

questions.s: A parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to a battery while its plate separation is doubled. The electric field between the plates
questions.e: The battery fixes V, and for a uniform field E = V/d, so doubling d halves E. 'Stays the same' is the result for an isolated capacitor, where the charge and hence σ/ε₀ stay fixed.

questions.s: An isolated charged parallel-plate capacitor (not connected to any battery) has its plate separation doubled. Which statement is correct?
o: V doubles and E stays the same
V stays the same and E halves
V halves and E stays the same
questions.e: Q is fixed, so E = σ/ε₀ = Q/(ε₀A) is unchanged. C = ε₀A/d halves, so V = Q/C doubles (equivalently V = Ed with d doubled). 'V stays the same and E halves' describes a capacitor still connected to its battery.

questions.s: A parallel-plate capacitor of capacitance C has plate separation d. A metal slab of thickness d/2, of the same area as the plates, is inserted parallel to them without touching either plate. The new capacitance is
questions.e: The field inside a conductor is zero, so the slab simply removes d/2 of the gap: C′ = ε₀A/(d − d/2) = 2C. Its position between the plates does not matter. C/2 assumes the metal acts like extra separation, when in fact it shortens the gap.

questions.s: A parallel-plate capacitor in air has capacitance C and plate separation d. A dielectric slab of dielectric constant 2 and thickness d/2 is placed between the plates, covering their full area. The new capacitance is
questions.e: The arrangement acts as two capacitors in series: the air gap of thickness d/2 gives 2C and the slab gives 2 × 2C = 4C. Then 1/C′ = 1/(2C) + 1/(4C) = 3/(4C), so C′ = 4C/3. 2C would need the slab to fill the whole gap.

questions.s: Two capacitors give 9 μF when connected in parallel and 2 μF when connected in series. Their values are
questions.e: C₁ + C₂ = 9 and C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂) = 2, so C₁C₂ = 18. The numbers with sum 9 and product 18 are 3 and 6. The pair 4 and 5 has the right sum but gives 20/9 ≈ 2.2 μF in series.

questions.s: Four identical capacitors are first connected in parallel and then in series. The ratio of the parallel equivalent capacitance to the series equivalent capacitance is
questions.e: In parallel C_p = 4C and in series C_s = C/4, so C_p/C_s = 4C ÷ (C/4) = 16. The value 4 compares only one of the combinations with a single capacitor.

questions.s: Three capacitors of 3 μF each are available. An equivalent capacitance of 4.5 μF is obtained by connecting
o: two in series, then in parallel with the third
two in parallel, then in series with the third
questions.e: Two in series give 1.5 μF, and adding the third in parallel gives 1.5 + 3 = 4.5 μF. Two in parallel (6 μF) in series with 3 μF give only 2 μF, while all series gives 1 μF and all parallel 9 μF.

questions.s: Two charges of 3 μC each are 0.1 m apart in a medium of relative permittivity 9. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the force between them is
questions.e: In air F = (9 × 10⁹)(9 × 10⁻¹²)/0.01 = 8.1 N; the medium divides this by εᵣ = 9, giving 0.9 N. 8.1 N ignores the medium, and 2.7 N divides by √9 instead of 9.

questions.s: The field-line pattern of two equal positive point charges shows
o: a neutral point midway between them
lines running from one charge to the other
a uniform field between the charges
questions.e: Lines leave both charges and bend away from each other, so the fields cancel at the midpoint, giving a neutral point. Lines run from one charge to the other only for unlike charges, and electrostatic lines never form closed loops.

questions.s: A particle of mass m and charge q enters a uniform electric field E with speed v at right angles to the field. After travelling a distance L along its original direction, its sideways deflection is
questions.e: The time to cover L is t = L/v and the sideways acceleration is a = qE/m, so y = ½at² = qEL²/(2mv²). qEL²/(mv²) forgets the ½ in ½at², and qEL²/(2mv) has the wrong dimensions.

questions.s: A charge is carried once round a closed path in an electrostatic field and returned to its starting point. The net work done by the field is
questions.e: The electrostatic field is conservative: work depends only on the start and end potentials, W = q(V_start − V_end), which is zero when they are the same point. It does not depend on the path.

questions.s: The potential at point A is +50 V and at point B is −30 V. The work an external agent must do to move a +2 μC charge slowly from B to A is
questions.e: W = q(V_A − V_B) = (2 × 10⁻⁶)(50 − (−30)) = (2 × 10⁻⁶)(80) = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ J, positive because the positive charge is pushed to a higher potential. 4 × 10⁻⁵ J uses 50 − 30 = 20 V, ignoring the minus sign of V_B.

questions.s: A particle of mass 2 × 10⁻⁶ kg and charge 4 μC starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Ignoring gravity, its final speed is
questions.e: qV = (4 × 10⁻⁶)(100) = 4 × 10⁻⁴ J = ½mv², so v² = 2(4 × 10⁻⁴)/(2 × 10⁻⁶) = 400 and v = 20 m s⁻¹. 400 m s⁻¹ forgets the square root, and 14 m s⁻¹ (√200) drops the 2 from ½mv².

questions.s: A parallel-plate capacitor holding charge Q stays connected to its battery while a slab of dielectric constant 3 is inserted to fill the gap. The charge on the plates becomes
questions.e: The battery keeps V fixed, and C rises to 3C, so Q = CV becomes 3Q; the battery supplies the extra charge. 'Q' would be correct only if the capacitor had been disconnected first, in which case V would fall instead.

questions.s: A 2 μF capacitor charged to 100 V and a 4 μF capacitor charged to 40 V are joined positive plate to positive plate and negative to negative. Their common potential is
questions.e: Total charge = 2 × 100 + 4 × 40 = 360 μC on a total capacitance of 6 μF, so V = 360/6 = 60 V. 70 V is the simple average of the voltages, which ignores that the larger capacitor holds more charge per volt.

questions.s: For a capacitor discharging through a resistor R, a graph of ln V (natural log of the capacitor voltage) against time t is a straight line with
questions.e: V = V₀e⁻ᵗ/ᴿᶜ, so ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC: a straight line with intercept ln V₀ and slope −1/RC. Slope −RC confuses the time constant with its reciprocal, and a positive slope would mean the voltage grows, which happens only while charging.

questions.s: Two parallel plates 2 cm apart are kept at a potential difference of 400 V. The force on an electron between the plates is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: E = V/d = 400/0.02 = 2 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹, so F = eE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(2 × 10⁴) = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ N divides by 2 instead of 0.02 m, and 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁷ is eV, an energy in joules, not a force.

questions.s: Equal charges +q are placed at (−a, 0) and (a, 0). The magnitude of the electric field at the point (0, a) is
questions.e: Each charge is √2 a away, giving E = kq/(2a²). The x-components cancel and the y-components add: 2 × kq/(2a²) × (1/√2) = kq/(√2 a²). Zero holds only at the origin, where the two fields are exactly opposite.

questions.s: An electron moves, under electric forces alone, from a point at potential 50 V to a point at potential 200 V. Its kinetic energy
questions.e: ΔU = qΔV = (−e)(200 − 50) = −150 eV, so the potential energy falls by 150 eV and the kinetic energy rises by 150 eV; negative charges speed up towards higher potential. 'Decreases' would apply to a proton making the same move.

questions.s: An isolated conducting sphere of radius 0.3 m is at a potential of 9 kV. The electric field just outside its surface is
questions.e: At the surface V = kQ/R and E = kQ/R², so E = V/R = 9000/0.3 = 3 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. 10⁵ V m⁻¹ divides V by R², and 2.7 × 10³ multiplies V by R.

questions.s: Capacitors of 2 μF and 4 μF are connected in series across a battery. The ratio of the energy stored in the 2 μF capacitor to that in the 4 μF capacitor is
questions.e: In series both carry the same charge Q, and U = Q²/(2C) ∝ 1/C, so U₂:U₄ = (1/2):(1/4) = 2:1. 1:2 uses U ∝ C, which is true only for capacitors in parallel, where V is common.

questions.s: A 6 μF capacitor is connected in series with a parallel pair of 2 μF and 4 μF capacitors, and the network is connected to a 24 V battery. The charge on the 4 μF capacitor is
questions.e: The parallel pair is 6 μF, in series with 6 μF it gives 3 μF, so the total charge is 3 × 24 = 72 μC. The pair then has 72/6 = 12 V across it, so Q₄ = 4 × 12 = 48 μC. 72 μC is the charge on the 6 μF capacitor and on the pair as a whole, and 24 μC is on the 2 μF one.

questions.s: Air breaks down when the electric field exceeds about 3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹. The highest potential to which an isolated metal sphere of radius 1 cm can be charged in air is about
questions.e: For a sphere V = ER at the surface, so V_max = (3 × 10⁶)(0.01) = 3 × 10⁴ V. 3 × 10⁸ V divides by R instead of multiplying, and 3 × 10² V uses R = 10⁻⁴ m.

questions.s: Coulomb's law in the form F = kq₁q₂/r² applies strictly to
o: charges moving at very high speeds
charged bodies of any shape at any distance
questions.e: The law is stated for stationary point charges (or spherically symmetric bodies treated as points); for large, close bodies the distance r is not well defined. Moving charges also feel magnetic forces, so the simple form no longer gives the full force.

questions.s: Charges +q, −q, +q and −q are placed at the four corners of a square, taken in order round the square. At the centre of the square
questions.e: Opposite corners hold like charges at equal distances, so their fields cancel in pairs and E = 0. The potentials add as scalars: 2kq/r − 2kq/r = 0. E ≠ 0 would be right if the two positive charges were on adjacent corners, where the field vectors no longer cancel.

questions.s: A proton with kinetic energy 0.9 MeV, starting far away, moves head-on towards a proton held fixed. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the distance of closest approach is
questions.e: At closest approach all the kinetic energy has become potential energy: ke²/r = K. With K = 0.9 × 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.44 × 10⁻¹³ J and ke² = 2.304 × 10⁻²⁸ J m, r = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ m forgets to convert MeV to eV.

questions.s: A parallel-plate capacitor storing energy U stays connected to its battery while the plate separation is doubled. The stored energy becomes
questions.e: C = ε₀A/d halves while the battery holds V constant, so U = ½CV² halves to U/2. 2U is the result for an isolated capacitor, where Q stays fixed and U = Q²/(2C) doubles.

questions.s: For a capacitor, a graph of potential difference V (y-axis) against charge Q (x-axis) is a straight line through the origin. The slope of the line and the area under it represent
questions.e: V = Q/C, so the slope V/Q is 1/C. The area under the line is ½QV, the work done in charging, which is the energy stored. Slope C would be correct for a graph of Q against V.

questions.s: The field between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor is 6000 V m⁻¹. A dielectric of dielectric constant 3 is inserted to fill the gap completely. The field inside the dielectric becomes
questions.e: The polarised dielectric reduces the field by the factor εᵣ, so E = 6000/3 = 2000 V m⁻¹. 18000 V m⁻¹ multiplies by εᵣ, mixing up the effect on capacitance (which rises) with the effect on field (which falls).

questions.s: A charge +q is at x = 0 and a charge +4q is at x = 3 m. A third charge Q is placed so that all three charges are in equilibrium. Q and its position are
questions.e: Q must be between them where kq/x² = k(4q)/(3 − x)², so 3 − x = 2x and x = 1 m. For +q to be in equilibrium, Q must attract it with force equal to the 4q repulsion: kQq/1² = k(4q)q/3², so Q = −4q/9. A positive Q would push +q away, adding to the repulsion instead of balancing it.

questions.s: A point charge q is placed exactly at one corner of a cube. The electric flux through the cube as a whole is
questions.e: Eight such cubes meeting at that corner would enclose the charge completely and share the flux q/ε₀ equally, so one cube receives q/(8ε₀). q/(24ε₀) is the flux through each of the three faces not touching the charge, not through the whole cube.

questions.s: A proton gains 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁶ J of kinetic energy. Expressed in electron volts this is (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.e: Energy in eV = energy in J ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁶/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4 × 10³ eV = 4000 eV. 1.02 × 10⁻³⁴ multiplies by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ instead of dividing, and 400 eV slips one power of ten.

questions.s: Capacitors of 2 μF and 3 μF are connected in parallel across a 100 V supply. The total energy stored is
questions.e: In parallel C = 5 μF, so U = ½CV² = ½(5 × 10⁻⁶)(10⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁻² J. 6 × 10⁻³ J uses the series value 1.2 μF, and 5 × 10⁻² J forgets the ½.

questions.s: Two point charges of 1 μC each are 1 m apart in air. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the force between them is
questions.e: F = kq₁q₂/r² = (9 × 10⁹)(10⁻⁶)(10⁻⁶)/1² = 9 × 10⁻³ N. 9 × 10³ N converts only one of the two charges from μC to C, and 10⁻¹² N leaves out k.

questions.s: Two point charges exert a force F on each other. If one charge is tripled and the distance between them is also tripled, the force becomes
questions.e: F ∝ q₁q₂/r²: tripling one charge multiplies F by 3, and tripling r divides it by 9, so the new force is 3F/9 = F/3. 'F' assumes the two changes cancel, forgetting that r is squared.

questions.s: Two equal and opposite point charges 0.2 m apart attract each other with a force of 0.9 N. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the magnitude of each charge is
questions.e: q² = Fr²/k = (0.9)(0.04)/(9 × 10⁹) = 4 × 10⁻¹², so q = 2 × 10⁻⁶ C = 2 μC. 4 μC forgets to take the square root of q².

questions.s: When measuring an electric field with a test charge, the test charge should be very small because
o: it barely disturbs the source field
it feels a larger force per coulomb
it keeps the potential at zero
questions.e: A large test charge would push or pull on the charges producing the field and change their arrangement, so E = F/q would no longer describe the original field. The force per coulomb, F/q, does not depend on the size of the test charge, so a small charge is not chosen to increase it.

questions.s: The electric field at a point is 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. The force on a charge of 5 μC placed there is
questions.e: F = qE = (5 × 10⁻⁶)(2 × 10⁴) = 10 × 10⁻² = 0.1 N. 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ N divides q by E, and 4 × 10⁹ N divides E by q.

questions.s: Point charges +q and +9q are 8 cm apart. The electric field is zero at a point on the line between them at a distance from the +q charge of
questions.e: E = 0 where kq/x² = k(9q)/(8 − x)², so (8 − x)/x = 3, giving x = 2 cm. 0.8 cm uses the ratio 1:9 without the square root, and 6 cm is the distance from the 9q charge.

questions.s: A closed surface encloses an electric dipole, made of charges +q and −q, and no other charge. The net electric flux through the surface is
questions.e: By Gauss's law Φ = Q_enclosed/ε₀ and the enclosed charge is q + (−q) = 0, so the net flux is zero: every line leaving +q ends on −q inside. 2q/ε₀ adds the magnitudes of the charges instead of their algebraic sum.

questions.s: A square sheet of side 10 cm lies in a uniform electric field of 300 N C⁻¹, with the plane of the sheet making an angle of 30° with the field lines. The electric flux through the sheet is
questions.e: If the plane makes 30° with E, the normal makes 60° with E. Then Φ = EA cos 60° = 300 × 0.01 × ½ = 1.5 N m² C⁻¹. 1.5√3 uses 30° as the angle with the normal, and 15 uses the side 0.1 m in place of the area 0.01 m².

questions.s: Which of the following quantities is a scalar?
questions.e: Potential is work per unit charge, so it has magnitude only, and potentials from several charges simply add as numbers. Field, force and dipole moment all have direction and add as vectors.

questions.s: Moving a charge of 30 μC from point B to point A takes 6 mJ of work against the electric field. The potential difference V_A − V_B is
questions.e: V = W/q = (6 × 10⁻³ J)/(30 × 10⁻⁶ C) = 200 V. 2 × 10⁵ V treats 6 mJ as 6 J, and 1.8 × 10⁻⁷ multiplies W by q instead of dividing.

questions.s: A point P is 0.3 m from a charge of +3 nC and 0.1 m from a charge of −1 nC. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the electric potential at P is
questions.e: V = k(3 × 10⁻⁹)/0.3 + k(−1 × 10⁻⁹)/0.1 = 90 V − 90 V = 0. 180 V adds the two magnitudes, forgetting that the negative charge gives a negative potential.

questions.s: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2 kV. Its kinetic energy is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: K = eV = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(2 × 10³) = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ J, which is 2000 eV. 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J uses 2 V, forgetting the kilo prefix, and 1.25 × 10²² divides V by e.

questions.s: An electron is released from rest in a uniform electric field of 1000 V m⁻¹ and moves 1 cm (opposite to the field direction, as an electron does). The kinetic energy it gains is
questions.e: The potential difference crossed is ΔV = Ed = 1000 × 0.01 = 10 V, so the energy gained is e × 10 V = 10 eV. 1000 eV uses the field strength as if it were a voltage, and 10⁵ eV multiplies by 100 instead of 0.01.

questions.s: The capacitance of a parallel-plate air capacitor increases when
o: the plate area is made smaller
questions.e: C = εᵣε₀A/d, so C rises when d falls (plates closer), when A grows or when a dielectric is added. Moving the plates apart, reducing the area or removing the dielectric all reduce C.

questions.s: A 10 μF capacitor stores 0.2 J of energy. The potential difference across it is
questions.e: U = ½CV² gives V² = 2U/C = 0.4/10⁻⁵ = 4 × 10⁴, so V = 200 V. 4 × 10⁴ V forgets the square root, and 100 V leaves out the factor 2 from ½CV².

questions.s: Capacitors of 4 μF and 12 μF are connected in series, and this pair is connected in parallel with a 6 μF capacitor. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.e: The series pair gives 4 × 12/(4 + 12) = 3 μF; in parallel with 6 μF the total is 3 + 6 = 9 μF. 22 μF adds all three as if in parallel, and 3 μF stops after the first step.

questions.s: An uncharged capacitor C is charged fully by a battery of emf V through a resistor. The energy converted to heat in the resistor during charging is
questions.e: The battery moves charge Q = CV through emf V, doing work QV = CV². The capacitor stores only ½CV², so the other ½CV² is dissipated in the resistor, whatever its resistance. 'Zero' assumes all the battery's work ends up stored.

questions.s: A 50 μF capacitor is connected in series with a 20 kΩ resistor. The time constant of the circuit is
questions.e: τ = RC = (2 × 10⁴ Ω)(5 × 10⁻⁵ F) = 1 s. 1000 s treats μF as mF, while 0.4 s and 2.5 s come from dividing 20 and 50 instead of multiplying them.

questions.s: A capacitor discharges through a resistor. After about how many time constants has its charge fallen to roughly 5 % of the initial value? (e ≈ 2.7)
questions.e: q/Q₀ = e⁻ⁿ after n time constants: e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37, e⁻² ≈ 0.14 and e⁻³ ≈ 1/20 = 0.05, so about 3 time constants. After 5 time constants less than 1 % remains, which is why 5RC is often taken as 'fully discharged'.

questions.s: A 100 μF capacitor charged to 10 V is connected across a resistor, and the current at the first instant is 2 mA. The time constant of the discharge is
questions.e: At the start the full 10 V is across R, so R = V₀/I₀ = 10/(2 × 10⁻³) = 5 kΩ. Then τ = RC = (5 × 10³)(10⁻⁴) = 0.5 s. 5 s comes from taking R as 50 kΩ by a slip in the powers of ten.

questions.s: A charge of 120 C flows past a point in a wire in 1 minute. The current in the wire is
questions.e: I = Q/t = 120 C / 60 s = 2 A. The time must be in seconds; using t = 1 gives 120 A, and multiplying Q by t gives 7200 A, which has the wrong unit altogether.

questions.s: A current of 1.6 mA flows through a wire. The number of electrons passing a cross-section of the wire each second is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: n = I/e = (1.6 × 10⁻³)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1 × 10¹⁶ electrons per second. Forgetting the milli prefix gives 10¹⁹, and treating 1.6 mA as 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ A gives 10¹³. Multiplying I by e instead of dividing gives the meaningless 2.56 × 10⁻²².

questions.s: A potential difference of 12 V across a conductor drives a current of 0.4 A through it. The resistance of the conductor is
questions.e: By Ohm's law R = V/I = 12/0.4 = 30 Ω. Multiplying V and I gives 4.8, which is the power in watts, not a resistance; I/V gives 0.033 Ω.

questions.s: A uniform wire of resistance R is stretched so that its length becomes double while its volume stays the same. Its new resistance is
questions.e: Volume constant means A falls to A/2 when L doubles. R = ρL/A, so R′ = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4R. The answer 2R comes from doubling the length but forgetting that the cross-sectional area also halves.

questions.s: A carbon resistor has colour bands in the order yellow, violet, red, gold. Its resistance is
questions.e: Yellow = 4, violet = 7, red multiplier = 10², gold tolerance = ±5%. R = 47 × 100 = 4700 Ω = 4.7 kΩ ± 5%. Reading red as the third digit 2 gives 472 Ω, but the third band of a four-band resistor is the multiplier.

questions.s: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in parallel, and this combination is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor. The total resistance is
questions.e: Three equal resistors in parallel give 6/3 = 2 Ω. Adding the 4 Ω in series gives 2 + 4 = 6 Ω. The answer 22 Ω treats all four resistors as if in series, and 2 Ω forgets the series 4 Ω.

questions.s: A bulb is rated 100 W, 220 V. The resistance of its filament when glowing normally is
questions.e: P = V²/R, so R = V²/P = 220²/100 = 48400/100 = 484 Ω. Using R = V/P gives 2.2 Ω, and R = VP gives 22000 Ω; neither formula is correct for resistance.

questions.s: A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to an external resistor of 2.5 Ω. The terminal potential difference of the cell is
questions.e: I = E/(R + r) = 1.5/(2.5 + 0.5) = 0.5 A. Terminal p.d. V = IR = 0.5 × 2.5 = 1.25 V (or E − Ir = 1.5 − 0.25). The value 0.25 V is the lost volts across the internal resistance, not the terminal voltage.

questions.s: A battery of emf E and internal resistance r is connected to a variable external resistor R. The power delivered to R is maximum when
questions.e: By the maximum power transfer theorem, the power in the load is greatest when the load resistance equals the internal resistance, R = r, giving P = E²/4r. At R = 0 the current is largest but no power goes to the load, and for very large R the current is almost zero.

questions.s: Kirchhoff's first rule (the junction rule) is a consequence of the law of conservation of
questions.e: The junction rule says the total current into a junction equals the total current out, because charge cannot pile up at or vanish from a junction. Conservation of energy is the basis of the second (loop) rule, the usual confusion.

questions.s: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge P = 10 Ω, Q = 20 Ω and R = 15 Ω, with the balance condition P/Q = R/S. The value of S is
questions.e: P/Q = R/S gives S = RQ/P = 15 × 20/10 = 30 Ω. Inverting the ratio (S = RP/Q) gives 7.5 Ω, which would unbalance the bridge.

questions.s: A potentiometer measures the emf of a cell more accurately than a moving-coil voltmeter because
o: it has a very low resistance wire
it draws no current from the cell at balance
it uses a sensitive ammeter in series
its wire has a very high temperature coefficient
questions.e: At the balance point the galvanometer shows zero deflection, so no current is drawn from the cell and there is no drop across its internal resistance; the full emf is measured. A voltmeter always draws some current, so it reads the terminal p.d., slightly less than the emf.

questions.s: As the temperature of an NTC thermistor rises, its resistance
questions.e: NTC means negative temperature coefficient: heating frees more charge carriers in the semiconductor, so the resistance falls, usually very steeply. A rise in resistance with temperature is the behaviour of metals and PTC devices.

questions.s: A copper coil has a resistance of 10 Ω at 0 °C. Taking the temperature coefficient of resistance of copper as 0.004 K⁻¹, its resistance at 50 °C is
questions.e: R = R₀(1 + αΔT) = 10(1 + 0.004 × 50) = 10 × 1.2 = 12 Ω. The answer 10.2 Ω adds αΔT = 0.2 directly to R₀ instead of multiplying R₀ by (1 + αΔT).

questions.s: A wire of cross-sectional area 1 mm² carries a current of 1.6 A. If the number of free electrons per unit volume is 1 × 10²⁹ m⁻³, the drift velocity of the electrons is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: v = I/(nAe) with A = 1 mm² = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m². nAe = 10²⁹ × 10⁻⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6 × 10⁴, so v = 1.6/(1.6 × 10⁴) = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m/s. Taking 1 mm² as 10⁻³ m² gives 10⁻⁷ m/s; the area conversion is squared.

questions.s: Wires A and B are made of the same metal. A is twice as long as B and has half the diameter of B. The ratio of their resistances R_A : R_B is
questions.e: R = ρL/A and A ∝ d². Halving the diameter makes the area one quarter, so R_A/R_B = (2)/(1/4) = 8. The answer 4 : 1 comes from treating area as proportional to diameter rather than diameter squared.

questions.s: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. The current through the 12 Ω resistor is
questions.e: 6 Ω ∥ 12 Ω = 72/18 = 4 Ω, so the total is 8 Ω and the battery current is 12/8 = 1.5 A. The p.d. across the parallel pair is 1.5 × 4 = 6 V, so the 12 Ω resistor carries 6/12 = 0.5 A. The value 1.5 A is the total current, which splits between the two branches.

questions.s: Ayesha's 1000 W heater runs for 2 hours a day for 30 days. If electricity costs Rs 50 per unit (kWh), the cost of running it is
questions.e: Energy = 1 kW × 2 h × 30 = 60 kWh = 60 units, costing 60 × 50 = Rs 3000. Rs 1500 uses only 30 hours (1 hour a day), and Rs 6000 doubles the energy by mistake.

questions.s: A cell drives a current of 0.5 A through a 2 Ω resistor and a current of 0.25 A through a 5 Ω resistor. The internal resistance of the cell is
questions.e: E = I(R + r): 0.5(2 + r) = 0.25(5 + r), so 1 + 0.5r = 1.25 + 0.25r, giving 0.25r = 0.25 and r = 1 Ω (E = 1.5 V). The value 1.5 is the emf in volts, not the internal resistance.

questions.s: A battery has emf 12 V and internal resistance 3 Ω. The maximum power it can deliver to an external resistor is
questions.e: Maximum power occurs when R = r = 3 Ω: I = 12/6 = 2 A and P = I²R = 4 × 3 = 12 W, i.e. E²/4r = 144/12. The answer 48 W is E²/r, the power the cell would dissipate internally on short circuit, not the load maximum.

questions.s: Between points X and Y there are three parallel branches: a 12 V cell in series with 2 Ω, a 6 V cell in series with 2 Ω (both cells with positive terminal towards X), and a 2 Ω resistor alone. The cells have no internal resistance. The current through the 6 V cell is
questions.e: Let V be the potential of X above Y. Junction rule: (12 − V)/2 + (6 − V)/2 = V/2, giving 18 − 2V = V and V = 6 V. The 6 V branch then carries (6 − 6)/2 = 0 A, while the 12 V branch sends (12 − 6)/2 = 3 A through the 2 Ω resistor. 3 A is the current in the lone resistor, not in the 6 V cell.

questions.s: A Wheatstone bridge has P = 2 Ω, Q = 4 Ω in one arm pair and R = 3 Ω, S = 6 Ω in the other, with a galvanometer joining the P-Q and R-S junctions. A 9 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across the bridge. The current drawn from the battery is
questions.e: P/Q = R/S = 1/2, so the bridge is balanced and the galvanometer carries no current; it can be removed. The two paths (2 + 4) = 6 Ω and (3 + 6) = 9 Ω are in parallel: 54/15 = 3.6 Ω, so I = 9/3.6 = 2.5 A. 0.6 A wrongly adds all four resistors in series (15 Ω).

questions.s: On a potentiometer wire, a standard cell of emf 1.5 V balances at 60 cm. Another cell balances at 80 cm on the same wire with the same driver current. Its emf is
questions.e: E ∝ balancing length, so E₂ = 1.5 × 80/60 = 2.0 V. Using the ratio upside down (1.5 × 60/80) gives 1.125 V, which would mean a larger emf balances at a shorter length.

questions.s: Which of the following is a typical use of a thermistor?
o: as a rectifier in a power supply
as the standard reference cell in a potentiometer
as a temperature sensor in an alarm circuit
as a fuse in household wiring
questions.e: A thermistor's resistance changes sharply with temperature, so it is used to sense temperature, for example in fire alarms, thermostats and electronic thermometers. Rectification needs a diode, and a fuse depends on melting, not on a controlled change in resistance.

questions.s: Ohm's law, V ∝ I, is obeyed by
o: a metallic conductor at constant temperature
a filament lamp whose temperature rises as it glows
questions.e: Ohm's law holds for metallic conductors provided physical conditions, especially temperature, stay constant. A diode conducts mainly in one direction, and a filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats, so neither gives a straight-line V-I graph through the origin.

questions.s: In a gas discharge tube, 2 × 10¹⁸ electrons move towards the anode and 1 × 10¹⁸ positive ions (each of charge +e) move towards the cathode across a cross-section every second. The current in the tube is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: Negative charge moving one way and positive charge moving the other way both give conventional current in the same direction, so the contributions add: I = (2 + 1) × 10¹⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.48 A. Subtracting them gives 0.16 A, and counting only the electrons gives 0.32 A.

questions.s: The drift velocity of free electrons in a copper wire carrying an ordinary current is of the order of
questions.e: Electrons drift very slowly, typically about 10⁻⁴ m/s (a fraction of a millimetre per second). 10⁵ m/s is the order of their random thermal speed, and 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed at which the electric field signal travels, not the electrons themselves.

questions.s: Two copper wires of diameters 1 mm and 2 mm are joined end to end and carry a steady current. The ratio of the drift velocity in the thin wire to that in the thick wire is
questions.e: Same current and same material, so I = nAev gives v ∝ 1/A ∝ 1/d². The thin wire has one quarter of the area, so its drift velocity is 4 times larger: 4 : 1. The answer 2 : 1 forgets that area depends on the square of the diameter.

questions.s: The resistivity of a metal wire depends on
questions.e: Resistivity ρ is a property of the material at a given temperature; it does not change when the wire is cut, stretched or thickened. Length and area affect the resistance R = ρL/A, not ρ itself.

questions.s: A wire 2 m long with cross-sectional area 0.5 mm² has a resistance of 0.2 Ω. The resistivity of its material is
questions.e: ρ = RA/L = 0.2 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 5 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²). Multiplying by L instead of dividing gives 2 × 10⁻⁷, and taking 1 mm² as 10⁻³ m² gives 5 × 10⁻⁵.

questions.s: A platinum resistance thermometer has a resistance of 2.0 Ω at 0 °C and 2.6 Ω at 100 °C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of platinum is
questions.e: α = (R − R₀)/(R₀ΔT) = (2.6 − 2.0)/(2.0 × 100) = 0.003 K⁻¹. Leaving out R₀ gives 0.006 K⁻¹, and dividing by R at 100 °C instead of R₀ gives about 0.0023 K⁻¹.

questions.s: A metal wire has a resistance of 5 Ω at 20 °C and 6 Ω at 70 °C. Assuming R = R₀(1 + αθ), the temperature at which its resistance is 7 Ω is
questions.e: R varies linearly with θ: a 50 °C rise adds 1 Ω, so another 1 Ω needs another 50 °C, giving 70 + 50 = 120 °C. Check: 1 = 230α gives α = 1/230 per °C and R₀ = 4.6 Ω; 7 = 4.6(1 + θ/230) gives θ = 120 °C. 140 °C comes from doubling 70 °C, as if R were proportional to θ.

questions.s: A resistor has colour bands brown, black, orange, silver. Its value is
questions.e: Brown = 1, black = 0, orange multiplier = 10³, silver = ±10%. R = 10 × 1000 = 10 kΩ ± 10%. Gold, not silver, means ±5%, and the third band is a multiplier, not a third digit.

questions.s: Which colour band sequence marks a 220 Ω ± 5% carbon resistor?
questions.e: 220 = 22 × 10¹, so the bands are red (2), red (2), brown (multiplier 10¹), gold (±5%). Red as multiplier gives 2.2 kΩ, and black gives only 22 Ω.

questions.s: Five identical resistors have a combined resistance R_s in series and R_p in parallel. The ratio R_s/R_p is
questions.e: For n equal resistors R, R_s = nR and R_p = R/n, so R_s/R_p = n² = 25. The answer 5 forgets that the parallel value also divides by n, and 1/25 is the ratio inverted.

questions.s: Two resistors have a combined resistance of 9 Ω in series and 2 Ω in parallel. Their values are
questions.e: R₁ + R₂ = 9 and R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 2, so R₁R₂ = 18. The pair adding to 9 with product 18 is 3 and 6 (check: 18/9 = 2 Ω). 4 and 5 add to 9 but give 20/9 ≈ 2.2 Ω in parallel.

questions.s: A uniform wire of resistance 16 Ω is bent into a circle. The resistance between two points on the circle that are a quarter of the circumference apart is
questions.e: The two arcs are a quarter (4 Ω) and three quarters (12 Ω) of the wire, and they are in parallel: 4 × 12/(4 + 12) = 48/16 = 3 Ω. 4 Ω is the resistance between diametrically opposite points (8 ∥ 8), not between points a quarter apart.

questions.s: A 60 W, 220 V bulb and a 100 W, 220 V bulb are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Which statement is correct?
questions.e: R = V²/P, so the 60 W bulb has the larger resistance (about 807 Ω against 484 Ω). In series both carry the same current, and P = I²R is larger for the larger resistance, so the 60 W bulb is brighter. The 100 W bulb is brighter only when the bulbs are in parallel.

questions.s: A heater rated 40 W at 220 V is connected to a 110 V supply. Assuming its resistance does not change, the power it now consumes is
questions.e: P = V²/R with R fixed, so halving V makes P one quarter: 40/4 = 10 W. The answer 20 W assumes power is proportional to V rather than to V².

questions.s: An electric kettle of power 2 kW is switched on for 3 minutes. The electrical energy it uses is
questions.e: E = Pt = 2000 W × 180 s = 360 000 J = 360 kJ. Using t = 3 (minutes) without converting gives 6 kJ, and using one minute gives 120 kJ.

questions.s: A cell of emf 2 V gives a current of 10 A when its terminals are joined by a thick wire of negligible resistance. The internal resistance of the cell is
questions.e: On short circuit the only resistance is r, so I = E/r and r = E/I = 2/10 = 0.2 Ω. 5 Ω comes from I/E, the inverted ratio, and 20 Ω from multiplying E by I.

questions.s: A 12 V battery with internal resistance 0.5 Ω is being charged with a current of 2 A. The potential difference across its terminals during charging is
questions.e: During charging current is forced into the positive terminal, so the charger must supply the emf plus the internal drop: V = E + Ir = 12 + 2 × 0.5 = 13 V. 11 V is E − Ir, which applies when the battery is discharging.

questions.s: A high-resistance voltmeter reads 1.5 V across a cell on open circuit and 1.2 V when a 6 Ω resistor is connected across the cell. The internal resistance of the cell is
questions.e: With the resistor connected, I = V/R = 1.2/6 = 0.2 A. The lost volts are 1.5 − 1.2 = 0.3 V, so r = 0.3/0.2 = 1.5 Ω. 7.5 Ω is E/I, which is the total resistance R + r, and 0.3 is the lost voltage, not a resistance.

questions.s: When a battery delivers maximum power to an external resistor, the efficiency of the circuit (power in the load ÷ total power from the battery) is
questions.e: Maximum power transfer needs R = r, so the same current flows through equal resistances and the load and the internal resistance dissipate equal power. Efficiency = R/(R + r) = 1/2 = 50%. 100% would need r = 0.

questions.s: A cell delivers the same power to an external resistor of 4 Ω as to one of 9 Ω. The internal resistance of the cell is
questions.e: P = E²R/(R + r)², so 4/(4 + r)² = 9/(9 + r)². Taking square roots, 2/(4 + r) = 3/(9 + r), so 18 + 2r = 12 + 3r and r = 6 Ω (in general r = √(R₁R₂)). 6.5 Ω is the average of 4 and 9, not the geometric mean.

questions.s: At a junction of four wires, currents of 3 A and 5 A flow in through two of the wires and 2 A flows out through the third. The current in the fourth wire is
questions.e: By the junction rule, current in = current out: 3 + 5 = 2 + I, so I = 6 A flowing out. 10 A adds all three numbers, ignoring that the 2 A is already leaving.

questions.s: A cell of emf 9 V and a cell of emf 3 V, each of internal resistance 1 Ω, are connected in series with their positive terminals facing each other (in opposition), together with a 4 Ω resistor. The terminal potential difference of the 3 V cell is
questions.e: Net emf = 9 − 3 = 6 V, total resistance = 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 Ω, so I = 1 A. The current is driven into the positive terminal of the 3 V cell, which is being charged: V = E + Ir = 3 + 1 = 4 V. 2 V wrongly uses E − Ir, as if this cell were supplying the current.

questions.s: In a metre bridge, an unknown resistance X is in the left gap and a 10 Ω resistor in the right gap. The balance point is 75 cm from the left end. The value of X is
questions.e: At balance X/10 = l/(100 − l) = 75/25, so X = 30 Ω. Swapping the lengths gives 10 × 25/75 ≈ 3.3 Ω; the larger resistance must sit on the side of the longer wire segment.

questions.s: A steady current flows through a uniform potentiometer wire. The potential difference across any part of the wire is proportional to
o: the square root of its length
questions.e: For a uniform wire the resistance of a section is proportional to its length, and with a steady current V = IR, so V ∝ l. This is the basic principle of the potentiometer; nothing in V = IR involves l² or √l.

questions.s: On a potentiometer, a cell balances at 75 cm on open circuit. When a 4 Ω resistor is connected across the cell, the balance length becomes 60 cm. The internal resistance of the cell is
questions.e: E ∝ 75 and the terminal p.d. V ∝ 60. r = R(E − V)/V = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂ = 4 × 15/60 = 1 Ω. Dividing by l₁ instead of l₂ gives 4 × 15/75 = 0.8 Ω, which uses the emf instead of the terminal voltage.

questions.s: In a simple model of an atom, an electron moves in a circular orbit, completing 6.25 × 10¹⁵ revolutions per second. The equivalent current due to its motion is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: Each revolution carries charge e past any point of the orbit, so I = ef = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 6.25 × 10¹⁵ = 1 × 10⁻³ A = 1 mA. Dividing e by f instead of multiplying gives a meaninglessly tiny value.

questions.s: The current in a conductor rises uniformly from 0 to 4 A in 10 s. The charge that passes through the conductor in this time is
questions.e: Charge is the area under the I-t graph: ½ × 10 × 4 = 20 C (equivalently, average current 2 A for 10 s). 40 C uses the final current for the whole time, ignoring that the current started at zero.

questions.s: Hamza plots current I (vertical axis) against potential difference V (horizontal axis) for two metal resistors A and B. Both graphs are straight lines through the origin, and the line for A is steeper. Which statement is correct?
o: A and B have equal resistance
A does not obey Ohm's law
questions.e: The slope of an I-V graph is I/V = 1/R, so the steeper line belongs to the smaller resistance. If V were on the vertical axis, a steeper line would mean a larger resistance, which is the usual mix-up.

questions.s: A wire of resistance 12 Ω is cut into three equal pieces, and the pieces are then connected in parallel. The resistance of the combination is
questions.e: Each piece has resistance 12/3 = 4 Ω, and three 4 Ω resistors in parallel give 4/3 Ω. 4 Ω is the value of one piece, forgetting the parallel connection.

questions.s: A wire of resistance R is drawn out (keeping its volume constant) until its radius becomes half of the original. Its new resistance is
questions.e: Halving the radius makes the area A/4; constant volume then makes the length 4L. R′ = ρ(4L)/(A/4) = 16R. 4R accounts for only one of the two changes, either the smaller area or the greater length.

questions.s: The resistance of a metal increases with temperature mainly because
o: the number of free electrons per unit volume falls sharply
the lattice ions vibrate more, so collisions are more frequent
the wire contracts, so its cross-section decreases
the free electrons lose part of their charge
questions.e: In a metal the number of free electrons hardly changes with temperature, but hotter lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude, so drifting electrons collide more often and the resistance rises. A fall in carrier number is the opposite of what happens in semiconductors, where heating releases more carriers.

questions.s: Which of the following materials has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance?
questions.e: Germanium is a semiconductor: heating frees more charge carriers, so its resistance falls and α is negative. Copper, tungsten and nichrome are metals or alloys with positive α (nichrome's is very small but still positive).

questions.s: A carbon resistor has the bands brown, green, red, gold. The greatest value its actual resistance can have within the tolerance is
questions.e: Brown = 1, green = 5, red multiplier 10², so the nominal value is 1500 Ω; gold means ±5%, i.e. ±75 Ω. The maximum is 1500 + 75 = 1575 Ω. 1425 Ω is the minimum, and 1650 Ω uses a ±10% (silver) tolerance.

questions.s: A 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor are joined in series, and this pair is connected in parallel with a 3 Ω resistor. The equivalent resistance is
questions.e: The series pair is 2 + 4 = 6 Ω; 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω gives 18/9 = 2 Ω. 9 Ω treats all three as in series, and 4.33 Ω wrongly puts 2 Ω and 4 Ω in parallel and then adds 3 Ω.

questions.s: Three resistors of 6 Ω each are to be combined to give a resistance of 4 Ω. This is done by
o: connecting two in series and the third in parallel with them
connecting two in parallel and the third in series with them
questions.e: Two in series give 12 Ω, and 12 Ω in parallel with 6 Ω gives 72/18 = 4 Ω. Two in parallel (3 Ω) plus one in series gives 9 Ω; all in series gives 18 Ω and all in parallel 2 Ω.

questions.s: Bilal's electric iron is rated 2.2 kW, 220 V. The most suitable fuse for its plug, from those available, is
questions.e: Normal current I = P/V = 2200/220 = 10 A. The fuse should be rated a little above the normal current, so 13 A. A 3 A or 5 A fuse would blow at once, and a 30 A fuse would let a dangerously large fault current flow.

questions.s: Resistors of 2 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel across a battery. The ratio of the power dissipated in the 2 Ω resistor to that in the 3 Ω resistor is
questions.e: In parallel both have the same p.d., so P = V²/R ∝ 1/R, giving P₂ : P₃ = 3 : 2. 2 : 3 would be the ratio for resistors in series, where P = I²R ∝ R.

questions.s: A heater coil rated 900 W is shortened by cutting off one quarter of its length, and the rest is connected to the same supply. The power of the heater now is
questions.e: The remaining coil has resistance 3R/4. With the same supply voltage, P = V²/R ∝ 1/R, so P′ = 900 × 4/3 = 1200 W. 675 W multiplies by 3/4, which would be right only if the current, not the voltage, stayed the same.

questions.s: Two heaters, each rated 1000 W at 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. The total power drawn is
questions.e: Each heater has R = V²/P = 48.4 Ω, so in series the total is 96.8 Ω and P = 220²/96.8 = 500 W (half of one heater's power). 2000 W would be drawn if they were in parallel; 250 W is the power of each heater in series.

questions.s: The emf of a cell is best described as
o: the energy supplied by the cell per unit charge
the force that the cell exerts on each charge
the p.d. across its terminals when current flows
the charge it supplies per unit time
questions.e: Emf is the energy converted from other forms (chemical) into electrical energy per coulomb of charge passing through the source, measured in J/C = V. Despite its name it is not a force, and the terminal p.d. while current flows is less than the emf by Ir.

questions.s: A graph of terminal potential difference V (vertical) against current I (horizontal) for a cell is a straight line that meets the V-axis at 3 V and the I-axis at 6 A. The emf and internal resistance of the cell are
questions.e: V = E − Ir, so the V-intercept (I = 0) is E = 3 V and the magnitude of the slope is r = 3/6 = 0.5 Ω. The I-intercept is the short-circuit current E/r = 6 A, not the emf; 2 Ω inverts the slope.

questions.s: Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series to a 4 Ω resistor. The current in the circuit is
questions.e: In series the emfs add to 6 V and the internal resistances to 2 Ω, so I = 6/(4 + 2) = 1 A. Ignoring internal resistance gives 1.5 A, and counting only one cell's internal resistance gives 6/4.5 ≈ 1.33 A.

questions.s: A battery of emf 10 V and internal resistance 2 Ω delivers 12 W to an external resistor R. One possible value of R is
questions.e: P = E²R/(R + r)²: 12 = 100R/(R + 2)², giving 3R² − 13R + 12 = 0, so R = 3 Ω or 4/3 Ω. Check: 3 Ω gives I = 2 A and P = 4 × 3 = 12 W. R = 2 Ω is the maximum power case and gives 12.5 W, not 12 W.

questions.s: When applying Kirchhoff's loop rule, a resistor R carrying current I is crossed in the same direction as the current. The change in potential to be written is
questions.e: Conventional current flows from higher to lower potential through a resistor, so moving with the current the potential falls by IR: write −IR. +IR applies when the resistor is crossed against the current.

questions.s: A 6 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected between A (positive) and B. Two branches join A to B: one is 1 Ω then 2 Ω, with junction C between them; the other is 2 Ω then 1 Ω, with junction D between them. The potential difference between C and D is
questions.e: Each branch is 3 Ω and carries 2 A. C is 2 × 1 = 2 V below A, so V_C = 4 V; D is 2 × 2 = 4 V below A, so V_D = 2 V. V_C − V_D = 2 V. 0 V would hold only for a balanced bridge, but here 1/2 ≠ 2/1.

questions.s: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced. If the positions of the battery and the galvanometer are interchanged, then
o: the bridge can no longer be balanced
the galvanometer reads the battery current
questions.e: The balance condition P/Q = R/S can be rearranged as P/R = Q/S, which is exactly the condition for the interchanged bridge, so the galvanometer still shows zero deflection. The resistances themselves do not change.

questions.s: A Wheatstone bridge has P = Q = 100 Ω, a variable resistor R and an NTC thermistor S, with P/Q = R/S at balance. It is balanced at room temperature. When the thermistor is warmed, to restore balance R must be
o: replaced by a wire of zero resistance
questions.e: With P = Q, balance requires R = S. Warming an NTC thermistor lowers S, so R must be decreased to match it. Increasing R is the correct response for a metal resistance thermometer, whose resistance rises when heated.

questions.s: Two cells of emfs E₁ and E₂ (E₁ > E₂) are connected in series. On a potentiometer, the pair balances at 90 cm when the cells aid each other and at 30 cm when they oppose each other. The ratio E₁ : E₂ is
questions.e: E₁ + E₂ ∝ 90 and E₁ − E₂ ∝ 30. Adding and subtracting: 2E₁ ∝ 120 and 2E₂ ∝ 60, so E₁ : E₂ = 120 : 60 = 2 : 1. 3 : 1 is just 90 : 30, the ratio of the sum to the difference.

questions.s: Sana wants her potentiometer to measure small emfs more precisely by lowering the potential drop per centimetre of wire. She should
o: use a shorter wire with the same driver cell
increase the current through the wire
use a longer wire with the same driver cell
connect a resistor in parallel with the galvanometer
questions.e: The potential gradient is the p.d. across the wire divided by its length; a longer wire with the same driver p.d. gives fewer volts per cm, so a given emf balances over a longer, more precisely read length. Increasing the current raises the gradient and makes it less sensitive.

questions.s: An NTC thermistor and a 1 kΩ fixed resistor are connected in series across a 6 V supply, and the output is taken across the fixed resistor. The thermistor's resistance is 2 kΩ at 20 °C and 1 kΩ at 60 °C. As the temperature goes from 20 °C to 60 °C, the output voltage
questions.e: Potential divider: V_out = 6 × 1/(1 + R_T). At 20 °C V_out = 6 × 1/3 = 2 V; at 60 °C V_out = 6 × 1/2 = 3 V, so it rises from 2 V to 3 V. 4 V to 3 V is the change across the thermistor, not across the fixed resistor.

questions.s: Free electrons in a wire drift at 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m/s. The time an electron would take to drift along 1 m of the wire is
questions.e: t = d/v = 1/(2.5 × 10⁻⁴) = 4 × 10³ s, more than an hour. A lamp still lights at once because the electric field, not the individual electrons, travels through the circuit at nearly the speed of light. 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ s multiplies distance by speed instead of dividing.

questions.s: Wires A and B have the same cross-sectional area and carry the same current. The number of free electrons per unit volume in A is twice that in B. The ratio of drift velocities v_A : v_B is
questions.e: I = nAev with I and A equal gives v ∝ 1/n, so v_A : v_B = 1 : 2. With twice as many carriers, each needs to drift only half as fast to carry the same current; 2 : 1 assumes v ∝ n.

questions.s: The direction of conventional current in a metal wire is
o: from the negative terminal to the positive terminal through the external circuit
opposite to the direction of electron flow
the same as the direction of electron flow
perpendicular to the electric field in the wire
questions.e: Conventional current is taken as the flow of positive charge, from + to − in the external circuit. In metals the carriers are electrons, which move the other way, so conventional current is opposite to electron flow. The first option describes the electron flow itself.

questions.s: A filament lamp takes a current of 0.5 A at 6 V and 0.75 A at 12 V. As the voltage rises from 6 V to 12 V, the resistance of the filament increases by
questions.e: Resistance is V/I at each point: 6/0.5 = 12 Ω and 12/0.75 = 16 Ω, an increase of 4 Ω as the filament heats. 24 Ω is ΔV/ΔI = 6/0.25, the reciprocal slope of the curve, which is not the resistance of a non-ohmic device.

questions.s: Two wires are made of the same metal and have equal masses. Their lengths are in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their resistances is
questions.e: Equal mass and density means equal volume, so A = V/L and R = ρL/A = ρL²/V ∝ L². The ratio is 1² : 2² = 1 : 4. 1 : 2 ignores that the longer wire must also be thinner.

questions.s: The SI unit of electrical conductivity is
questions.e: Conductivity σ = 1/ρ, and resistivity has the unit Ω m, so σ is measured in Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹ (siemens per metre). Ω m is the unit of resistivity itself.

questions.s: Alloys such as manganin and constantan are used to make standard resistors because they have
o: a very low resistivity, even lower than that of copper
a resistance that hardly changes with temperature
a melting point lower than that of solder
questions.e: A standard resistor must keep its value as it warms, so it is made from an alloy with a very small temperature coefficient of resistance. These alloys actually have a high resistivity compared with copper, and a large negative α is the property of a thermistor.

questions.s: A carbon resistor (α = −5 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹) and an iron resistor (α = 5 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹) are joined in series. Their total resistance is 22 Ω and does not change for small changes of temperature. The resistance of the iron resistor is
questions.e: For no change in total resistance, the rise in one must cancel the fall in the other: R_iron × 5 × 10⁻³ = R_carbon × 5 × 10⁻⁴, so R_carbon = 10 R_iron. With R_iron + R_carbon = 22 Ω, R_iron = 2 Ω and R_carbon = 20 Ω. 20 Ω is the carbon resistor, which must be the larger because its α is smaller in size.

questions.s: A low-value resistor is marked with the bands yellow, violet, gold, gold. Its resistance is
questions.e: Yellow = 4, violet = 7, and gold in the third (multiplier) position means × 0.1, so R = 47 × 0.1 = 4.7 Ω; the fourth gold band is ±5%. Silver as a multiplier would mean × 0.01, giving 0.47 Ω.

questions.s: Resistors of 1 Ω, 2 Ω and 3 Ω can be combined in different ways. The ratio of the largest possible resistance to the smallest possible resistance is
questions.e: Largest: all in series, 6 Ω. Smallest: all in parallel, 1/(1 + 1/2 + 1/3) = 6/11 Ω. Ratio = 6 ÷ (6/11) = 11. 1/11 is the ratio taken the wrong way up, and 6 compares the series value with 1 Ω.

questions.s: Three identical bulbs A, B and C are connected to a fixed voltage supply: A is in series with a parallel pair formed by B and C. If the filament of C breaks, then
o: A becomes brighter and B dimmer
A becomes dimmer and B brighter
A and B both become brighter
A and B both become dimmer
questions.e: Before: total resistance 1.5R, so A carries 2V/3R and B carries V/3R. After C breaks: total 2R, so A and B each carry V/2R. A's current falls (dimmer) and B's rises (brighter). Assuming everything dims misses that B now carries the whole current through A.

questions.s: An electric motor connected to a 220 V supply draws a current of 5 A. The resistance of its coil is 4 Ω. The rate at which heat is produced in the coil is
questions.e: Heat in the coil is I²R = 5² × 4 = 100 W. The input power is VI = 1100 W, of which 1000 W becomes mechanical work. 12100 W uses V²/R, which is wrong because the motor's back emf means V ≠ IR for the coil.
