questions.s: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor in parallel are connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor across a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The power dissipated in the 3 Ω resistor is
questions.e: 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω, total 4 Ω, so I = 3 A and the p.d. across the parallel pair is 3 × 2 = 6 V. P = V²/R = 36/3 = 12 W. 27 W wrongly sends the full 3 A through the 3 Ω resistor, and 6 W is the power in the 6 Ω resistor.

questions.s: The terminal potential difference of a cell is equal to its emf when
o: no current is drawn from the cell
questions.e: V = E − Ir, so V = E only when I = 0, i.e. on open circuit. On short circuit the terminal p.d. is zero, and with R = r it is E/2.

questions.s: Two identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, are connected in parallel (positive to positive) across a 1.5 Ω resistor. The current in the resistor is
questions.e: Identical cells in parallel act as one cell of emf 2 V with internal resistance 1/2 = 0.5 Ω, so I = 2/(1.5 + 0.5) = 1 A. Using r = 1 Ω gives 0.8 A, and ignoring internal resistance gives 1.33 A. Adding the emfs to 4 V is wrong for a parallel connection.

questions.s: A graph of the power delivered by a battery to a variable external resistor R has its peak at R = 5 Ω, where the power is 20 W. The emf of the battery is
questions.e: The peak occurs at R = r, so r = 5 Ω, and P_max = E²/4r gives E² = 4 × 5 × 20 = 400, so E = 20 V. Using E² = P r gives 10 V, and 400 V forgets the square root.

questions.s: A 12 V battery (negligible internal resistance) sends current through a 3 Ω resistor to point X and returns from point Y. Between X and Y are two parallel branches: a 6 Ω resistor, and a 2 Ω resistor in series with a 4 V cell whose positive terminal faces X. The current drawn from the battery is
questions.e: Take Y as 0 V and X at V. Junction rule at X: (12 − V)/3 = V/6 + (V − 4)/2. Multiplying by 6: 24 − 2V = V + 3V − 12, so V = 6 V and the battery current is (12 − 6)/3 = 2 A (1 A in each branch). Ignoring the 4 V cell gives 12/4.5 ≈ 2.67 A.

questions.s: In part of a circuit a current of 2 A flows from A to B through a 3 Ω resistor, then through a 5 V cell (entering at its negative terminal), then through a 1 Ω resistor. The potential difference V_A − V_B is
questions.e: Going from A to B: −2 × 3 (drop) + 5 (rise from − to + through the cell) − 2 × 1 (drop) = −3 V, so V_B = V_A − 3 and V_A − V_B = 3 V. 13 V gives the cell the wrong sign, and 8 V ignores the cell.

questions.s: A Wheatstone bridge measures resistance accurately mainly because
o: it passes a very large current through the unknown
it needs no battery at all
it needs a galvanometer of zero resistance
the galvanometer's scale need not be calibrated
questions.e: It is a null method: at balance the galvanometer shows zero, so only the absence of current is detected, and errors in the meter's scale or resistance do not affect the result. A large current would heat the resistors and spoil the measurement.

questions.s: In a Wheatstone bridge P = 10 Ω, Q = 20 Ω, R = 10 Ω and S = 30 Ω, and balance requires P/Q = R/S. To balance the bridge, the resistance that must be connected in parallel with S is
questions.e: Balance needs S = RQ/P = 20 Ω. A resistor X in parallel with 30 Ω must give 20 Ω: 30X/(30 + X) = 20, so 30X = 600 + 20X and X = 60 Ω. 20 Ω is the required effective value of the S arm, not the resistor to be added in parallel.

questions.s: A potentiometer wire 100 cm long has a resistance of 4 Ω. It is connected in series with a 6 Ω resistor and a driver cell of emf 2 V and negligible internal resistance. The potential gradient along the wire is
questions.e: I = 2/(4 + 6) = 0.2 A, so the p.d. across the wire is 0.2 × 4 = 0.8 V over 100 cm: 0.008 V/cm. 0.02 V/cm ignores the series resistor, and 0.012 V/cm uses the 1.2 V across the 6 Ω resistor.

questions.s: A long uniform resistance wire with a sliding contact is connected across a 10 V supply and used as a potential divider. The output taken between one end and the sliding contact can be varied from
questions.e: Moving the contact from one end to the other takes the output from zero (contact at the reference end) to the full 10 V (contact at the far end), varying smoothly in proportion to length. This continuous range from zero is the advantage of a potential divider over a series rheostat.

questions.s: A typical NTC thermistor used as a temperature sensor is made of
o: pure copper drawn into a fine coil
an alloy of nickel and chromium
questions.e: Thermistors are made from semiconducting metal oxides (for example of manganese, nickel or cobalt) pressed and heated into beads or discs. Copper, nichrome and tungsten are metallic conductors whose resistance rises with temperature, not falls.

questions.s: A 9 V battery of negligible internal resistance, a 1 kΩ resistor and an NTC thermistor are connected in series. When the thermistor is heated, the current rises to 3 mA. The thermistor's resistance is now
questions.e: Total resistance = 9 V/3 mA = 3 kΩ, so the thermistor has 3 − 1 = 2 kΩ. 3 kΩ is the whole circuit's resistance, forgetting the fixed 1 kΩ resistor.

questions.s: For an NTC thermistor over a wide range of temperatures, a graph of resistance against temperature shows the resistance
o: falling, steeply at first and then gradually
falling in a straight line to zero
questions.e: An NTC thermistor's resistance falls roughly exponentially with temperature: a large drop at low temperatures and a smaller drop at higher ones, a non-linear curve. A straight rising line describes a metal, and the resistance never falls to zero.

questions.s: One ampere of current is equivalent to
questions.e: Current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t, so 1 A = 1 coulomb per second. 1 J/C is the volt, and 1 C s would mean charge multiplied by time, which is not a rate.

questions.s: A current of 0.5 A flows in a wire for 2 minutes. The number of electrons that pass a point in the wire is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: Q = It = 0.5 × 120 = 60 C, and n = Q/e = 60/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 3.75 × 10²⁰. Using t = 2 instead of 120 s gives Q = 1 C and 6.25 × 10¹⁸, and multiplying Q by e gives 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁸.

questions.s: A 5 V supply is connected across a 20 Ω resistor. The current through the resistor is
questions.e: I = V/R = 5/20 = 0.25 A. Dividing R by V gives 4 A, and multiplying them gives 100, which would be in V Ω, not amperes.

questions.s: Two wires of the same material and the same length have diameters in the ratio 1 : 3. The ratio of their resistances is
questions.e: R = ρL/A with A ∝ d², so R ∝ 1/d². The ratio is 3² : 1² = 9 : 1, the thinner wire having the larger resistance. 3 : 1 forgets to square the diameter ratio, and 1 : 9 inverts it.

questions.s: A tungsten filament has a resistance of 20 Ω at 0 °C. Taking α = 0.005 K⁻¹ and R = R₀(1 + αθ), the temperature at which its resistance is 60 Ω is
questions.e: 60 = 20(1 + 0.005θ) gives 1 + 0.005θ = 3, so 0.005θ = 2 and θ = 400 °C. 600 °C comes from using 60/20 = 3 directly as 0.005θ, forgetting to subtract the 1.

questions.s: A resistor has colour bands green, blue, black, gold. Its value is
questions.e: Green = 5, blue = 6, black multiplier = 10⁰ = 1, gold = ±5%. R = 56 × 1 = 56 Ω ± 5%. Treating black as 10¹ gives 560 Ω, and ±10% would need a silver fourth band.

questions.s: In a circuit where several resistors are connected in series, the quantity that is the same for every resistor is the
questions.e: A series circuit has only one path, so the same current flows through every resistor. The p.d. and power are shared in proportion to the resistances; it is in a parallel circuit that the p.d. is the same for each branch.

questions.s: Resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel across a 6 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The total current from the supply is
questions.e: 4 ∥ 12 = 48/16 = 3 Ω, so I = 6/3 = 2 A (1.5 A in the 4 Ω branch plus 0.5 A in the 12 Ω branch). 0.375 A treats the resistors as in series (16 Ω), and 1.5 A and 0.5 A are the separate branch currents.

questions.s: One kilowatt-hour, the commercial unit of electrical energy, is equal to
questions.e: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. 3.6 × 10³ J forgets the factor 1000 for kilo, and 6 × 10⁴ J uses one minute instead of one hour.

questions.s: A car headlamp is rated 12 V, 24 W. Its resistance when working normally is
questions.e: R = V²/P = 144/24 = 6 Ω (the current is P/V = 2 A, and 12/2 = 6 Ω). 2 Ω is the current in amperes, not the resistance, and 288 Ω multiplies V by P.

questions.s: A battery of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 5 Ω resistor. The power wasted inside the battery is
questions.e: I = 6/(5 + 1) = 1 A, so the power dissipated in the internal resistance is I²r = 1 × 1 = 1 W. 5 W is the power in the external resistor, and 6 W is the total power EI.

questions.s: Zainab increases the external resistance connected to a cell of constant emf and internal resistance. The terminal potential difference of the cell
questions.e: A larger external resistance means a smaller current, so the lost volts Ir fall and V = E − Ir increases towards E. It equals E only on open circuit, when no current flows.

questions.s: Hamza has a battery of emf 6 V and internal resistance 2 Ω. He chooses an external resistor so that it receives the greatest possible power. That power is
questions.e: Maximum power occurs for R = r = 2 Ω: I = 6/4 = 1.5 A and P = I²R = 2.25 × 2 = 4.5 W (= E²/4r = 36/8). 9 W is the total power EI drawn from the battery, half of which is wasted inside it; 18 W is E²/r.

questions.s: At a junction, a current of 4 A divides into three wires. Two of the wires carry 1 A and 2.5 A away from the junction. The current in the third wire is
questions.e: By Kirchhoff's junction rule the outgoing currents must total 4 A: 1 + 2.5 + I = 4, so I = 0.5 A away from the junction. 7.5 A adds all three given currents, and 3.5 A is the sum of the two known outgoing currents.

questions.s: A cell of emf 6 V and one of emf 4 V, each of internal resistance 1 Ω, are connected in parallel (positive to positive) with no external load. The potential difference across the combination is
questions.e: The cells drive a circulating current I = (6 − 4)/(1 + 1) = 1 A round the loop. The common terminal p.d. is 6 − 1 × 1 = 5 V, which also equals 4 + 1 × 1 for the cell being charged. 10 V adds the emfs as if the cells were in series.

questions.s: In a metre bridge, a 5 Ω resistor is in the left gap and an unknown resistor X in the right gap. The balance point is 40 cm from the left end. The value of X is
questions.e: At balance 5/X = 40/60, so X = 5 × 60/40 = 7.5 Ω. Inverting the length ratio gives 3.33 Ω; since X sits opposite the longer 60 cm segment it must be larger than 5 Ω.

questions.s: A Wheatstone bridge has P = 1 Ω and Q = 2 Ω in one path and R = 2 Ω and S = 4 Ω in the other, with a 5 Ω galvanometer joining the P-Q and R-S junctions. A 6 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across the bridge. The current drawn from the battery is
questions.e: P/Q = R/S = 1/2, so the bridge is balanced and the galvanometer carries no current; its 5 Ω does not matter. The paths of 3 Ω and 6 Ω are in parallel: 18/9 = 2 Ω, so I = 6/2 = 3 A. 2 A counts only the 3 Ω path, and 0.67 A puts all four resistors in series.

questions.s: A standard cell of emf 1.08 V balances at 54 cm on a potentiometer wire. A second cell balances at 75 cm on the same wire with the same driver current. The emf of the second cell is
questions.e: The potential gradient is 1.08/54 = 0.02 V/cm, so E = 0.02 × 75 = 1.5 V. Using the inverse ratio 1.08 × 54/75 gives about 0.78 V, smaller than the standard even though it balances at a longer length.

questions.s: A potentiometer wire 100 cm long has a resistance of 10 Ω. It is driven by a 2 V cell of negligible internal resistance through a series resistor. To obtain a potential gradient of 0.01 V/cm, the series resistor must be
questions.e: A gradient of 0.01 V/cm over 100 cm means 1 V across the wire, so I = 1/10 = 0.1 A. The total resistance must be 2/0.1 = 20 Ω, leaving 20 − 10 = 10 Ω for the series resistor. 20 Ω is the total circuit resistance, not the added resistor.

questions.s: In a fire alarm, an NTC thermistor is connected in series with a fixed resistor across a steady supply. As a fire heats the thermistor, the potential difference across the thermistor
questions.e: Heating lowers the NTC thermistor's resistance, so it takes a smaller share of the supply voltage in the potential divider and its p.d. falls, while the p.d. across the fixed resistor rises and can trigger the alarm. Saying it rises confuses the thermistor with the fixed resistor.

questions.s: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. The magnetic field at a distance of 2 cm from the wire is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
questions.e: For a long straight wire B = μ₀I/(2πr) = (2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10)/0.02 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ T. Using 1 cm instead of 2 cm gives 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ T, and using the loop formula μ₀I/(2r) gives 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ T; neither applies to a straight wire at 2 cm.

questions.s: The magnetic field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are
o: Lines radially outward from the wire
questions.e: The field of a straight current forms closed concentric circles in planes perpendicular to the wire, with direction given by the right-hand grip rule. Radial lines describe the electric field of a line charge, not the magnetic field of a current.

questions.s: A solenoid 50 cm long has 500 turns and carries a current of 4 A. The magnetic field inside it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
questions.e: Turns per metre n = 500/0.5 = 1000 m⁻¹, so B = μ₀nI = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 4 = 1.6π × 10⁻³ T. Using N = 500 directly instead of turns per metre gives 0.8π × 10⁻³ T, and dividing by 50 cm without converting to metres gives 1.6π × 10⁻⁵ T.

questions.s: A closed loop encloses two long parallel wires carrying currents of 3 A and 5 A in opposite directions. The magnitude of ∮B·dL around the loop is
questions.e: Ampere's law gives ∮B·dL = μ₀ × (net current enclosed). The currents are opposite, so the net current is 5 − 3 = 2 A and the integral is 2μ₀ T m. Adding the currents to get 8μ₀ ignores their directions.

questions.s: The number of turns per unit length of a long solenoid is doubled and the current through it is halved. The magnetic field inside the solenoid
questions.e: B = μ₀nI depends on the product nI. Doubling n and halving I leaves nI, and so B, unchanged. Choosing 'four times' wrongly treats both changes as increases.

questions.s: A straight wire 0.5 m long carries 4 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. The force on the wire is
questions.e: F = BIL sin θ = 0.2 × 4 × 0.5 × sin 90° = 0.4 N. The answer 0.8 N comes from forgetting the factor 0.5 m for the length.

questions.s: A wire 0.8 m long carrying 5 A lies in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T, making an angle of 30° with the field. The magnitude of the force on it is (√3 ≈ 1.73)
questions.e: F = BIL sin θ = 0.5 × 5 × 0.8 × sin 30° = 2.0 × 0.5 = 1.0 N. Using cos 30° instead of sin 30° gives about 1.7 N; the angle in BIL sin θ is between the wire and the field.

questions.s: Two long parallel wires 5 cm apart each carry 10 A in the same direction. The force per metre between them is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
questions.e: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10 × 10/0.05 = 4 × 10⁻⁴ N/m. Parallel currents in the same direction attract; only opposite currents repel.

questions.s: A horizontal wire of mass 0.02 kg per metre lies at right angles to a horizontal magnetic field of 0.5 T. The current needed for the magnetic force to support its weight is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: For balance BIL = mg, so I = (m/L)g/B = 0.02 × 10/0.5 = 0.4 A. Forgetting g gives 0.04 A, which supports only a tenth of the weight.

questions.s: A coil of 100 turns and area 20 cm² carries 0.5 A in a uniform field of 0.4 T, with the plane of the coil parallel to the field. The torque on the coil is
questions.e: With the plane parallel to B the torque is maximum: τ = NIAB = 100 × 0.5 × 20 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.4 = 0.04 N m. 'Zero' is the torque when the plane is perpendicular to the field, and 0.4 N m comes from taking 20 cm² as 2 × 10⁻² m².

questions.s: A rectangular coil of 50 turns and area 0.01 m² carries 2 A in a uniform field of 0.2 T. The plane of the coil makes an angle of 60° with the field. The torque on the coil is (√3 ≈ 1.73)
questions.e: τ = NIAB cos α, where α is the angle between the plane of the coil and the field: 50 × 2 × 0.01 × 0.2 × cos 60° = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.10 N m. Using sin 60° gives 0.17 N m, which treats 60° as the angle between the field and the coil's normal.

questions.s: The force on a straight current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field is maximum when the conductor is
questions.e: F = BIL sin θ is largest when sin θ = 1, that is θ = 90°. Parallel or antiparallel conductors have sin θ = 0 and feel no force at all.

questions.s: An electron moves at 2 × 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.5 T. The magnetic force on it is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.e: F = qvB sin 90° = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10⁶ × 0.5 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N. Omitting the factor 0.5 for B gives 3.2 × 10⁻¹³ N.

questions.s: A charged particle moves through a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on the particle
questions.e: F = q(v × B) is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed and kinetic energy stay constant; only the direction changes. The force is proportional to q, so it does depend on the charge.

questions.s: A particle of mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T at right angles with speed 2 × 10⁶ m/s. The radius of its circular path is
questions.e: r = mv/(qB) = (1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2 × 10⁶)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.1) = 3.2 × 10⁻²¹/1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ = 0.2 m. Dropping the factor 0.1 of B in the denominator gives 0.02 m.

questions.s: A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles with the same speed. The ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to that of the proton is
questions.e: r = mv/(qB), so r ∝ m/q at equal speed. The alpha particle has 4 times the mass and 2 times the charge, so r_α/r_p = 4/2 = 2. Answer 1/2 inverts the ratio.

questions.s: A proton and an alpha particle with the same kinetic energy move at right angles to the same uniform magnetic field. The ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to that of the proton is
questions.e: With momentum p = √(2mK), r = √(2mK)/(qB) ∝ √m/q at equal K. For the alpha particle √4/2 = 1 relative to the proton's √1/1 = 1, so the ratio is 1. The answer 2 holds for equal speeds, not equal kinetic energies.

questions.s: A charged particle moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled, the time it takes for one revolution
questions.e: T = 2πr/v and r = mv/(qB), so T = 2πm/(qB), which does not depend on speed. Doubling v doubles the radius, and the longer path exactly cancels the higher speed, so 'halved' is wrong.

questions.s: In a velocity selector, crossed fields E = 3 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.2 T are used. The speed of the ions that pass through undeflected is
questions.e: Undeflected ions have qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 3 × 10⁴/0.2 = 1.5 × 10⁵ m/s. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 6.0 × 10³ m/s, and B/E gives 6.7 × 10⁻⁶ m/s.

questions.s: In an e/m experiment, electrons accelerated from rest through 250 V move in a circle of radius 5 cm in a uniform magnetic field of 1.0 × 10⁻³ T. The value of e/m obtained is
questions.e: From eV = ½mv² and r = mv/(eB), e/m = 2V/(B²r²) = 500/(10⁻⁶ × 25 × 10⁻⁴) = 500/(2.5 × 10⁻⁹) = 2.0 × 10¹¹ C/kg. Dropping the factor 2 gives 1.0 × 10¹¹ C/kg, and treating 5 cm as the diameter gives 8.0 × 10¹¹ C/kg.

questions.s: A charged particle is projected parallel to a uniform magnetic field. Its path is a
questions.e: For v parallel to B, F = qvB sin 0° = 0, so the particle continues in a straight line at constant velocity. A circle needs v perpendicular to B, and a helix needs an angle between 0° and 90°.

questions.s: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field with its velocity at 30° to the field direction. Its path in the field is
questions.e: The velocity component v cos 30° along B is unaffected, while the component v sin 30° perpendicular to B produces circular motion. The combination is a helix. A parabola would need a constant force in a fixed direction, as in an electric field.

questions.s: A circular coil of 10 turns and radius 10 cm carries a current of 2 A. The magnetic field at its centre is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
questions.e: At the centre of a circular coil B = μ₀NI/(2R) = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10 × 2/(2 × 0.1) = 4π × 10⁻⁵ T. Using the diameter 0.2 m as R gives half this, 2π × 10⁻⁵ T.

questions.s: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 5 A each in opposite directions. The magnetic field at the point midway between them is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
questions.e: Each wire gives B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 5/0.05 = 2 × 10⁻⁵ T at the midpoint. With opposite currents the two fields point the same way between the wires and add to 4 × 10⁻⁵ T. 'Zero' is the result for currents in the same direction.

questions.s: A moving coil galvanometer is converted into an ammeter by connecting
questions.e: An ammeter must carry the large circuit current while only the small full-scale current passes through the coil, so a low resistance (shunt) is placed in parallel to divert the rest. A high resistance in series is the voltmeter conversion.

questions.s: To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, we connect
questions.e: A voltmeter must draw very little current, so a high resistance is added in series; the full-scale current then flows only when the chosen maximum voltage is applied. A low parallel resistance would turn it into an ammeter.

questions.s: A galvanometer of resistance 99 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 10 mA. The shunt needed to convert it into an ammeter of range 0-1 A is
questions.e: The shunt carries I − Ig = 1 − 0.01 = 0.99 A at the same p.d. as the coil: S = IgG/(I − Ig) = 0.01 × 99/0.99 = 1 Ω. Dividing by the full 1 A instead of 0.99 A gives the tempting 0.99 Ω.

questions.s: A galvanometer has resistance 100 Ω and gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA. The resistance needed in series to make it a voltmeter of range 0-10 V is
questions.e: The total resistance must be V/Ig = 10/0.001 = 10000 Ω, so the series resistance is 10000 − 100 = 9900 Ω. Choosing 10000 Ω forgets that the coil's own 100 Ω is already part of the total.

questions.s: A galvanometer of resistance 45 Ω is shunted by a 5 Ω resistor. The fraction of the total current that passes through the galvanometer is
questions.e: Parallel branches share current inversely to resistance: Ig/I = S/(G + S) = 5/(45 + 5) = 1/10. The value 1/9 is the ratio of the two branch currents, Ig/Is = 5/45, not the fraction of the total.

questions.s: A voltmeter of range 0-5 V has a resistance of 1000 Ω. The extra resistance needed in series to extend its range to 0-20 V is
questions.e: Full-scale current is 5/1000 = 5 mA. For 20 V the total resistance must be 20/0.005 = 4000 Ω, so the extra series resistance is 4000 − 1000 = 3000 Ω. The answer 4000 Ω is the new total, not the addition.

questions.s: An ideal voltmeter should have
o: a resistance equal to the circuit's
questions.e: A voltmeter is connected in parallel and should take no current from the circuit, so its ideal resistance is infinite. Zero resistance is the ideal for an ammeter, which is connected in series.

questions.s: The current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer can be increased by
o: increasing the area of the coil
questions.e: Deflection θ = NBA I/c, so θ/I rises with larger N, B or A and with a smaller torsional constant c. A stiffer suspension increases c and reduces the sensitivity.

questions.s: In a moving coil galvanometer, concave pole pieces and a soft iron core give a radial magnetic field so that
o: the coil stays cool at large currents
the restoring torque is cancelled out
the deflection is proportional to current
the coil's resistance is kept very low
questions.e: In a radial field the plane of the coil is always parallel to B, so the deflecting torque NIAB does not depend on the angle and θ = NBAI/c is proportional to I, giving a linear scale. The restoring torque of the suspension is still needed to balance it.

questions.s: The range of an ammeter made from a galvanometer of resistance G is to be 10 times the galvanometer's full-scale current. The shunt resistance required is
questions.e: With I = 10Ig, the shunt carries 9Ig at the same p.d.: S × 9Ig = G × Ig, so S = G/9. G/10 would make the range 11 times Ig.

questions.s: Two 2000 Ω resistors are connected in series with a 12 V cell of negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter of resistance 2000 Ω is connected across one of the resistors. The voltmeter reads
questions.e: The voltmeter and the resistor in parallel give 1000 Ω, so the total is 3000 Ω and the current is 12/3000 = 4 mA. The p.d. across the parallel pair is 4 mA × 1000 Ω = 4 V. The answer 6 V is what an ideal voltmeter would read; a real voltmeter loads the circuit.

questions.s: In Fleming's left-hand rule for a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, the thumb points along the
questions.e: With the forefinger along the field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb gives the direction of motion, that is the force on the conductor. The induced emf belongs to the right-hand (dynamo) rule.

questions.s: An electron moves towards the east in a uniform magnetic field directed vertically upward. The magnetic force on the electron is directed towards the
questions.e: For a positive charge v × B with v east and B up gives south (east × up = south). The electron is negative, so the force is reversed and points north. Choosing south forgets the negative charge.

questions.s: A proton moves towards the north in a uniform magnetic field directed towards the west. The magnetic force on the proton is directed
questions.e: F = q(v × B) with v north and B west. Taking east = x, north = y, up = z: y × (−x) = −(y × x) = +z, so the force on the positive proton is vertically upward. The force must be perpendicular to both v and B, which rules out east and south.

questions.s: One tesla is equal to
questions.e: From F = BIL, B = F/(IL), so 1 T = 1 N/(1 A × 1 m) = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ (also 1 Wb m⁻²). The other combinations do not follow from F = BIL.

questions.s: A uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T passes through a flat surface of area 0.05 m². The normal to the surface makes an angle of 60° with the field. The magnetic flux through the surface is
questions.e: Φ = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal: 0.4 × 0.05 × cos 60° = 0.02 × 0.5 = 0.01 Wb. The value 0.02 Wb ignores the angle, and 0.017 Wb uses sin 60°.

questions.s: A coil of area 0.5 m² is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T so that the plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the field. The flux through one turn is (√3 ≈ 1.73)
questions.e: If the plane makes 30° with B, the normal makes 60° with B, so Φ = BA cos 60° = 0.2 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.05 Wb. Using cos 30° gives 0.087 Wb, which mistakes the plane for the normal.

questions.s: The weber, the SI unit of magnetic flux, is equivalent to
questions.e: Faraday's law ε = −ΔΦ/Δt gives the unit of flux as volt × second, so 1 Wb = 1 V s (also 1 T m²). V A is the watt and A s is the coulomb.

questions.s: In a mass spectrometer, singly charged ions of masses 20 u and 22 u enter the same magnetic field at right angles with the same speed. The lighter ions move in a circle of radius 10 cm. The radius for the heavier ions is
questions.e: r = mv/(qB), so with equal v, q and B the radius is proportional to mass: r = 10 × 22/20 = 11 cm. The value 12.1 cm wrongly assumes r ∝ m².

questions.s: An electron (mass mₑ) and a proton (mass mₚ) are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference and then enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles. The ratio of the radius of the proton's path to that of the electron is
questions.e: Both gain kinetic energy eV, so momentum p = √(2meV) and r = p/(eB) ∝ √m since the charges have equal magnitude. Hence rₚ/rₑ = √(mₚ/mₑ). The ratio mₚ/mₑ would apply only if both had the same speed.

questions.s: A particle of mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. Its angular velocity is
questions.e: From qvB = mv²/r, ω = v/r = qB/m = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.5/1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ = 5.0 × 10⁷ rad/s. The value 8.0 × 10⁶ is the frequency f = ω/2π in hertz, not the angular velocity.

questions.s: The magnetic field well inside a long current-carrying solenoid is
questions.e: Inside a long solenoid the fields of the turns combine into a uniform field B = μ₀nI parallel to the axis. Circular field lines around an axis describe a straight wire or a toroid, not the inside of a solenoid.

questions.s: The magnetic field at 6 cm from a long straight current-carrying wire is 3 × 10⁻⁵ T. The field at 2 cm from the same wire is
questions.e: B = μ₀I/(2πr) ∝ 1/r, so reducing r from 6 cm to 2 cm triples the field to 9 × 10⁻⁵ T. The value 27 × 10⁻⁵ T assumes an inverse-square law, which applies to a point charge's electric field, not a wire's magnetic field.

questions.s: An alpha particle (charge 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 5 × 10⁵ m/s at 30° to a magnetic field of 0.4 T. The magnetic force on it is
questions.e: F = qvB sin θ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5 × 10⁵ × 0.4 × 0.5 = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Leaving out sin 30° gives 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, and using cos 30° gives about 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ N.

questions.s: The magnetic flux through each turn of a 200-turn coil falls from 0.05 Wb to 0.01 Wb in 0.2 s. The average emf induced in the coil is
questions.e: ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 200 × (0.05 − 0.01)/0.2 = 200 × 0.04/0.2 = 40 V. Leaving out N gives 0.2 V, and adding the two flux values instead of subtracting gives 60 V.

questions.s: Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of
questions.e: The induced current always opposes the change that produces it, so work must be done against it and that work appears as electrical energy. If the induced current aided the change, energy would be created from nothing, violating conservation of energy.

questions.s: A straight rod 0.5 m long moves at 4 m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.3 T, with the rod perpendicular to both its velocity and the field. The emf induced across its ends is
questions.e: Motional emf ε = BLv = 0.3 × 0.5 × 4 = 0.6 V. Leaving out the speed gives BL = 0.15 V, but the emf grows in proportion to how fast the rod cuts the field.

questions.s: A rod 0.2 m long slides at a constant 5 m/s on two parallel rails in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The total resistance of the circuit is 2 Ω. The external force needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed is
questions.e: ε = BLv = 0.5 × 0.2 × 5 = 0.5 V, so I = 0.5/2 = 0.25 A. The magnetic force opposing the motion is BIL = 0.5 × 0.25 × 0.2 = 0.025 N, and the applied force must equal it. The answer 0.25 N is the current in amperes, not a force.

questions.s: A conducting rod 0.4 m long moves at 10 m/s on rails at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.5 T. The circuit has a total resistance of 4 Ω. The rate at which heat is produced in the circuit is
questions.e: ε = BLv = 0.5 × 0.4 × 10 = 2 V and P = ε²/R = 4/4 = 1 W. Taking the current ε/R = 0.5 A as the power gives 0.5 W, and forgetting to divide ε² by R gives 4 W; the mechanical power supplied, Fv, also equals 1 W.

questions.s: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards one face of a closed coil. As the magnet approaches, that face of the coil behaves as
o: a south pole, attracting the magnet
a north pole, repelling the magnet
a north pole, attracting the magnet
a south pole, repelling the magnet
questions.e: By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the approach, so the near face becomes a north pole and repels the incoming north pole. A south pole would attract the magnet and increase the change, which would create energy from nothing.

questions.s: A strong bar magnet is dropped vertically through a long vertical copper tube. While inside the tube, its acceleration is
questions.e: The falling magnet changes the flux through the tube walls, inducing eddy currents whose magnetic field opposes its motion (Lenz's law). This retarding force makes its acceleration less than g; it is not zero at the start because the magnet begins at rest with no induced current.

questions.s: The henry, the SI unit of inductance, is equal to
questions.e: From ε = L ΔI/Δt, L = ε Δt/ΔI, so 1 H = 1 V s A⁻¹ (also 1 Wb A⁻¹). Wb A multiplies instead of dividing by the current.

questions.s: The current in a coil of self-inductance 0.2 H falls steadily from 5 A to 1 A in 0.1 s. The magnitude of the self-induced emf is
questions.e: ε = L ΔI/Δt = 0.2 × (5 − 1)/0.1 = 0.2 × 40 = 8 V. Adding the currents gives 12 V, and leaving out L gives 40 V.

questions.s: A steady current of 4 A flows through an inductor of 0.5 H. The energy stored in its magnetic field is
questions.e: U = ½LI² = ½ × 0.5 × 16 = 4 J. Forgetting the factor ½ gives 8 J, and forgetting to square I gives 1 J.

questions.s: When the current through an inductor is increased from 2 A to 4 A, the energy stored in it increases by 6 J. The inductance is
questions.e: ΔU = ½L(I₂² − I₁²) = ½L(16 − 4) = 6L = 6 J, so L = 1 H. Using (ΔI)² = 4 instead of the difference of squares gives 3 H, and omitting the ½ gives 0.5 H.

questions.s: The mutual inductance between two coils is 0.3 H. If the current in the primary changes at a rate of 20 A/s, the emf induced in the secondary is
questions.e: ε = M ΔI/Δt = 0.3 × 20 = 6 V. Dividing the rate by M gives 66.7 V, which has the wrong dependence: a larger mutual inductance gives a larger emf.

questions.s: The self-induced emf in a coil always opposes
o: the steady current through the coil
any change in the current through it
the resistance of the coil's wire
the terminal voltage of the source
questions.e: ε = −L ΔI/Δt exists only while the current changes and acts against that change, as Lenz's law requires. With a steady current there is no self-induced emf at all.

questions.s: A solenoid 0.5 m long has 1000 turns and a cross-sectional area of 10 cm². Its self-inductance is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
questions.e: L = μ₀N²A/l = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10⁶ × 10⁻³/0.5 = 8π × 10⁻⁴ H. Using N instead of N² gives 8π × 10⁻⁷ H, and taking 10 cm² as 0.1 m² gives 8π × 10⁻² H.

questions.s: A long solenoid is rewound with twice the number of turns over the same length and cross-section. Its self-inductance becomes
questions.e: L = μ₀N²A/l, so doubling N multiplies L by 2² = 4. 'Double' forgets that N enters twice: once in the field B = μ₀NI/l and once in the flux linkage NΦ.

questions.s: According to Faraday's law, the emf induced in a coil is proportional to
o: the rate of change of flux
questions.e: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt: the emf depends on how fast the flux linkage changes, not on the flux itself. A large but steady flux induces no emf.

questions.s: A circular loop lies in the plane of the page in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. If the field is increasing, the induced current in the loop, as seen by a viewer facing the page, is
questions.e: The inward flux is increasing, so the induced current must produce a field out of the page inside the loop. By the right-hand grip rule that current is anticlockwise. A clockwise current would add to the inward flux.

questions.s: A coil of 100 turns and area 0.02 m² is in a uniform field of 0.5 T with its plane perpendicular to the field. It is turned in 0.1 s until its plane is parallel to the field. The average emf induced is
questions.e: The flux per turn falls from BA = 0.5 × 0.02 = 0.01 Wb to zero, so ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 0.01/0.1 = 10 V. The value 20 V would apply to a half-turn, where the flux reverses from +BA to −BA.

questions.s: The flux through each turn of a 50-turn coil of total resistance 10 Ω changes by 0.02 Wb. The charge that flows through the coil is
questions.e: I = ε/R = NΔΦ/(RΔt), so the charge q = IΔt = NΔΦ/R = 50 × 0.02/10 = 0.1 C, independent of how fast the change happens. Leaving out N gives 0.002 C.

questions.s: A metal rod 0.5 m long rotates at 20 rad/s about one end in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. The emf between the ends of the rod is
questions.e: Points on the rod move at speeds from 0 to ωL, so the average speed is ωL/2 and ε = ½BωL² = ½ × 0.4 × 20 × 0.25 = 1.0 V. Using the tip speed ωL for the whole rod gives 2.0 V.

questions.s: The iron core of a transformer is made of thin insulated laminations in order to
questions.e: Thin insulated sheets break the large closed paths in which eddy currents would circulate, so the heating loss in the core falls sharply. Laminating does not increase the flux linkage, which depends on the core material and the windings.

questions.s: A straight conductor 1 m long moves at 2 m/s in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The conductor is perpendicular to both the field and its velocity, and the velocity makes 30° with the field. The emf induced is (√3 ≈ 1.73)
questions.e: Only the velocity component perpendicular to B cuts the field lines: ε = BLv sin θ = 0.5 × 1 × 2 × sin 30° = 0.5 V. Ignoring the angle gives 1.0 V, and using cos 30° gives 0.87 V.

questions.s: An aircraft with a wingspan of 40 m flies horizontally at 250 m/s where the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field is 5 × 10⁻⁵ T. The emf between its wing tips is
questions.e: The wings cut the vertical component of the field: ε = BLv = 5 × 10⁻⁵ × 40 × 250 = 0.5 V. Slipping a power of ten in 5 × 10⁻⁵ gives 0.05 V or 5 V.

questions.s: A current of 2 A in a primary coil produces a flux of 4 × 10⁻⁴ Wb through each of the 500 turns of a nearby secondary coil. The mutual inductance of the pair is
questions.e: M = NₛΦₛ/Iₚ = 500 × 4 × 10⁻⁴/2 = 0.1 H. Multiplying by the current instead of dividing gives 0.4 H, and leaving out the 500 turns gives 2 × 10⁻⁴ H.

questions.s: A generator coil of 100 turns and area 0.02 m² rotates at an angular speed of 50 rad/s in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The peak emf generated is
questions.e: For a rotating coil ε = NABω sin ωt, so the peak value is ε₀ = NABω = 100 × 0.02 × 0.5 × 50 = 50 V. Halving it to 25 V confuses the peak with an average-type value.

questions.s: An AC generator works on the principle of
questions.e: Rotating the coil in a magnetic field changes the flux linked with it, inducing an emf by Faraday's law. The motor effect, the force on a current in a field, is the principle of the motor, the reverse device.

questions.s: In an AC generator, the emf induced in the rotating coil is maximum at the instant when the plane of the coil is
questions.e: ε = NABω sin ωt is largest when the flux through the coil is zero but changing fastest, which happens when the plane of the coil is parallel to B. When the plane is perpendicular to B the flux is maximum but momentarily not changing, so the emf is zero.

questions.s: The speed of rotation of an AC generator's coil is doubled. The effect on the peak emf and on the frequency is
questions.e: Peak emf ε₀ = NABω and frequency f = ω/2π are both proportional to ω, so both double. The emf does not rise four times because ω appears only once in NABω.

questions.s: In a DC motor, the split-ring commutator
o: reverses the coil current every half turn
reduces the resistance of the coil
changes the mains AC into steady DC
questions.e: Every half rotation the commutator reverses the current in the coil, so the torque keeps acting in the same sense and the coil turns continuously. It does not change the field or the coil's resistance.

questions.s: A DC motor connected to a 220 V supply has an armature resistance of 2 Ω and draws 10 A when running normally. The back emf is
questions.e: V = ε_b + IR, so ε_b = 220 − 10 × 2 = 200 V. The value 20 V is only the drop across the armature resistance, and 240 V adds that drop instead of subtracting it.

questions.s: A DC motor with armature resistance 4 Ω runs on 120 V and develops a back emf of 100 V at full speed. The current at the instant of switching on is
questions.e: At switch-on the armature is at rest, so there is no back emf and I = V/R = 120/4 = 30 A. The value 5 A is the running current (120 − 100)/4, which flows only once the back emf has built up.

questions.s: A DC motor works on 200 V, has an armature resistance of 5 Ω and draws 4 A at full speed. Ignoring friction, the mechanical power it develops is
questions.e: Back emf ε_b = 200 − 4 × 5 = 180 V, and the mechanical power is ε_b I = 180 × 4 = 720 W. The input is VI = 800 W, of which I²R = 80 W is wasted as heat, so 800 W is not the output.

questions.s: A DC motor is suddenly given a heavier load, so it slows down. As a result
o: back emf rises and current falls
both back emf and current fall
both back emf and current rise
back emf falls and current rises
questions.e: Back emf is proportional to the speed, so it falls when the motor slows. Since I = (V − ε_b)/R, the current rises and supplies the extra torque. This is why an overloaded or stalled motor can overheat.

questions.s: A transformer does not work with a steady DC supply because
o: DC heats the core too much
DC flows only in the secondary
questions.e: A transformer relies on mutual induction, which needs a changing flux in the core. A steady direct current gives a constant flux, so no emf is induced in the secondary.

questions.s: An ideal transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 2000 turns on the secondary. If the primary is connected to 220 V AC, the secondary voltage is
questions.e: Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ = 2000/100 = 20, so Vₛ = 20 × 220 = 4400 V. Inverting the turns ratio gives 11 V, which would be a step-down transformer.

questions.s: An ideal transformer steps 220 V down to 11 V. The secondary supplies a current of 4 A. The primary current is
questions.e: For an ideal transformer VₚIₚ = VₛIₛ, so Iₚ = 11 × 4/220 = 0.2 A. Multiplying by the voltage ratio the wrong way gives 80 A; a step-down transformer has a smaller current in its primary.

questions.s: A transformer of efficiency 90% steps 240 V down to 12 V. The secondary supplies 9 A to a load. The primary current is
questions.e: Output power = 12 × 9 = 108 W, so the input power is 108/0.9 = 120 W and Iₚ = 120/240 = 0.5 A. Ignoring the efficiency gives 108/240 = 0.45 A, which is the ideal-transformer value.

questions.s: Electric power is transmitted over long distances at very high voltage mainly because
o: the current, and so I²R loss, is smaller
questions.e: For a fixed power P = VI, a higher V means a smaller I, and the heat lost in the cables, I²R, falls as the square of the current. Transformers are exactly what make the high voltage possible, and the frequency is unchanged.

questions.s: A power station sends 100 kW at 10 kV through cables of total resistance 5 Ω. The power lost as heat in the cables is
questions.e: The line current is I = P/V = 100000/10000 = 10 A, so the loss is I²R = 100 × 5 = 500 W. Using V²/R with the full 10 kV gives 2 × 10⁷ W, but 10 kV is not the voltage across the cables.

questions.s: The peak value of an alternating voltage is 200√2 V. Its rms value is
questions.e: For a sinusoidal voltage V_rms = V₀/√2 = 200√2/√2 = 200 V. The value 100√2 V comes from dividing by 2 instead of √2.

questions.s: The rms value of an alternating current is 5 A. Its peak value is
questions.e: I₀ = √2 × I_rms = 5√2 A, about 7.1 A. The value 2.5√2 A results from dividing by √2 instead of multiplying.

questions.s: An alternating voltage is given by V = 100 sin(100πt) volts. Its rms value and frequency are
questions.e: Comparing with V₀ sin ωt: V₀ = 100 V, so V_rms = 100/√2 = 50√2 V, and ω = 100π gives f = ω/2π = 50 Hz. Reading 100 Hz directly from 100π confuses ω with f.

questions.s: For a 50 Hz alternating current, the time taken for the current to rise from zero to its peak value is
questions.e: The period is T = 1/50 = 20 ms, and the current goes from zero to peak in a quarter cycle, T/4 = 5 ms. The value 10 ms is half a cycle, from zero back to zero.

questions.s: The average value of a sinusoidal alternating voltage of peak V₀ over one complete cycle is
questions.e: The positive and negative half cycles are equal and opposite, so the average over a full cycle is zero. 2V₀/π is the average over a half cycle only, and V₀/√2 is the rms value.

questions.s: In a purely inductive AC circuit, the current compared with the applied voltage
questions.e: The self-induced emf opposes changes in current, so the current reaches its maximum a quarter cycle after the voltage: it lags by 90° (π/2). Leading by 90° is the behaviour of a pure capacitor.

questions.s: In a purely capacitive AC circuit, the current
o: is in phase with the voltage
questions.e: Current I = C dV/dt is largest when the voltage is changing fastest, that is when V passes through zero, so the current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage: it leads by π/2. Lagging by π/2 describes a pure inductor.

questions.s: An alternating voltage is V = 200 sin(100πt) volts. Its instantaneous value at t = 1/600 s is
questions.e: At t = 1/600 s, 100πt = π/6, so V = 200 sin 30° = 200 × ½ = 100 V. Using cos 30° gives 100√3 V.

questions.s: A sinusoidal current of peak value 4 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is
questions.e: I_rms = 4/√2 = 2√2 A, so P = I_rms²R = 8 × 10 = 80 W. Using the peak current gives I₀²R = 160 W, which is the maximum instantaneous power, not the average.

questions.s: The inductive reactance of a coil of inductance 0.1/π H in a 50 Hz supply is
questions.e: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.1/π = 10 Ω. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 5 Ω.

questions.s: The reactance of a capacitor of capacitance 100/π μF in a 50 Hz supply is
questions.e: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 10⁻⁴/π) = 1/0.01 = 100 Ω. Slipping a power of ten when converting 100 μF to 10⁻⁴ F gives 10 Ω or 1000 Ω.

questions.s: When the frequency of the AC supply is increased, the reactance of a capacitor
questions.e: X_C = 1/(2πfC), so the reactance is inversely proportional to frequency and falls as f rises. An inductor behaves the opposite way, with X_L = 2πfL rising with frequency.

questions.s: Which component blocks steady DC but allows AC to pass?
questions.e: For DC, f = 0, so X_C = 1/(2πfC) is infinite and a capacitor blocks it, while for AC its reactance is finite. An inductor or choke does the reverse: X_L = 0 for DC.

questions.s: A series circuit has a resistance of 30 Ω and an inductive reactance of 40 Ω. Its impedance is
questions.e: The voltages across R and L are 90° out of phase, so Z = √(R² + X_L²) = √(900 + 1600) = 50 Ω. Adding them directly to get 70 Ω ignores the phase difference.

questions.s: A 60 Ω resistor and a capacitor of reactance 80 Ω are connected in series across a 200 V rms supply. The rms current is
questions.e: Z = √(60² + 80²) = 100 Ω, so I = 200/100 = 2 A. Adding R and X_C to 140 Ω gives 1.4 A, which ignores the phase difference.

questions.s: In a series RL circuit the resistance equals the inductive reactance. The phase relation between current and supply voltage is
questions.e: tan φ = X_L/R = 1, so φ = 45°, and in an inductive circuit the current lags the voltage. A lag of 90° occurs only for a pure inductor with R = 0.

questions.s: A series RLC circuit has R = 40 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω and X_C = 50 Ω. Its impedance is
questions.e: X_L and X_C are opposite in phase, so the net reactance is 80 − 50 = 30 Ω, and Z = √(40² + 30²) = 50 Ω. Adding R to the net reactance gives 70 Ω, and adding everything gives 170 Ω.

questions.s: In a series RLC circuit, the rms voltages across the resistor, inductor and capacitor are 30 V, 60 V and 20 V. The rms supply voltage is
questions.e: V_L and V_C are 180° apart, so their net is 60 − 20 = 40 V, at 90° to V_R: V = √(30² + 40²) = 50 V. Simply adding the three readings to get 110 V ignores the phases.

questions.s: A series circuit contains an inductor of 0.1 H and a capacitor of 10 μF. Its resonant frequency is
questions.e: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) with LC = 0.1 × 10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁶, so √(LC) = 10⁻³ s and f₀ = 1000/(2π) = 500/π Hz, about 159 Hz. The value 1000/π Hz forgets the 2 in 2π.

questions.s: At resonance, the impedance of a series RLC circuit is
questions.e: At resonance X_L = X_C, so the reactances cancel and Z = √(R² + 0) = R, the minimum value, giving maximum current. It is a parallel resonant circuit, not a series one, whose impedance is maximum.

questions.s: The power factor of a series RLC circuit at resonance is
questions.e: At resonance the net reactance is zero, current and voltage are in phase (φ = 0) and cos φ = R/Z = 1. A power factor of 0 belongs to a purely reactive circuit.

questions.s: The average power consumed by an ideal inductor connected to an AC supply is
questions.e: P = V_rms I_rms cos φ and for an ideal inductor φ = 90°, so cos φ = 0 and P = 0. Energy stored in the field during one quarter cycle is returned to the supply in the next.

questions.s: In an AC circuit, V_rms = 220 V, I_rms = 5 A and the current lags the voltage by 60°. The average power consumed is
questions.e: P = V_rms I_rms cos φ = 220 × 5 × cos 60° = 1100 × 0.5 = 550 W. The value 1100 W ignores the power factor, and 950 W uses sin 60° instead of cos 60°.

questions.s: A 60 Ω resistor and a capacitor of reactance 80 Ω are in series across a 100 V rms supply. The average power consumed by the circuit is
questions.e: Z = √(60² + 80²) = 100 Ω, so I_rms = 1 A. Only the resistor dissipates power: P = I²R = 1 × 60 = 60 W (equivalently VI cos φ with cos φ = 0.6). The value 100 W is V_rms I_rms, which ignores the power factor.

questions.s: A coil of inductance 1/π H is connected in series with a capacitor. For the circuit to resonate at 50 Hz, the capacitance must be
questions.e: X_L = 2π × 50 × 1/π = 100 Ω, and resonance needs X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × C) = 100 Ω, so C = 1/(10⁴π) F = 100/π μF. Checking 10/π μF gives X_C = 1000 Ω, which does not match X_L.

questions.s: In AC circuits a choke coil is preferred to a resistor for reducing current because
o: it wastes very little power as heat
it makes the power factor one
it stores charge on its turns
questions.e: A choke has large inductive reactance but small resistance, so its power factor is close to zero and it limits the current while dissipating very little energy. A resistor would turn the dropped voltage into heat.

questions.s: In a series LC circuit the inductance is made four times larger while the capacitance is unchanged. The resonant frequency becomes
questions.e: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) ∝ 1/√L, so multiplying L by 4 divides f₀ by √4 = 2. 'A quarter' forgets the square root.

questions.s: A pure inductor of inductance 1.1/π H is connected to a 220 V rms, 50 Hz supply. The rms current is
questions.e: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 1.1/π = 110 Ω, so I = 220/110 = 2 A. Forgetting the factor 2 in 2πf gives X_L = 55 Ω and 4 A.

questions.s: In a series RC circuit across a 100 V rms supply, the rms voltage across the resistor is 80 V. The rms voltage across the capacitor is
questions.e: V² = V_R² + V_C², so V_C = √(100² − 80²) = √3600 = 60 V. Subtracting directly to get 20 V ignores the 90° phase difference between V_R and V_C.

questions.s: A series RL circuit with R = 80 Ω has an inductive reactance of 30 Ω at 50 Hz. Its impedance at 100 Hz is
questions.e: X_L = 2πfL is proportional to f, so at 100 Hz X_L = 60 Ω and Z = √(80² + 60²) = 100 Ω. About 85 Ω is the impedance at 50 Hz, forgetting that the reactance doubles.

questions.s: The rms value of an alternating current is
o: the mean of all instantaneous values
the steady current giving the same heating
the value at one quarter of the period
questions.e: The rms value is the steady (DC) current that produces heat at the same rate in a given resistor; for a sine wave it equals I₀/√2. The mean of the instantaneous values over a cycle is zero, so it cannot measure the effect of AC.

questions.s: A series RLC circuit with R = 30 Ω, X_L = 70 Ω and X_C = 30 Ω is connected to a 100 V rms supply. The average power consumed is
questions.e: Z = √(30² + (70 − 30)²) = 50 Ω, so I_rms = 2 A and P = I²R = 4 × 30 = 120 W. The value 200 W is V_rms I_rms, which ignores the power factor cos φ = 30/50 = 0.6.

questions.s: A lamp in series with an air-cored coil glows on an AC supply. A soft iron rod is slowly pushed into the coil. The lamp
questions.e: The iron core greatly increases the inductance L, so X_L = 2πfL and the impedance rise, the current falls and the lamp dims. It does not go out, since the impedance stays finite and some current still flows; 'brighter' would need the impedance to fall.

questions.s: A long straight wire carries a current of 20 A. The magnetic field at 5 cm from it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
questions.e: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 20/0.05 = 8 × 10⁻⁵ T. Leaving r as 5 instead of 0.05 m gives 8 × 10⁻⁷ T, and using the loop formula μ₀I/(2r) gives about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ T.

questions.s: A long solenoid has 1000 turns per metre. The current needed to produce a field of 2π × 10⁻³ T inside it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
questions.e: I = B/(μ₀n) = 2π × 10⁻³/(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1000) = 2π × 10⁻³/(4π × 10⁻⁴) = 5 A. Inverting the ratio of the π terms gives 2 A.

questions.s: A wire 2 m long carries 3 A towards the north in a uniform magnetic field of 5 × 10⁻⁵ T that also points north. The magnetic force on the wire is
questions.e: F = BIL sin θ and here the current is parallel to the field, so θ = 0° and F = 0. The value 3 × 10⁻⁴ N is BIL, which would apply only if the wire were perpendicular to the field.

questions.s: An electron moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. Which quantity remains constant?
questions.e: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed, and so the kinetic energy, stays constant. Velocity, momentum and acceleration are vectors whose directions keep changing around the circle.

questions.s: An electron (mass 9 × 10⁻³¹ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 4 × 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ T. The radius of its path is
questions.e: r = mv/(eB) = (9 × 10⁻³¹ × 4 × 10⁶)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 4.5 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.6 × 10⁻²⁴/7.2 × 10⁻²³ = 0.05 m = 5 cm. A slip of one power of ten in the numerator gives 0.5 cm or 50 cm.

questions.s: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 2 mA. The series resistance needed to convert it into a voltmeter of range 0-20 V is
questions.e: The total resistance must be 20/0.002 = 10000 Ω, so the series resistance is 10000 − 50 = 9950 Ω. Choosing 10000 Ω forgets the galvanometer's own 50 Ω, and 10050 Ω adds it instead of subtracting.

questions.s: A galvanometer of resistance 20 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 5 mA. The shunt needed to convert it into an ammeter of range 0-1 A is approximately
questions.e: S = IgG/(I − Ig) = 0.005 × 20/0.995 ≈ 0.1/1 = 0.1 Ω. The shunt must be much smaller than G because it carries almost all of the 1 A; 4 Ω would let far too much current through the coil.

questions.s: A coil is held at rest in a strong but steady magnetic field. The emf induced in the coil is
questions.e: Induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux linkage, ε = −NΔΦ/Δt. A steady field and a stationary coil give no change in flux, so the emf is zero however strong the field is. NBA is the flux linkage, not an emf.

questions.s: A metal rod 0.25 m long moves at 8 m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T, with the rod perpendicular to both. The emf between its ends is
questions.e: ε = BLv = 0.5 × 0.25 × 8 = 1 V. Leaving out the rod length gives 4 V, which would be the emf per metre of rod.

questions.s: A square loop of side 0.1 m and resistance 0.5 Ω is pulled at a steady 2 m/s out of a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T that is perpendicular to the loop. One side is outside the field and the opposite side is still inside. The induced current is
questions.e: Only the side still in the field cuts flux: ε = BLv = 0.4 × 0.1 × 2 = 0.08 V, so I = 0.08/0.5 = 0.16 A. The value 0.08 is the emf in volts, not the current.

questions.s: An emf of 12 V is induced in a coil when the current through it changes at 40 A/s. The self-inductance of the coil is
questions.e: ε = L ΔI/Δt, so L = 12/40 = 0.3 H. Dividing 40 by 12 gives 3.3 H, and multiplying gives 480 H; neither follows from L = ε/(ΔI/Δt).

questions.s: An inductor of 2 H stores 25 J of energy in its magnetic field. The current through it is
questions.e: U = ½LI², so I² = 2U/L = 50/2 = 25 and I = 5 A. Stopping at I² = 25 and giving 25 A forgets the square root.

questions.s: An ideal transformer steps 240 V down to 12 V. Its primary has 1000 turns. The number of secondary turns is
questions.e: Nₛ = Nₚ × Vₛ/Vₚ = 1000 × 12/240 = 50 turns. Using the ratio the wrong way gives 20000 turns, which would make a step-up transformer.

questions.s: A small DC motor runs on a 24 V supply and draws 3 A. Its armature resistance is 2 Ω. The back emf is
questions.e: V = ε_b + IR, so ε_b = 24 − 3 × 2 = 18 V. The value 6 V is only the IR drop across the armature, and 30 V adds that drop to the supply.

questions.s: The rms value of the mains voltage in Pakistan is 220 V. Its peak value is about (√2 ≈ 1.41)
questions.e: V₀ = √2 × V_rms = 1.41 × 220 ≈ 311 V. Dividing by √2 gives 156 V, which is backwards: the peak is larger than the rms value.

questions.s: An inductor has a reactance of 50 Ω at 50 Hz. Its reactance at 200 Hz is
questions.e: X_L = 2πfL ∝ f, so multiplying the frequency by 4 multiplies the reactance by 4: 50 × 4 = 200 Ω. The value 12.5 Ω would be correct for a capacitor, whose reactance falls with frequency.

questions.s: A 40 Ω resistor and a capacitor of reactance 30 Ω are in series across an AC supply. The power factor of the circuit is
questions.e: Z = √(40² + 30²) = 50 Ω and power factor cos φ = R/Z = 40/50 = 0.8. The value 0.6 is X_C/Z, which is sin φ, not cos φ.

questions.s: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω and L = 0.1 H is driven at its resonant angular frequency of 1000 rad/s by a 50 V rms supply. The rms voltage across the inductor is
questions.e: At resonance Z = R, so I = 50/10 = 5 A. X_L = ωL = 1000 × 0.1 = 100 Ω, so V_L = 5 × 100 = 500 V. This is larger than the supply because V_L and V_C cancel each other; assuming V_L cannot exceed the supply leads to 50 V.

questions.s: Positive ions pass undeflected through crossed fields E = 2 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.1 T. They then enter a region of the same magnetic field alone and move in a circle of radius 5 cm. Their charge-to-mass ratio q/m is
questions.e: The selector gives v = E/B = 2 × 10⁴/0.1 = 2 × 10⁵ m/s. In the field alone r = mv/(qB), so q/m = v/(Br) = 2 × 10⁵/(0.1 × 0.05) = 4 × 10⁷ C/kg. Using r = 5 instead of 0.05 m changes the result by a factor of 100 and is wrong.

questions.s: The coil of an AC generator rotates at 3000 revolutions per minute. The frequency of the emf it produces is
questions.e: One revolution gives one complete cycle of emf, so f = 3000/60 = 50 revolutions per second = 50 Hz. Using 3000 Hz forgets to convert minutes to seconds.

questions.s: The SI unit of stress is
questions.e: Stress is force per unit area, F/A, so its unit is N/m² = N m⁻², the pascal. N m is the unit of torque or work, and N m⁻¹ is the unit of a spring constant. Strain, not stress, has no unit.

questions.s: Tensile strain is
questions.e: Strain = extension/original length, ΔL/L, a ratio of two lengths, so it has no unit. N m⁻² is the unit of stress (and of Young's modulus), not strain.

questions.s: A load of 100 N hangs from a wire of cross-sectional area 2 mm². The tensile stress in the wire is
questions.e: 2 mm² = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m², so stress = F/A = 100/(2 × 10⁻⁶) = 5 × 10⁷ Pa. 50 Pa forgets to convert mm² to m², and 5 × 10⁴ Pa converts with 10⁻³ instead of 10⁻⁶.

questions.s: A wire 2 m long with cross-sectional area 1 mm² stretches by 1 mm under a force of 100 N. The Young's modulus of the material is
questions.e: Stress = 100/10⁻⁶ = 1 × 10⁸ Pa and strain = 10⁻³/2 = 5 × 10⁻⁴, so Y = stress/strain = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa. 1 × 10¹¹ Pa forgets to divide the extension by the original length of 2 m.

questions.s: A steel wire 4 m long with cross-sectional area 2 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries a load of 200 N. Young's modulus of steel is 2 × 10¹¹ Pa. The extension of the wire is
questions.e: Stress = 200/(2 × 10⁻⁶) = 1 × 10⁸ Pa, strain = 10⁸/(2 × 10¹¹) = 5 × 10⁻⁴, and extension = strain × L = 5 × 10⁻⁴ × 4 = 2 × 10⁻³ m = 2 mm. Forgetting to multiply by the length leaves 0.5 mm.

questions.s: A copper wire is stretched beyond its elastic limit and the load is then removed. The wire
questions.e: Beyond the elastic limit the deformation is plastic: some of the extension remains after the load is removed (a permanent set). Only below the elastic limit does the wire return fully to its original length. Breaking happens later, at the breaking stress.

questions.s: A wire extends by 3 mm under a load of 60 N. Assuming Hooke's law holds, its extension under a load of 100 N is
questions.e: Within the proportional limit extension ∝ load, so e = 3 × 100/60 = 5 mm. 1.8 mm inverts the ratio (3 × 60/100).

questions.s: Wires A and B are made of the same material and have the same length. The diameter of B is twice that of A. When the same load is hung from each, the extension of B is
questions.e: e = FL/(AY) and A = πd²/4, so e ∝ 1/d². Doubling the diameter makes the area four times larger, so B stretches 1/4 as much as A. Choosing 1/2 treats the area as proportional to d instead of d².

questions.s: A wire is stretched by 2 mm by a force that rises steadily from zero to 200 N, within the elastic limit. The elastic potential energy stored in the wire is
questions.e: Energy = ½ × F × e = ½ × 200 × 0.002 = 0.2 J. 0.4 J forgets the factor ½, which arises because the force grows from zero to its final value. 400 J uses e = 2 instead of 0.002 m.

questions.s: A material that breaks soon after its elastic limit, showing almost no plastic deformation, is called
questions.e: Brittle materials such as glass and cast iron fracture with little or no plastic region. Ductile materials such as copper show a large plastic region and can be drawn into wires; malleable materials can be hammered into sheets.

questions.s: For a wire obeying Hooke's law, on a stress-strain graph the Young's modulus is given by
o: stress at the point of fracture
questions.e: In the proportional region stress/strain is constant, and this ratio is Y, the slope of the straight part of the graph. The area under a stress-strain graph gives energy stored per unit volume, and the highest stress is the ultimate tensile strength.

questions.s: A wire stretches by e under a load. A second wire of the same material has twice the length and twice the diameter. Under the same load its extension is
questions.e: e = FL/(AY) with A ∝ d². Doubling L doubles e, and doubling d makes the area four times larger, dividing e by 4; the net factor is 2/4 = 1/2, so the extension is e/2. e/4 forgets the effect of the longer length.

questions.s: In a metal such as copper, the valence band and the conduction band
o: are separated by a large gap
questions.e: In conductors the bands overlap (or the conduction band is partly filled), so many free electrons are available even at low temperature. A gap of about 1 eV is typical of semiconductors such as silicon, and a large gap marks an insulator.

questions.s: The forbidden energy gap is largest in
questions.e: Diamond is an insulator with a gap of about 5-6 eV. Silicon (about 1.1 eV) and germanium (about 0.7 eV) are semiconductors, and copper is a conductor with no gap at all.

questions.s: At absolute zero temperature, pure silicon behaves as
questions.e: At 0 K no electrons have enough thermal energy to cross the band gap, so the valence band is full, the conduction band empty, and silicon cannot conduct: it acts as an insulator. It becomes a semiconductor only as temperature rises.

questions.s: When the temperature of a pure germanium crystal rises, its resistivity
questions.e: Heating gives more electrons enough energy to jump the band gap, creating more electron-hole pairs, so conductivity rises and resistivity falls; semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient. Resistivity increases with temperature in metals, not semiconductors.

questions.s: To make n-type silicon, pure silicon is doped with a small amount of
questions.e: Phosphorus has five valence electrons; four bond with silicon and the fifth becomes a free electron, giving n-type material. Boron, aluminium and indium are trivalent and produce holes, giving p-type material.

questions.s: In a p-type semiconductor, the majority charge carriers are
questions.e: Trivalent acceptor atoms each leave a missing bond, a hole, so holes far outnumber the thermally produced electrons. The ions formed are fixed in the lattice and do not carry current.

questions.s: An n-type semiconductor, taken as a whole, is
questions.e: Each donor atom that gives up a free electron becomes a positive ion, so the extra electrons are exactly balanced by positive donor ions and the crystal stays neutral. 'n' refers to the negative majority carriers, not to a net charge.

questions.s: A trivalent impurity atom such as gallium added to silicon is called
questions.e: A trivalent atom forms only three bonds and leaves a hole that can accept an electron, so it is an acceptor and makes the material p-type. Pentavalent atoms such as arsenic are donors.

questions.s: The depletion region of an unbiased p-n junction contains
questions.e: Near the junction, electrons diffusing from n to p fill holes, leaving behind fixed positive donor ions on the n-side and fixed negative acceptor ions on the p-side. The region is depleted of mobile carriers, which is why it acts as an insulating layer.

questions.s: A p-n junction diode is forward biased when
o: the p-side is joined to the positive terminal
the n-side is joined to the positive terminal
both sides are at the same potential
questions.e: Connecting p to the positive terminal and n to the negative terminal pushes holes and electrons towards the junction, narrowing the depletion region so a large current flows. Joining the n-side to positive is reverse bias.

questions.s: The potential barrier of a silicon p-n junction at room temperature is about
questions.e: For silicon the barrier potential is about 0.7 V, so a forward-biased silicon diode conducts noticeably only above this voltage. About 0.3 V is the value for germanium.

questions.s: When a p-n junction is reverse biased, the width of its depletion region
questions.e: Reverse bias pulls holes and electrons away from the junction, uncovering more fixed ions, so the depletion region widens and only a tiny minority-carrier current flows. It narrows under forward bias.

questions.s: A full-wave rectifier is supplied with 50 Hz alternating voltage. The frequency of the pulses in its output is
questions.e: A full-wave rectifier turns both half-cycles into pulses in the same direction, so there are two pulses per input cycle: 2 × 50 = 100 Hz. 50 Hz is the output pulse frequency of a half-wave rectifier.

questions.s: The number of diodes used in a bridge rectifier is
questions.e: A bridge rectifier uses four diodes; in each half-cycle two of them conduct in series, so both halves reach the load in the same direction. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and a centre-tap full-wave rectifier uses two.

questions.s: In a half-wave rectifier circuit, the diode conducts during
questions.e: The diode is forward biased only during the half-cycle in which its anode is positive, so current flows through the load for half of each cycle and the other half is blocked. A diode that conducted all the time would not rectify at all.

questions.s: A bridge rectifier made of silicon diodes (0.7 V drop each when conducting) is fed with an AC voltage of peak value 10 V. The peak voltage across the load is about
questions.e: In a bridge rectifier two diodes are in series with the load in each half-cycle, so the drop is 2 × 0.7 = 1.4 V and the peak output is 10 − 1.4 = 8.6 V. 9.3 V counts only one diode, which is true for a half-wave or centre-tap circuit.

questions.s: The pulsating output of a rectifier is smoothed by connecting
o: a capacitor in series with the load
questions.e: A capacitor in parallel with the load charges near each peak and discharges slowly through the load between peaks, filling in the gaps and reducing the ripple. A capacitor in series would block the DC output altogether.

questions.s: In a bipolar junction transistor, the region that is thinnest and most lightly doped is the
questions.e: The base is made very thin and lightly doped so that most carriers injected from the heavily doped emitter cross it into the collector instead of recombining, which keeps the base current small. The collector is the largest region, and the emitter is the most heavily doped.

questions.s: In a transistor the emitter current is 10 mA and the collector current is 9.8 mA. The base current is
questions.e: I_E = I_B + I_C, so I_B = 10 − 9.8 = 0.2 mA. 19.8 mA adds the currents instead of subtracting, and 2 mA misplaces the decimal point.

questions.s: A transistor with current gain β = 100 has a base current of 20 μA. Its collector current is
questions.e: I_C = βI_B = 100 × 20 μA = 2000 μA = 2 mA. 0.2 mA and 20 mA come from slips in converting μA to mA.

questions.s: In a transistor the base current is 50 μA and the collector current is 4.95 mA. The ratio α = I_C/I_E is
questions.e: I_E = I_C + I_B = 4.95 + 0.05 = 5.00 mA, so α = 4.95/5.00 = 0.99. 99 is β = I_C/I_B, not α, and α can never exceed 1 because I_C is always less than I_E.

questions.s: For a transistor to work as an amplifier, its junctions must be biased as follows
questions.e: In the active region the emitter-base junction is forward biased so carriers are injected into the base, and the collector-base junction is reverse biased so it collects them. Both forward biased is saturation (switch ON), and both reverse biased is cut-off (switch OFF).

questions.s: In a common-emitter amplifier, β = 100, the collector resistor is 2 kΩ and the input resistance is 1 kΩ. An input signal of amplitude 10 mV gives an output of amplitude
questions.e: Voltage gain A_v = βR_C/r_in = 100 × 2/1 = 200 in magnitude (the output is inverted). Output = 200 × 10 mV = 2000 mV = 2 V. 20 V comes from a gain of 2000, which mixes units by taking R_C in ohms but the input resistance in kΩ.

questions.s: When a transistor is used as a switch and is fully ON (saturated), the voltage between its collector and emitter is
questions.e: In saturation the transistor behaves like a closed switch: almost all the supply voltage appears across the load and V_CE is close to zero (about 0.2 V). V_CE equals the supply voltage when the transistor is OFF (cut-off).

questions.s: The Boolean expression for the output X of a NOT gate with input A is
questions.e: A NOT gate (inverter) gives the complement of its input: X = Ā, so 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1. A · A = A and A + 1 = 1 in Boolean algebra, so neither inverts the input.

questions.s: The output of a two-input NAND gate is 0 only when
questions.e: NAND is AND followed by NOT: X = NOT(A · B). A · B = 1 only when both inputs are 1, so the NAND output is 0 only then and 1 for every other combination. Both inputs 0 gives 0 for a NOR or AND gate, not a NAND.

questions.s: For which input combination (A, B) is the output of a two-input NOR gate equal to 1?
questions.e: NOR = NOT(A + B). A + B is 0 only when both inputs are 0, so the NOR output is 1 only for (0, 0). Any input at 1 makes the OR part 1 and the NOR output 0.

questions.s: Inputs A and B feed an OR gate. The OR output and a third input C feed an AND gate, whose output passes through a NOT gate to give X. The Boolean expression for X is
questions.e: The OR gate gives A + B, the AND gate gives (A + B) · C, and the NOT gate inverts the whole of this: X = NOT[(A + B) · C]. NOT(A + B) · C would place the inverter before the AND gate. For A = 1, B = 0, C = 0, X = NOT(0) = 1.

questions.s: A force of 500 N acts at right angles on a cross-sectional area of 5 × 10⁻⁴ m². The stress produced is
questions.e: Stress = F/A = 500/(5 × 10⁻⁴) = 1 × 10⁶ Pa. 2.5 × 10⁻¹ Pa multiplies F by A instead of dividing, and 1 × 10⁵ Pa is a slip of one power of ten.

questions.s: A wire 2.0 m long stretches by 0.4 mm under a load. The tensile strain in the wire is
questions.e: Strain = ΔL/L = 0.4 × 10⁻³/2.0 = 2 × 10⁻⁴. 0.2 forgets to convert mm to m, and 5 × 10³ inverts the ratio (L/ΔL).

questions.s: The Young's modulus of a wire depends on
questions.e: Young's modulus is a property of the material: changing the length, area or load changes the stress and strain, but their ratio stays the same within the proportional limit. A thicker wire stretches less, but its Y is unchanged.

questions.s: A logic gate gives output 1 for inputs (0, 0), (0, 1) and (1, 0), and output 0 for inputs (1, 1). The gate is
questions.e: Output 0 only when both inputs are 1 is the inverse of AND, which is NAND. A NOR gate gives 1 only for (0, 0), and an OR gate gives 1 for (1, 1) as well.

questions.s: In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor at room temperature,
o: electron and hole numbers are equal
there are no holes at all
questions.e: In an intrinsic semiconductor every electron that jumps to the conduction band leaves exactly one hole in the valence band, so the numbers of free electrons and holes are equal. Unequal numbers occur only after doping.

questions.s: Germanium doped with a small amount of gallium becomes
questions.e: Gallium is trivalent, so each gallium atom leaves a hole in the germanium lattice, making holes the majority carriers: p-type. A pentavalent impurity such as arsenic would give n-type material.

questions.s: A bridge rectifier is supplied with 50 Hz AC. The time between two successive peaks of the rectified output is
questions.e: Full-wave rectification gives two peaks per input cycle, so the output peak frequency is 100 Hz and the time between peaks is 1/100 = 0.01 s. 0.02 s is the input period, which applies to a half-wave rectifier.

questions.s: A transistor has a collector current of 3 mA when its base current is 30 μA. Its current gain β is
questions.e: β = I_C/I_B = 3 mA/0.03 mA = 100. 0.01 inverts the ratio, and 10 or 1000 come from slips in converting μA to mA.

questions.s: A steel wire 2 m long with cross-sectional area 1 mm² is stretched by 2 mm by a force of 200 N, within its elastic limit. The elastic energy stored per unit volume of the wire is
questions.e: Stress = 200/10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁸ Pa and strain = 0.002/2 = 1 × 10⁻³. Energy per unit volume = ½ × stress × strain = ½ × 2 × 10⁸ × 10⁻³ = 1 × 10⁵ J m⁻³. 2 × 10⁵ forgets the ½, and 2 × 10¹¹ Pa is the Young's modulus, not an energy density.

questions.s: Both inputs of a NAND gate are joined together and used as a single input. The gate now behaves as which gate?
questions.e: With A = B, the output is NOT(A · A) = NOT A, so the gate inverts its input and acts as a NOT gate. This is one reason NAND is called a universal gate. It would act as AND only if a further inverter followed it.

questions.s: According to the second postulate of the special theory of relativity, the speed of light in vacuum
o: depends on the speed of the source
is the same for all inertial observers
depends on the speed of the observer
is greater along the direction of the Earth's motion
questions.e: Einstein's second postulate states that light in vacuum travels at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s for every inertial observer, whatever the motion of the source or observer. Adding the source's speed to c is the Galilean idea that the Michelson-Morley experiment failed to confirm.

questions.s: A clock on a spacecraft moving at 0.8c relative to the Earth records 6.0 s between two events that occur at the same place on the craft. The time interval measured by an observer on the Earth is
questions.e: For v = 0.8c, √(1 − v²/c²) = √(1 − 0.64) = 0.6, so t = t₀/0.6 = 6.0/0.6 = 10 s. Moving clocks run slow, so the Earth observer measures a longer interval. Multiplying by 0.6 instead of dividing gives 3.6 s, and dividing by 0.8 gives 7.5 s.

questions.s: A rod has a length of 10 m when at rest. Its length measured by an observer past whom it moves along its length at 0.6c is
questions.e: L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²) = 10 × √(1 − 0.36) = 10 × 0.8 = 8.0 m. Length contracts along the direction of motion, so the answer must be less than 10 m. Using 0.6 itself as the factor gives 6.0 m, and dividing by 0.8 gives 12.5 m.

questions.s: If a mass of 1 g is completely converted into energy, the energy released is (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
questions.e: E = mc² = (1 × 10⁻³ kg)(3 × 10⁸ m/s)² = 10⁻³ × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 9 × 10¹³ J. Forgetting to convert grams to kilograms gives 9 × 10¹⁶ J, and forgetting to square c gives 3 × 10⁵ J.

questions.s: Using the relation m = m₀/√(1 − v²/c²), the mass of a body moving at 0.6c in terms of its rest mass m₀ is
questions.e: √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8, so m = m₀/0.8 = 1.25 m₀. The moving mass is larger than the rest mass. Writing m = 0.8 m₀ multiplies by the root factor instead of dividing by it.

questions.s: At what speed relative to an observer must a clock move so that the observer finds it running at half its normal rate?
questions.e: Half the rate means t = 2t₀, so √(1 − v²/c²) = 1/2. Then 1 − v²/c² = 1/4, v²/c² = 3/4 and v = (√3/2)c ≈ 0.87c. Taking v = 0.5c confuses the factor 1/2 with the speed ratio, and 0.71c comes from setting v²/c² = 1/2.

questions.s: An inertial frame of reference is a frame
o: in which Newton's first law of motion holds
that rotates at a constant angular speed
that moves with a constant acceleration
attached to a car turning round a corner
questions.e: An inertial frame is one that is not accelerating, so a body with no net force on it stays at rest or moves with uniform velocity: Newton's first law holds. A rotating frame has centripetal acceleration even at constant angular speed, so it is non-inertial, as are the other two.

questions.s: A muon has a lifetime of 2.2 μs in its own rest frame. It moves through the laboratory at a speed for which 1/√(1 − v²/c²) = 5. Its lifetime measured in the laboratory is
questions.e: Time dilation gives t = γt₀ = 5 × 2.2 = 11 μs. The laboratory observer sees the moving muon's clock running slow, so it lives longer in the lab. Dividing by 5 (0.44 μs) applies the factor the wrong way.

questions.s: The kinetic energy of a particle is two-thirds of its rest mass energy. The speed of the particle is
questions.e: Total energy = rest energy + kinetic energy = m₀c² + (2/3)m₀c² = (5/3)m₀c², so γ = 5/3. Then √(1 − v²/c²) = 3/5, so v²/c² = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25 and v = 0.8c. Using γ = 2/3 or equating v/c to 2/3 gives the wrong 0.67c.

questions.s: Light of a fixed frequency above the threshold frequency falls on a metal. Increasing the intensity of the light increases
o: the threshold frequency of the metal
the work function of the metal
the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons
the number of electrons emitted per second
questions.e: Greater intensity at the same frequency means more photons per second, each of the same energy hf, so more electrons are ejected per second. The maximum kinetic energy, hf − φ, depends only on frequency, and the threshold frequency and work function are properties of the metal.

questions.s: Photons of energy 3.5 eV fall on a metal surface whose work function is 2.0 eV. The stopping potential is
