questions.e: K.E.max = hf − φ = 3.5 − 2.0 = 1.5 eV, and eV₀ = K.E.max, so V₀ = 1.5 V. Adding the work function instead of subtracting it gives 5.5 V; the stopping potential is set by the kinetic energy, not the photon energy.

questions.s: The work function of a metal is 2.48 eV. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, its threshold wavelength is
questions.e: λ₀ = hc/φ = 1240/2.48 = 500 nm. Light of longer wavelength than 500 nm has too little energy per photon to eject electrons. Dividing 1240 by 2 rather than 2.48 gives 620 nm.

questions.s: Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the energy of a photon of violet light of wavelength 400 nm is
questions.e: E = hc/λ = 1240 eV nm / 400 nm = 3.1 eV. Visible photons carry a few electronvolts, so answers of 31 eV or 310 eV point to a slip in the power of ten. 0.31 eV would be an infrared photon.

questions.s: In a photoelectric experiment, the stopping potential V₀ is plotted on the y-axis against the frequency f of the incident light on the x-axis. The slope of the straight line obtained is
questions.e: From eV₀ = hf − φ, V₀ = (h/e)f − φ/e, a straight line of slope h/e and y-intercept −φ/e. The slope is the same for every metal. φ/e is the size of the intercept, not the slope, and h alone would be the slope of a graph of K.E.max (in joules) against f.

questions.s: Light of frequency f ejects photoelectrons of maximum kinetic energy K from a metal of work function φ. If the frequency is doubled, the new maximum kinetic energy is
questions.e: Originally hf = K + φ. With frequency 2f, K′ = 2hf − φ = 2(K + φ) − φ = 2K + φ. The kinetic energy more than doubles because the work function is subtracted only once; 2K would hold only if φ were zero.

questions.s: Photoelectrons are emitted from a metal surface without any measurable time delay, even in very weak light of suitable frequency. This observation supports
o: the nuclear model of the atom
questions.e: A single photon delivers its whole energy hf to one electron at once, so emission is immediate. On the wave picture, energy would spread over the surface and weak light would need time to build up enough energy in an electron, so the wave model fails here.

questions.s: In a photocell, the intensity of the incident light is doubled while its frequency is kept the same. Which of the following is correct?
o: the saturation current doubles; the stopping potential is unchanged
the saturation current is unchanged; the stopping potential doubles
the saturation current and the stopping potential both double
neither the saturation current nor the stopping potential changes
questions.e: Doubling the intensity doubles the photons per second and hence the electrons emitted per second, so the saturation current doubles. Each photon still has energy hf, so K.E.max = hf − φ and the stopping potential do not change. Thinking brighter light gives faster electrons is the classical mistake.

questions.s: When light of wavelength λ falls on a metal surface, the stopping potential is 4V₀. With light of wavelength 2λ it is V₀. The threshold wavelength of the metal is
questions.e: hc/λ = 4eV₀ + φ and hc/2λ = eV₀ + φ. Subtracting gives hc/2λ = 3eV₀, so eV₀ = hc/6λ, and φ = hc/2λ − hc/6λ = hc/3λ. Hence λ₀ = hc/φ = 3λ. Assuming the stopping potential is simply proportional to 1/λ ignores φ and leads to wrong values such as 4λ.

questions.s: Photons of energy 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J fall on a metal of work function 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Taking the electron mass as 9.0 × 10⁻³¹ kg, the maximum speed of the photoelectrons is
questions.e: K.E.max = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Then v² = 2K/m = 9.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 9.0 × 10⁻³¹ = 1.0 × 10¹², so v = 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s. Dropping the factor 2 gives 7.1 × 10⁵ m/s, and using the full photon energy gives 1.3 × 10⁶ m/s.

questions.s: The SI unit of Planck's constant is
questions.e: From E = hf, h = E/f, so its unit is J ÷ s⁻¹ = J s. J s⁻¹ is the watt, a unit of power, and kg m s⁻² is the newton.

questions.s: The Compton effect, in which X-rays scattered by electrons have a longer wavelength, shows that
o: photons carry momentum and collide like particles
X-rays are longitudinal waves travelling through matter
electrons behave as waves inside metal crystals
atoms emit light only at certain fixed energies
questions.e: Compton treated the X-ray photon as a particle of momentum h/λ that collides elastically with an electron, giving part of its energy and momentum to it; the longer scattered wavelength fits this exactly. Electron waves are shown by electron diffraction, not by the Compton effect.

questions.s: In Compton scattering by free electrons of rest mass m₀, the maximum change in wavelength of the scattered photon and the scattering angle at which it occurs are
questions.e: Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ) is largest when cos θ = −1, that is θ = 180°, giving Δλ = 2h/(m₀c). At 90° the shift is h/(m₀c), which is the Compton wavelength but not the maximum shift.

questions.s: Take h/(m₀c) = 2.4 pm for the electron. An X-ray photon is Compton-scattered through 120° by a free electron. The increase in its wavelength is
questions.e: Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos 120°) = 2.4 × (1 + 0.5) = 3.6 pm. Taking cos 120° as +0.5 gives 1.2 pm; 4.8 pm is the maximum shift, at 180°.

questions.s: An X-ray photon of wavelength 7.2 pm is scattered back through 180° by a free electron. Taking h/(m₀c) = 2.4 pm, the fraction of the photon's energy given to the electron is
questions.e: λ′ = 7.2 + 2 × 2.4 = 12 pm. Photon energy is proportional to 1/λ, so E′/E = 7.2/12 = 0.6; the electron receives 1 − 0.6 = 0.4, or 40 %. The tempting 60 % is the fraction the scattered photon keeps, not what the electron gains.

questions.s: The minimum energy a photon must have to produce an electron-positron pair is
questions.e: The photon must supply the rest energy of two particles: 2m₀c² = 2 × 0.51 MeV = 1.02 MeV. 0.51 MeV is the rest energy of only one electron, and 931 MeV is the energy equivalent of 1 u.

questions.s: An electron and a positron, both practically at rest, annihilate each other. The radiation produced consists of
o: two photons of 0.51 MeV each, moving in opposite directions
two photons of 1.02 MeV each, moving in the same direction
two photons of 0.51 MeV each, moving in the same direction
one photon of 1.02 MeV moving in any direction
questions.e: The total rest energy 2 × 0.51 MeV = 1.02 MeV is shared by the photons. The initial momentum is zero, so a single photon (which always has momentum E/c) is impossible; two equal photons moving in opposite directions keep the total momentum zero, each with 0.51 MeV.

questions.s: Pair production by a γ-ray photon takes place only near a heavy nucleus and not in empty space, because the nucleus is needed to
o: provide the rest mass of the pair
questions.e: A photon of energy E carries momentum E/c, but a pair created near threshold has almost no momentum, so momentum and energy cannot both be conserved in empty space. The nucleus recoils and takes up the extra momentum. Charge is conserved anyway, since the pair has total charge zero.

questions.s: A γ-ray photon of energy 3.02 MeV produces an electron-positron pair near a nucleus. Neglecting the recoil of the nucleus and assuming the two particles share the kinetic energy equally, the kinetic energy of each particle is (rest energy of an electron = 0.51 MeV)
questions.e: Rest energy of the pair = 2 × 0.51 = 1.02 MeV, so the kinetic energy available is 3.02 − 1.02 = 2.00 MeV, which is 1.00 MeV each. 2.00 MeV is the total for both particles, and 1.51 MeV is simply half the photon energy, which forgets the rest energy of the pair.

questions.s: Two particles have the same de Broglie wavelength. They must have the same
questions.e: λ = h/p, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta. Particles of different masses can share a momentum at different speeds and with different kinetic energies (K = p²/2m), so speed, energy and mass need not match.

questions.s: An electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference V has de Broglie wavelength λ. If the accelerating potential difference is made 4V, the wavelength becomes
questions.e: eV = p²/2m gives p = √(2meV) and λ = h/√(2meV), so λ ∝ 1/√V. Making V four times larger divides λ by √4 = 2. λ/4 forgets the square root.

questions.s: A cricket ball of mass 0.10 kg moves at 6.6 m/s. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, its de Broglie wavelength is
questions.e: p = mv = 0.10 × 6.6 = 0.66 kg m/s, so λ = h/p = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ / 0.66 = 1.0 × 10⁻³³ m. This is far smaller than any slit or atom, which is why the wave nature of everyday objects is never observed. Dividing h by 6.6 only, forgetting the mass, gives 1.0 × 10⁻³⁴ m.

questions.s: A proton and an alpha particle (mass 4 times and charge 2 times that of the proton) are each accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to that of the alpha particle is
questions.e: λ = h/√(2mqV). For the alpha particle mq is 4 × 2 = 8 times that of the proton, so λp/λα = √8 = 2√2. Using only the mass ratio gives √4 = 2, and inverting the ratio gives 1/(2√2).

questions.s: An electron is accelerated from rest through 150 V. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, its de Broglie wavelength is about
questions.e: λ = h/√(2meV); 2meV = 2 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 150 ≈ 4.37 × 10⁻⁴⁷, whose square root is about 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s. So λ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the size of an atom. Leaving out the 2 under the root gives 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

questions.s: The diffraction of a beam of electrons by a crystal, first observed by Davisson and Germer, confirmed
questions.e: Diffraction is a wave property; the electron beam produced a diffraction pattern whose wavelength matched de Broglie's λ = h/p. The photon nature of light is shown by the photoelectric and Compton effects, and the nucleus by alpha-particle scattering.

questions.s: An electron microscope can resolve much finer detail than an optical microscope mainly because
o: electrons move faster than visible light in vacuum
electrons are never absorbed by the specimen
glass lenses focus electrons more sharply than light
electrons can have far shorter wavelengths than light
questions.e: Resolving power improves as wavelength decreases. Electrons accelerated through a few kilovolts have de Broglie wavelengths of the order of 10⁻¹¹ m, thousands of times shorter than visible light (about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m). Electrons cannot move faster than light, and they are focused by magnetic or electric lenses, not glass.

questions.s: According to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, if the position of an electron is measured more precisely, the uncertainty in its momentum
questions.e: Δx Δp is at least of the order of h, so making Δx smaller forces Δp to become larger. Both can never be zero together; this limit comes from the wave nature of matter, not from poor instruments.

questions.s: An electron is located within a region of width 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Using Δx Δp ≈ h with h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the uncertainty in its momentum is about
questions.e: Δp ≈ h/Δx = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ / 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 3.0 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s. A slip in the powers of ten gives 3.0 × 10⁻²³, and halving the width wrongly gives 6.0 × 10⁻²⁴.

questions.s: An atom stays in an excited state for about 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ s before emitting a photon. Using ΔE Δt ≈ h, the spread in frequency of the emitted light is about
questions.e: ΔE ≈ h/Δt and ΔE = hΔf, so Δf ≈ 1/Δt = 1/(1.0 × 10⁻⁸) = 10⁸ Hz. This is tiny compared with the frequency of visible light itself, about 10¹⁴-10¹⁵ Hz, which is why spectral lines are sharp. Choosing 10¹⁴ Hz confuses the spread with the frequency of the light.

questions.s: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle Δx Δp ≈ h relates the uncertainties in
o: the mass and charge of a particle
x-position and y-momentum of a particle
the speed and mass of a particle
position and momentum along the same axis
questions.e: The principle links the uncertainty in position along a direction with the uncertainty in momentum along that same direction (for example x and pₓ). Position along x and momentum along y can be known together, and mass and charge are fixed properties, not conjugate quantities.

questions.s: According to Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the angular momentum of the electron in the nth allowed orbit is
questions.e: Bohr's quantum condition is mvr = nh/2π, so angular momentum comes in whole multiples of h/2π. nh is too large by a factor 2π, and h/2πn would decrease for higher orbits, which is wrong.

questions.s: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is 0.053 nm. The orbit of radius 0.477 nm is the one with n equal to
questions.e: rₙ = n²r₁, so n² = 0.477/0.053 = 9 and n = 3. Answering 9 forgets that the radius grows as the square of n.

questions.s: In hydrogen, Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. The energy needed to remove the electron completely from the n = 3 level is
questions.e: E₃ = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV, so 1.51 eV raises it to E = 0, the ionised state. 12.09 eV is the energy for the jump from n = 1 to n = 3, and 4.53 eV divides by n instead of n².

questions.s: The total energy of the electron in the ground state of hydrogen is −13.6 eV. Its electric potential energy in this state is
questions.e: In a Bohr orbit K.E. = ke²/2r and P.E. = −ke²/r, so P.E. = −2 K.E. and the total is −K.E. With total −13.6 eV, K.E. = +13.6 eV and P.E. = −27.2 eV. +13.6 eV is the kinetic energy, not the potential energy.

questions.s: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, rₙ ∝ n² and vₙ ∝ 1/n. The ratio of the time for one revolution in the n = 2 orbit to that in the n = 1 orbit is
questions.e: T = 2πr/v ∝ n²/(1/n) = n³. So T₂/T₁ = 2³ = 8. Using only r ∝ n² gives 4, and forgetting that the speed falls gives the wrong idea that T ∝ n².

questions.s: According to Bohr's postulates, the electron in a hydrogen atom emits radiation when it
o: revolves in an allowed stationary orbit
jumps from a higher orbit to a lower one
jumps from a lower orbit to a higher one
questions.e: In an allowed orbit the electron does not radiate, despite being accelerated. A photon of energy hf = Eᵢ − E_f is emitted only when it drops to a lower orbit. A jump to a higher orbit needs energy to be absorbed, not emitted.

questions.s: Using Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, the energy of the photon emitted when the electron in a hydrogen atom falls from n = 4 to n = 2 is
questions.e: E₄ = −0.85 eV and E₂ = −3.40 eV, so the photon energy is −0.85 − (−3.40) = 2.55 eV, a blue-green Balmer line. 12.75 eV is the energy for 4 → 1, and 3.40 eV ignores the energy of the upper level.

questions.s: For a hydrogen-like ion of atomic number Z, Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV. The energy needed to ionise a singly ionised helium atom (He⁺) from its ground state is
questions.e: For He⁺, Z = 2 and n = 1, so E₁ = −13.6 × 4 = −54.4 eV and the ionisation energy is 54.4 eV. Using Z instead of Z² gives 27.2 eV, and 122.4 eV corresponds to Z = 3 (Li²⁺).

questions.s: The lines of the Balmer series of the hydrogen spectrum lie in the
questions.e: Balmer lines end on n = 2 and have wavelengths from about 656 nm down to 365 nm, mostly visible. The Lyman series (ending on n = 1) is ultraviolet and the Paschen series (ending on n = 3) is infrared.

questions.s: Taking the Rydberg constant R = 1.1 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, the shortest wavelength in the Paschen series of hydrogen is about
questions.e: For the Paschen series 1/λ = R(1/3² − 1/n²); the shortest wavelength is the series limit n → ∞, so λ = 9/R = 9/(1.1 × 10⁷) ≈ 8.2 × 10⁻⁷ m. 9.1 × 10⁻⁸ m (1/R) is the Lyman limit and 3.6 × 10⁻⁷ m (4/R) is the Balmer limit.

questions.s: The ratio of the longest wavelength of the Lyman series to the longest wavelength of the Balmer series of hydrogen is
questions.e: Longest Lyman line (2 → 1): 1/λ_L = R(1 − 1/4) = 3R/4. Longest Balmer line (3 → 2): 1/λ_B = R(1/4 − 1/9) = 5R/36. So λ_L/λ_B = (5/36)/(3/4) = 5/27. 27/5 is the inverted ratio, which would make the ultraviolet line longer.

questions.s: Electrons in a sample of hydrogen gas are excited to the n = 4 level. As they return to the ground state by all possible routes, the number of different spectral lines that can be emitted is
questions.e: Any pair of the levels 1, 2, 3, 4 can give a line, so the number is n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6 (4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1, 2→1). Answering 3 counts only one step-by-step route, and 10 is the value for n = 5.

questions.s: The spectrum of hydrogen gas in a discharge tube consists of sharp lines of particular wavelengths because
o: hydrogen atoms in the tube all move at the same speed
the nucleus of hydrogen emits light of fixed colours
hydrogen gas absorbs every other wavelength present
the electron's energy in the atom can take only certain values
questions.e: The electron can occupy only discrete energy levels, so a jump between two levels emits a photon of one definite energy hf = Eᵢ − E_f, giving one sharp line. The light comes from electron transitions, not from the nucleus, and the speed of the atoms has nothing to do with the line positions.

questions.s: In an X-ray tube, the continuous part of the X-ray spectrum is produced by
o: transitions of inner electrons in the target atoms
sudden slowing down of fast electrons near target nuclei
radioactive decay of the target metal
heating of the filament to a high temperature
questions.e: Fast electrons are decelerated by the electric fields of the target nuclei and radiate X-rays of every energy up to eV (braking radiation), giving a continuous spectrum. Transitions of inner electrons produce the sharp characteristic lines, not the continuous background.

questions.s: The shortest wavelength of the X-rays coming from an X-ray tube is 0.062 nm. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the potential difference across the tube is
questions.e: The shortest wavelength is produced when an electron gives all its energy eV to one photon: eV = hc/λmin, so V = 1240/0.062 = 20 000 V = 20 kV. The other choices come from slips in the powers of ten.

questions.s: The potential difference across an X-ray tube is increased, with the same target. Which of the following is correct?
o: the cut-off wavelength decreases; the characteristic lines keep their wavelengths
the cut-off wavelength increases; the characteristic lines keep their wavelengths
the cut-off wavelength and the characteristic wavelengths both decrease
the cut-off wavelength and the characteristic wavelengths both stay the same
questions.e: λmin = hc/eV, so a larger V gives a shorter cut-off wavelength. The characteristic lines depend only on the energy levels of the target atoms, so their wavelengths do not change. Expecting the lines to shift as well confuses the tube voltage with a property of the target.

questions.s: The penetrating power (hardness) of the X-rays from an X-ray tube is increased by
o: using a target of larger area
questions.e: Penetrating power depends on photon energy, and the maximum photon energy is eV, so a higher accelerating voltage gives harder X-rays. A larger filament current gives more electrons and therefore more X-rays (greater intensity), but not more energetic ones.

questions.s: The Kα line in the characteristic X-ray spectrum of a target is emitted when an electron moves from the
o: K shell to the L shell
M shell to the L shell
M shell to the K shell
L shell to the K shell
questions.e: A fast electron knocks out a K-shell electron; when an electron from the next shell (L) fills the vacancy, the Kα photon is emitted. The jump M → K gives the Kβ line, and K → L would need energy to be absorbed rather than emitted.

questions.s: The word LASER stands for
o: Light Amplification by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Stimulated Absorption of Radiation
Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Absorption by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
questions.e: A laser amplifies light by stimulated emission: an incoming photon triggers an excited atom to emit an identical photon. Spontaneous emission happens randomly and gives ordinary incoherent light, and absorption removes photons rather than amplifying them.

questions.s: For laser action, a population inversion must be produced. This means that
o: more atoms are in a higher (metastable) state than in the lower state
more atoms are in the ground state than in any excited state
all the atoms have been ionised by the pumping source
the atoms emit photons in random directions and phases
questions.e: Normally most atoms are in the lower state, so photons are absorbed more than they stimulate emission. Pumping atoms into a long-lived metastable level so that the upper level holds more atoms than the lower one lets stimulated emission dominate. More atoms in the ground state is the normal, non-inverted situation.

questions.s: In a helium-neon laser, the laser light is emitted by
o: helium atoms, after neon atoms excite them by collision
helium and neon atoms equally, by spontaneous emission
electrons of the discharge striking the mirrors
neon atoms, after helium atoms excite them by collision
questions.e: The discharge excites helium atoms to metastable levels; they pass this energy to neon atoms in collisions, producing a population inversion in neon. Stimulated emission from neon gives the red 632.8 nm light. Helium only acts as the energy carrier, so it is not the source of the laser light.

questions.s: In stimulated emission, the photon emitted by the atom, compared with the photon that stimulates it, has
o: the same frequency but a random phase
the same frequency, phase and direction
twice the frequency and the same direction
the same phase but the opposite direction
questions.e: The stimulated photon is an exact copy of the incoming one: same frequency, same phase and same direction, which is why laser light is coherent and highly directional. Random phase is a feature of spontaneous emission.

questions.s: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of lead ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb is
questions.e: Neutron number N = A − Z = 206 − 82 = 124. 82 is the number of protons, 206 the total number of nucleons, and 288 comes from adding A and Z.

questions.s: The nuclei ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. Such nuclei are called
questions.e: Nuclei with equal mass number A but different atomic number Z are isobars. Isotopes have the same Z and different A (such as ¹²C and ¹⁴C), and isotones have the same number of neutrons.

questions.s: Take the mass of a proton as 1.0073 u, of a neutron as 1.0087 u and of a helium-4 nucleus as 4.0015 u, with 1 u = 931 MeV. The binding energy of the helium-4 nucleus is about
questions.e: Mass of 2 protons + 2 neutrons = 2.0146 + 2.0174 = 4.0320 u, so the mass defect is 4.0320 − 4.0015 = 0.0305 u. Binding energy = 0.0305 × 931 ≈ 28.4 MeV. 7.1 MeV is the binding energy per nucleon, not the total.

questions.s: Take the mass of a proton as 1.0073 u, of a neutron as 1.0087 u and of a deuteron (²₁H nucleus) as 2.0136 u, with 1 u = 931 MeV. The binding energy per nucleon of the deuteron is about
questions.e: Mass defect = 1.0073 + 1.0087 − 2.0136 = 0.0024 u, so the binding energy = 0.0024 × 931 ≈ 2.2 MeV. The deuteron has 2 nucleons, so the binding energy per nucleon is about 1.1 MeV. 2.2 MeV is the total binding energy, which is the tempting slip.

questions.s: The binding energy per nucleon is greatest, so that the nucleus is most stable, for nuclei of mass number close to that of
questions.e: The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve peaks at about 8.8 MeV near A = 56 (iron), making iron among the most tightly bound nuclei. Uranium has a lower value (about 7.6 MeV), which is why it releases energy on fission.

questions.s: Energy is released when a uranium-235 nucleus splits into two medium-sized nuclei because the product nuclei have
o: a smaller total number of nucleons
a smaller binding energy per nucleon
more protons than the uranium nucleus
a larger binding energy per nucleon
questions.e: Medium-mass nuclei lie near the peak of the binding-energy curve (about 8.5 MeV per nucleon) while uranium has about 7.6 MeV per nucleon. The products are more tightly bound, so their total mass is less and the difference appears as energy. The number of nucleons is conserved in the reaction.

questions.s: The strong nuclear force that holds nucleons together in a nucleus is
o: inversely proportional to the square of distance
questions.e: The nuclear force is much stronger than the electric repulsion between protons, but acts only over about 10⁻¹⁵ m. It acts between all nucleons (p-p, n-n and p-n), and it does not follow an inverse-square law like gravity or the Coulomb force.

questions.s: An alpha particle is
questions.e: An alpha particle is ⁴₂He, two protons and two neutrons, with charge +2e. A fast electron is a beta particle and a high-energy photon is a gamma ray.

questions.s: Thorium ²³²₉₀Th decays through a series of alpha and beta-minus emissions to stable lead ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb. The numbers of alpha and beta particles emitted are
questions.e: Only α decay changes A: (232 − 208)/4 = 6 α particles. These reduce Z by 12, to 78, but the final Z is 82, so Z must rise by 4 through 4 β⁻ emissions. 6 α and 2 β forgets that each β⁻ raises Z by 1, not 2.

questions.s: A radioactive sample of mass 64 mg has a half-life of 5 days. The mass of the sample still undecayed after 20 days is
questions.e: 20 days is 20/5 = 4 half-lives, so the remaining mass is 64 × (1/2)⁴ = 64/16 = 4 mg. Dividing 64 by 4 (16 mg) treats decay as linear, and 8 mg stops after three half-lives.

questions.s: The fraction of the nuclei of a radioactive sample that have decayed after three half-lives is
questions.e: After three half-lives the fraction remaining is (1/2)³ = 1/8, so the fraction decayed is 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. Choosing 1/8 gives the undecayed fraction instead of the decayed one.

questions.s: A radioactive nuclide has a half-life of 693 s. Taking ln 2 = 0.693, its decay constant is
questions.e: λ = 0.693/T½ = 0.693/693 = 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Taking λ = 1/T½ gives 1.4 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹, and inverting the relation gives 1.0 × 10³ s⁻¹, which has the wrong size.

questions.s: When a nucleus emits a gamma ray,
o: neither its mass number nor its atomic number changes
questions.e: A gamma ray is a photon with no charge and no rest mass; it only carries away the excess energy of an excited nucleus, so A and Z stay the same. A falls by 4 and Z by 2 in α decay, and Z rises by 1 in β⁻ decay.

questions.s: Which of the following correctly orders alpha, beta and gamma radiations by their ionising power, from greatest to least?
questions.e: Alpha particles are heavy and doubly charged, so they ionise very strongly and are stopped by a sheet of paper; gamma rays are uncharged and ionise least. Penetrating power runs the other way, γ > β > α, which is the tempting confusion.

questions.s: In the fission reaction ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + x ¹₀n, the value of x is
questions.e: Mass numbers must balance: 235 + 1 = 140 + 94 + x, so 236 = 234 + x and x = 2. The atomic numbers check: 92 = 54 + 38. Forgetting the incoming neutron on the left gives x = 1.

questions.s: Each fission of uranium-235 releases about 200 MeV. Taking 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J, the number of fissions per second needed in a reactor core producing 32 MW of power is
questions.e: Energy per fission = 200 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J. Fissions per second = 32 × 10⁶ / 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ = 1.0 × 10¹⁸. Treating 32 MW as 32 × 10³ W or slipping a power of ten in the MeV conversion gives the smaller choices.

questions.s: In a nuclear reactor, the main function of the control rods, made of cadmium or boron, is to
o: carry heat out of the core
questions.e: Cadmium and boron absorb neutrons strongly; moving the rods in or out sets how many neutrons cause further fissions, keeping the chain reaction steady. Slowing neutrons is the job of the moderator (graphite or heavy water), and the coolant carries heat away.

questions.s: In the fusion reaction ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n, the masses are ²H = 2.0141 u, ³H = 3.0160 u, ⁴He = 4.0026 u and n = 1.0087 u. With 1 u = 931 MeV, the energy released is about
questions.e: Mass before = 2.0141 + 3.0160 = 5.0301 u; mass after = 4.0026 + 1.0087 = 5.0113 u. Mass defect = 0.0188 u, so the energy released = 0.0188 × 931 ≈ 17.5 MeV. 175 MeV results from misplacing the decimal point in the mass defect.

questions.s: A detector shows the path of each charged particle as a visible line of tiny droplets formed on ions in a supersaturated vapour. The detector is a
questions.e: In a Wilson cloud chamber, sudden expansion makes the vapour supersaturated, and droplets condense on the ions left along a particle's path, making its track visible. A Geiger-Muller counter only counts particles as electrical pulses and shows no tracks.

questions.s: A technician works near a small gamma-ray source. The simplest effective way to reduce the radiation dose received is to
o: work at a greater distance from the source
look at the source through a glass window
handle the source quickly with bare hands
switch off the room lights while working
questions.e: Intensity from a small source falls roughly as 1/r², so doubling the distance cuts the dose to about a quarter; time and shielding (lead) are the other two safety rules. Ordinary glass hardly stops gamma rays, and sources must always be handled with tongs, never bare hands.

questions.s: A Geiger-Muller counter detects radiation because the radiation
o: condenses vapour into droplets along its path
heats a fine wire inside the tube
ionises the low-pressure gas, causing a pulse of current
ejects photoelectrons from a glass window
questions.e: Radiation entering the tube ionises a few gas atoms; the high voltage accelerates these electrons, which ionise more atoms in an avalanche, giving one pulse of current that is counted. Condensation of droplets on ions is how the cloud chamber works.

questions.s: The gray, the SI unit of absorbed dose of radiation, is equal to
questions.e: Absorbed dose is the energy absorbed per unit mass, so 1 Gy = 1 J kg⁻¹. 1 s⁻¹ is the becquerel, the unit of activity, and 1 J s⁻¹ is the watt.

questions.s: A laser of power 3.0 mW emits light of wavelength 660 nm. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the number of photons emitted per second is
questions.e: Photon energy E = hc/λ = (6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(6.6 × 10⁻⁷) = 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Photons per second = P/E = 3.0 × 10⁻³ / 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.0 × 10¹⁶. Using 3.0 W instead of 3.0 mW, or slipping the nm conversion, gives a wrong power of ten.

questions.s: The activity of a radioactive sample falls from 800 Bq to 50 Bq in 24 hours. The half-life of the nuclide is
questions.e: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 is four halvings, so 4 half-lives = 24 h and T½ = 6 h. Counting three halvings gives 8 h; the activity does not fall by a fixed amount each hour.

questions.s: When a nucleus emits a β⁻ particle, the daughter nucleus has
o: atomic number one less, same mass number
atomic number two less, mass number four less
atomic number and mass number both unchanged
atomic number one more, same mass number
questions.e: In β⁻ decay a neutron changes into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino. Z rises by 1 while the total number of nucleons A stays the same. Z one less fits β⁺ decay, and Z two less with A four less is α decay.

questions.s: A spaceship is 100 m long when at rest. Ali on the Earth measures its length as 60 m while it flies past him. The speed of the spaceship is
questions.e: L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²) gives √(1 − v²/c²) = 60/100 = 0.6, so v²/c² = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64 and v = 0.8c. Taking the speed equal to the length ratio gives 0.6c, which is wrong.

questions.s: The work function of a metal is 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, its threshold frequency is
questions.e: φ = hf₀, so f₀ = φ/h = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ = 0.5 × 10¹⁵ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, in the visible range. Writing 0.5 × 10¹⁵ as 5.0 × 10¹⁵ is the common slip.

questions.s: An electron and a proton move with the same speed. Taking the proton mass as about 1836 times the electron mass, which statement about their de Broglie wavelengths is correct?
o: the electron's is about 1836 times longer
the electron's is about 43 times longer
the proton's is about 1836 times longer
questions.e: λ = h/mv; at equal speeds λ ∝ 1/m, so the lighter electron has the longer wavelength, by the mass ratio of about 1836. The factor √1836 ≈ 43 applies when the two have the same kinetic energy, not the same speed.

questions.s: Which of the following statements about X-rays is correct?
o: they are bent by magnetic fields
they travel slower than light in vacuum
questions.e: X-rays are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength (about 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻⁸ m), so they are uncharged, are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields and travel at c in vacuum. Cathode rays (electrons) are the ones bent by magnetic fields.

questions.s: Using Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, a hydrogen atom in its ground state absorbs a photon of energy 12.75 eV. The electron moves to the level
questions.e: After absorption E = −13.6 + 12.75 = −0.85 eV. Then n² = 13.6/0.85 = 16, so n = 4. A 12.09 eV photon would reach n = 3 and 10.2 eV would reach n = 2.

questions.s: A sample contains 4.0 × 10¹⁸ nuclei of a radioactive nuclide of half-life 693 s. Taking ln 2 = 0.693, the activity of the sample is
questions.e: λ = 0.693/693 = 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹, and activity A = λN = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × 4.0 × 10¹⁸ = 4.0 × 10¹⁵ Bq. Using λ = 1/T½ gives about 5.8 × 10¹⁵ Bq, and multiplying N by T½ instead of dividing gives 2.8 × 10²¹.

questions.s: The rest energy of an electron is 0.51 MeV. Using relativistic mechanics, the kinetic energy of an electron moving at 0.6c is about
questions.e: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.36) = 1.25, so the total energy = 1.25 × 0.51 ≈ 0.64 MeV and K.E. = 0.64 − 0.51 = 0.13 MeV. The classical ½m₀v² = ½ × 0.51 × 0.36 ≈ 0.09 MeV underestimates it at such speeds, and 0.64 MeV is the total, not the kinetic, energy.

questions.s: The first line of the Balmer series of hydrogen (n = 3 → n = 2) has wavelength 656 nm. The wavelength of the second line (n = 4 → n = 2) is about
questions.e: 1/λ ∝ (1/4 − 1/n²): for 3 → 2 this is 5/36 and for 4 → 2 it is 3/16. So λ₂ = 656 × (5/36)/(3/16) = 656 × 20/27 ≈ 486 nm. 434 nm and 410 nm are the lines from n = 5 and n = 6.

questions.s: Nuclear fusion of light nuclei takes place only at temperatures of millions of kelvin because
o: the nuclei must overcome their electric repulsion
the neutrons must first be slowed down
the electrons must be removed from the nuclei
the strong force works only at high temperature
questions.e: Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other; only at very high temperatures do they move fast enough to come within about 10⁻¹⁵ m, where the attractive strong force takes over. Slowing neutrons matters in fission reactors, not in fusion.
